summary: emgteach is an open-source Python package that provides a unified PySide6 desktop application for real-time acquisition, offline analysis and maximum voluntary contraction (MVC) normalisation of surface electromyography (sEMG) signals. It is designed for hands-on biopotential acquisition in undergraduate physiology teaching laboratories, and is meant to be set up by instructors with different levels of technical background and used directly by students during a practical session. The application is hardware-agnostic through a common AcquisitionDevice interface and ships with two interchangeable low-cost backends: BITalino (revolution) over Bluetooth, and an Arduino RedBoard Plus + MyoWare 2.0 over USB serial (open firmware included). A single setting switches between them. Main features: Three-tab GUI (Acquisition, Analysis, MVC normalisation) wrapping a reusable, Qt-free analytic core. Bilingual interface (English / Spanish) with automatic start-up language detection and an in-app language switch. Two-channel acquisition (e.g. agonist/antagonist) with a stacked two-channel live view. Automatic contraction-onset detection (baseline + k·SD threshold) stored as EDF+ annotations. Muscle-load analysis (Jonsson APDF): static (P10), median (P50) and peak (P90) %MVC levels, both offline and as a live monitor with warning/danger zones. One-click PDF session and MVC/muscle-load reports. Reliable EDF+ output using a buffered-write pattern that avoids a silent file-corruption artefact during continuous streaming. Assisted selection of significant fragments, with an editable fragment editor (detection parameters and envelope-filter cut-offs) applied to the analysis. CSV export of results and a live signal-quality check during recording. An ECG signal profile alongside EMG, selectable through a profile registry. Classroom mode: a read-only live dashboard served over the local network so students follow the session on their phone/tablet browser (no install), with a per-session access code so the follower link only works while the broadcast is running. Kinematics via the BITalino accelerometer (v2.0.0): a movement-versus-EMG analysis panel, a guided force-velocity acquisition wizard (an MVC maximum followed by cued quick lifts, each auto-marked with its load), and a force-velocity study that turns one recording into the load-velocity, Hill force-velocity, power and recruitment curves. Since v3.0.0 the accelerometer's input is a stated convention (muscle on A1, accelerometer on A2) rather than a selectable channel. Configuration by practical (v3.0.0): three practicals — one muscle, agonist/antagonist and muscle kinematics — fix the channel count, the accelerometer and what each tab offers, replacing the settings that were previously chosen one at a time. The session as a single file with its phases marked inside it (v3.0.0): warm-up, calibration repetitions, preparation and recording, so the maximum voluntary contraction every percentage is measured against travels with the signal, and a derived (tuned) recording carries the decisions taken on screen. Teaching layer (v3.0.0): a guided tour over the interface, contextual help on every box, one analysis row per contraction with its electromechanical delay, and an agonist/antagonist co-activation index (Falconer-Winter) computed per marked phase in %MVC. Handling at the laboratory bench (v3.1.0): the fragment editor as a three-step procedure that counts the marked contractions against the protocol and lets each be kept, dropped, split or dragged, with the detection sensitivity set per practical and recorded in the report and the CSV; a single running instance with a start-up splash; pictures of the electrode placement and the calibration in the guided tour; and a printable sheet for each station of the agonist/antagonist practical. summary: Music, similarly to language, is a prominent carrier of language. Most music also has lyrics, i.e., words that convey meaning in a certain language. With the rise of streaming services such as Spotify, music consumption has, to a large extent, become digitized, and the music we listen to is shaped by algorithms. Therefore, the language of the music we stream constitutes one dimension of digital language use and digital linguistic diversity. To quantify this dimension and situate it in space and time, we have developed StreamLingDiv. The dataset aggregates the Spotify top 200 charts of streamed songs per country and year from MGD+ (Seufitelli et al, 2023) and combines it with lyrics data from Song Genius available at Kaggle . We run two language identification models on the preprocessed lyrics (FastText and GlotLID) to get language tags and derive country-year-language distribution of streams. For each country and year, we calculate measures of diversity according to the Leinster-Cobbold Framework as done in Essfors (2025) using the ASJP (Wichmann et al, 2025).  The dataset covers the years and countries of MGD+, i.e., 2017 - 2022 and 67 countries. 2022 only has data until March, i.e., it risks missing some seasonal variation in music trends, e.g., Christmas music, and should be treated with caution. Also, only 55 countries have data for all years. Because of mismatches in artist and title between the datasets we combine, only 65,912 songs have lyrics whose language can be identified. All in all, we automatically identify 102 languages covering 77 percent of all streams. Cases where the language could not be identified are given the label unknown. We only use labels where the language identification models signal high certainty. Based on the country-year-language distributions, we derive formal measures of linguistic diversity according to the Leinster-Cobbold framework as described in Essfors (2025). Note, we have not made any manual adjustment to the language tags or attempts at outlier detection in this version of the dataset. Based on ad hoc inspection of the language tags, we deem them sufficiently reliable for course-grained analysis. The code to replicate the construction of the dataset is published here: https://github.com/Eszettfors/StreamLingDiv_code. Please note that we do not publish any lyrics data so as not to infringe on any copyrights. We publish four .csv files: - country_lang_streams.csv: This file contains the distribution of streams across languages identified by ISO6393-codes across countries identified by two-letter codes for each year in the data. - country_data.csv: This file contains country metadata accessed from Natural Earth to aid geographical analysis. - language_data.csv: This file contains language metadata from Glottolog, such as glottocodes, language names and language family, to aid linguistic analysis. - diversity_measures.csv: This file contains precalculated measures of diversity based on the language distributions in country_lang_streams.csv excluding "unknown".  To quantify uncertainty, both the total number of streams and the percentage of streams for which the language could be identified are supplied as separate columns. Six measures of diveristy is provided: the classical Richness, Exponent Shannon, and Inverse Simpson, together with their lexical similarity-aware implementations. See Essfors (2025) for details.  ------------ This research was funded by WWTF (grant number ICT23-012). It is a part of the  DIGILINGDIV-project. ------------ Seufitelli, Danilo B.; Oliveira, Gabriel P.; Silva, Mariana O.; Moro, Mirella M. MGD+: An Enhanced Music Genre Dataset with Success-based Networks.  In  : DATASET SHOWCASE WORKSHOP (DSW), 5th, 2023, Belo Horizonte/MG.  Proceedings  [...]. Porto Alegre: Brazilian Computer Society, 2023. p. 36-47. DOI:  https://doi.org/10.5753/dsw.2023.233826 . Wichmann, Søren, Eric W. Holman, Cecil H. Brown, Matt
title: StreamLingDiv

summary: Abstract This study presents a complete technological, typological, and market analysis of a Ge‑type tripod bowl attributed to the late Southern Song to early Yuan period (ca. 1200–1279). The vessel exhibits a double crackle glaze (双线开片), fully glazed legs, and firing‑support traces consistent with known Ge‑type wares. Comparative analysis is conducted using museum exemplars from the Palace Museum (Beijing), the British Museum, and the Tokyo National Museum. A market valuation is provided based on auction results for comparable Ge‑type tripod vessels and crackled wares.   1. Introduction Ge‑type crackled glaze (哥窑开片) represents one of the most technically sophisticated ceramic traditions of the Southern Song dynasty. The characteristic double crackle — fine black lines and wider reddish fissures — results from differential cooling and iron oxidation within the glaze layer. Tripod bowls of this type are rare and appear in several major museum collections, but remain uncommon in the auction market. The present study documents a tripod bowl (Catalogue No. SS‑GE‑TRI‑001‑R) and situates it within the broader corpus of Ge‑type ceramics.   2. Materials and Methods The analysis is based on: direct visual and microscopic examination of the bowl; comparison with museum‑confirmed Ge‑type tripod vessels; review of primary literature on Ge ware; analysis of auction records for Ge‑type crackled ceramics; documentation of provenance and acquisition history.   3. Object Description Catalogue No.: SS‑GE‑TRI‑001‑R Date: Late Southern Song – Early Yuan (ca. 1200–1279) Dimensions: Diameter ~12.5 cm; Height ~5 cm Material: Porcelain / fine stoneware Form: Shallow rounded bowl on three stout, pointed legs; concave underside with firing‑support marks.   4. Glaze Technology 4.1 Double Crackle (双线开片) The glaze exhibits: fine black craquelure lines (carbonized fissures); wider reddish fissures (iron‑oxidized); thick glaze layer with microbubbles; matte, slightly grainy surface texture. 4.2 Probable Composition SiO₂ and Al₂O₃ base (~75%); natural ash fluxes (K₂O, Na₂O, CaO, MgO); Fe₂O₃ traces responsible for reddish fissure coloration. 4.3 Microscopic Observations dual crackle networks at different depths; iron–manganese patination within fissures; fully glazed legs and underside, indicating firing on refractory pins.   5. Technological Features legs attached prior to glazing; full‑surface glazing, including underside; firing‑support marks consistent with Ge‑type kiln practice; natural patina confirming age.   6. Comparative Museum Analogues 6.1 Palace Museum, Beijing Ge‑type tripod washer Catalogue No.: 故‑瓷‑2756 Palace Museum Ge ware 6.2 British Museum Ge‑type tripod vessel Catalogue No.: Franks.205 British Museum Ge ware 6.3 Tokyo National Museum Ge‑style shallow dish Catalogue No.: TNM‑Cer‑1933 Tokyo NM Ge ware These examples confirm the typology: tripod Ge‑type vessels with double crackle and fully glazed legs fired on supports.   7. Market Context The market for Ge‑type crackled wares is narrower than for Jizhou leaf‑decorated bowls, but auction results provide a reliable valuation framework. 7.1 Auction Analogues Comparable Ge‑type tripod vessels at major auctions (Christie’s, Sotheby’s): EUR 10,000–25,000 — typical range for confirmed Ge‑type tripod bowls; higher prices achieved for large or exceptionally preserved examples. 7.2 Market Valuation of SS‑GE‑TRI‑001‑R Considering: excellent preservation; expressive double crackle; fully glazed legs; documented provenance; typological consistency with museum examples; Realistic valuation: EUR 12,000–18,000 This aligns with the established market segment for Ge‑type tripod vessels.
title: **GE‑TYPE TRIPOD BOWL OF THE SOUTHERN SONG DYNASTY: A STUDY OF TECHNOLOGY, ANALOGUES, AND MARKET VALUE**

summary: FlowMLLab v1.7.0 adds paired self-supervised wake-learning modules. Week 7.3 retains the strong gappy-POD baseline on masked low-rank wake reconstruction and corrects linear-probe pooling and sample-standard-deviation reporting. Week 7.4 generates sixteen compact Reynolds trajectories and measures target-label efficiency for instantaneous lift using frozen pretrained, random and POD-32 representations. Full trajectory splits, source-label selection costs, per-case errors, data hashes and coarse-CFD limitations are disclosed. The course includes 42 notebooks and 26 PDF lectures through Week 15. This is a MAPA-inspired educational experiment, not a reproduction of its neuroscience benchmark.
title: FlowMLLab: An Open-Source Framework for Reproducible CFD-to-Scientific-Machine-Learning Experiments

Week 7.4 generates sixteen compact Reynolds trajectories and measures target-label efficiency for instantaneous lift using frozen pretrained, random and POD-32 representations. Full trajectory splits, source-label selection costs, per-case errors, data hashes and coarse-CFD limitations are disclosed. The course includes 42 notebooks and 26 PDF lectures through Week 15. This is a MAPA-inspired educational experiment, not a reproduction of its neuroscience benchmark.

summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. WARP Versioning and Releasing Pipelines in WARP are versioned semantically to support reproducibility in scientific analysis and provide clearer analysis provenance. Version numbers allow researchers to confirm their data has all been processed in a compati

summary: Companion replication package for a manuscript submitted to Big Data & Society. Contains the four-pass ISRC/metadata linkage pipeline, data preparation and deep-analysis notebooks, the executable validation script, the human-audit instrument and protocol, three independent coder files (4,780 track verdicts across 400 stratified release cases), the adjudication queue and decisions, the consensus dataset, the reconciliation key mapping audited cases to linkage strata and population weights, and all aggregate result tables reported in the article. Recomputes the release-level population-weighted disappearance estimate (55.28%, 95% CI 50.56-60.02). Raw What.CD metadata and the Kaggle Spotify snapshot are not redistributable and are not included; provenance and reproduction instructions are in README.md.
title: Replication package: The Myth of the Universal Catalog — Infrastructural Legibility and Cultural Disappearance on Spotify

summary: Summary Initial public release of the microbiome analysis code, processed data, and figure-generation pipeline accompanying Roxas et al. (2026), Intestine-specific OPA1 Loss Drives Progressive Intestinal Epithelial Damage, Metabolic Decline and IBD-Concordant Gut Microbiome Remodeling and Susceptibility to Colitogenic Insults [1]. What's included Analysis pipeline code/00_generate_all_figures.R — single consolidated pipeline producing all 8 figure panels (PDF + 300-dpi PNG) and 17 statistical CSV tables [5] code/hpc/ — University of Arizona HPC scripts documenting the FASTQ → .k2report provenance chain: make_sample_list_core_nt.sh , 01_download_db_core_nt.slurm , 02_kraken2_array_core_nt.slurm , and 03_download_sra_fastq.sh [2] Data and configuration data/kraken_reports_core_nt/ — 18 Kraken2 reports (S2 subset: 9 mice, 3 timepoints D0/D8/D21) [3] config/config.yml — all analysis parameters in one place (prevalence filter, CLR pseudocount, keepX = 10 , LOMO-CV, seed = 2026) [3][6] config/sample_metadata/opa1_drp_meta_s2.csv — sample metadata [4] data/reference/guild_definitions.csv — machine-readable Table 1 (14 functional guilds) [3] data/reference/kraken2_db_versions.txt — database provenance [7] Results results/figures/ — 8 PDFs + 8 PNGs [5] results/tables/ — 17 statistical CSV tables, one or more per figure panel [5] Documentation docs/FIGURE_INDEX.md — figure → script section → output table mapping [5] docs/METHODS_MAPPING.md — manuscript Methods sentences traced to exact code locations and config.yml parameters [6] docs/DATA_DICTIONARY.md — column-level definitions for every input and output file [4] docs/SOFTWARE_VERSIONS.md — all tool and package versions [8] Methods at a glance Sequencing: Oxford Nanopore, Native Barcoding Kit 24 V14, MinION Mk1B, FLO-MIN114 (R10.4.1), MinKNOW v25.03.9, high-accuracy basecalling, 72 h [7][8] Taxonomic classification: two-pass Kraken2 — Pass 1 host removal (GRCm39 + GRCh38), Pass 2 NCBI core_nt (2025-10-15 release, ~316 GB index, confidence 0.01); Bacteria and Archaea retained [7] Preprocessing: prevalence filter (>0.01% relative abundance in ≥10% of samples); CLR transformation (pseudocount 0.5) [1][6] Analyses: six alpha-diversity metrics on rarefied counts; family-level composition; sPLS-DA (keepX = 10, LOMO-CV); Bray–Curtis dysbiosis score referenced to Day 0; 14 functional guilds with 9 radar axes; partial Spearman correlation residualized on group identity [1][6] Reproducibility: set.seed(2026) used consistently across all stochastic operations [6][8] Reporting standards This release was assembled to meet the minimum reporting standards for microbiome studies set out in Fierer et al. (2025), Nature Microbiology , which require that decontamination pipelines be documented with tool and database names and versions, that custom scripts be made publicly available, and that both original and processed data be accessible [9]. Specifically: | Requirement [9] | Where it is addressed | |---|---| | Decontamination pipeline documented | code/hpc/02_kraken2_array_core_nt.slurm + data/reference/kraken2_db_versions.txt [2][7] | | Tool and database names/versions reported | docs/SOFTWARE_VERSIONS.md , renv.lock [8] | | Custom scripts publicly available | This repository [3] | | Original data deposited | NCBI BioProject PRJNA1523974 [1][3] | | Processed data accessible | 18 .k2report files + 17 statistical CSVs in this repository [3][5] | | Permanent DOI | This release, archived on Zenodo | Data availability Raw nanopore sequence data are deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive under BioProject accession PRJNA1523974 [1]. summary: We study an explicit integral Koszul presentation arising in the graded-syzygy analysis of a previously constructed Huneke-Wiegand family. For every integer p>=8, its cokernel contains a direct summand isomorphic to (Z/2)^floor(((p-2)^2+3)/12). The classes are indexed by all strictly increasing nonnegative triples of sum p-2. Reflection-symmetric interval potentials give explicit original integral sources for twice each class. Relative parity functionals, supported on ten to twelve original rows, detect the classes independently and vanish on every complete connecting image; extension over the remaining target gives a nonconstructive retraction. A previously tracked four-row vector is integrally congruent to one selected class, with an explicit source for the difference. We also give its full twice-source, two short kernel-domain corrections, and a neighboring integral potential basis of rank binomial(p-1,2) with at most seven-row images. Independent finite computations check the signed identities and complete-sector parity certificates, preserving all tested sources in lossless archives. A failed local search yields an exact locality obstruction. The uniform theorem follows from signed reconstruction, exhaustive source classification, and an elementary counting recurrence, not finite rank extrapolation. The full cokernel, an upper bound, and identification with earlier isolated subpresentations remain unresolved. The family-to-presentation identification is an imported premise. Son Pham retains priority for the original public Huneke-Wiegand counterexample. Source code, computation records and archived sources: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH .

summary: For every integer p>=4, a previously constructed symmetric numerical semigroup ring R_p and rigid two-generated monomial ideal determine a conductor ideal T_p whose special fiber C_p = F(T_p) is one-dimensional Cohen-Macaulay, generated in degree one by 10p monomials, and has multiplicity 24p. We prove that this fiber cone admits the explicit standard-graded parametrization C_p ≅ 𝕜[xy^a : a ∈ G_p] ⊆ 𝕜[x,y]/(y^24p), with deg(xy^a) = 1, where G_p is the exact degree-one offset set. If P_p = 𝕜[X_a : a ∈ G_p] and J_p is the defining ideal, then √J_p = L_p = (X_a : a > 0), J_p is L_p-primary. Thus the complete primary decomposition has one component. The nilradical of C_p has sharp nilpotency index 24p: its (24p-1)st power is nonzero, while its 24p-th power vanishes. Dehomogenization at X_0 gives C_p/(X_0-1) ≅ 𝕜[y]/(y^24p). Consequently Proj(C_p) is a saturated length-24p curvilinear fat point with one-dimensional Zariski tangent space. It is locally Gorenstein, although its homogeneous coordinate ring has Cohen-Macaulay type 10p+1 and is neither level nor Gorenstein. We also compute its affine Kähler differential module, including the exact characteristic split. The proof is deductive from previously proved offset-basis and Cohen-Macaulay input theorems. We further give the complete reduced Gröbner basis for graded reverse lexicographic order with X_0 last. Its degree profile is (50p^2-17p, 5p-1, p-2) in degrees two, three, and four, with no later elements. No minimal leading monomial contains X_0, yielding a flat Cohen-Macaulay monomial degeneration. Exact parameter sweeps, an independently encoded clique-based recomputation, and an all-parameter Presburger boundary certificate validate the formulas and run negative controls, but do not replace the deductive arguments. The results concern the conductor fiber cones of this explicit family; they do not assert that arbitrary monomial fiber cones are primary, curvilinear, Cohen-Macaulay or locally Gorenstein. Source code, compact artifacts, premise hashes and proofs: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH .

summary: In March 2026, the Canadian Cardiovascular Harmonized National Guideline Endeavour (C-CHANGE) published the first Canadian clinical practice guideline to jointly address brain, heart, and mental health conditions, replacing the disease-specific silos that had previously left family physicians without unified guidance for patients carrying multiple, interacting chronic conditions. This review synthesizes that guideline for a Canadian primary care audience, examining in turn its recommendations for managing heart failure and atrial fibrillation in patients with comorbid cognitive impairment, its guidance on cognitive screening and silent cerebral infarct detection in cardiac patients, its proposed integrated care pathway linking cardiology, neurology, and mental health services, and its shared decision-making framework for reconciling competing treatment priorities. The evidence indicates that cognitive status materially changes cardiac management decisions, that brief validated screening tools can identify at-risk patients within a standard visit, and that team-based models such as the Patient's Medical Home already provide much of the infrastructure the guideline's integrated pathway requires. What remains incomplete is implementation: screening tools, referral pathways, and electronic medical record supports exist individually but are rarely deployed together in the same practice. Family physicians are positioned to close that gap and are the clinicians most likely to see these patients before either a cardiac or neurologic event forces a reactive referral. Moving this guideline from publication into everyday Canadian family practice will require deliberate investment in the team-based infrastructure that makes integrated, patient-centred brain-heart care practical rather than aspirational.
title: Integrated Brain-Heart-Mental Health Care: A Review of the 2026 C-CHANGE Guideline

summary: In July 2026 a counterexample to Goemans' cost version of the Dinitz–Garg–Goemans theorem was announced publicly, outside peer review, and circulated widely. We report an independent verification of that finite object by exact rational enumeration, performed without executing or importing the proposer's verifier, together with quantitative and structural content that the announcement did not state. Title Quality-controlled gradient-tower meteorological profiles and derived surface-flux estimates from the Huancayo Geophysical Observatory, Peruvian central Andes Alternative short title HYGO gradient-tower profiles and derived surface-flux dataset Description This dataset contains quality-controlled gradient-tower meteorological profiles, derived thermodynamic variables, and method-dependent surface-flux estimates from the Huancayo Geophysical Observatory (HYGO) of the Instituto Geofísico del Perú. HYGO is located in the Mantaro Valley of the central Peruvian Andes, an area characterized by high elevation, strong diurnal forcing, seasonal moisture contrasts, agricultural land use, and mountain–valley–slope circulations. Native 1-min observations of air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and wind direction were processed using a reproducible workflow that includes timestamp auditing, pre-deployment sensor harmonization, conservative bit-mask quality control, thermodynamic derivation, 30-min aggregation, flux-specific pre-calculation screening, independent MOST and BRN_ANC calculations, method-status diagnostics, defensive post-calculation checks, applicability diagnostics, and sensitivity analyses. The quality-controlled multi-level meteorological profiles are the primary observational product. The surface-flux variables are derived, method-dependent estimates and should not be interpreted as direct eddy-covariance measurements or as independently validated absolute flux observations. Dataset period 15 May 2018 to 31 July 2026 The released L2 time coordinate extends from 15 May 2018 at 19:00 UTC to 1 August 2026 at 04:59 UTC, corresponding to the local observational period ending at 23:59 on 31 July 2026 in America/Lima (UTC−5). Geographic coverage Huancayo Geophysical Observatory, Mantaro Valley, central Peruvian Andes, Peru Latitude: −12.04145° Longitude: −75.31875° Elevation: 3315 m above sea level Measurement heights Meteorological profile levels used for the flux-gradient calculations: 2 m AGL 6 m AGL 12 m AGL 24 m AGL Wind-direction monitoring levels: 18 m AGL: source channel dir_wind_01 29 m AGL: source channel dir_wind_02 The 18 and 29 m direction measurements are used to diagnose vertical wind turning and directional shear. They are not treated as additional scalar-profile levels in the MOST or BRN_ANC calculations. Temporal resolution 1 min for the quality-controlled meteorological profiles. 1 min for the corresponding high-frequency derived flux estimates. 30 min for aggregated profiles, availability statistics, MOST and BRN_ANC flux estimates, applicability diagnostics, and sensitivity products. Time conventions The L2 quality-controlled profile NetCDF uses a UTC time coordinate. The current L3 1-min and 30-min flux products retain local wall-clock timestamps and declare America/Lima (UTC−5) in the time-coordinate metadata. Users combining L2 and L3 products must convert timestamps according to the metadata of each file before matching observations. A timezone-naive decoded timestamp should not automatically be assumed to use the same convention in all products. Main variables Observed meteorological variables Air temperature at 2, 6, 12, and 24 m AGL Relative humidity at 2, 6, 12, and 24 m AGL Wind speed at 2, 6, 12, and 24 m AGL Wind direction at 18 and 29 m AGL Derived thermodynamic variables Atmospheric pressure estimated at the site eleva

Native 1-min observations of air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and wind direction were processed using a reproducible workflow that includes timestamp auditing, pre-deployment sensor harmonization, conservative bit-mask quality control, thermodynamic derivation, 30-min aggregation, flux-specific pre-calculation screening, independent MOST and BRN_ANC calculations, method-status diagnostics, defensive post-calculation checks, applicability diagnostics, and sensitivity analyses. The quality-controlled multi-level meteorological profiles are the primary observational product. The surface-flux variables are derived, method-dependent estimates and should not be interpreted as direct eddy-covariance measurements or as independently validated absolute flux observations. Dataset period 15 May 2018 to 31 July 2026 The released L2 time coordinate extends from 15 May 2018 at 19:00 UTC to 1 August 2026 at 04:59 UTC, corresponding to the local observational period ending at 23:59 on 31 July 2026 in America/Lima (UTC−5). Geographic coverage Huancayo Geophysical Observatory, Mantaro Valley, central Peruvian Andes, Peru Latitude: −12.04145° Longitude: −75.31875° Elevation: 3315 m above sea level Measurement heights Meteorological profile levels used for the flux-gradient calculations: 2 m AGL 6 m AGL 12 m AGL 24 m AGL Wind-direction monitoring levels: 18 m AGL: source channel dir_wind_01 29 m AGL: source channel dir_wind_02 The 18 and 29 m direction measurements are used to diagnose vertical wind turning and directional shear. They are not treated as additional scalar-profile levels in the MOST or BRN_ANC calculations. Temporal resolution 1 min for the quality-controlled meteorological profiles. 1 min for the corresponding high-frequency derived flux estimates. 30 min for aggregated profiles, availability statistics, MOST and BRN_ANC flux estimates, applicability diagnostics, and sensitivity products. Time conventions The L2 quality-controlled profile NetCDF uses a UTC time coordinate. The current L3 1-min and 30-min flux products retain local wall-clock timestamps and declare America/Lima (UTC−5) in the time-coordinate metadata. Users combining L2 and L3 products must convert timestamps according to the metadata of each file before matching observations. A timezone-naive decoded timestamp should not automatically be assumed to use the same convention in all products. Main variables Observed meteorological variables Air temperature at 2, 6, 12, and 24 m AGL Relative humidity at 2, 6, 12, and 24 m AGL Wind speed at 2, 6, 12, and 24 m AGL Wind direction at 18 and 29 m AGL Derived thermodynamic variables Atmospheric pressure estimated at the site eleva

summary: Ontario's Education Act requires every district school board to identify, place, and support students with special education needs, yet the province's own 2026 auditor general special report found that the system does not consistently fulfill that legal obligation. This audit examines Ontario's special education policy architecture, comprising the Education Act, Regulation 181/98, Regulation 306, and the Identification, Placement and Review Committee (IPRC) and Individual Education Plan (IEP) processes, against the lived experience of students, families, and educators who navigate it. Drawing on stakeholder analysis, a PESTEL scan of the policy environment, and a comparative review of the United States' Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) and the United Kingdom's Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) system, the audit finds that Ontario's framework is legally sound in principle but structurally inconsistent in practice: assessment wait times exceeding one year at multiple boards, educational assistant absences left unfilled between roughly half and three-quarters of the time, and individualized education plans that frequently lack measurable goals or documented parent input. The audit does not conclude that Ontario's approach has failed; rather, it finds that the policy's core entitlements are strong but under-resourced and unevenly enforced across the province's 72 district school boards. The United States and United Kingdom experiences are considered as useful points of comparison, not as models for direct replication, and the audit closes with recommendations for standardizing identification timelines, strengthening IEP quality assurance, and improving public accountability for special education outcomes across Ontario.
title: Equitable Access to Special Education in Ontario: A Policy and Equity Audit of Programs and Services

summary: Artifact of the IEEE S&P 2027 paper "Quiet Triggers, Loud Footprints: A Tri-Space Measurement Study of Backdoor Stealthiness". Code: backdoor-stealthiness-sp2027-artifact.tar.gz is a complete source tree (measurement library with the sixteen input-, feature- and parameter-space footprint metrics, record loaders, the per-record evaluation driver, table-regeneration scripts, defenses, derived analyses with their per-configuration results, setup and data-download scripts) with the five attack implementations included; README.md, setup.sh and the claim scripts are also attached individually for reference. The code is released under the MIT license (LICENSE inside the archive). Data: the backdoored image classifiers (ResNet18 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Imagenette; a VGG16 subset) with their poisoned training and test data (record.tar), the saved penultimate-layer features, test predictions, activation differences and t-SNE embeddings the footprint metrics were computed from, the datasets in the layout the code expects (data.tar), and the retrained replicates used in the robustness analyses (record_seeds, record_targets, record_reruns, vgg_records); scripts/download_data.py in the archive fetches and verifies every tarball. Development continues in the linked GitHub repository.
title: Quiet Triggers, Loud Footprints: A Tri-Space Measurement Study of Backdoor Stealthiness -- code and data

summary: Cyber threats directed against space systems (spanning orbital payloads, tracking and telemetry ground stations, downlinks, and upstream manufacturing supply chains) have evolved into acute operational hazards. Concurrently, national security and commercial defenders face an intelligence volume crisis where telemetry and vulnerability disclosures outpace human cognitive bandwidth. While autonomous multi-agent pipelines powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) offer scalable automation, they introduce severe epistemic liabilities: hallucination, source detachment, uncalibrated certainty, and susceptibility to indirect prompt injection. This paper presents Space-Cyber Brief Crew, a multi-agent cyber threat intelligence (CTI) architecture that automates space-domain intelligence synthesis under an explicit governance layer. Built on a decoupled CrewAI orchestration, the system routes structured reporting through a three-stage sequential pipeline (Collector, Analyst, Writer) governed by ten operational rules. Crucially, the architecture establishes a structural boundary between action capabilities and generative synthesis: downstream analysis agents operate in zero-tool sandboxes, restricting the execution attack surface by construction. We evaluate the framework against a tri-domain threat corpus spanning satellite imagery manipulation, ground industrial control systems (ICS), and global navigation satellite system (GNSS) spoofing. In our evaluation, the governed architecture eliminated identifier fabrication (from 23.3% to 0.0%), preserved 100% provenance retention, and neutralized indirect prompt injection attacks that succeeded in 80% of unconstrained baseline runs. Finally, we examine the institutional, regulatory, and oversight implications, establishing technical criteria for federal procurement and intelligence integration.

title: Governing the Intelligence Loop: Architectural Mitigations for Epistemic Fragility in Autonomous Space-Cyber Threat Analysis

summary: Cyber threats directed against space systems (spanning orbital payloads, tracking and telemetry ground stations, downlinks, and upstream manufacturing supply chains) have evolved into acute operational hazards. Concurrently, national security and commercial defenders face an intelligence volume crisis where telemetry and vulnerability disclosures outpace human cognitive bandwidth. While autonomous multi-agent pipelines powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) offer scalable automation, they introduce severe epistemic liabilities: hallucination, source detachment, uncalibrated certainty, and susceptibility to indirect prompt injection. This paper presents Space-Cyber Brief Crew, a multi-agent cyber threat intelligence (CTI) architecture that automates space-domain intelligence synthesis under an explicit governance layer. Built on a decoupled CrewAI orchestration, the system routes structured reporting through a three-stage sequential pipeline (Collector, Analyst, Writer) governed by ten operational rules. Crucially, the architecture establishes a structural boundary between action capabilities and generative synthesis: downstream analysis agents operate in zero-tool sandboxes, restricting the execution attack surface by construction. We evaluate the framework against a tri-domain threat corpus spanning satellite imagery manipulation, ground industrial control systems (ICS), and global navigation satellite system (GNSS) spoofing. In our evaluation, the governed architecture eliminated identifier fabrication (from 23.3% to 0.0%), preserved 100% provenance retention, and neutralized indirect prompt injection attacks that succeeded in 80% of unconstrained baseline runs. Finally, we examine the institutional, regulatory, and oversight implications, establishing technical criteria for federal procurement and intelligence integration.

summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . Interactive studio: https://tailwatch.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1, descending frame 124D_04854_171313 (2016-2018), redistributed under the Copernicus free-and-open licence with LiCSBAS attribution (Morishita et al. 2020); provenance in data/derived/tw-real-cf.provenance.json.

summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across diverse applications, raising critical questions for governance, accountability, and data provenance. Understanding which training data most influenced a model's output remains a fundamental open problem. We address this challenge through training data attribution (TDA) for auto-regressive LLMs by expanding upon the inverse formulation: How would training data be affected if the model had seen the generated output during training? Our method perturbs the base model using bidirectional gradient optimization (gradient ascent and descent) on a generated text sample and measures the resulting change in loss across training samples. Our framework supports attribution at arbitrary data granularity, enabling both factual and stylistic attribution. We evaluate our method against baselines on pretrained models with known datasets, and show that it outperforms previous work on influence metrics, thereby enhancing model interpretability, an essential requirement for accountable AI systems.
title: Data Attribution in Large Language Models via Bidirectional Gradient Optimization

summary: Robot behavior is often validated through simulation-based testing, yet the replicability of such campaigns depends critically on transparent documentation of how tests are configured, executed, and post-processed. We argue that data provenance, coupled with the FAIR principles (findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability), addresses this gap by explicitly tracking links between artifacts and by attaching machine-readable metadata about file origins and key design decisions. Moreover, provenance and metadata cannot be treated as an afterthought confined to final datasets; they must be integrated into the testing processes that generate those datasets so that evidence can be reconstructed end-to-end. We demonstrate this by augmenting an existing simulation-based testing framework with provenance tracking and metadata collection mechanisms, and by using these extensions to enrich a mobile robot navigation dataset with structured provenance and FAIR-aligned metadata. Finally, we discuss obstacles encountered in this integration -- such as vocabulary alignment, attribute selection, and adoption of domain standards -- and provide actionable recommendations for implementing provenance-centric, FAIR metadata in robotics validation workflows.
title: Replicable Simulation-Based Robot Validation through Provenance

summary: We present SemRepo, an RDF knowledge graph comprising over 81 million triples describing nearly 200,000 GitHub repositories associated with scientific research. SemRepo captures repository-level metadata, such as contributors, issues, and programming languages, and interlinks this information with external scholarly knowledge graphs. In particular, repository authors are linked to their profiles in SemOpenAlex, repositories are connected to scholarly publications in LPWC, and research artifacts, such as datasets and experiments, are linked via MLSea-KG. This integration enables queries that span publications and their scholarly artifacts, which are typically fragmented across separate platforms. SemRepo supports analyses that are difficult to perform with existing resources in isolation, including provenance reconstruction across repositories and publications, as well as the systematic identification of risks to research reproducibility and software sustainability. By unifying research software with its scholarly context in a single graph, SemRepo provides an important infrastructure for large-scale analysis of software within the broader scientific research ecosystem.
title: SemRepo: A Knowledge Graph for Research Software and Its Scholarly Ecosystem

summary: Handwritten archival tables contain rich historical information, yet transforming them into structured representations, such as Knowledge Graphs, requires integrating table structure recognition, handwriting recognition, and semantic interpretation - a complex multimodal process. End-to-end AI implementations can obscure these steps, resulting in opaque algorithmic operations that hinder human oversight, critical assessment, and trust. To address this, we present a modular, provenance-aware pipeline to convert handwritten tabular images into KGs supporting human-AI collaboration. The pipeline decomposes the workflow into three stages - table reconstruction, information extraction, and KG construction - while exposing intermediate representations for inspection, evaluation, and correction. A key contribution of our approach is the systematic integration of data provenance at every stage, ensuring that all extracted entities and literals remain traceable to their visual and textual origins. The proposed pipeline is demonstrated through a number of experiments on real-world archival material concerning military careers. The results across three different table reconstruction variants highlight the importance of modularisation. By coupling modularity with data provenance, our work advances transparent and collaboratively controllable image-to-KG pipelines for complex historical data.

summary: The rise of generative AI has enabled the production of high-fidelity synthetic tabular data across fields such as healthcare, finance, and public policy, raising growing concerns about data provenance and misuse. Watermarking offers a promising solution to address these concerns by ensuring the traceability of synthetic data, but existing methods face many limitations: they are computationally expensive due to reliance on the inverse process of large diffusion models, struggle with mixed discrete-continuous data, or lack robustness to common post-processing attacks. To address these limitations, we propose TAB-DRW, an efficient and robust post-editing watermarking scheme for synthetic tabular data. TAB-DRW embeds watermark signals in the frequency domain: it normalizes heterogeneous features via the Yeo-Johnson transformation and standardization, applies the discrete Fourier transform (DFT), and adjusts the imaginary parts of adaptively selected entries according to precomputed pseudorandom bits. To further enhance robustness and efficiency, we introduce a novel rank-based pseudorandom bit generation method that enables row-wise retrieval without incurring storage overhead. Experiments on five benchmark tabular datasets show that TAB-DRW achieves strong detectability and robustness against post-processing and adaptive attacks, while preserving high data fidelity and fully supporting mixed-type features.

To address these limitations, we propose TAB-DRW, an efficient and robust post-editing watermarking scheme for synthetic tabular data. TAB-DRW embeds watermark signals in the frequency domain: it normalizes heterogeneous features via the Yeo-Johnson transformation and standardization, applies the discrete Fourier transform (DFT), and adjusts the imaginary parts of adaptively selected entries according to precomputed pseudorandom bits. To further enhance robustness and efficiency, we introduce a novel rank-based pseudorandom bit generation method that enables row-wise retrieval without incurring storage overhead. Experiments on five benchmark tabular datasets show that TAB-DRW achieves strong detectability and robustness against post-processing and adaptive attacks, while preserving high data fidelity and fully supporting mixed-type features.
title: Robust Spectral Watermark for Synthetic Tabular Data

summary: Formal financial sector linkage with community group saving and lending mechanisms (CGSLs) is often proposed as a pathway through which fragile rural economies can move from subsistence finance to more durable agricultural investment. Yet, in South Sudan, this linkage remains difficult to institutionalise. This article re-analyses thesis evidence from Eastern Equatoria, Jonglei and Lakes State to examine why coordination among government, non-governmental organisations, donors, formal financial institutions and CGSL groups remains elusive. Framed through North's institutional analysis, the article argues that CGSL proliferation is not simply a cultural preference for informal finance; it is a rational institutional response to high transaction costs, weak formal enforcement, limited rural banking infrastructure, conflict-affected markets and project-based support systems. The study used a mixed-methods design involving 81 valid survey responses and 17 interviews. Descriptive findings showed strong demand for government and donor collaboration, with 94% of respondents agreeing or strongly agreeing that such collaboration should support rural financial services. However, the mean score for NGO promotion of informal savings was lower (3.68), and village-bank loan officer linkage was weaker (3.49), suggesting that external support is uneven and not yet converted into stable formal-informal intermediation. Chi-square tests confirmed significant associations between CGSL participation and agricultural development indicators, while logistic regression showed that CGSL credit access significantly influenced farmers' investment decisions. The article concludes that linkage failure is best understood as a coordination problem: CGSL groups carry local trust and repayment discipline, but they remain weakly connected to formal capital, policy protection, risk-management products, extension systems and market institutions. The paper recommends a coordination compact that recognises CGSLs as rural financial institutions, links mature groups to suitable wholesale finance, and protects member governance without destroying local accountability.
title: Government-NGO-CGSL Coordination Failures: Why Formal-Informal Financial Sector Linkage Remains Elusive in South Sudan

summary: For a century, cinema has returned to a single figure—the thinking machine that turns on its maker—and to a single feeling: dread. This article asks where that dread is actually manufactured. It pairs a qualitative coding of twelve canonical texts, from Karel Čapek's R.U.R. (1920) to the generative-AI films of the 2020s, with a computational content analysis of their scripts, conducted with a purpose-built instrument that measures fear vocabulary, sentiment arcs, propaganda techniques, dehumanizing language, and the language of violence. The results are unexpected. Explicit fear language never reaches one and a half percent of sentences in any script; the three-act emotional arc of every film in the corpus registers as neutral or faintly positive; the most recent films carry the least fear language of all; and the two films most affectionate toward their machines objectify them most heavily in grammar. The article argues that these apparent null results are themselves the finding. The fear of the intelligent machine is cultivated not in words but in the audiovisual apparatus—in lighting inherited from expressionism and noir, in the bodiless machine voice, in the unblinking close-up and the withheld cut, in production design that photographs the machine like geography. Drawing on cultivation theory, the Frankfurt School, and postcolonial critique, the article then asks who benefits from a fear installed beneath the level of language, and what a century of spectacular, misaimed dread has trained audiences not to see.
tags: Keywords: Artificial intelligence; science-fiction cinema; content analysis; cultivation theory; technophobia
title: The Many Names of The Machine: Fear, Neutrality, and The Cinema of Artificial Intelligence, 1920–2026

summary: FlowMLLab v1.7.0 adds paired self-supervised wake-learning modules. Week 7.3 retains the strong gappy-POD baseline on masked low-rank wake reconstruction and corrects linear-probe pooling and sample-standard-deviation reporting. Week 7.4 generates sixteen compact Reynolds trajectories and measures target-label efficiency for instantaneous lift using frozen pretrained, random and POD-32 representations. Full trajectory splits, source-label selection costs, per-case errors, data hashes and coarse-CFD limitations are disclosed. The course includes 42 notebooks and 26 PDF lectures through Week 15. This is a MAPA-inspired educational experiment, not a reproduction of its neuroscience benchmark.
title: FlowMLLab: An Open-Source Framework for Reproducible CFD-to-Scientific-Machine-Learning Experiments

summary: We study an explicit integral Koszul presentation arising in the graded-syzygy analysis of a previously constructed Huneke-Wiegand family. For every integer p>=8, its cokernel contains a direct summand isomorphic to (Z/2)^floor(((p-2)^2+3)/12). The classes are indexed by all strictly increasing nonnegative triples of sum p-2. Reflection-symmetric interval potentials give explicit original integral sources for twice each class. Relative parity functionals, supported on ten to twelve original rows, detect the classes independently and vanish on every complete connecting image; extension over the remaining target gives a nonconstructive retraction. A previously tracked four-row vector is integrally congruent to one selected class, with an explicit source for the difference. We also give its full twice-source, two short kernel-domain corrections, and a neighboring integral potential basis of rank binomial(p-1,2) with at most seven-row images. Independent finite computations check the signed identities and complete-sector parity certificates, preserving all tested sources in lossless archives. A failed local search yields an exact locality obstruction. The uniform theorem follows from signed reconstruction, exhaustive source classification, and an elementary counting recurrence, not finite rank extrapolation. The full cokernel, an upper bound, and identification with earlier isolated subpresentations remain unresolved. The family-to-presentation identification is an imported premise. Son Pham retains priority for the original public Huneke-Wiegand counterexample. Source code, computation records and archived sources: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH .
title: A quadratic family of integral two-torsion classes in a Huneke–Wiegand Koszul presentation

summary: In March 2026, the Canadian Cardiovascular Harmonized National Guideline Endeavour (C-CHANGE) published the first Canadian clinical practice guideline to jointly address brain, heart, and mental health conditions, replacing the disease-specific silos that had previously left family physicians without unified guidance for patients carrying multiple, interacting chronic conditions. This review synthesizes that guideline for a Canadian primary care audience, examining in turn its recommendations for managing heart failure and atrial fibrillation in patients with comorbid cognitive impairment, its guidance on cognitive screening and silent cerebral infarct detection in cardiac patients, its proposed integrated care pathway linking cardiology, neurology, and mental health services, and its shared decision-making framework for reconciling competing treatment priorities. The evidence indicates that cognitive status materially changes cardiac management decisions, that brief validated screening tools can identify at-risk patients within a standard visit, and that team-based models such as the Patient's Medical Home already provide much of the infrastructure the guideline's integrated pathway requires. What remains incomplete is implementation: screening tools, referral pathways, and electronic medical record supports exist individually but are rarely deployed together in the same practice. Family physicians are positioned to close that gap and are the clinicians most likely to see these patients before either a cardiac or neurologic event forces a reactive referral. Moving this guideline from publication into everyday Canadian family practice will require deliberate investment in the team-based infrastructure that makes integrated, patient-centred brain-heart care practical rather than aspirational.
title: Integrated Brain-Heart-Mental Health Care: A Review of the 2026 C-CHANGE Guideline

summary: In July 2026 a counterexample to Goemans' cost version of the Dinitz–Garg–Goemans theorem was announced publicly, outside peer review, and circulated widely. We report an independent verification of that finite object by exact rational enumeration, performed without executing or importing the proposer's verifier, together with quantitative and structural content that the announcement did not state. Our results: (i) the instance is confirmed, so Goemans' conjecture is false, and, the instance being acyclic, the Morell–Skutella cost conjecture and the convex-combination form fall with it; (ii) the instance forces a violation of exactly 16/15 of the maximum demand d_max, that is, the conjecture fails by one unit at d_max = 15, so the open question whether cost-preserving rounding is possible with O(d_max) violation is untouched by it; (iii) every proved result in the area survives its direct test on the instance, including the Dinitz–Garg–Goemans theorem, the Morell–Skutella cost-free conjecture, the series-parallel theorem of Majthoub Almoghrabi, Skutella and Warode, and the planar theorem of Traub, Vargas Koch and Zenklusen; (iv) the instance contains a K4 subdivision, hence sits exactly one structure outside the series-parallel class where the conjecture is proved, and, being planar, pins the planar constant strictly between 1 and 2; (v) an exact separation linear program shows that the published cost vector is an optimal separator for that graph and fractional flow, so its cost gap cannot be improved by any reweighting; and (vi) a first minimality result, that no single-terminal instance is a counterexample for any nonnegative cost vector, together with a necessary condition at two terminals. The verification is a replication; items (ii) and (iv)-(vi) are, to our knowledge, new. The two-terminal case remains open, and we show why a natural argument for it fails. The counterexample instance is not ours, and no claim is made about priority or attribution. Source code, data and computational records: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH (problems/optimization-geometry/unsplittable-flow-cost).
title: An independent exact verification of the 2026 counterexample to Goemans' unsplittable-flow cost conjecture, with the violation constant it forces

Title Quality-controlled gradient-tower meteorological profiles and derived surface-flux estimates from the Huancayo Geophysical Observatory, Peruvian central Andes Alternative short title HYGO gradient-tower profiles and derived surface-flux dataset Description This dataset contains quality-controlled gradient-tower meteorological profiles, derived thermodynamic variables, and method-dependent surface-flux estimates from the Huancayo Geophysical Observatory (HYGO) of the Instituto Geofísico del Perú. HYGO is located in the Mantaro Valley of the central Peruvian Andes, an area characterized by high elevation, strong diurnal forcing, seasonal moisture contrasts, agricultural land use, and mountain–valley–slope circulations. Native 1-min observations of air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and wind direction were processed using a reproducible workflow that includes timestamp auditing, pre-deployment sensor harmonization, conservative bit-mask quality control, thermodynamic derivation, 30-min aggregation, flux-specific pre-calculation screening, independent MOST and BRN_ANC calculations, method-status diagnostics, defensive post-calculation checks, applicability diagnostics, and sensitivity analyses. The quality-controlled multi-level meteorological profiles are the primary observational product. The surface-flux variables are derived, method-dependent estimates and should not be interpreted as direct eddy-covariance measurements or as independently validated absolute flux observations. Dataset period 15 May 2018 to 31 July 2026 The released L2 time coordinate extends from 15 May 2018 at 19:00 UTC to 1 August 2026 at 04:59 UTC, corresponding to the local observational period ending at 23:59 on 31 July 2026 in America/Lima (UTC−5). Geographic coverage Huancayo Geophysical Observatory, Mantaro Valley, central Peruvian Andes, Peru Latitude: −12.04145° Longitude: −75.31875° Elevation: 3315 m above sea level Measurement heights Meteorological profile levels used for the flux-gradient calculations: 2 m AGL 6 m AGL 12 m AGL 24 m AGL Wind-direction monitoring levels: 18 m AGL: source channel dir_wind_01 29 m AGL: source channel dir_wind_02 The 18 and 29 m direction measurements are used to diagnose vertical wind turning and directional shear. They are not treated as additional scalar-profile levels in the MOST or BRN_ANC calculations. Temporal resolution 1 min for the quality-controlled meteorological profiles. 1 min for the corresponding high-frequency derived flux estimates. 30 min for aggregated profiles, availability statistics, MOST and BRN_ANC flux estimates, applicability diagnostics, and sensitivity products. Time conventions The L2 quality-controlled profile NetCDF uses a UTC time coordinate. The current L3 1-min and 30-min flux products retain local wall-clock timestamps and declare America/Lima (UTC−5) in the time-coordinate metadata. Users combining L2 and L3 products must convert timestamps according to the metadata of each file before matching observations. A timezone-naive decoded timestamp should not automatically be assumed to use the same convention in all products. Main variables Observed meteorological variables Air temperature at 2, 6, 12, and 24 m AGL Relative humidity at 2, 6, 12, and 24 m AGL Wind speed at 2, 6, 12, and 24 m AGL Wind direction at 18 and 29 m AGL Derived thermodynamic variables Atmospheric pressure estimated at the site eleva
title: Data-set of gradient tower for quality-controlled and surface-flux estimations in the Peruvian central Andes

summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . Interactive studio: https://tailwatch.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1, descending frame 124D_04854_171313 (2016-2018), redistributed under the Copernicus free-and-open licence with LiCSBAS attribution (Morishita et al. 2020); provenance in data/derived/tw-real-cf.provenance.json.
title: TailWatch: An InSAR Deformation-Monitoring and Inverse-Velocity Failure-Forecasting Studio, on Synthetic Sentinel-1 and Real Campi Flegrei

summary: Data will be added in the next version.  This corrected U.S. Civic Rigor Framework adapts the Universal Civic Rigor Checklist to the institutional realities of U.S. federal elections. It evaluates how presidential and congressional platforms use evidence, scale fiscal claims, respect constitutional limits, disclose uncertainty, engage opposing arguments, anticipate legislative feasibility, and acknowledge judicial constraints. The framework consists of ten criteria across constitutional competence, fiscal scale, definitional guardrails, historical context, disclosure and causal honesty, committee and veto hearing, rhetorical register, legislative and administrative blueprint, federal agency provenance, and judicial review. This version corrects grade-band arithmetic, resolves overlap between criteria, and restores missing concepts from the original UK model. It is designed for reproducible scoring of U.S. federal platforms and is directly derived from the UK Civic Rigor Framework (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22766473). This framework is an adaptation of the Universal Civic Rigor Checklist originally developed for UK general election manifestos.   Related identifier (isDerivedFrom): 10.5281/zenodo.22766473

summary: Data will be added in the next version.  This corrected U.S. Civic Rigor Framework adapts the Universal Civic Rigor Checklist to the institutional realities of U.S. federal elections. It evaluates how presidential and congressional platforms use evidence, scale fiscal claims, respect constitutional limits, disclose uncertainty, engage opposing arguments, anticipate legislative feasibility, and acknowledge judicial constraints. The framework consists of ten criteria across constitutional competence, fiscal scale, definitional guardrails, historical context, disclosure and causal honesty, committee and veto hearing, rhetorical register, legislative and administrative blueprint, federal agency provenance, and judicial review. This version corrects grade-band arithmetic, resolves overlap between criteria, and restores missing concepts from the original UK model. It is designed for reproducible scoring of U.S. federal platforms and is directly derived from the UK Civic Rigor Framework (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22766473). This framework is an adaptation of the Universal Civic Rigor Checklist originally developed for UK general election manifestos.   Related identifier (isDerivedFrom): 10.5281/zenodo.22766473

summary: This dataset contains the complete computational records from two 500-sequence demonstration runs performed with ENZTRA (Enzyme Redesign and Triage Automation), a reproducible and resumable workflow for reference-guided enzyme redesign. ENZTRA integrates reference preparation, RFdiffusion2 backbone generation, LigandMPNN sequence design, DLKcat and CatPred kinetic prediction, strict kinetic selection, Boltz-2 structural assessment, quality control, provenance tracking, and publication-oriented reporting. Both demonstrations used an active Escherichia coli phytase derived from PDB 1DKP and myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (IHP; phytate) as the reference enzyme-substrate system. Each run generated 50 RFdiffusion2 backbones and 10 LigandMPNN sequences per backbone, yielding 500 candidate sequences. The deposit contains two project archives: release-500: A short-scaffold demonstration using a requested design-length range of 150-180 residues. Fourteen of the 500 candidates satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion and proceeded to Boltz-2 structural assessment. The remaining 486 candidates were rejected, and no data-quality failures were detected. release-500b: A full-length comparison using a requested scaffold length of 410 residues, matching the reference sequence length. All 500 candidates passed the specified data-quality checks, but none satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion because their predicted turnover numbers were below the reference prediction. Consequently, no candidate proceeded to Boltz-2 assessment. The ENZTRA strict kinetic gate requires both a predicted turnover number ( k cat) above the corresponding reference value and a predicted Michaelis constant ( K m) below the reference value. Passing data-quality checks is therefore distinct from passing kinetic selection. The archives include validated biological inputs, design requests, RFdiffusion2 specifications and execution records, generated backbones, TRB and functional-site mappings, LigandMPNN outputs, consolidated sequence files, DLKcat and CatPred inputs and predictions, kinetic and selection tables, Boltz-2 inputs and outputs where applicable, quality-control tables, publication figures, workflow-state records, qualification reports, and reproducibility manifests. These results are computational predictions intended to demonstrate workflow execution, traceability, recovery, candidate selection, and reporting. They do not establish catalytic activity, structural correctness, expression, stability, or experimental improvement. All prioritized candidates require appropriate experimental validation. ENZTRA source code, installation instructions, and a step-by-step reproduction tutorial are available at: https://github.com/Olanrewaju-Durojaye/ENZTRA

summary: Reproducibility package for the manuscript: Maintenance-Aware Replica Selection for Deadline-Constrained Distributed Scientific Data Transfers This release contains the complete computational artifact used for the submitted study, including: simulation and analysis code; deterministic random seeds; controlled workload inputs; public SCINet maintenance-event provenance data; raw and processed numerical results; baseline and robustness experiments; exact small-instance oracle comparisons; runtime-scaling results; figure-generation scripts; software requirements; validation scripts; and SHA-256 integrity manifests. The archived results include the 6,000-instance controlled experiment and the 9,000-instance public-maintenance-event-conditioned validation. No proprietary production data are included. Public maintenance records are used only as documented event provenance and outage-duration inputs; workload characteristics remain controlled/synthetic. Authors: Abdulaziz M. D. Aljohani Khaled M. Alhawiti University of Tabuk, Saudi Arabia

summary: A 3D city model is only as accurate as its building heights, and a model built from open data mostly infers those heights, from a mapped floor count, a height raster or a default value, rather than taking them from a mapped height. Maqueta reconstructs real places from open geospatial layers, with terrain from the Copernicus GLO-30 surface model, building footprints and roads from Overture Maps, water, green areas and rail from OpenStreetMap, population from GHS-POP, and building heights from the Google Open Buildings 2.5D raster where it has coverage, and it records for every building how its height was obtained. Across the 118 baked places and 4.05 million buildings, 8.8% of heights come from a mapped height attribute, 6.4% from a mapped floor count, 73.2% from the Open Buildings 2.5D height raster, itself a model estimate from satellite imagery, and 11.6% from a default prior of 8 m. A public LoD2 reference exists for two of the places, both in the Netherlands, where the raster has no coverage. Against the 3D BAG, the fused heights have a root-mean-square error of 3.1 m at Delft, with a bias of -0.1 m, and of 8.3 m at Amsterdam, with a bias of -6.6 m; the Amsterdam figure rests on 50 reference buildings. The raster heights, which supply most of the buildings, are not validated by this benchmark, and public ground truth for open-data building heights is scarce. Interactive tool and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RES_Maqueta . Fusion core: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_GeoScena .

summary: A 3D city model is only as accurate as its building heights, and a model built from open data mostly infers those heights, from a mapped floor count, a height raster or a default value, rather than taking them from a mapped height. Maqueta reconstructs real places from open geospatial layers, with terrain from the Copernicus GLO-30 surface model, building footprints and roads from Overture Maps, water, green areas and rail from OpenStreetMap, population from GHS-POP, and building heights from the Google Open Buildings 2.5D raster where it has coverage, and it records for every building how its height was obtained. Across the 118 baked places and 4.05 million buildings, 8.8% of heights come from a mapped height attribute, 6.4% from a mapped floor count, 73.2% from the Open Buildings 2.5D height raster, itself a model estimate from satellite imagery, and 11.6% from a default prior of 8 m.
