summary: This record contains the complete R and Python code and supporting documentation for the independent sensitivity reanalysis associated with the manuscript “Swab-based stool collection largely preserves gut microbiome structure with small device-dependent effects: an intra-individual evaluation of sampling devices and processing conditions.” The archive includes scripts to reconstruct and validate anonymous sample metadata from the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) run report and FASTQ filenames; perform preliminary read-quality and paired-read overlap assessments; process forward (R1) and reverse (R2) reads separately using DADA2; infer ASVs; assign taxonomy using the SILVA SSU NR99 release 138.2 training set; construct phylogenetic trees; evaluate sequencing-depth dependence; calculate standardized alpha- and beta-diversity metrics, including Faith’s phylogenetic diversity, weighted UniFrac, and Bray–Curtis dissimilarity; compare the R1 and R2 results; assess sensitivity to rarefaction depth and unusually long terminal branches; and generate the corresponding tables and figures. The archive also contains a complete execution guide, software dependencies and versions, random seeds, original R session information, reference-database details, and file-integrity checksums. Sample metadata and analytical outputs are generated locally by the documented workflow and are not distributed as precomputed files. Raw paired-end sequencing data are publicly available from the European Nucleotide Archive under accession PRJEB107991. The DADA2-formatted SILVA 138.2 taxonomic training set is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14169026 . The independent ASV analyses complement, but do not reproduce or replace, the proprietary MicrobAT® workflow used for the primary OTU-based analysis. MicrobAT® algorithms, OTU-assignment parameters, and the release of its embedded reference database were not disclosed by the software provider. Accordingly, this archive supports reproducibility of the independent R1/R2 ASV sensitivity analyses and downstream analyses of the published MicrobAT® outputs, but not reconstruction of the proprietary MicrobAT®-generated OTU and taxonomic profiles. This version supersedes the earlier R-only archive by adding the Python utilities, complete operational documentation, software-environment records, random seeds, integrity checks, and portable figure-generation scripts.

summary: Version 1.2.0 code and aggregate-results archive for urinary DEHP metabolites and fasting insulin, glucose, HOMA-IR and C-peptide in NHANES adults without diagnosed diabetes. It includes the analyses completed through 13 September 2026, including all 39 paired insulin-glucose comparisons. The principal analysis covers 2005-2018 and the complementary historical analysis covers 2003-2004. These are cross-sectional samples from the same survey, not an external validation cohort. The historical C-peptide finding is exploratory and does not pass the specified multiple-testing correction. The coefficient decomposition is algebraic and does not establish mediation or a causal effect. Later specifications followed knowledge of earlier results and are not prospective preregistrations.   The six files contain two code packages, two aggregate-data attachments, README and SHA256SUMS. Individual participant records, raw CDC datasets, the manuscript and full supplementary narrative are excluded. Reconstruction retrieves public CDC/NCHS source data. README documents release boundaries, historical reconstruction evidence, licensing and file integrity. Version 1.2.0 updates Code 1 documentation and its integrity metadata without changing statistical computations, numerical outputs or figures; Code 2 and both data attachments retain their original bytes.   Original code is licensed under MIT; original aggregate results, figures and documentation are CC BY 4.0. CDC/NCHS and third-party materials retain their own terms and are not relicensed.   Creators: Jie Li, Xiubo Sun, Jing Zhang, Lijie Zhai and Ling Yu. Corresponding author: Ling Yu, Department of Pharmacy, The Second Hospital of Jilin University. Funding: Jilin Province Tianhua Health Public Welfare Foundation Project, J2025JKJ012 to Ling Yu. OpenAI Codex assisted source review, code and figure-code development, statistical checks and drafting; its use and verification limits are disclosed in the study materials. Human authors retain responsibility. This is a code/results archive, not a manuscript, preprint or preregistration.

summary: FPGA-Accelerated Sub-Microsecond Union-Find Decoding for Real-Time Surface-Code Quantum Memory Architecture manuscript. Latency, power, and resource figures are design estimates unless otherwise marked as measured. Related FPGA Union-Find implementations (Helios / Collision Clustering) are cited for comparison. Abstract Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires continuous decoding of stabilizer syndromes within cycle times that, for superconducting processors, are often 200 ns–1 μs. Host-processor decoders are subject to operating-system jitter, DMA overhead, and memory-hierarchy latency, which make deterministic sub-microsecond service difficult. This paper describes a fully pipelined FPGA architecture for a Union-Find decoder aimed at surface-code quantum memory. The pipeline integrates Aurora-based syndrome acquisition, streaming defect extraction, a path-halving Union-Find engine with hazard forwarding, localized peeling, and dual-port Pauli-frame updates. All latency-critical state is on-chip (BRAM, UltraRAM, distributed RAM). At a target clock of 400 MHz the design estimate for end-to-end latency is 170–390 ns below threshold, with a conservative worst-case bound near 500 ns—inside a 1 μs cycle. Memory for a decoding window scales as O(d³) with the space-time graph, not as O(d³) measurements per cycle. Power is estimated at 3–6 W per logical patch at the FPGA, which remains at room temperature. The contribution is a single deterministic pipeline that does not require a host CPU in the inner loop. It is an architecture and resource plan; it does not replace measured implementations such as Helios. Keywords: surface code; quantum error correction; Union-Find decoder; FPGA; real-time decoding; Pauli frame; clock gating. 1. Introduction Surface-code fault tolerance proceeds by repeated stabilizer measurement and classical decoding of the syndrome stream [1], [9], [10]. Superconducting cycle times commonly fall in T_cycle ~ 200 ns–1 μs [13]. Software decoders on CPUs or GPUs introduce scheduling jitter, DMA cost, cache misses, and synchronization [14]–[16]. Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) is accurate but worst-case cubic in the number of defects and heavy for large distance [17], [18]. The Union-Find decoder of Delfosse and Nickerson is almost-linear and close to MWPM in accuracy, which makes it a natural hardware target [3]. FPGA and ASIC decoders have already shown that real-time surface-code decoding is possible. Das et al. gave a Union-Find micro-architecture; Liyanage et al. (Helios) implemented distributed Union-Find on a VCU129 up to d = 21 with mean times of order 10 ns per round under phenomenological noise, and a resource-optimized d = 51 point near 544 ns per round [14], [15]. Collision Clustering, another Union-Find variant, has been mapped to FPGA and ASIC with sub-microsecond times at large patch size [16]. The present manuscript specifies a single-tile, fully streaming pipeline—acquisition through Pauli frame—with explicit memory equations, banked Find ports, path-halving (not recursive compression), clock-enable power control, and a latency budget written against T_cycle = 1 μs. It is intended as a self-contained hardware architecture that can be implemented or compared against those measured designs. 2. System Architecture The decoder is a fixed-depth pipeline. Stages are registered and advance on the same clock. After fill, a new syndrome frame can be accepted every cycle from the control layer; variable work inside Union-Find is bounded by a worst-case iteration budget, not by a host thread. Stages: •     Syndrome acquisition and deserialization (Aurora 64B/66B over GTY). •     Defect extraction unit (DEU): frame-to-frame XOR and sparse packing. •     Pipelined Union-Find engine: growth, union, path-halving find, boundary test. •     Localized peeling

Superconducting cycle times commonly fall in T_cycle ~ 200 ns–1 μs [13]. Software decoders on CPUs or GPUs introduce scheduling jitter, DMA cost, cache misses, and synchronization [14]–[16]. Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) is accurate but worst-case cubic in the number of defects and heavy for large distance [17], [18]. The Union-Find decoder of Delfosse and Nickerson is almost-linear and close to MWPM in accuracy, which makes it a natural hardware target [3]. FPGA and ASIC decoders have already shown that real-time surface-code decoding is possible. Das et al. gave a Union-Find micro-architecture; Liyanage et al. (Helios) implemented distributed Union-Find on a VCU129 up to d = 21 with mean times of order 10 ns per round under phenomenological noise, and a resource-optimized d = 51 point near 544 ns per round [14], [15]. Collision Clustering, another Union-Find variant, has been mapped to FPGA and ASIC with sub-microsecond times at large patch size [16]. The present manuscript specifies a single-tile, fully streaming pipeline—acquisition through Pauli frame—with explicit memory equations, banked Find ports, path-halving (not recursive compression), clock-enable power control, and a latency budget written against T_cycle = 1 μs. It is intended as a self-contained hardware architecture that can be implemented or compared against those measured designs. 2. System Architecture The decoder is a fixed-depth pipeline. Stages are registered and advance on the same clock. After fill, a new syndrome frame can be accepted every cycle from the control layer; variable work inside Union-Find is bounded by a worst-case iteration budget, not by a host thread. Stages: •     Syndrome acquisition and deserialization (Aurora 64B/66B over GTY). •     Defect extraction unit (DEU): frame-to-frame XOR and sparse packing. •     Pipelined Union-Find engine: growth, union, path-halving find, boundary test. •     Localized peeling
title: FPGA-Accelerated Sub-Microsecond Union-Find Decoding for Real-Time Surface-Code Quantum Memory

summary: The RNA world hypothesis faces two core challenges: first, the error threshold paradox—the contradiction between the length required for RNA replication and its fidelity; second, the transition from free RNA to a primitive cell (membrane-encapsulated system)—how to spontaneously form a selectively permeable compartmental structure. Dual Information Cybernetics states that internal information (the intrinsic determinacy of a system) possesses four attributes: wholeness, potentiality, self-consistency, and dominance. Among these, dominance drives the system from disorder to order and delimits the boundary of possibility for all local processes. Based on this theory, this paper proposes two mutually supporting experimental protocols: (1) the RNA condensate experiment—under mild wet-dry cycling conditions, observing whether RNA with secondary structure spontaneously forms condensates and testing whether the replication fidelity within the condensate is higher than that of single molecules, thereby verifying that "collective synergy" can bypass the error threshold; (2) the RNA-lipid co-assembly experiment—under the same mild conditions, observing whether RNA actively attracts lipid molecules and drives vesicle formation, forming an RNA-containing protocell model, thereby verifying the "active nest-building" behavior driven by the dominance of internal information. Both experiments share the same theoretical framework and mild-condition design; their results corroborate each other and can provide direct visualizable evidence for the dominance of internal information. This paper describes in detail the experimental materials, apparatus, observational indicators, expected results, and significance, aiming to provide an actionable research protocol for experimental researchers and to advance the information-theoretic perspective on the origin of life.
title: Two Experimental Protocols for Verifying the Dominance of Internal Information in RNA From the Error Threshold to Protocell Construction

summary: FlowMLLab v1.7.0 adds paired self-supervised wake-learning modules. Week 7.3 retains the strong gappy-POD baseline on masked low-rank wake reconstruction and corrects linear-probe pooling and sample-standard-deviation reporting. Week 7.4 generates sixteen compact Reynolds trajectories and measures target-label efficiency for instantaneous lift using frozen pretrained, random and POD-32 representations. Full trajectory splits, source-label selection costs, per-case errors, data hashes and coarse-CFD limitations are disclosed. The course includes 42 notebooks and 26 PDF lectures through Week 15. This is a MAPA-inspired educational experiment, not a reproduction of its neuroscience benchmark.
title: FlowMLLab: An Open-Source Framework for Reproducible CFD-to-Scientific-Machine-Learning Experiments

summary: Companion replication package for a manuscript submitted to Big Data & Society. Contains the four-pass ISRC/metadata linkage pipeline, data preparation and deep-analysis notebooks, the executable validation script, the human-audit instrument and protocol, three independent coder files (4,780 track verdicts across 400 stratified release cases), the adjudication queue and decisions, the consensus dataset, the reconciliation key mapping audited cases to linkage strata and population weights, and all aggregate result tables reported in the article. Recomputes the release-level population-weighted disappearance estimate (55.28%, 95% CI 50.56-60.02). Raw What.CD metadata and the Kaggle Spotify snapshot are not redistributable and are not included; provenance and reproduction instructions are in README.md.

summary: We study an explicit integral Koszul presentation arising in the graded-syzygy analysis of a previously constructed Huneke-Wiegand family. For every integer p>=8, its cokernel contains a direct summand isomorphic to (Z/2)^floor(((p-2)^2+3)/12). The classes are indexed by all strictly increasing nonnegative triples of sum p-2. Reflection-symmetric interval potentials give explicit original integral sources for twice each class. Relative parity functionals, supported on ten to twelve original rows, detect the classes independently and vanish on every complete connecting image; extension over the remaining target gives a nonconstructive retraction. A previously tracked four-row vector is integrally congruent to one selected class, with an explicit source for the difference. We also give its full twice-source, two short kernel-domain corrections, and a neighboring integral potential basis of rank binomial(p-1,2) with at most seven-row images. Independent finite computations check the signed identities and complete-sector parity certificates, preserving all tested sources in lossless archives. A failed local search yields an exact locality obstruction. The uniform theorem follows from signed reconstruction, exhaustive source classification, and an elementary counting recurrence, not finite rank extrapolation. The full cokernel, an upper bound, and identification with earlier isolated subpresentations remain unresolved. The family-to-presentation identification is an imported premise. Son Pham retains priority for the original public Huneke-Wiegand counterexample. Source code, computation records and archived sources: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH .
title: A quadratic family of integral two-torsion classes in a Huneke–Wiegand Koszul presentation

summary: For every integer p>=4, a previously constructed symmetric numerical semigroup ring R_p and rigid two-generated monomial ideal determine a conductor ideal T_p whose special fiber C_p = F(T_p) is one-dimensional Cohen-Macaulay, generated in degree one by 10p monomials, and has multiplicity 24p. We prove that this fiber cone admits the explicit standard-graded parametrization C_p ≅ 𝕜[xy^a : a ∈ G_p] ⊆ 𝕜[x,y]/(y^24p), with deg(xy^a) = 1, where G_p is the exact degree-one offset set. If P_p = 𝕜[X_a : a ∈ G_p] and J_p is the defining ideal, then √J_p = L_p = (X_a : a > 0), J_p is L_p-primary. Thus the complete primary decomposition has one component. The nilradical of C_p has sharp nilpotency index 24p: its (24p-1)st power is nonzero, while its 24p-th power vanishes. Dehomogenization at X_0 gives C_p/(X_0-1) ≅ 𝕜[y]/(y^24p). Consequently Proj(C_p) is a saturated length-24p curvilinear fat point with one-dimensional Zariski tangent space. It is locally Gorenstein, although its homogeneous coordinate ring has Cohen-Macaulay type 10p+1 and is neither level nor Gorenstein. We also compute its affine Kähler differential module, including the exact characteristic split. The proof is deductive from previously proved offset-basis and Cohen-Macaulay input theorems. We further give the complete reduced Gröbner basis for graded reverse lexicographic order with X_0 last. Its degree profile is (50p^2-17p, 5p-1, p-2) in degrees two, three, and four, with no later elements. No minimal leading monomial contains X_0, yielding a flat Cohen-Macaulay monomial degeneration. Exact parameter sweeps, an independently encoded clique-based recomputation, and an all-parameter Presburger boundary certificate validate the formulas and run negative controls, but do not replace the deductive arguments. The results concern the conductor fiber cones of this explicit family; they do not assert that arbitrary monomial fiber cones are primary, curvilinear, Cohen-Macaulay or locally Gorenstein. Source code, compact artifacts, premise hashes and proofs: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH .
title: Curvilinear Geometry, Primary Structure, and Gröbner Degenerations of Conductor Fiber Cones in a Huneke–Wiegand Family

summary: In July 2026 a counterexample to Goemans' cost version of the Dinitz–Garg–Goemans theorem was announced publicly, outside peer review, and circulated widely. We report an independent verification of that finite object by exact rational enumeration, performed without executing or importing the proposer's verifier, together with quantitative and structural content that the announcement did not state. Our results: (i) the instance is confirmed, so Goemans' conjecture is false, and, the instance being acyclic, the Morell–Skutella cost conjecture and the convex-combination form fall with it; (ii) the instance forces a violation of exactly 16/15 of the maximum demand d_max, that is, the conjecture fails by one unit at d_max = 15, so the open question whether cost-preserving rounding is possible with O(d_max) violation is untouched by it; (iii) every proved result in the area survives its direct test on the instance, including the Dinitz–Garg–Goemans theorem, the Morell–Skutella cost-free conjecture, the series-parallel theorem of Majthoub Almoghrabi, Skutella and Warode, and the planar theorem of Traub, Vargas Koch and Zenklusen; (iv) the instance contains a K4 subdivision, hence sits exactly one structure outside the series-parallel class where the conjecture is proved, and, being planar, pins the planar constant strictly between 1 and 2; (v) an exact separation linear program shows that the published cost vector is an optimal separator for that graph and fractional flow, so its cost gap cannot be improved by any reweighting; and (vi) a first minimality result, that no single-terminal instance is a counterexample for any nonnegative cost vector, together with a necessary condition at two terminals. The verification is a replication; items (ii) and (iv)-(vi) are, to our knowledge, new. The two-terminal case remains open, and we show why a natural argument for it fails. The counterexample instance is not ours, and no claim is made about priority or attribution. Source code, data and computational records: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH (problems/optimization-geometry/unsplittable-flow-cost).
title: An independent exact verification of the 2026 counterexample to Goemans' unsplittable-flow cost conjecture, with the violation constant it forces

Title Quality-controlled gradient-tower meteorological profiles and derived surface-flux estimates from the Huancayo Geophysical Observatory, Peruvian central Andes Alternative short title HYGO gradient-tower profiles and derived surface-flux dataset Description This dataset contains quality-controlled gradient-tower meteorological profiles, derived thermodynamic variables, and method-dependent surface-flux estimates from the Huancayo Geophysical Observatory (HYGO) of the Instituto Geofísico del Perú. HYGO is located in the Mantaro Valley of the central Peruvian Andes, an area characterized by high elevation, strong diurnal forcing, seasonal moisture contrasts, agricultural land use, and mountain–valley–slope circulations. Native 1-min observations of air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and wind direction were processed using a reproducible workflow that includes timestamp auditing, pre-deployment sensor harmonization, conservative bit-mask quality control, thermodynamic derivation, 30-min aggregation, flux-specific pre-calculation screening, independent MOST and BRN_ANC calculations, method-status diagnostics, defensive post-calculation checks, applicability diagnostics, and sensitivity analyses. The quality-controlled multi-level meteorological profiles are the primary observational product. The surface-flux variables are derived, method-dependent estimates and should not be interpreted as direct eddy-covariance measurements or as independently validated absolute flux observations. Dataset period 15 May 2018 to 31 July 2026 The released L2 time coordinate extends from 15 May 2018 at 19:00 UTC to 1 August 2026 at 04:59 UTC, corresponding to the local observational period ending at 23:59 on 31 July 2026 in America/Lima (UTC−5). Geographic coverage Huancayo Geophysical Observatory, Mantaro Valley, central Peruvian Andes, Peru Latitude: −12.04145° Longitude: −75.31875° Elevation: 3315 m above sea level Measurement heights Meteorological profile levels used for the flux-gradient calculations: 2 m AGL 6 m AGL 12 m AGL 24 m AGL Wind-direction monitoring levels: 18 m AGL: source channel dir_wind_01 29 m AGL: source channel dir_wind_02 The 18 and 29 m direction measurements are used to diagnose vertical wind turning and directional shear. They are not treated as additional scalar-profile levels in the MOST or BRN_ANC calculations. Temporal resolution 1 min for the quality-controlled meteorological profiles. 1 min for the corresponding high-frequency derived flux estimates. 30 min for aggregated profiles, availability statistics, MOST and BRN_ANC flux estimates, applicability diagnostics, and sensitivity products. Time conventions The L2 quality-controlled profile NetCDF uses a UTC time coordinate. The current L3 1-min and 30-min flux products retain local wall-clock timestamps and declare America/Lima (UTC−5) in the time-coordinate metadata. Users combining L2 and L3 products must convert timestamps according to the metadata of each file before matching observations. A timezone-naive decoded timestamp should not automatically be assumed to use the same convention in all products. Main variables Observed meteorological variables Air temperature at 2, 6, 12, and 24 m AGL Relative humidity at 2, 6, 12, and 24 m AGL Wind speed at 2, 6, 12, and 24 m AGL Wind direction at 18 and 29 m AGL Derived thermodynamic variables Atmospheric pressure estimated at the site eleva
title: Data-set of gradient tower for quality-controlled and surface-flux estimations in the Peruvian central Andes

summary: Ontario's Education Act requires every district school board to identify, place, and support students with special education needs, yet the province's own 2026 auditor general special report found that the system does not consistently fulfill that legal obligation. This audit examines Ontario's special education policy architecture, comprising the Education Act, Regulation 181/98, Regulation 306, and the Identification, Placement and Review Committee (IPRC) and Individual Education Plan (IEP) processes, against the lived experience of students, families, and educators who navigate it. Drawing on stakeholder analysis, a PESTEL scan of the policy environment, and a comparative review of the United States' Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) and the United Kingdom's Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) system, the audit finds that Ontario's framework is legally sound in principle but structurally inconsistent in practice: assessment wait times exceeding one year at multiple boards, educational assistant absences left unfilled between roughly half and three-quarters of the time, and individualized education plans that frequently lack measurable goals or documented parent input. The audit does not conclude that Ontario's approach has failed; rather, it finds that the policy's core entitlements are strong but under-resourced and unevenly enforced across the province's 72 district school boards. The United States and United Kingdom experiences are considered as useful points of comparison, not as models for direct replication, and the audit closes with recommendations for standardizing identification timelines, strengthening IEP quality assurance, and improving public accountability for special education outcomes across Ontario.
title: Equitable Access to Special Education in Ontario: A Policy and Equity Audit of Programs and Services

summary: Artifact of the IEEE S&P 2027 paper "Quiet Triggers, Loud Footprints: A Tri-Space Measurement Study of Backdoor Stealthiness". Code: backdoor-stealthiness-sp2027-artifact.tar.gz is a complete source tree (measurement library with the sixteen input-, feature- and parameter-space footprint metrics, record loaders, the per-record evaluation driver, table-regeneration scripts, defenses, derived analyses with their per-configuration results, setup and data-download scripts) with the five attack implementations included; README.md, setup.sh and the claim scripts are also attached individually for reference. The code is released under the MIT license (LICENSE inside the archive). Data: the backdoored image classifiers (ResNet18 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Imagenette; a VGG16 subset) with their poisoned training and test data (record.tar), the saved penultimate-layer features, test predictions, activation differences and t-SNE embeddings the footprint metrics were computed from, the datasets in the layout the code expects (data.tar), and the retrained replicates used in the robustness analyses (record_seeds, record_targets, record_reruns, vgg_records); scripts/download_data.py in the archive fetches and verifies every tarball. Development continues in the linked GitHub repository.
title: Quiet Triggers, Loud Footprints: A Tri-Space Measurement Study of Backdoor Stealthiness -- code and data

summary: Cyber threats directed against space systems (spanning orbital payloads, tracking and telemetry ground stations, downlinks, and upstream manufacturing supply chains) have evolved into acute operational hazards. Concurrently, national security and commercial defenders face an intelligence volume crisis where telemetry and vulnerability disclosures outpace human cognitive bandwidth. While autonomous multi-agent pipelines powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) offer scalable automation, they introduce severe epistemic liabilities: hallucination, source detachment, uncalibrated certainty, and susceptibility to indirect prompt injection. This paper presents Space-Cyber Brief Crew, a multi-agent cyber threat intelligence (CTI) architecture that automates space-domain intelligence synthesis under an explicit governance layer. Built on a decoupled CrewAI orchestration, the system routes structured reporting through a three-stage sequential pipeline (Collector, Analyst, Writer) governed by ten operational rules. Crucially, the architecture establishes a structural boundary between action capabilities and generative synthesis: downstream analysis agents operate in zero-tool sandboxes, restricting the execution attack surface by construction. We evaluate the framework against a tri-domain threat corpus spanning satellite imagery manipulation, ground industrial control systems (ICS), and global navigation satellite system (GNSS) spoofing. In our evaluation, the governed architecture eliminated identifier fabrication (from 23.3% to 0.0%), preserved 100% provenance retention, and neutralized indirect prompt injection attacks that succeeded in 80% of unconstrained baseline runs. Finally, we examine the institutional, regulatory, and oversight implications, establishing technical criteria for federal procurement and intelligence integration.

summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . Interactive studio: https://tailwatch.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1, descending frame 124D_04854_171313 (2016-2018), redistributed under the Copernicus free-and-open licence with LiCSBAS attribution (Morishita et al. 2020); provenance in data/derived/tw-real-cf.provenance.json.
title: TailWatch: An InSAR Deformation-Monitoring and Inverse-Velocity Failure-Forecasting Studio, on Synthetic Sentinel-1 and Real Campi Flegrei

summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across diverse applications, raising critical questions for governance, accountability, and data provenance. Understanding which training data most influenced a model's output remains a fundamental open problem. We address this challenge through training data attribution (TDA) for auto-regressive LLMs by expanding upon the inverse formulation: How would training data be affected if the model had seen the generated output during training? Our method perturbs the base model using bidirectional gradient optimization (gradient ascent and descent) on a generated text sample and measures the resulting change in loss across training samples. Our framework supports attribution at arbitrary data granularity, enabling both factual and stylistic attribution. We evaluate our method against baselines on pretrained models with known datasets, and show that it outperforms previous work on influence metrics, thereby enhancing model interpretability, an essential requirement for accountable AI systems.
title: Data Attribution in Large Language Models via Bidirectional Gradient Optimization

summary: We present SemRepo, an RDF knowledge graph comprising over 81 million triples describing nearly 200,000 GitHub repositories associated with scientific research. SemRepo captures repository-level metadata, such as contributors, issues, and programming languages, and interlinks this information with external scholarly knowledge graphs. In particular, repository authors are linked to their profiles in SemOpenAlex, repositories are connected to scholarly publications in LPWC, and research artifacts, such as datasets and experiments, are linked via MLSea-KG. This integration enables queries that span publications and their scholarly artifacts, which are typically fragmented across separate platforms. SemRepo supports analyses that are difficult to perform with existing resources in isolation, including provenance reconstruction across repositories and publications, as well as the systematic identification of risks to research reproducibility and software sustainability. By unifying research software with its scholarly context in a single graph, SemRepo provides an important infrastructure for large-scale analysis of software within the broader scientific research ecosystem.
title: SemRepo: A Knowledge Graph for Research Software and Its Scholarly Ecosystem

summary: Handwritten archival tables contain rich historical information, yet transforming them into structured representations, such as Knowledge Graphs, requires integrating table structure recognition, handwriting recognition, and semantic interpretation - a complex multimodal process. End-to-end AI implementations can obscure these steps, resulting in opaque algorithmic operations that hinder human oversight, critical assessment, and trust. To address this, we present a modular, provenance-aware pipeline to convert handwritten tabular images into KGs supporting human-AI collaboration. The pipeline decomposes the workflow into three stages - table reconstruction, information extraction, and KG construction - while exposing intermediate representations for inspection, evaluation, and correction. A key contribution of our approach is the systematic integration of data provenance at every stage, ensuring that all extracted entities and literals remain traceable to their visual and textual origins. The proposed pipeline is demonstrated through a number of experiments on real-world archival material concerning military careers. The results across three different table reconstruction variants highlight the importance of modularisation. By coupling modularity with data provenance, our work advances transparent and collaboratively controllable image-to-KG pipelines for complex historical data.
title: From Historical Tabular Image to Knowledge Graphs: A Provenance-Aware Modular Pipeline

summary: The rise of generative AI has enabled the production of high-fidelity synthetic tabular data across fields such as healthcare, finance, and public policy, raising growing concerns about data provenance and misuse. Watermarking offers a promising solution to address these concerns by ensuring the traceability of synthetic data, but existing methods face many limitations: they are computationally expensive due to reliance on the inverse process of large diffusion models, struggle with mixed discrete-continuous data, or lack robustness to common post-processing attacks. To address these limitations, we propose TAB-DRW, an efficient and robust post-editing watermarking scheme for synthetic tabular data. TAB-DRW embeds watermark signals in the frequency domain: it normalizes heterogeneous features via the Yeo-Johnson transformation and standardization, applies the discrete Fourier transform (DFT), and adjusts the imaginary parts of adaptively selected entries according to precomputed pseudorandom bits. To further enhance robustness and efficiency, we introduce a novel rank-based pseudorandom bit generation method that enables row-wise retrieval without incurring storage overhead. Experiments on five benchmark tabular datasets show that TAB-DRW achieves strong detectability and robustness against post-processing and adaptive attacks, while preserving high data fidelity and fully supporting mixed-type features.
title: Robust Spectral Watermark for Synthetic Tabular Data

summary: This dataset contains the complete computational records from two 500-sequence demonstration runs performed with ENZTRA (Enzyme Redesign and Triage Automation), a reproducible and resumable workflow for reference-guided enzyme redesign. ENZTRA integrates reference preparation, RFdiffusion2 backbone generation, LigandMPNN sequence design, DLKcat and CatPred kinetic prediction, strict kinetic selection, Boltz-2 structural assessment, quality control, provenance tracking, and publication-oriented reporting. Both demonstrations used an active Escherichia coli phytase derived from PDB 1DKP and myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (IHP; phytate) as the reference enzyme-substrate system. Each run generated 50 RFdiffusion2 backbones and 10 LigandMPNN sequences per backbone, yielding 500 candidate sequences. The deposit contains two project archives: release-500: A short-scaffold demonstration using a requested design-length range of 150-180 residues. Fourteen of the 500 candidates satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion and proceeded to Boltz-2 structural assessment. The remaining 486 candidates were rejected, and no data-quality failures were detected. release-500b: A full-length comparison using a requested scaffold length of 410 residues, matching the reference sequence length. All 500 candidates passed the specified data-quality checks, but none satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion because their predicted turnover numbers were below the reference prediction. Consequently, no candidate proceeded to Boltz-2 assessment. The ENZTRA strict kinetic gate requires both a predicted turnover number ( k cat) above the corresponding reference value and a predicted Michaelis constant ( K m) below the reference value. Passing data-quality checks is therefore distinct from passing kinetic selection. The archives include validated biological inputs, design requests, RFdiffusion2 specifications and execution records, generated backbones, TRB and functional-site mappings, LigandMPNN outputs, consolidated sequence files, DLKcat and CatPred inputs and predictions, kinetic and selection tables, Boltz-2 inputs and outputs where applicable, quality-control tables, publication figures, workflow-state records, qualification reports, and reproducibility manifests. These results are computational predictions intended to demonstrate workflow execution, traceability, recovery, candidate selection, and reporting. They do not establish catalytic activity, structural correctness, expression, stability, or experimental improvement. All prioritized candidates require appropriate experimental validation. ENZTRA source code, installation instructions, and a step-by-step reproduction tutorial are available at: https://github.com/Olanrewaju-Durojaye/ENZTRA
title: ENZTRA demonstration dataset: reference-guided phytase redesign and kinetic-structural triage

summary: Reproducibility package for the manuscript: Maintenance-Aware Replica Selection for Deadline-Constrained Distributed Scientific Data Transfers This release contains the complete computational artifact used for the submitted study, including: simulation and analysis code; deterministic random seeds; controlled workload inputs; public SCINet maintenance-event provenance data; raw and processed numerical results; baseline and robustness experiments; exact small-instance oracle comparisons; runtime-scaling results; figure-generation scripts; software requirements; validation scripts; and SHA-256 integrity manifests. The archived results include the 6,000-instance controlled experiment and the 9,000-instance public-maintenance-event-conditioned validation. No proprietary production data are included. Public maintenance records are used only as documented event provenance and outage-duration inputs; workload characteristics remain controlled/synthetic. Authors: Abdulaziz M. D. Aljohani Khaled M. Alhawiti University of Tabuk, Saudi Arabia
title: Maintenance-Aware Replica Selection for Deadline-Constrained Distributed Scientific Data Transfers

summary: A 3D city model is only as accurate as its building heights, and a model built from open data mostly infers those heights, from a mapped floor count, a height raster or a default value, rather than taking them from a mapped height. Maqueta reconstructs real places from open geospatial layers, with terrain from the Copernicus GLO-30 surface model, building footprints and roads from Overture Maps, water, green areas and rail from OpenStreetMap, population from GHS-POP, and building heights from the Google Open Buildings 2.5D raster where it has coverage, and it records for every building how its height was obtained. Across the 118 baked places and 4.05 million buildings, 8.8% of heights come from a mapped height attribute, 6.4% from a mapped floor count, 73.2% from the Open Buildings 2.5D height raster, itself a model estimate from satellite imagery, and 11.6% from a default prior of 8 m. A public LoD2 reference exists for two of the places, both in the Netherlands, where the raster has no coverage. Against the 3D BAG, the fused heights have a root-mean-square error of 3.1 m at Delft, with a bias of -0.1 m, and of 8.3 m at Amsterdam, with a bias of -6.6 m; the Amsterdam figure rests on 50 reference buildings. The raster heights, which supply most of the buildings, are not validated by this benchmark, and public ground truth for open-data building heights is scarce. Interactive tool and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RES_Maqueta . Fusion core: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_GeoScena .
title: Maqueta: Height Provenance in Open-Data 3D Urban Reconstruction Across 118 Places

summary: This deposit contains the analysis code, fitted parameters, output files, audit records, supplements, and citation list supporting the working paper "Power-Law Claims in Production and Supply Networks: What Survives a Uniform Certification Audit" (version 16, September 2026, posted on SSRN) by Bruce Rishel (Independent Scholar, ORCID 0009-0000-8324-4331) and Melissa Rishel (Independent Scholar, ORCID 0009-0001-4919-0728). Melissa Rishel contributed the independent validation of the statistical analysis and the mathematical derivations. The audit applies the Clauset-Shalizi-Newman 2009 maximum-likelihood estimation protocol with semi-parametric bootstrap goodness-of-fit testing and likelihood-ratio tests against alternative distributions, together with the Broido-Clauset 2019 five-category corpus classification, to a verified population of 20 published power-law claims in the supply chain operational literature. Three widely cited datasets are re-analyzed. The manuscript reports four distributions: Acemoglu et al. 2012's sectoral input-output out-degree (BEA 1997 Use Table), Liu, Shen, Tan 2021's international trade product networks in both the out-degree and in-degree directions (BACI HS92 Y2024 current release, 1,217 networks), and Axtell 2001's US firm-size distribution (SUSB 2017, n = 5,996,900 firms via the Virkar-Clauset 2014 binned-data MLE). The Acemoglu influence vector is analyzed separately and treated as exploratory, described under the version note below. The remaining 17 audit targets are characterized at methodology rigor level without independent data re-analysis. Every audit-target citation is verified against its publisher record for title, authors, DOI, and the cited claim text. Contents of the deposit: analysis/: Python implementation of the audit's re-analysis pipeline: BACI parsing and corpus fitting, BEA 1997 Use Table reconstruction, SUSB binned-data MLE via Virkar-Clauset 2014, Vuong likelihood-ratio tests, Broido-Clauset 2019 corpus classification, semi-parametric bootstrap goodness-of-fit, the exploratory influence-vector sensitivity engine, and cross-validation of the Acemoglu first-order out-degree re-analysis against the published Alstott et al. 2014 powerlaw Python library, where fitted exponents and Kolmogorov-Smirnov distances match to four decimal places. The influence-vector exponent reflects that library's default parameter-range cap at 3.0 and is treated as exploratory; the closed-form maximum-likelihood value on the same input lies above 3. outputs/: JSON output files containing per-target fitted parameters, x_min values, KS distances, bootstrap p-values, Vuong test statistics, and corpus aggregate statistics, plus the powerlaw-library cross-validation output and the exploratory influence-vector sensitivity results. audit_records/: per-target audit records for the three re-analyzed datasets (Acemoglu et al. 2012, Liu-Shen-Tan 2021, Axtell 2001), including methodology grade, data acquisition tier, sample sizes, fit details, and audit verdict. audit_targets/: structured audit-target list of all 20 verified entries with author, title, venue, year, DOI, verification status, data tier, methodology rigor level, and re-analysis results. verification_protocol.md: the citation-verification procedure used to assemble the audit population. references.md: the manuscript's numbered reference list. figures/: three figures from the manuscript, the BACI corpus alpha distributions, the Acemoglu d_i CCDF with fitted power law, and the SUSB firm-size CCDF with fitted power law. README.md: file inventory, dependency versions, reproducibility instructions, and citation guidance. CHANGELOG.md: version history of this deposit. LICENSE: MIT License (code), CC-BY 4.0 (documentation). Data sources used by the audit code are public and free: the BEA 1997 detailed Use Table (Bureau of Economic Analysis), the BACI HS92 Y2024 release (CEPII), and the SUSB 2017 US enterprise-size brackets (US Census Bureau). Source URLs

summary: Direct numerical simulation (DNS) dataset of incompressible turbulent flow around a wall-mounted square cylinder, used as the training and evaluation data for Diff-SPORT, a diffusion-based framework for optimal sensor placement and sparse reconstruction of turbulent flows in urban environments (Vishwasrao et al., Nature Communications, in press; preprint arXiv:2506.00214). The simulation was performed with the open-source spectral-element code Nek5000 for an obstacle of width-to-height ratio b/h = 0.25 at a Reynolds number Re_h = 2000 based on the obstacle height h and the free-stream velocity. The computational domain spans -1 <= x/h <= 5, 0 <= y/h <= 2 and -1.5 <= z/h <= 1.5, and the velocity field is interpolated onto a uniform mesh. Snapshots are stored in convective time units with a sampling interval of 0.005. The simulation set-up and validation are documented in Martinez-Sanchez et al., J. Fluid Mech. 967, A1 (2023), https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2023.423. Files: U.mat, V.mat contain the streamwise, vertical velocity components, respectively, for a chunk of the three-dimensional DNS data (MATLAB v7.3 / HDF5 format).
title: DNS dataset of turbulent flow around a wall-mounted square cylinder (Re_h = 2000) for Diff-SPORT: Diffusion-based sensor placement optimization and reconstruction of turbulent flows in urban environments

summary: # FaultNet This archive contains the trained models, example earthquake catalog, and Jupyter notebook used to apply **FaultNet**, a deep-learning framework for reconstructing three-dimensional fault structures from earthquake hypocenters. FaultNet uses two PointNet++-based models followed by agglomerative clustering and fault surface reconstruction by radial basis function. The first model, denoising model, identifies fault-related earthquakes and removes background seismicity. The second model, feature learning model, maps the remaining earthquakes into an embedding space in which earthquakes associated with the same fault have similar representations. Pairwise similarities estimated from overlapping spatial windows are combined into a global distance matrix and used for clustering. The resulting earthquake clusters can then be reconstructed as continuous three-dimensional fault surfaces using radial basis function (RBF) interpolation. ## Files and directories - `apply_FaultNet.ipynb`     Main notebook demonstrating the complete FaultNet inference workflow, including:   1. loading the trained models;   2. loading and visualizing an earthquake catalog;   3. selecting a sliding-window size;   4. identifying fault-related earthquakes;   5. learning feature embedding and agglomerative clustering;   6. reconstructing fault surfaces using RBF interpolation; and   7. evaluating and visualizing the reconstructed surfaces. - `example_catalog.npy`   Example earthquake catalog used in the notebook. The array has shape `(N, 5)`, with columns:   `x, y, z, horizontal_location_error, vertical_location_error`.   Spatial coordinates and location uncertainties should use consistent distance units (km in the provided example).   Users can replace it with another earthquake catalog following the same format. Coordinates and uncertainties should be expressed in a consistent Cartesian coordinate system and distance unit. - `example_prediction.npy`     Example FaultNet clustering output corresponding to `example_catalog.npy`. It contains one integer label per earthquake. A label of `-1` denotes background seismicity or clusters excluded by the minimum-size criterion (50 events); non-negative integers identify reconstructed fault clusters. - `model_I_denoising/`     Trained denoising model for distinguishing fault-related earthquakes from background seismicity. The trained weights used by the notebook are stored in `checkpoints/best_model.pth`. - `model_II_feature_learning/`     Trained feature learning model for generating 8-dimensional embedding representations of fault-related earthquakes. The trained weights used by the notebook are stored in `checkpoints/best_model.pth`. - `Pointnet_Pointnet2_pytorchmaster/`     PointNet++ implementation and supporting source code used by the FaultNet models. This directory is based on a PyTorch implementation of PointNet/PointNet++ and retains its associated license information. - `requirements.txt`     Python packages required by the main FaultNet notebook. ## Installation Python 3 is required. To install the main dependencies, run: ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt ``` The supplied notebook loads the trained neural networks on the CPU by default. PyTorch can be configured separately for CUDA-enabled GPU execution if desired.   ## Citation If you use FaultNet or the materials in this archive, please cite the associated FaultNet publication and this Zenodo record. .. 10.5281/zenodo.22837108 ## Acknowledgments This work was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences (Award No. DE-SC0026319). ## License Please refer to the license information distributed with the relevant source-code components. Before public release, add the license selected for the FaultNet-specific code and trained models to the top-level archive.
title: FaultNet: Inferring Complex Fault Structures from Earthquake Hypocenter Distributions

summary: Overview Ouranos Reconstruction – RDPS-CaPA (ORRC) version 1.0 is a dataset designed to approximate the Canadian Surface Reanalysis (CaSR)  and provide continuity beyond the CaSR period. It is produced from the  Regional Deterministic Prediction System (RDPS) , with precipitation fields adjusted using the 6-hour and 24-hour Regional Deterministic Precipitation Analysis (RDPA)  products generated by the CaPA system. ORRC v1.0 provides hourly surface and near-surface meteorological fields at 0.09° (~10 km) resolution on a rotated regular latitude–longitude grid covering North America, Central America, and nearly all of Greenland, from 2015 to present. It supports near-real-time climate monitoring and is intended for operational climate services, event monitoring, and the routine update of climate indicators without waiting for future CaSR releases. Temporal coverage: 2015-01-01 to near-present Spatial resolution: 0.09° (~10 km) Temporal resolution: Hourly and daily File format: NetCDF  Data provider: Ouranos Version: 1.0 Products Two products are available: ORRC v1.0 : The original hourly and daily meteorological fields. ORRC-a v1.0 : A bias-adjusted daily product available for daily mean precipitation and daily mean, minimum, and maximum near-surface air temperature. ORRC-a v1.0 is adjusted relative to CaSR v3.2 using the 2020–2024 overlap period. Day-of-year mean corrections are calculated using a 31-day moving window. Additive corrections are applied to temperature, and multiplicative corrections are applied to precipitation. ORRC-a is recommended for applications requiring closer consistency with the historical conditions represented by CaSR v3.2. The original ORRC product retains the characteristics of the operational products from which it is constructed and may be preferable when these characteristics are important, when hourly data are required, or for variables for which the bias-adjustment approach is not appropriate.  Variables ORRC v1.0 includes precipitation (CaPA reconstructed and model precipitation), near-surface air temperature, dew point temperature, specific humidity, relative humidity, surface and sea-level pressure, downwelling shortwave and longwave radiation, near-surface wind components, wind speed, and wind direction. A complete table of variable names, units, frequencies, and source identifiers is provided in the accompanying technical documentation . Code, documentation, and data availability The ORRC-ORRC-v1.0.1.zip archive contains a snapshot of the source code and documentation associated with ORRC v1.0. The accompanying technical report describes the input data, processing workflow, precipitation adjustment, bias adjustment, evaluation, and known limitations. The complete ORRC and ORRC-a datasets are hosted separately and can be accessed through the Ouranos THREDDS Data Server . Archived source release: https://github.com/Ouranosinc/ORRC/releases/tag/ORRC-v1.0.1   GitHub repository: https://github.com/Ouranosinc/ORRC Version specific view: https://github.com/Ouranosinc/ORRC/tree/ORRC-v1.0.1
title: Ouranos Reconstruction – RDPS-CaPA (ORRC) v1.0 / Reconstruction Ouranos – RDPS‑CAPA (RORC) v1.0

summary: How can a critical interpretation of geopolitical narratives remain hermeneutically open while becoming explicit enough to be evaluated, contested, compared, and revised? This article develops Geopolitical Hermeneutics of Suspicion (HGS) as a second-order interpretive methodology for that problem. HGS translates philosophical and critical commitments into explicit epistemic obligations, operational criteria, evidence rules, contradiction tests, temporal safeguards, uncertainty registers, and revision procedures. The method comprises a five-phase analytical workflow—deconstruction of foundational dualisms; mapping of discursive production; symptomatic reading; analysis of material and institutional correlates; and multipolar contrast with reflexive review—and places an epistemic control architecture around it. A qualitative Hermeneutic Robustness Matrix records evidentiary convergence across material, discursive, and historical-comparative dimensions while keeping the dimensions analytically distinct. Two contrastive demonstrations, Libya 2011 and Ukraine 2022, show how the protocol constrains inferential moves from correlation to causation, from omission to constitutive silence, and from repetition to independent corroboration. A third demonstration, applying the identical protocol to the contested Anomalous Health Incidents narrative, functions as a disconfirming test case in which the same evidentiary rules yield a Weak classification, showing that the method can register non-confirmation rather than only confirm suspicion. The article argues that the methodological value of HGS lies in making the conditions of interpretation visible, its evidentiary burdens explicit, its vulnerabilities to error diagnosable, and its conclusions revisable.
title: Geopolitical Hermeneutics of Suspicion: An Epistemically Disciplined Method for Interpretive Evaluation

summary: Depression and anxiety among university students have risen alongside problematic social media use, and while traditional interventions are effective, they face barriers to scalability and accessibility. AI-driven chatbots offer a scalable, real-time, anonymous alternative, with recent meta-analyses showing comparable reductions in depressive symptoms relative to standard interventions. This poster presents the protocol for a two-arm, parallel-group randomized controlled non-inferiority trial evaluating whether a Social Media Wellness Chatbot is non-inferior to an active psychoeducational control in reducing depressive symptoms among high-risk university students (PHQ-9 ≥ 10, social media use ≥ 2 hrs/day). Approximately 320 students will be randomized 1:1 to the chatbot (CBT-based exercises, mood tracking, and social media habit coaching, 4-5x/week for 10-15 min/day) or a 6-week online psychoeducational toolkit ("Social Media and Mental Wellness Toolkit"). The primary outcome is change in PHQ-9 score from baseline to 6-week post-test, evaluated against a non-inferiority margin of Δ ≈ 3 points. Secondary outcomes include anxiety (GAD-7), stress (PSS), well-being (WHO-5), and engagement metrics. As this is a study protocol, results are not yet available. If non-inferiority is established, the chatbot's accessibility, scalability, and on-demand availability would support its integration into university mental health services. Presented at the First Annual HCAP (Health, Community, and Policy) Research Forum, University of Texas at San Antonio, April 25, 2025.
title: Social Media Wellness Chatbot for Students: A Randomized Controlled Non-Inferiority Trial Protocol of an AI-Driven Mental Health Intervention in High-Risk University Populations

summary: Replication package for the article "Weaponised Reserves and the Return of Gold: Central Banks, the Triffin Dilemma, and the Political Economy of 'Bretton Woods III'" (submitted to New Political Economy , 2026). The paper examines the post-2022 shift of central bank reserves from US Treasury securities toward monetary gold — the first gold-over-Treasuries crossover since 1996 — combining the Triffin dilemma literature, the weaponised-interdependence framework and the empirical safe-haven literature into a single account of "generalised political-risk hedging". This package reproduces every quantitative element of the paper. It contains: (a) a self-contained Python script implementing the three-factor Shapley decomposition of the 2025 rise in gold's reserve share (price revaluation vs. net purchases vs. FX-denominator growth), with sensitivity analysis and the Treasury-side mechanical-compression calculation; (b) a script that regenerates both figures at 600 dpi; (c) a CSV documenting all 25 quantitative anchors cited in the paper, each with value, period, source and URL (IMF COFER, World Gold Council, European Central Bank, LBMA, ICE, OMFIF, Congressional Budget Office); (d) the central bank net gold purchases series 2010–2025 (World Gold Council, Gold Demand Trends); and (e) the two figures as submitted. No proprietary or confidential data are used: all statistics are from publicly available official and industry sources, as documented in data/stylized_facts_sources.csv . Requirements: Python 3.10+ with numpy and matplotlib. See README.md for instructions. Code is released under the MIT License; text and figures under CC-BY 4.0.
title: Replication package: Weaponised Reserves and the Return of Gold — Central Banks, the Triffin Dilemma, and the Political Economy of 'Bretton Woods III'

summary: A mineral prospectivity map stacks geophysical, geochemical and structural evidence over a study area and outputs, per cell, the probability that a deposit is there. Such maps are typically presented with an area-under-curve (AUC) and a posterior, and both numbers can be inflated in two specific, well-understood ways. ProspectMap is an interactive tool that computes such a map by Weights of Evidence, a Bayesian log-odds update, and makes those two inflations first-class, measuring them rather than hiding them. This report quantifies both on the real US Midcontinent Mississippi-Valley-type zinc-lead belt (the open Critical Minerals Mapping Initiative dataset of Lawley et al., 2022) and on ten synthetic cases. The first inflation is evaluation: reporting AUC under random cross-validation, which lets spatially adjacent cells leak between train and test, overstates prospective skill. On the real belt, with thresholds, weights and prior fitted on the training folds only and every map cell scored, the Weights-of-Evidence AUC falls from 0.74 under random cross-validation to 0.65 under spatial block cross-validation, an inflation of 0.09, the second largest of the eleven cases. Under the same spatial folds a learned classifier reaches 0.91, but a baseline that ranks cells by their distance to the nearest training deposit reaches 0.90, so this protocol does not show that the classifier learned more than proximity to known deposits. The second inflation is modelling: Weights of Evidence assumes the evidence layers are conditionally independent given a deposit, and on the real belt they are not. The posterior probabilities sum to 1124 against 858 deposit cells (omnibus z = 8.3), so the posterior is overconfident. The six layers' contrasts are individually significant (studentized contrasts 2.45 to 5.80; exact one-sided p ≤ 1.9 × 10⁻³), but four of them come from thresholds that leave no deposit outside the pattern, where the weight outside the pattern is set by a zero-count correction. The tool displays the spatial-CV AUC, the conditional-independence test and the per-layer significance beside the inflated values; every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive tool and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_ProspectMap . Interactive tool: https://prospectmap.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: Critical Minerals Mapping Initiative US Mississippi-Valley-type Zn-Pb belt dataset (Lawley et al. 2022, doi:10.1016/j.oregeorev.2021.104635).
title: ProspectMap: The Two Ways a Mineral Prospectivity Map Lies, Quantified on the Real US Mississippi-Valley-Type Belt

summary: This study analyzes the decarbonization trajectories of the Moroccan agri-food industry by 2050 in a context of strengthening climate policies and increasing exposure to the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). A bottom-up  energy optimization model based on OSeMOSYS was developed to evaluate four scenarios: baseline (BAU), deep decarbonization (DO), national strategy (SN) and carbon tax (TC). The results show that an 85% reduction in emissions is technically feasible through the electrification of thermal processes and the massive deployment of high-temperature heat pumps (heat pumps). This transition increases the cost of the system by about 15%, with a marginal abatement cost of €51/tCO₂. The CBAM's prospective analysis indicates a cumulative cost of around €422 million between 2025 and 2050. However, a carbon tax alone does not allow for a profound technological transformation. The success of the transition therefore requires a decarbonization of the electricity system and investment support mechanisms.
title: Modeling the decarbonization trajectories of the Moroccan agri-food industry: a prospective analysis with OSeMOSYS

summary: Benchmark package accompanying the manuscript “Failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems: residual-error decoupling, an attainable-accuracy bound and an identifiability benchmark”. The package contains: the exact solution of the beam–two-mass moving-load benchmark and the modal and RK4 reference baselines on the same grid; the training campaign with random seeds, network configurations, collocation densities, training budgets, measured wall-clock times, residuals and relative-L2 errors for every run; the inverse-problem (speed and load-amplitude) campaign with its identifiability verdict; the weights of the reference physics-informed network; and the scripts that regenerate every figure, table and number of the paper. It supports two results of the paper: the residual–error decoupling for moving singular sources, and the attainable-accuracy bound obtained by fitting the same architecture to the exact solution. All runs are seeded, so the accuracy–cost comparison reported in the paper can be re-derived without retraining.
title: Benchmark package — failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems (v1.0)

summary: Code and experimental evidence supporting Calibrated Residual Tube Projection During Conditional Diffusion Sampling for Thermal Time Series , by Hyojin Park and Jinhong Yang (corresponding author). The release contains the selected B6 checkpoint, original method implementations, exact simulator and score settings, frozen selections, per-context evaluation records, diagnostic analyses, frozen detector coefficients, author-created figures, and a simulator reconstruction fixture. CPU audits verify saved aggregates, paired intervals, event metrics, decision criteria, cohort separation, journal chains, file hashes, and eight reconstructed fit trajectories. The study uses one fixed noiseless two-node thermal simulator and one selected diffusion generator. Repeated correction reduced true-equation residual by 11.07% and 10.53% on two three-stream cohorts, while both failed the original event-preservation and rollback criteria. A separate controlled detector showed lower T2 timing loss with corrected-only than raw-only synthetic training; real-only training retained lower loss. Deterministic ridge regression nearly recovered the simulator response. Original and later evaluation criteria remain distinguished. This is an evidence and code companion, not a self-contained one-command full retraining release. Full generated-trajectory arrays, other adapters' weights, the manuscript, internal authoring files, and AI-Hub source data are excluded. Historical runners retain original paths and execution gates. The measured-battery branch is represented by derived applicability counts only; no real-battery warning efficacy or broad physical generalization is claimed. License scope: original Python source in dt_diffpinn/ and tools/ is MIT; original synthetic data, results, model weights, figures, documentation, and metadata are CC BY 4.0. These licenses apply to their respective file categories. Third-party dependencies and AI-Hub data are not redistributed or relicensed. No journal acceptance or article publication is asserted. title: Calibrated Residual Tube Projection During Conditional Diffusion Sampling for Thermal Time Series — Code and Experimental Evidence

summary: Version 1.1 (2026-09-19). Version 1.0 stated that the English rebuild could not be compared against the published English store, because the cleaning pass behind that store no longer exists as a script. That was wrong: the missing script only prevents reproducing the Japanese/Chinese method, while the old English store and its index were on disk throughout. The comparison is now made, with the control questions generated from the old store's own chunk text — exactly what the old index encoded — over 400 articles sampled by uniform stride from the both-store intersection. Whole corpus, nprobe 128: the old store returns recall@1 19.5, recall@5 33.5, MRR 25.1; v11b returns 39.2, 59.5 and 47.9, a gain of +22.8 MRR while searching a corpus 2.9 times larger. Section 8.4 is new and records how four passes of review let an untested caveat stand. The results of version 1.0 are unchanged. We re-read three Wikipedia retrieval indexes we had published ourselves and had been using in production — English, Japanese and Chinese, FAISS over intfloat/multilingual-e5-large — and found three defects, none of which had ever produced an error message. Chunks were cut by character count in front of a token window, so 13.7 % of the published Japanese chunks and 18.5 % of the Chinese ones ran past the encoder's 512-token limit and lost 21.7 % and 27.0 % of their tokens at embed time. The Kiwix licence footer, 184 characters of English legal text, sat inside 97.1 % of the published Japanese chunks and 92.9 % of the Chinese ones. The index type, IndexIVFPQ(m=64) , returned 45.4–47.1 % of the exact top-10 and cost 7.8 MRR in Japanese and 10.7 in English against exact search. Rebuilding the whole pipeline moved retrieval against the previously published artifact from 26.6 to 43.3 MRR in Japanese and 26.2 to 47.5 in Chinese, on a control question set generated from the old extractor's own output. The components are not separated, and the rebuild is not uniformly better: indexed-article coverage falls in two of three languages. Two results may generalise. Our own first benchmark ranked the defective extractor higher , because it queried by article title, a field the index also stores. And clipping the scalar quantiser's range to the 0.1–99.9 percentile of the residuals rather than their min/max raises top-10 agreement with exact search from 81.6 % to 85.2 % at the same 4 bits per dimension; the first attempt computed the quantiles on raw vectors and made the index substantially worse, because an IVF index encodes residuals. Three rounds of adversarial review are reported at equal prominence with the results. Round one rejected the first rebuild. Round two found sixteen unsupported statements in the draft. Round three found a defect in the release that the first two had both passed — the acceptance script had not been re-run on two of the three shipped indexes after they were re-encoded — and three measurements that round two had itself introduced while correcting other numbers. Scope. This reports what happened to three specific artifacts. It does not claim these defects are common elsewhere. The retrieval numbers come from synthetic questions generated by one local model with no human relevance judgements and no answerability check; the reconstructed standard error of one MRR figure is 2.2–2.9 points. Index-type comparisons were run on pools of 150,000–206,000 vectors, not at the shipped scale of 3–15.6 million. Nothing here is peer reviewed, certified, or independently replicated; every reviewer was a model instance commissioned by the author. AI co-observer disclosure. The forensic measurements, the rebuild, the three review rounds and the drafting were carried out with Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic) as a working instrument under human direction. The registered author is the human author alone.
title: What a Retrieval Index Loses Before Anyone Notices: Three Silent Defects in Three Published Wikipedia Embedding Indexes

summary: This work studies how small perturbations of the Enchan local time-rate field propagate through fine spatial structure in the same field. The problem is motivated by the hard-wall boundary used in a previous Enchan two-route interference study: rather than imposing a primitive material opacity or an S=0 wall, the present work asks whether finite structure in the Enchan field itself can generate scale-selective transmission and reflection. Starting from the reduced finite-tension branch S_tt = div[mu(D) grad S] - S with mu(D) = 1/(1 + D^(3/2)), the field is decomposed as a structured background plus a small propagating perturbation. Stage A uses a predeclared one-dimensional frozen structured background and compares it with a matched smooth/homogenized control. The response is banded rather than a monotonic low-pass: long-scale perturbations remain comparatively transmissive while strong reflection bands appear when the perturbation resolves the fine structure. At ka = 2 the mean Stage-A structured transmission is approximately 6.25e-4 while the smooth control remains approximately 0.989; at ka = 4 the structured transmission is approximately 1.07e-14 while the smooth control remains approximately 0.962. Stage B replaces the hand-constructed surrogate with three previously frozen source-free Enchan final states from the published localized-field study. The source files are SHA-256 checked against the original run manifest before analysis. All three source profiles remain within the declared positive longitudinal branch and reproduce a scale-dependent structured-versus-smooth transmission difference. The largest Stage-B mean differences occur near ka = 1.0 and 1.5, where structured transmission is approximately 0.330 and 0.358 while the smooth controls remain approximately 0.994 and 0.988. The maximum Stage-B conservation residual is approximately 1.89e-15. Stage C extends the test to a full three-dimensional propagation study using the same three previously frozen source-free Enchan field configurations. A total of 54 cases were evaluated across structured, smooth, and vacuum controls, three selected spatial scales, and both normal and 30° oblique incidence. The scale-dependent scattering observed in the one-dimensional diagnostics persists in three dimensions. Structured backgrounds show reduced forward transmission together with increased reflection and lateral scattering relative to the matched controls. At ka = 4 under normal incidence, the mean structured transmission is approximately 0.486, compared with approximately 0.527 for the smooth control and 0.532 for vacuum. The maximum three-dimensional energy-accounting residual remains below 1.2% across all 54 cases. The result supports a model-level statement: fine S-field structure can act as a wavelength-selective barrier for small time-rate perturbations within the declared linearized Enchan branch. It does not identify ordinary matter with the tested surrogate or source-free structures, does not claim monotonic high-frequency blocking, and does not claim that a macroscopic material wall has been reconstructed. The Zenodo deposit contains the Version 1.1 manuscript PDF together with the complete reproducibility package for Stages A, B, and C, including the frozen numerical code, Stage-C configuration, archived source states, full numerical results, summary tables, execution manifest, README, LICENSE, and SHA-256 integrity records. The manuscript PDF is generated directly from the final Version 1.1 TeX source and is set as the default Zenodo preview. Version 1.1 update: Version 1.1 adds the completed Stage-C three-dimensional validation, updates the manuscript and reproducibility package accordingly, and preserves the Stage-A and Stage-B results unchanged. title: Scale-Selective Propagation of Time-Rate Waves Through Fine Structure in the Enchan Field

summary: Replication package for the paper 'Immaterial Apart, Material Together: Statement-Level Disclosure Regulation under Cheap Machine Aggregation'. The archive carries the event list and every logged score: the four scoring models on the main sample, the re-identification probe, the entity-masked and name-only arms, the post-cutoff holdout, and the frozen same-batch collection. summary: Interstellar communication is not merely slow. It is strategically stale. A message received across distance reports a sender that may no longer occupy the same strategic state, while replies and irreversible actions are chosen on different local clocks. This paper develops a delayed Bayesian interaction game in which each civilisation’s benign or hostile state evolves as a continuous-time Markov chain. An exact filtering equation separates source-time inference from predictive ageing during light-speed transit. Strategic temporal opacity is defined as the loss of discriminatory power between past benign and hostile states; for the two-state process it equals 1 - exp[-( α + β ) a ]. The model derives posterior floors and ceilings, a finite assurance horizon beyond which even perfect benign evidence cannot prevent pre-emption, a warning horizon beyond which hostile evidence becomes obsolete, and a signal-specific decision-reversal time. A two-way query is valued exactly with a Markov-modulated hostile hazard and becomes irrational beyond a critical delay. Asynchronous decision clocks generate a closed-form probability of crossed irreversible actions before either side can observe the other’s commitment. Numerical illustrations show that distance can destroy reassurance, erase warning and increase reciprocal commitment even without increasing intrinsic hostility. Cosmic silence and pre-emption are therefore conditional consequences of causal delay, state volatility, offensive feasibility and decision tempo.
title: Strategic Temporal Opacity in Interstellar Interaction: Light-Speed Delay, Outdated Beliefs and Asynchronous Action in a Bayesian Game
