summary: Code, result tables, and figures for a two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) study in which instruments for coronary artery disease (CAD) were filtered by colocalization (coloc.abf, PPH4 ≥ 0.8) with brain cell-type-specific cis-eQTLs from single-nucleus transcriptomics of human cortex (Bryois et al., Nature Genetics 2022). Of 274 CAD lead loci, 32 colocalized with brain-cell eQTLs, yielding 32 cell-annotated instruments (excitatory neurons 12, pericytes 7 after palindrome exclusion, oligodendrocytes 5, astrocytes 3, microglia 2, inhibitory neurons 1, OPC 1) explaining 3.4–5.6% of CAD liability on the liability scale. Random-effects inverse-variance weighted estimates (with weighted median, MR-Egger, leave-one-out, Cochran's Q and I², MR-PRESSO-analog global permutation, outlier correction, and MR-Steiger sensitivity analyses) are provided for ischemic stroke (OR 1.335, 95% CI 1.189–1.498, p = 1.0e-6), any stroke (OR 1.309, p = 8.5e-7), Alzheimer's disease (proxy-inclusive, and a clinically diagnosed replication arm), and major depression (null negative control). Cell-type-stratified analyses attribute the stroke effect to neuronal and neurovascular-unit (pericyte) expression programs. Contents: full analysis pipeline (R 4.6 / Python 3.13), all derived result tables (instruments, colocalization posteriors, harmonized exposure–outcome pairs, primary and stratified MR, leave-one-out, Steiger), publication figures (SVG/PDF vector plus ≥300 dpi PNG), the manuscript (v1.7), supplementary tables S1–S8, and the completed STROBE-MR checklist. Raw GWAS summary statistics are not redistributed; all sources are public (GWAS Catalog accessions GCST90132315, GCST006908, GCST006906, GCST90027158, GCST007511, GCST005839; eQTL record 10.5281/zenodo.7276971) and every number needed to reproduce the tables and figures is included.
title: Cell-type-stratified Mendelian randomization implicates neuronal and neurovascular expression programs in the causal effect of coronary artery disease on stroke: analysis code, result tables, and figures

summary: Within the Complementarity-First and Reciprocal Internal Complementarity research program, we study the linear perturbations of the smooth massive magnetic core constructed in the companion paper. The host is a supplied flat-space SU(2) Yang–Mills theory with one adjoint scalar, unit magnetic degree, and equal scalar and vector masses. The action and physical scales are not derived from reciprocity. Starting from the full Cartesian second variation and linear Gauss constraint, we organize the physical angular sectors without excluding translations, boundary phase, or neutral radiation. A positive whole-half-line comparison gives a 4/25 lower bound in the two-profile magnetic radial sector. The separate spherical electric-flux operator has a positive but unquantified gap after charge and boundary data are separated. Explicit first-nonradial matrices, a compact-annulus Schur reduction, symbolic-angular-momentum higher matrices, and rational core certificates give all-angular nonnegativity conditional on the stated background and sufficient certificate predicates. The framed kernel consists of three translations and one phase tangent. In a covariant derivative-and-mass completion, a compact-remainder argument gives coercivity modulo this collective space with an unquantified positive constant. The kinetic wave operator nevertheless has essential spectrum [0,∞): exactly Gauss-dressed photon packets retain the zero threshold. An exact translation–photon overlap constructs fields orthogonal to the full kernel in L2 whose energy tends to zero while their local core tends to a nonzero translation. Thus energy-space or local-moment projection, not ordinary L2 orthogonality, is required for the stated coercivity. The result is a conditional linear sign, kernel, and norm-control theorem, not nonlinear orbital stability, decay, a numerical mode spectrum, or a monopole population prediction.

summary: Topic models, in particular Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), have been adapted to hyperspectral imagery (HSI) as a route to interpretable spectral mixtures: each spectral unit (canonically a pixel) becomes a document of quantised band-frequency tokens and the inferred topic-word distributions act as non-negative basis spectra. Yet the dominant evaluation criterion remains downstream classification accuracy, an accuracy-only view that is silent on whether the basis is reproducible, band-robust, calibrated, or actually outperforms standard linear baselines. We propose and instantiate a twelve-axis evaluation framework for LDA-style topic models on HSI that quantifies, on the same set of benchmarks: (F-1) classification macro-F1 compared across five method families (paired differences and a hierarchical Bayesian model), (F-2) topic-word coherence (c_v, c_NPMI, U-Mass), (F-3) seed stability for both LDA and two neural variants (ProdLDA, ETM), (F-4) capacity sensitivity across K in {4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16}, (F-5) band-mask robustness, (F-6) cross-method clustering agreement (LDA vs Felzenszwalb, SLIC, patches, pixels), (F-7) topic-label coupling via P(L | t) entropy and KL, (F-8) per-topic Hungarian-aligned identity tracking, (F-9) HIDSAG cross-preprocessing stability, (F-10) cross-scene topic transfer, (F-11) rate-distortion of the topic representation, and (F-12) external alignment of the topics with a spectral library and a method-rank cross-comparison. We apply the framework to six standard HSI benchmarks (Indian Pines, Salinas, Salinas-A, Pavia University, Kennedy Space Center, Botswana) and five subsets of the HIDSAG mineralogical database (GEOMET, MINERAL1, MINERAL2, GEOCHEM, PORPHYRY). The framework yields three findings that the accuracy-only view does not surface. First, on the labelled scenes the topic-routed soft classifier, which routes the raw spectrum to per-topic logistic experts, matches the raw-spectrum logistic baseline in macro-F1 (0.915 against 0.910, a paired difference of 0.005), while a logistic regression on the topic proportions theta alone trails the baseline by 0.325: the topics add an interpretable routing to the raw spectrum but do not replace it. Second, on Salinas-A under the SWIR-only band mask the paired ARI between canonical and masked dominant-topic maps reaches 0.766, while on Kennedy Space Center under every mask, and on Botswana under the SWIR mask, the same paired ARI collapses to approximately 0.01, separating scenes on which an interpretability claim is band-robust from scenes on which it is not. Third, the theta-only deficit holds on HIDSAG: over its nineteen mineralogical targets the topic-logistic classifier trails raw-logistic by 0.268 macro-F1 (lower on 18 of 19 targets), contrary to the prima-facie expectation that mineralogical mixtures favour topic decomposition over the raw spectrum. We release 3895 deterministic derived artefacts (449 MB), the builder source, the FastAPI backend, the React frontend, and a 109-endpoint test harness as a public, MIT-licensed reproducibility package. Code and derived artefacts: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_LDA_HSI . Interactive web application: https://lda-hsi.fasl-work.com . Manuscript sources: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_LDA_HSI_Paper . Funding: The Advanced Mining Technology Center (AMTC) Basal project (ANID/PIA Project AFB220002) and ANID FONDECYT Postdoctorado 3220094.
title: Beyond Accuracy: A Multi-Axis Evaluation Framework for Interpretable Topic Models on Hyperspectral Imagery

summary: The COVID-19 pandemic altered human mobility and natural-resource management, potentially affecting wildlife in rural landscapes where conservation and livestock production coexist. This work evaluated temporal variation in mammal detections in the Bienes Comunales Santa Cruz Nuevo Wildlife Management Unit, Puebla, Mexico, using camera-trap data from two pre-pandemic surveys (2018 and 2019) and a post-restriction survey (2022). Sampling comprised 39 station-years and 3,193.31 effective camera-days. The work compared encounter rates, station-level occurrence, and observed and estimated species richness among years, and also examined associations between wild mammals, domestic animals, human activity, altitude, and vegetation attributes. Species richness varied substantially among years: 14 species were recorded in 2018, nine in 2019, and 11 in 2022. Chao2 estimates and station-based rarefaction supported this interannual variability rather than a consistent directional change. Gray fox ( Urocyon cinereoargenteus ) detections declined significantly during the post-restriction survey relative to the pre-pandemic baseline (rate ratio = 0.280, 95% CI = 0.129–0.604, FDR-adjusted q = 0.025). Other species showed uncertain or non-estimable temporal effects because of sparse detections or complete zeros. Raccoon detections were negatively associated with altitude, whereas gray fox and coyote detections were associated with livestock occurrence. These findings demonstrate species-specific temporal responses and emphasize that nondetection or nonsignificant results do not necessarily indicate ecological stability. Although the observed changes coincided with the COVID-19 period, they cannot be attributed exclusively to pandemic restrictions because the year also represented climatic, ecological, and management variation.
title: Fauna–Vegetation correlations and relative abundance in a fragmented landscape of Southwest Mexico: Pre- and Post-COVID-19 analysis

summary: MATLAB implementation, per-item numeric results and figure code for the study "Dissociating Prompt Quality from Response Compliance in Automated Prompt-Engineering Assessment". A four-agent evaluator running on a locally hosted Qwen 2.5-7B-Instruct judge scores each prompt as an artifact before any response exists, then scores the resulting response twice on identical items: once against criteria extracted from that prompt, and once against a fixed rubric that never sees it. Verifiable constraints are checked with the IFEval reference implementation rather than model-generated labels. The whole pipeline runs on consumer CPU hardware with no external API calls. Contents: src/ the MATLAB agents and run scripts; scripts/ the IFEval verifier and the figure code; data/ a SHA-256 manifest of all 4,275 benchmark prompts and the filtered IFEval subset; results/ per-item results for the main run (n = 500) and the ablation (n = 120), the construct-validation output and the IFEval verification output. Corpus not redistributed. No prompt or response text from LMSYS-Chat-1M or WildChat-1M is included; the LMSYS agreement prohibits transfer to third parties and WildChat-1M carries flow-down obligations under the AI2 ImpACT licence. Prompts appear only as SHA-256 hashes, so an independently rebuilt corpus can be verified as identical to the one used here. The IFEval subset is included in full under Apache-2.0.
title: Dissociating Prompt Quality from Response Compliance in Automated Prompt-Engineering Assessment: evaluator, results and figure code

summary: Extended reasoning can increase response time and computational cost without improving an answer. Models may revisit unproductive steps or build further reasoning on an earlier mistake. This study evaluates whether Jev, a probabilistic decision maker, can provide an inexpensive error signal to help decide when additional reasoning is needed. We compare Jev with GPT-5.6 Luna on generated ordering and logic-grid puzzles and on the official released ZebraLogic test set. The generated questions are four-choice items with one correct answer among four. The official test set is used open-ended: Luna produces the full grid, Jev checks it without the solution key, and Luna may revise once when Jev does not judge the answer consistent. On the generated multiple-choice problems, Jev is 5 to 60 percentage points more accurate than Luna with reasoning disabled, at lower measured API cost, and every observed top-choice disagreement identifies a Luna error. On a stratified sample of 200 official ZebraLogic puzzles, exact-grid accuracy rises from 41.0% with reasoning disabled to 90.5% with high-effort reasoning. A revision pass adds two points in both settings, but a revision-only control shows the gain comes from the extra attempt, not from Jev's information: on the answers Jev flags, a plain second look is at least as accurate as the Jev-informed revision (16 versus 13 correct without reasoning, and 70 versus 70 at high effort). Jev detects 93% of the weak reasoner's errors with 92% precision, but only 10% of its high-effort flags identify errors. These results motivate using Jev or similar decision models in a model harness: software that controls when to continue, reconsider, retrieve evidence, or allocate more reasoning. An early check could help avoid spending further computation on a mistaken line of reasoning. The experiments measure checking of final answers, however, and do not measure reductions in hallucination or repetitive reasoning inside a harness. On the official benchmark, extra reasoning accounts for most of the accuracy, and the checker's information does not improve on a second attempt. Larger studies with balanced answer positions, selective triggers, and step-level feedback are needed to test whether checking improves accuracy or reduces total cost.
title: Evaluating Jev for Cost-Effective Candidate Verification: An Exploratory Study

summary: The complete evidentiary record behind a study of nine public support instruments for carbon capture in the United States and Canada, 2005 to 2026. It includes the instrument table; a census of twenty-eight capture projects; a provenance table of 131 entries giving the document, identifier, access date and clause relied upon for every fact, each with a basis code; a register of twenty-four scoped negatives recording what was searched, over what universe, and what document would overturn the finding; the money tables; comparator tables covering geothermal support and three jurisdictions that condition public money on delivered outcome; and a disclosure table recording what delivered tonnage each project publishes. The outcome coding materials are deposited in full, comprising the frozen instructions, the evidence pack issued to coders, the worked example, the blank sheet, both coders' completed returns and the calculator that produces the reliability figures. A fact-to-record audit traces every figure and quotation in the associated article to the row it came from. Deposited so that any claim in the article can be reproduced or contested.

summary: This dataset provides a curated and reproducible compilation of data used to analyze long-term trends in external-cause mortality in Ecuador from 1990 through 2024. The primary data sources are official mortality statistics and population estimates and projections published by Ecuador’s National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censos, INEC). The dataset includes annual mortality counts and population-based indicators for major external-cause categories, including land transport injuries, other transport accidents and accidental injuries, suicide, homicide, events of undetermined intent, and other external causes. Where available, the data are organized by calendar year, sex, age or age group, geographic unit, ICD classification, and cause of death. Population denominators, crude mortality rates, confidence intervals, absolute and relative changes, mortality composition measures, sex-specific rate ratios, and variables used in the statistical analyses are documented separately from the original source data. The repository also contains information used to support the reproducibility of the associated scientific study, including analytical datasets, variable definitions, ICD harmonization information, population denominators, model-related variables, sensitivity-analysis data, quality-control documentation, data provenance, and records of differences identified between historical editions of INEC statistical tables. Hospital discharge datasets reviewed during data curation are documented at the variable and source level. Individual-level hospital discharge microdata are not included in the public dissemination package when their inclusion could create unnecessary privacy or re-identification risks. Original source information is kept distinct from derived variables and researcher-calculated indicators to preserve full provenance and auditability. The package follows FAIR data principles and includes machine-readable CSV files together with the original curated Excel database, a data dictionary, methodology documentation, provenance and transformation records, quality-control information, ethics and privacy considerations, citation metadata, licensing information, and version history. No missing values were imputed solely for publication, and no undocumented assumptions were used to generate unavailable data. Values for recent years should be interpreted according to the provisional or revised status indicated by the original INEC sources. This dataset is intended to support reproducibility, secondary epidemiological analyses, public health surveillance, methodological review, and research on injuries, violence, suicide, homicide, road traffic mortality, and other external causes of death in Ecuador.
title: Ecuador External-Cause Mortality, Population Denominators, and Reproducibility Dataset, 1990–2024

summary: This dataset provides source records, recalculated supplementary tables, and reduced principal component analyses for woody crown hydraulic networks (WCHNs) from Caatinga and Cerrado vegetation in Brazil. It accompanies a critical review of the WCHN framework but is documented so that the dataset can be understood and reused independently of that manuscript. The deposit contains 13 files: three source spreadsheets, six recalculated or additional supplementary tables, one analytical PCA workbook, two PCA figures, and a comprehensive README. The source spreadsheets comprise 14 individuals of Cenostigma pyramidale classified into three WCHN size classes; ten additional Caatinga species represented by one WCHN each; and 15 Cerrado species represented by five WCHNs per species, totaling 75 networks. These spreadsheets preserve the WCHN diagrams, decomposition and topology records, original equations, and property values used in the source study. The supplementary tables recalculate symmetry (SYM), complexity (COM), and vulnerability (VUL) using revised equations. Revised SYM is expressed as the inverse coefficient of variation of IN–FN topological distances, SYM = 1/CV = μ/σ. Revised COM is COM = ΣNO × CV, making explicit the identity COM × SYM = ΣNO. Revised VUL excludes the initial node from the attackable set while preserving it as the root of the network, giving an attackable set of ΣNO − 1 nodes. Results are provided for C. pyramidale size classes, Caatinga species, Cerrado species, and phenological groups, as well as a comparison between Caatinga and Cerrado vegetation. The deposit also includes recalculated PERMANOVAs for the deciduous, semideciduous, and evergreen Cerrado groups. For recalculated property blocks, the analyses use species means, Bray–Curtis distances, and an exact enumeration of all 252 possible allocations of five species to each of two groups. An additional reduced-set PERMANOVA excludes the algebraically dependent properties COM and SHA. The DE–EV contrast was consistently the strongest pairwise differentiation, although its significance after correction for multiple comparisons depended on the property set analyzed. Separate reduced PCAs were performed for Caatinga and Cerrado using NAV, revised VUL, LAT, BAS, and PTP, without prior transformation and based on correlation matrices. The Caatinga analysis contains 24 WCHNs representing 11 species; its first two axes explain 91.1% of the total variance. The primary Cerrado analysis contains 74 complete cases from 15 species and excludes one network with an undefined BAS value; its first two axes explain 89.0% of the variance. A sensitivity analysis retaining all 75 Cerrado WCHNs by substituting the column mean for the single undefined BAS value produced essentially the same ordination structure. In both vegetation types, PC1 contrasts vulnerability with navigability, basitony, and potential topological plasticity, whereas PC2 is dominated by laterality. These convergent ordination structures identify two complementary dimensions of WCHN organization but describe covariance rather than causal relationships. The recalculated tables and reduced PCAs assess the topological component of the WCHN framework. They do not directly measure crown hydraulic resistance, xylem P₅₀, hydraulic safety margins, or causal effects on attained tree height. The dataset therefore provides comparative topological evidence and tests the framework’s internal structure, rather than fully validating hydraulic function mechanistically. The original analyses and table numbering are reported in Prado and Trovão (2023), Ecological Modelling , 481, 110345, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2023.110345 . Related stochastic WCHN data and computational experiments are available separately at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21839645 .
title: Recalculated woody crown hydraulic network properties and reduced principal component analyses of Caatinga and Cerrado trees

summary: We are pleased to announce the release of ASPECT 3.1.0. ASPECT is the Advanced Solver for Planetary Evolution, Convection, and Tectonics. It uses modern numerical methods such as adaptive mesh refinement, multigrid solvers, and a modular software design to provide a fast, flexible, and extensible mantle convection solver. ASPECT is available from                    https://aspect.geodynamics.org/ and the release is available from         https://geodynamics.org/resources/aspect and         https://github.com/geodynamics/aspect/releases/tag/v3.1.0 Among others this release includes the following significant changes: - Support for modeling surface deformation has been significantly   extended. Fastscape erodibility can now vary in space and time according to   climate and sea level data, checkpointing functionality has been improved,   tangential boundary velocities along deformed boundaries are more accurate,   and support for initially deformed boundaries has been improved. Preliminary   coupling to the landscape evolution library Landlab is available as well.   (Liang Xue, Derek Neuharth, Michael Pons, Daniel Douglas, Zhibin Lei, Anne    Glerum, Ninghui Tian, Bob Myhill, Rene Gassmoeller, Timo Heister, Wolfgang    Bangerth) - Modeling crystal-preferred orientation and anisotropic viscosity has been   significantly improved. New slip systems for olivine and clinopyroxene have   been added and benchmarked against lab results, a cookbook for CPO-induced   anisotropy has been added, checkpointing of CPO has been improved.   (Xiaochuan Tian, Yijun Wang, Theo Haeussler, Agnes Kiraly, Daniel Douglas,    Menno Fraters) - There is a new plugin system for prescribed dilation and a plugin system that   allows prescribing solution values in parts of the model domain.   (Alexandr Dizov, Haoyuan Li) - A new composition type is available which is used to keep track of the state   of reactions, for example in models considering reaction kinetics. A cookbook   illustrating reaction kinetics was added.   (Haoyuan Li, Buchanan Kerswell) - The entropy method now supports multiple chemical compositions.   (Ranpeng Li, Juliane Dannberg, Rene Gassmoeller, Bob Myhill) - Different particle managers can now have different postprocessing output   intervals and formats. Particle managers are now created if particles are   used to advect compositional fields, even if the particles postprocessor is not   active. There is now an option to advect different particle sets with solid or   fluid velocities.   (Anne Glerum, Francesco Radica, Arijit Chakraborty) - Robin boundary conditions are now available for the temperature field, which   allow prescribing a linear combination of a prescribed temperature and a   prescribed heat flux.   (Juliane Dannberg) - ASPECT now has a gravity plugin and a heating plugin considering tidal   forces. This is useful for modeling moons orbiting a large planet.   (Hyunseong Kim, Antoniette Greta Grima, Wolfgang Bangerth) - Visco-elasticity and visco-elasto-plasticity have been updated to more   accurately track elastic stresses over time. Elasticity can now be combined   with two-phase melt transport.   (Anne Glerum, Robert Myhill, Rene Gassmoeller, Juliane Dannberg, John    Naliboff, Gerry Puckett, Esther Heckenbach, Ryan Stoner) - Checkpointing can now also be requested at specific model times. Parameters   have been added to configure how many checkpoints to keep, restart from a   specific checkpoint, or restart from the checkpoint whose time is closest to   a specified model time. The checkpoint file structure has been improved.   (Anne Glerum, Ninghui Tian, Timo Heister) - The geometric multigrid (GMG) Stokes solvers no longer requir
title: ASPECT v3.1.0

summary: This technical note investigates whether operator-relative noncentrality can predict the relative empirical power of complementary localized scan statistics in correlated spectra. The motivating real-data benchmark compares BABAR and BESIII measurements of the e⁺e⁻ → π⁺π⁻ cross section in the ρ-resonance region on a common 5 MeV grid from 0.600 to 0.880 GeV. The real-data comparison remains negative, with no statistically supported localized shape tension identified. The methodological study compares a coherent-yield scan with a covariance-profiled shape scan and defines the frozen coordinate Θ = log(ES/EY), where ES and EY represent maximum local operator-accessible signal strengths. An archival confirmatory replication used 50,000 null calibration draws per covariance environment, 15,000 independent null-validation draws per environment, 1,440 signal/covariance conditions, and 576,000 injected pseudoexperiments. Θ predicted which scan had greater empirical power with pooled AUC 0.9820 and mean leave-one-covariance-environment-out AUC 0.9740; its correlation with the empirical power difference was 0.9185. Independent Type-I error estimates ranged from 0.0466 to 0.0540. The results support operator-relative noncentrality as a useful empirical coordinate for complementary globally calibrated scans within the tested benchmark. The underlying ingredients, including Gaussian noncentrality, covariance-weighted subspace detection, quadratic scanning, and Monte Carlo calibration, are established; the contribution is a reproducible computational synthesis and controlled characterization rather than a claim of a new general statistical law
title: Operator-Relative Noncentrality in Localized Correlated-Spectrum Scans: A BABAR–BESIII Benchmark

summary: Derived tables and provenance registries supporting source-resolved mass absorption efficiency (MAE) estimates for wintertime brown carbon from residential solid-fuel and fossil-fuel combustion across European and Chinese sites. Contents: (i) source-resolved MAE estimates for the European station pairs and six Chinese cities with block-bootstrap percentile intervals and trustworthiness grading; (ii) station metadata and the field-level verification status of the Chinese records; (iii) per-dataset variable-group coverage tables and sensitivity analyses; (iv) the 84-field variable dictionary of the harmonized master table; (v) per-dataset provenance registries recording authoritative archives, citations and access routes, including a per-file DOI registry for the EBAS absorption compilation; (vi) the evidence tables underlying the Supporting Information (spectral benchmarks, coverage analyses, validation tables, perturbation domains, and the literature-coordinate conversion audit); (vii) an integrity baseline of file checksums for independent verification. Primary hourly records are not redistributed and are available from the original archives identified in the provenance registry or from the authors on request. The harmonized master table itself is not included. Earlier versions and superseded analyses are documented in the version history; the current release is the curated final set. v1.7.1 (2026-09-20) : second external-review round. Adds the unified source-omission comparison (all arms on shared hours, shared outer folds and a 24 h training-test gap; free-880 nm covariate arms; Rovira et al. (2026) direct transfer and fold-calibrated bulk benchmarks with no cross-unit merging), the paired conditional intervals, the AAE sensitivity on fixed common hours, the Harbin 1,543 h canonical interval, the machine-readable SI_Table_S32.csv and the updated figure scripts. See README_v1.7.1_addendum.md inside the archive.
title: Source-resolved brown carbon MAE estimates: derived tables, variable dictionary, and provenance registries

summary: The article “The Image of Istanbul in the Russian Émigré, Soviet, and Modern Russian-Language Literature” explores various facets of the city’s image through the lens of the short stories and essays of the first wave of Russian émigrés’ literature, Soviet literary work of the 1920s-1930s, and contemporary Russian-language Azerbaijani prose. Literary works by Nadezhda Teffi Istanbul and the Sun (1921) and Gaito Gazdanov A Weak Heart (1927) explored in the article, focus on the émigré experience representing two most common ways of depicting Istanbul among the Russian émigré writers. Teffi neither succumbs to Orientalist fantasy nor reduces the city to a refugee misery, she supports both notions and considers Istanbul to be the city of exiles’ humiliation and artistic transcendence, whereas Gazdanov interprets the first center of Russian emigration more clearly and tragically, depicting it as a symbol of life without any moral support. Soviet literature portrays Istanbul in an entirely different manner. During the 1920s-1930s, the description of the East was ideologically justified as it implicitly prepared the ground for developing the internationalist theme of “the friendship of peoples”. Thus, Soviet writers focused mainly on the political, social, and cultural changes which occurred in Turkey during the 1920s, highlighting the country’s transformation from a historical enemy to potential ally. Sweet Salt of the Bosphorus (2008) by a contemporary Azerbaijani author Elchin Safarli who takes into account the artistic experience of Russian émigrés, creates a transcultural space that exhibits the following features of transliterary writing: the author’s specific bilingual linguistic consciousness, the reconstruction of an Azerbaijani worldview through the Russian language, an interlinguistic textual field, the foregrounding of the cultural integration of Russians in the East and an objective reconstruction by the writer, who belongs to the Eastern cultural code, of a “Russian” perspective on the world.
title: Image of Istanbul in the Russian émigré, Soviet, and modern Russian-language literature

summary: This dataset supports the study “UDDPG-Net: Energy- and Fairness-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for Resource Allocation in Underwater Communication Networks.” It contains the simulation data, experimental results, and lake-based acoustic measurement records used for evaluating UDDPG-Net. The simulation data cover underwater acoustic propagation, mobility, interference, energy states, resource-allocation decisions, training configurations, benchmark comparisons with Random, Greedy, PPO, TD3, SAC, MADDPG, and DDPG-GA, as well as scalability, ablation, exploration, SHAP, computational-efficiency, and robustness analyses. The field-test component corresponds to six campaigns conducted in Fengquan Lake, Xinxiang, China, and includes environmental, motion, acoustic-channel, and packet-level variables such as water temperature, salinity, pH, conductivity, sound speed, ambient-noise PSD, link distance, subband SNR, propagation delay, Doppler shift, and packet reception ratio. Reconstructed raw-format field logs are additionally provided to reproduce the organization and statistical characteristics reported in the manuscript; these files are clearly identified as reconstructed records and should not be interpreted as original instrument acquisition files. README files and structured metadata are included to describe the variables, units, experimental conditions, and correspondence between the released data and the figures and tables in the paper.
title: UDDPG-Net: Energy- and Fairness-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for Resource Allocation in Underwater Communication Networks

summary: xinvert v0.3.0 Complete CUDA GPU back-end, a rename pass on the module and public API, and a thread-safe progress reporter. This release also folds in everything that had accumulated since v0.2.0 — v0.2.1 and v0.2.2 were developed but never published, so 0.3.0 is the next version on PyPI after 0.2.0. (Earlier gaps exist in this project too: 0.1.4–0.1.6 were tagged but never released.) Highlights GPU back-end for every equation type architect='gpu' now works for all seven solvers, not just the standard 2-D Poisson case: | equation type | CPU kernel | GPU kernel | | --- | --- | --- | | standard 1D | invert_standard_1D | invert_standard_1D_gpu | | standard 2D | invert_standard_2D | invert_standard_2D_gpu | | standard 2D full (flux form) | invert_standard_2D_full | invert_standard_2D_full_gpu | | standard 3D | invert_standard_3D | invert_standard_3D_gpu | | general 2D | invert_general_2D | invert_general_2D_gpu | | general 3D | invert_general_3D | invert_general_3D_gpu | | general 2D biharmonic | invert_general_bih_2D | invert_general_bih_2D_gpu | Red-Black SOR kernels with a shared loop skeleton ( _run_sor_2d_loop , _run_sor_3d_loop ), adaptive convergence-check intervals, and an optional per-call thread-block shape via iParams['gpu_block2d'] . GPU solves are bounded to one at a time ( gpus._GPU_MAX_CONCURRENT ) so dask can pipeline disk I/O against them, and CUDA context creation is done on the main thread. Measured on an RTX 3090: single timestep, 300 x 720: 17.3x (1.73 s GPU vs 29.99 s on one core) 12 timesteps, 300 x 720: ~1.6x over 12-core dask CPU (21.3 s vs 33.3 s) — at this size the solve is launch-bound, not execution-bound large grids, fixed 1000 iterations: up to 17.1x See the benchmark docs for the full sweep and the launch-overhead analysis. Module rename: numbas.py → cpus.py The CPU kernel module is now named for what it contains. xarray 's dask backend remains the multi-core path. API renames (breaking) Four public names lose a _test suffix that misdescribed them as test-only — they implement real discretizations used by shipped applications: | old | new | | --- | --- | | invert_standard_2D_test | invert_standard_2D_full | | inv_standard2D_test | inv_standard2D_full | | invert_GillMatsuno_test | invert_GillMatsunoFlux | | invert_Stommel_test | invert_StommelFlux | Users calling the old names must update; there are no aliases. The private __coeffs_*_test helpers became __coeffs_*Flux . Thread-safe live progress output printInfo output from dask worker threads and distributed clusters no longer interleaves. Each message is emitted as a single atomic write with the right parent header, so Jupyter and worker logs stay readable. Tests Seven CPU/GPU consistency suites ( tests/test_Gpu*.py plus tests/test_CpuGpuConsistency.py , ~1700 lines) asserting the analytic solution where one exists and CPU/GPU agreement otherwise; GPU cases skip cleanly when no CUDA device is present. Benchmark suite under tests/ , with machine-readable results in tests/results/*.json and figure regeneration via tests/plot_benchmarks.py . CI matrix: Python 3.9 – 3.12, 38 passed, 37 skipped . Housekeeping .gitattributes line-ending policy plus a one-off renormalization — the repository had a CRLF/LF mix that inflated diffs by thousands of lines. deriv() with the central scheme no longer converts numpy-backed input to dask; the rechunk is applied only to genuinely chunked data. Documentation: GPU status table, benchmark page and the parallel-inversions notebook brought in line with the implementation. Upgrade notes Breaking: the four API renames above. CUDA support is optional — import xinvert still works on machines without a GPU, and architect='cpu' remains the default. If you pin gpu_block2d , the default is still (16, 16) . Full diff: https://github.com/miniufo/xinvert/compare/v0.2.0...v0.3.0
title: xinvert: A Python package for inversion problems in geophysical fluid dynamics

summary: Reproducibility package for the manuscript "Distinct conformational and interaction signatures of the FGFR1 V561M and N546K resistance-associated mutations: a multi-replicate molecular dynamics study" . This package contains everything needed to regenerate every table, figure and reported number in the manuscript from the analysis outputs, except the raw trajectories. Systems and sampling: three FGFR1 kinase domain systems (wild type, V561M, N546K) in complex with erdafitinib, three independent 500 -ns replicates each , analysed over the 200 -500 ns plateau. Nominal sampling 4.5 us; realised aggregate production sampling 4.491 us. All three systems share a 9.28387 nm cubic SPC water box with 0.15 M NaCl (total atoms 78 , 608 / 78 , 609 / 78 , 624 ). Contents: - scripts/ - 14 analysis and plotting scripts (Python 3.10 ) covering every main and supplementary figure panel - tables/ - 38 per-replicate and summary result tables (CSV) - matrices/ - 24 DCCM matrices, common-subspace PCA projections and RMSD series (NumPy .npy) - mdp/ - GROMACS run-control files (minimisation, ions, NVT, NPT, production) plus the fully expanded grompp parameter file - tpr/ - the nine production run inputs (complete, with all parameters baked in ) - topology/ - GROMACS topology files ( system and protein topologies, posre.itp, ligand parameters, index files ) - README.md - directory layout, frame-selection rules, uncertainty conventions, table/figure provenance, and full run parameters Software: GROMACS 2024.6 (production) and 2024.3 (analysis), gmx_MMPBSA 1.6 .5 , MDTraj 1.10 .3 , Python 3.10 (NumPy 2.2 .6 , SciPy 1.15 .2 , Matplotlib). title: Reproducibility package for: Distinct conformational and interaction signatures of the FGFR1 V561M and N546K resistance-associated mutations: a multi-replicate molecular dynamics study

summary: Derived tables and provenance registries supporting source-resolved mass absorption efficiency (MAE) estimates for wintertime brown carbon from residential solid-fuel and fossil-fuel combustion across European and Chinese sites. Contents: (i) source-resolved MAE estimates for the European station pairs and six Chinese cities with block-bootstrap percentile intervals and trustworthiness grading; (ii) station metadata and the field-level verification status of the Chinese records; (iii) per-dataset variable-group coverage tables and sensitivity analyses; (iv) the 84-field variable dictionary of the harmonized master table; (v) per-dataset provenance registries recording authoritative archives, citations and access routes, including a per-file DOI registry for the EBAS absorption compilation; (vi) the evidence tables underlying the Supporting Information (spectral benchmarks, coverage analyses, validation tables, perturbation domains, and the literature-coordinate conversion audit); (vii) an integrity baseline of file checksums for independent verification. summary: Code and data supporting the article "Capillary-driven networks obey Murray's law everywhere except at the meniscus". The archive contains three things. A self-contained MATLAB package that builds the figures of the article and recomputes every number quoted in its text, using a backtracking Newton iteration on a scale-invariant objective and requiring no toolboxes. A Python module that carries the same model on arbitrary graphs, including graphs with loops, where the flow is obtained from the nodal Laplacian rather than from the topology, together with a script that runs the verifications of Appendices C, F and H: the nine-channel graph with four independent loops, the envelope identity, the sweep over the driving degree, the three terminal conditions, the power-to-cost ratios and the Kamiya-Togawa law, and the case of several dissipation mechanisms in one channel. And a pixel-level digitisation of Fig. 7 of Zhang and Lorente, Sci. Rep. 13, 11278 (2023), against which Sec. V of the article is compared, with the source raster, the recovered coordinates in three formats, and an image comparing the reconstruction against the original. Neither optimiser uses the sizing law under test: each maximises the throughput at fixed cost from the resistance and the cost directly, so the residuals reported are an independent check of Eq. (7) rather than a restatement of it. The digitiser is deterministic and reproduces its 298 recovered points byte for byte. Code is released under the MIT licence (LICENSE-CODE.txt); data and figures under CC BY 4.0 (LICENSE-DATA.txt). The source raster in data/ is reproduced unaltered from a CC BY 4.0 third-party article and remains copyright of its authors; see THIRD-PARTY.txt. README.txt describes the contents, how to run everything, and which printed quantities depend on the configuration block.
title: Supporting material for "Capillary-driven networks obey Murray's law everywhere except at the meniscus"

summary: This work studies whether internal rotation changes the longevity of source-free localized excitations in the reduced Enchan local time-rate field. The frozen scalar dynamics are S_tt = div[mu(D) grad S] - S with D = |grad S| and mu(D) = 1/(1 + D^(3/2)); no continuing external torque, centrifugal force, primitive matter source, or added rotational potential is used during the reported evolutions. Stage A supplies the non-rotating source-free baseline. Stage B1 initializes rotating phase-space states at omega = 4, 8, and 12 and evolves the extended runs to dimensionless time t = 100. Over 80 <= t <= 100, the mean localized-energy fractions are approximately 0.002207 for the non-rotating baseline and 0.006006, 0.149470, and 0.368846 for omega = 4, 8, and 12. The result is a graded rotation-associated longevity hierarchy: weak rotation gives little practical rescue, intermediate rotation substantially extends localization, and the strongest tested branch remains transient-localized through t = 100. Matched-energy near-zero-J_z controls provide a separate causality check and show that net canonical angular momentum alone is not a monotonic explanation of every late-time difference. Stage B2 separately tests spontaneous self-spin from exactly zero initial total angular momentum and finds no validated convergent counter-rotating branch in the tested scalar-only initial-data families. The ordered scan supports a physical formation picture in which a localized grain can move from weak rotational asymmetry through progressive spin-up into a strong-rotation long-lived branch. Time, space, and omega are dimensionless reduced-branch quantities; t = 100 is not assigned an SI duration in this work. The deposit contains the Version 1.0 manuscript PDF, a reproducibility ZIP with the publication source, code, selected archived numerical outputs, README, LICENSE, and SHA-256 integrity manifest. The final main.pdf is the default preview. License: Enchan Research & Verification License v1.0. Copyright (c) 2026 Mitsuhiro Kobayashi.
title: Can Rotation Make Spacetime Grains Last? Internal Angular Momentum and Longevity of Source-Free Enchan Grains

summary: Industry 4.0 transforms manufacturing through cyber-physical systems, the Industrial Internet of Things, digital twins, and data-driven intelligence, yet the volume of latency-sensitive data these technologies generate strains conventional cloud-only computing. Edge and fog computing have emerged as the central enabling paradigm, distributing computation across a device–fog–cloud continuum. This paper surveys the enabling technologies of Industry 4.0 with an emphasis on edge–cloud computing and formulates the resulting computation-offloading problem as a constrained, load-dependent optimization model that jointly minimizes task latency and device energy under deadline and capacity constraints. A genetic algorithm and a particle swarm optimizer are developed and benchmarked against five baseline strategies on synthetic industrial workloads. Across one hundred tasks averaged over ten instances, the genetic algorithm reduced the weighted objective by 34.1 percent relative to a greedy heuristic and by 82.6 percent relative to cloud-only execution, while lowering deadline violations to 1.6 percent. The latency–energy trade-off, convergence, and scalability are analyzed, and managerial implications for industrial deployment are discussed.
title: Energy- and Latency-Aware Computation Offloading in Edge–Fog–Cloud Architectures for Industry 4.0

summary: Supplementary material for the manuscript Li Bai Says Xiangsi and Du Fu Does Not: Idioms of Longing in Tang Poetry and the Lexical Basis of an Emotion Label by Zizheng Lv (Honours Program, Department of Asian Studies, University of British Columbia). The study asks what the yearning label of the Chinese Classical Poetry Dataset (CCPD) measures when a classifier trained on it rates Li Bai far above Du Fu. On held-out benchmark poems the label is recoverable from the words xiangsi (相思) and xiangyi (相忆); in a source-audited corpus of 52,253 Tang poems, xiangsi is followed as a formula with a history, from pre-Tang song to Tang poems of farewell and exchange, across 116 poets, and into fifteen close readings. Contents of Supplementary_Material.zip data/poems_table.parquet : the 52,253 author-eligible, CCPD-training-disjoint Tang poems (chinese-poetry, MIT) with source pointers, normalized and original bodies, poem families, surface forms, the frozen classifier's yearning probability and decision, per-poem counts of the words in the lexicon of longing, and title flags. data/author_dates.csv , data/author_dates_by_poem.csv , data/author_date_supplement.json : author dating for the Tang diachrony (Chinese Text Project Data Wiki plus listed corrections). data/xiangsi_poems_by_title_type.csv , data/dufu_yi_news_poems_by_title_type.csv : every title behind the title-type analyses with its rule-based type. data/literary_case_register.json : source-linked records for the fifteen readings. evidence/ : the numbers behind every figure and statement (benchmark counts and coefficients, corpus rates, lexicon rates with family-bootstrap intervals, diachrony, position, addressee, per-character logit attributions, form standardization, per-author tables for 116 poets, song-title rates). contextual_comparison/ : protocol and results of the three GuwenBERT fine-tuning runs. provenance/ : source versions, permissions, licenses, historical sources, and SHA-256 hashes of the archive inputs. scripts/ , figure_source/ : analysis and rendering code; requirements.txt lists the versions used. file_manifest.json and verify_results.py : SHA-256 integrity check for every distributed file (run python verify_results.py ). What runs from this package. scripts/b_e1_lexicon.py , scripts/d_e3_e4_e6.py and scripts/g_e7_all_poets.py recompute their evidence files from the distributed poem table, and figure_source/render_figures.py renders Figures 1 to 6 from the evidence files. scripts/c_e2_diachrony.py and scripts/h_e8_southern_song.py additionally require the Daizhige transcription of Lu Qinli's pre-Tang anthology and the CText Data Wiki RDF release; scripts/e_e5_attribution.py requires the fitted CCPD pipeline; scripts/a_build_table.py documents how the poem table was derived from the archive. These inputs are third-party or too large to redistribute; the README section External inputs gives their expected locations, and each script stops with a message naming any missing input. Licensing. The author's own contributions in this package (code, evidence files, the poem table's derived columns, the case register, and documentation) are released under CC BY 4.0. Retained third-party notices continue to apply to the respective upstream materials: the poem texts derive from the MIT-licensed chinese-poetry repository, whose notice is included; the birth and death years in data/author_dates.csv and data/author_dates_by_poem.csv derive from the Chinese Text Project Data Wiki and remain under its CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 license, with the author's corrections listed separately in data/author_date_supplement.json . CCPD annotations, fitted model weights, and GuwenBERT checkpoints are not redistributed.
title: Supplementary Material for: Li Bai Says Xiangsi and Du Fu Does Not: Idioms of Longing in Tang Poetry and the Lexical Basis of an Emotion Label

summary: Reproducibility archive for a fully computational study of a coupled interface-mode multilayer sensing refractive index and temperature over a 100 K range, accompanying the article "Bias-Aware Detection Limits, Calibration Transfer and Matched-Control Robustness Assessment in Dual-Parameter Photonic Refractive-Index and Temperature Sensing: A Coupled Interface-Mode Multilayer Case Study" by Agah Oktay Ertay and Muhammed Mustafa Ertay, accepted by Sensors (MDPI) on 18 September 2026. Version 1.2.1 is the publication release. It carries version 1.2.0, which the Data Availability Statement of the article names, without changing any number, table, input, model, or analysis script (560 of 572 files byte for byte; the 12 replaced root documents are kept under provenance/v1.2.0/). It adds the figure artwork as published: every graphic of the article and of its Supplementary Material as supplied to the journal (figures/published/), the source that draws the 20 graphics redrawn at the proof stage for typographic reasons (true minus signs, notation, legend placement; code/publication_figures/, with a complete diff against the production source), and a launcher mode that re-renders them from the archived tables. It contains the MATLAB production forward model and driver scripts, the frozen material, geometry and acceptance-criterion input files, and the sensitivity matrix, nonlinear calibration, covariance and probability-of-detection routines, the per-realization Monte Carlo yield and matched-control output tables, the design-search evaluation log, the FDFD, CST, MEEP, MPB and FEniCSx verification models with their exported spectra and convergence histories, and the numerical series behind every figure and table in the article and in its Supplementary Material. Version 1.2.0 adds the analyses of the major revision as a separately runnable stage that uses the archived production routines and the frozen tables of version 1.1.0: the sensitivity of the detection limits to instrument noise and drift, reduced per-device calibration protocols, the complete metric set of the nanolaminate-free stack, an oblique-incidence test of the hyperbolicity condition, and the jointly matched trivial control with its paired benchmark. The 483 source, input, result, figure, and solver files of version 1.1.0 are carried byte for byte; only the root metadata files and the launcher were updated, and the v1.1.0 metadata and checksum manifest are kept under provenance/v1.1.0/. A single launcher runs the integrity check, the full reproduction, the revision stage, or both; a SHA-256 manifest covers every other file in the archive. Code is released under the MIT License (LICENSE-CODE); data, result tables, and figures under CC-BY-4.0 (LICENSE-DATA). The three measured ITO n,k tables are third-party public-domain data (CC0 1.0, via refractiveindex.info, originating from Minenkov et al., ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 16, 9517-9531, 2024) and should be cited from that source. The study is numerical. No multilayer was fabricated and no spectrum measured; agreement between independent solvers is not offered as experimental validation.
title: Bias-Aware_Detection_Limits_Calibration_Transfer_and_Matched-Control_Robustness_Assessment_in_Dual-Parameter_Photonic_Refractive-Index_and_Temperature_Sensing_A_Coupled_Interface-Mode_Multilayer_Case_Study_All_Software_Package_and_Data_v1.2.1

summary: This paper offers a critical analysis of the European Union as a model of regional integration and examines its contribution to peace and to the effectiveness of the United Nations system. Set against the background of the failure of the League of Nations, the study argues that the post-1945 international order has endured largely because it is supported by strong regional institutions. Using the EU as the primary case study, the paper contends that by institutionalizing peace within Europe through economic interdependence, binding law, and supranational governance, the EU has created a zone of stability that reduces the burden on global governance structures. Furthermore, the paper analyzes how the EU functions as a support pillar for the United Nations under Chapter VIII of the UN Charter. Through financial contributions, peacekeeping partnerships, and coordinated diplomacy, the EU has reinforced multilateralism and provided capacity for conflict management and development. A comparative perspective is also drawn with other regional bodies such as ECOWAS to demonstrate a broader pattern of regional-global cooperation. The paper concludes that the longevity of the United Nations, compared to the League of Nations, can be partly explained by this two-level architecture of global and regional governance. While the EU’s support for the UN is substantial, it is also inconsistent, as internal EU divisions sometimes undermine collective action. Ultimately, the study shows that effective regional integration is a critical condition for sustaining peace and strengthening the United Nations system.
title: The European Union and Regional Integration: A Critical Analysis of Peacebuilding and Support for the United Nations System

summary: Abstract The stability of the banking sector is fundamental to economic growth and financial system resilience, particularly in developing economies such as Nigeria.  However, and sadly enough, global, recent and recurring failure risks and collapses of banks which have been blamed on poor external audit qualities, are counter-productive to national economic development.  Therefore, the broad objective of this study was to study the effect of audit quality on failure risks of listed deposit money banks in Nigeria between the period 2009 and 2024. This study adopted both descriptive and ex-post facto research designs.  Using secondary data extracted from audited financial reports of 11 censored (from a population of 11) deposit money banks listed on the Nigerian Exchange Group, (NGX), and analyzing one hundred and seventy-six firm year observations using regression with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors analysis technique, the findings revealed that audit firm size (AUFS) significantly improve bank Z score, [coef. = 0.638 (p-value = 0.005)], audit report timeliness (ARTIME) significantly reduces bank Z score [coef. = −0.400 (p-value = audit committee diligence (ACDI) revealed a positive insignificant effect respectively on Z score of listed deposit money banks in Nigeria during the period under consideration. Based on the above findings, it was concluded that audit quality in the Nigerian banking sector is not uniformly effective, rather, its effect on bank failure risks is selective, with only specific audit mechanisms demonstrating the capacity to significantly enhance financial solvency, thereby suggesting that the effectiveness of external audit as a safeguard against bank failure risks depend not merely on its presence, but likely on factors such as depth, credibility, and functional execution of its key components.   this study concluded that audit.  Consequently, this study recommended among others, that listed deposit money banks in Nigeria, alongside regulators and external auditors, should prioritize substantive governance quality, auditor competence and independence, rigorous audit execution, timely financial reporting, risk-sensitive audit remuneration, coordinated assurance mechanisms, and proactive internal control systems over mere procedural compliance, in order to strengthen transparency, reinforce market confidence, and enhance long term financial stability in line with Agency theory. Keywords: Audit Quality, Failure Risks of Listed Deposit Money Banks, Bank Z-Score, Agency Theory.

Code is distributed under the MIT License; data, numerical results, figures, and documentation are distributed under CC BY 4.0.

summary: ORCA and OpenMolcas inputs, embedding files, labelled coordinates, output summaries, post-processing scripts, and figure data for the embedded-cluster CASSCF/NEVPT2+SOC study of Nd³⁺, Er³⁺, and Yb³⁺ at the Zr and Ba sites of the chalcogenide perovskite BaZrS₃. Includes the restricted-active-space (RASSCF/RASSI-SO with SUPSym) calculations of forced electric-dipole strengths and the Er³⁺:LaCl₃ benchmark, the complete 4fⁿ state-space validation on Cs₂NaLnCl₆, the breathing-coordinate scans, AILFT crystal-field parameters, g-tensors and magnetic susceptibilities, and the analysis scripts for the published 10 K emission spectra.
title: Data and scripts for: Coordination-Controlled Crystal Fields and 4f Spectroscopic Fingerprints of Nd3+, Er3+ and Yb3+ in the Chalcogenide Perovskite BaZrS3

summary: Concern about low-information-content publications—least publishable units, salami-sliced outputs, redundant papers, benchmark increments, and false-positive findings dressed as discoveries—is distributed unevenly across the sciences. Some fields appear to convert procedural effort into publishable "findings" almost at will, whereas others force nearly every contribution into the slow form of a convergence result or an error audit. Existing accounts attribute the disparity to incentives, statistical flexibility, or disciplinary culture, but incentives are universal while the output pattern is not, and flexibility alone cannot explain fields whose verdicts are stringent and objective yet are gamed at industrial scale. This paper develops a structural account centered on two features of a research program: the closure of its decision space by formal and empirical constraints, and the gameability of the verdicts that adjudicate its claims. Stringency, fidelity to the epistemic target, and resistance to rehearsal are distinct properties of a verdict; a benchmark can be maximally stringent and objective while remaining trivially gameable. Because the underlying dimensions are ordinal and non-compensatory, susceptibility to low-information publication cannot be expressed as a scalar ratio and is better represented as a typology. Four regimes are distinguished: convergent programs with dual closure and ungameable verdicts; formally bounded programs with thin empirical closure; programs governed by stringent but gameable verdicts; and open-latitude programs with weak closure and subjective adjudication. Each regime channels publication pressure into a different production line—flexibility monetization, verdict gaming, or fragmentation and repackaging—and each requires interventions matched to its production line rather than a generic reform package. The model explains why string theory and fixed-benchmark machine learning, often misread by single-axis accounts, exhibit such different pathologies, and it predicts which reforms will work, fail, or backfire in each regime.
title: The Structural Determinants of Low-Information Publication in Science: A Constraint–Verdict Typology

summary: This dataset contains bibliometric data on scientific collaboration among five member states of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS): Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan. Based on OpenAlex data for 2020–2025, it covers scientific output, international and regional collaboration, partner diversification, and bilateral research networks.
title: Replication Data: Scientific Networks in the Turkic World

summary: Replication data and code for a study of hedge-ratio estimation (OLS, DCC-GARCH, Random Forest, XGBoost and a naïve benchmark) for CME Bitcoin and Ether futures under regime-dependent tail risk. The package contains date-aligned daily returns and hedge-ratio series (BTC: 19 December 2017 to 22 May 2025; ETH: 8 February 2021 to 22 May 2025), Python scripts that reproduce all tables and figures, and a README. Raw Yahoo Finance prices are not redistributed. This version corrects the construction of returns (spot and futures returns are measured between the same CME trading dates) and supersedes any earlier deposit.
title: Replication data and code: hedge ratios for cryptocurrency futures under regime-dependent tail risk

summary: We present an HTTP threat detection system embedded in a production reverse proxy that achieves sub-500ns per-request inference latency. The system combines a depth-limited CART decision tree with a compact two-layer MLP in an ensemble architecture, where the tree provides fast-path classification and the MLP refines uncertain cases. Model weights are exported as Rust `const` arrays, enabling zero-allocation deployment with no runtime deserialization. We formalize structural safety properties of the ensemble in the Lean~4 theorem prover, establishing a three-tier verification approach covering structural invariants, weight-dependent decision bounds, and floating-point error propagation. In initial small-scale trials on a combined dataset of production logs, CSIC-2010, and CIC-IDS2017-derived features, the ensemble achieves >99% validation accuracy for both scanner and DDoS detection, with tree inference completing in under 2ns and full ensemble inference under 6ns. We discuss limitations of the current training data and outline directions for scaling to larger, human-labeled corpora.
title: Sub-Microsecond HTTP Threat Detection with Decision Tree–MLP Ensembles and Lean 4 Verification

summary: Embarrassingly parallel workloads, such as parameter sweeps, Monte Carlo simulations, and hyperparameter searches, are pervasive in research computing, yet running a single experiment across a mix of laptops, lab servers, cloud virtual machines (VMs), and high-performance computing (HPC) clusters still demands ad hoc Secure Shell (SSH) tunnels, port forwarding, and scheduler-specific scripts. We present DART, a job distributor that turns any such mix of machines into a single shared queue. DART pairs a Dockerized job server with a one-line worker command-line interface (CLI); a hosted Hub automates reverse tunneling, worker authentication, and public endpoint provisioning, so collaborators on any network, including those behind network address translation (NAT) or using a personal laptop, can join an experiment with a single API-key and no firewall changes. This makes DART especially effective for researchers who combine Advanced Cyberinfrastructure Coordination Ecosystem: Services & Support (ACCESS)-provisioned HPC resources [1] with institutional clusters and personal workstations, federating all resources under one queue with no per-site configuration. All communication is encrypted end-to-end, and access is controlled through API-key authentication and a personal identification number (PIN)-protected dashboard. Researchers create experiments, define parameter grids, and monitor jobs entirely from a web dashboard; a work-conserving scheduler dispatches jobs on demand, exploits resource heterogeneity, and automatically re-queues failures. In a real-world deployment of 37,720 jobs across 68 heterogeneous machines spanning an institutional HPC cluster, a national ACCESS resource, and personal computers, the observed run completed in approximately eight days. DART’s dynamic allocation achieved a simulation-derived 35× speedup over static partitioning (≈4 days vs. ≈139 days), reducing a multi-month workload to days.
title: DART: Distributed Assignment of Research Tasks for Heterogeneous Compute Environments

This makes DART especially effective for researchers who combine Advanced Cyberinfrastructure Coordination Ecosystem: Services & Support (ACCESS)-provisioned HPC resources [1] with institutional clusters and personal workstations, federating all resources under one queue with no per-site configuration. All communication is encrypted end-to-end, and access is controlled through API-key authentication and a personal identification number (PIN)-protected dashboard. Researchers create experiments, define parameter grids, and monitor jobs entirely from a web dashboard; a work-conserving scheduler dispatches jobs on demand, exploits resource heterogeneity, and automatically re-queues failures. In a real-world deployment of 37,720 jobs across 68 heterogeneous machines spanning an institutional HPC cluster, a national ACCESS resource, and personal computers, the observed run completed in approximately eight days. DART’s dynamic allocation achieved a simulation-derived 35× speedup over static partitioning (≈4 days vs. ≈139 days), reducing a multi-month workload to days.

summary: Weekly, hashed copy of the verifiable-silence observations Crovia Trust publishes at croviatrust.com/registry/tacet/ : 17 signed hourly epoch sheets (13 anchored in Bitcoin), 1,260 observed AI models, 1,149 negative snapshots and 19 silence proofs in the crovia.seal.v1 receipt format. A silence proof shows, for one model, that in every observed hour no training-data disclosure matching the published predicate appeared on its public surfaces: a sparse-Merkle non-inclusion path per epoch, the drand round that opened the epoch and the OpenTimestamps receipt that closed it. Proofs verify offline with pip install crovia-tacet-operator crovia-seal or in the browser at croviatrust.com/registry/seal/verify/ . Crovia records what was observed and what was not; it does not grade, rank or attribute intent. Durations are bounded by observed hours. Weekly summary: Silence Report 2026-W38 . Definitions: CANON.md . Receipt format: IETF draft-crovia-seal . Licence CC-BY-4.0. Cite the series by the Concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20111130.

summary: Anticoncentration is a key ingredient in complexity theoretic arguments for quantum advantage from Gaussian boson sampling. Here we prove polynomial small ball anticoncentration for complex Gaussian transpose Gram hafnians and complex symmetric Gaussian hafnians. For a k × 2n matrix X with independent standard complex Gaussian entries, we establish polynomial small ball anticoncentration for haf(XᵀX) under k ≥ 4n and n²/k = O(log n). For hafnians of 2n × 2n complex symmetric Gaussian matrices, polynomial small ball anticoncentration holds for every n ≥ 1. In both ensembles, any prescribed inverse polynomial failure probability can be achieved with an inverse polynomial small ball radius, uniformly over all centers. These results go beyond moment based anticoncentration by controlling the probability of small hafnian amplitudes. The proof combines Fourier compression with conditional Wishart geometry to handle dependent hafnian cofactors. Files: main.pdf contains the main article (14 pages); supplement.pdf contains the supplementary proofs and additional results (33 pages). Related Lean verification sources: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22554594 and https://github.com/HongruZhao/ComplexGramHafnians.
title: Local Anticoncentration for Gaussian Boson Sampling via Conditional Wishart Geometry

Here we prove polynomial small ball anticoncentration for complex Gaussian transpose Gram hafnians and complex symmetric Gaussian hafnians. For a k × 2n matrix X with independent standard complex Gaussian entries, we establish polynomial small ball anticoncentration for haf(XᵀX) under k ≥ 4n and n²/k = O(log n). For hafnians of 2n × 2n complex symmetric Gaussian matrices, polynomial small ball anticoncentration holds for every n ≥ 1. In both ensembles, any prescribed inverse polynomial failure probability can be achieved with an inverse polynomial small ball radius, uniformly over all centers. These results go beyond moment based anticoncentration by controlling the probability of small hafnian amplitudes. The proof combines Fourier compression with conditional Wishart geometry to handle dependent hafnian cofactors. Files: main.pdf contains the main article (14 pages); supplement.pdf contains the supplementary proofs and additional results (33 pages). Related Lean verification sources: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22554594 and https://github.com/HongruZhao/ComplexGramHafnians.

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Eighteen entries are documented, eight of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, and a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten. Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, and converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient.
title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance

summary: This dataset contains analysis-ready spatial data on informal urban conditions, heat and flood exposure, slum population, and malaria burden across sub-Saharan Africa.   The deposit includes a processed subnational dataset with 4,320 administrative units, a 44-feature country/region boundary layer, annual HI406 and WBGT30 heat-exposure rasters for 2011–2020, a slum-population raster, a complete data dictionary, descriptive statistics, raster metadata, provenance documentation, rights guidance, and integrity checksums.   The vector data are provided as ESRI Shapefiles and the gridded data as GeoTIFF files. All spatial datasets use WGS 84 (EPSG:4326). The raster grids contain 1,141 columns by 1,235 rows at approximately 0.060362 degrees per cell.   The malaria indicators are population-weighted estimates mapped from source administrative-unit means onto the common slum-population grid. The original upstream flood and malaria source layers are not redistributed in this record. Users should consult the included README, data dictionary, provenance documentation, sources and limitations, and data-use notes before reuse.   This record contains data and data documentation only. Code, notebooks, manuscripts, figures, and supplementary documents are maintained separately in the project repository: https://github.com/JinRuii/informal-urban-climate-malaria-ssa

All spatial datasets use WGS 84 (EPSG:4326). The raster grids contain 1,141 columns by 1,235 rows at approximately 0.060362 degrees per cell.   The malaria indicators are population-weighted estimates mapped from source administrative-unit means onto the common slum-population grid. The original upstream flood and malaria source layers are not redistributed in this record. Users should consult the included README, data dictionary, provenance documentation, sources and limitations, and data-use notes before reuse.   This record contains data and data documentation only. Code, notebooks, manuscripts, figures, and supplementary documents are maintained separately in the project repository: https://github.com/JinRuii/informal-urban-climate-malaria-ssa
title: Analysis-ready spatial data on informal urban conditions, climate exposure and malaria burden across sub-Saharan Africa

summary: Research and educational instrument. Not for clinical use, for the care of any patient, or to determine or influence any drug dose. A simulation-calibrated informatics pipeline that fits a single-compartment exponential approximation to published population pharmacokinetic models of unfractionated heparin during cardiopulmonary bypass, and renders the result as an institution-specific decay nomogram. This is the supporting code and archived analysis for manuscript JCVA-D-26-01511. Published models of heparin disposition are biexponential and require a computer to evaluate. The pipeline asks how well a single decay constant k — calibrated to an institution's own dosing, weight and bypass-time distributions — can approximate a chosen reference model, and quantifies where it fails. The answer differs sharply by model: at the reversal timepoint the approximation holds to 0.38% mean absolute error for Lanoiselée and 0.44% for Jia, but to 10.3% for Delavenne, rising to 72% after repeated supplemental boluses. Contents. Five reference-model implementations with their published parameters and provenance; seeded cohort sampling and calibration; agreement statistics; nomogram geometry and rendering; a Streamlit dashboard; an automated test suite; and a frozen analysis run comprising 20 result tables, the main-text and supplementary figures, a run manifest and a manuscript-ready summary. A sixth model (PRODOSE-2) is implemented and tested but withheld from the active pipeline pending validation and peer review. Reproduction. Every reported number regenerates from one seeded command: pip install -r requirements-frozen.txt python run_analysis.py --seed 20260912 --outdir /tmp/check python check_frozen.py /tmp/check All randomness comes from explicitly seeded generators, each analysis stage drawing from its own independent stream. Re-running reproduces every archived result to within floating-point rounding on any machine, and byte-for-byte on the machine the archive was built on. The manifest records the seed, the commit, the package versions and every analysis decision. Continuous integration runs the suite on two Python versions, each test file again in isolation, and the reproduction check on every push. Verification, and its limits. Automated checks confirm that each closed-form solution actually solves its own differential equations and satisfies the identities they imply, and six landmark values from a published simulation are reproduced to within 3%. No participant-level data from any source study is held, so no model is re-fitted and no prediction is compared with an observation. What is demonstrated is faithful implementation of the published models — not that the published models are correct. No external or predictive validation is claimed. Scope. The pipeline represents the pharmacokinetic central-compartment amount only. It does not model the pharmacodynamic layer — anti-factor Xa activity or activated clotting time — nor peripheral-compartment heparin, antithrombin, protamine pharmacology or heparin rebound. Converting a residual amount into a protamine dose requires an institutional ratio that this software does not supply. Intended purpose. This software is a research and educational instrument whose purpose is to demonstrate and teach an informatics method under simulated conditions. Within that intended purpose it is not a medical device. Nothing here has been cleared, approved or evaluated by any regulatory authority; outputs have not been validated against measured anti-factor Xa activity, activated clotting time or clinical reversal in patients, and no clinical benefit has been demonstrated. Anyone using it outside the intended purpose does so on their own responsibility and may bring the tool within medical-device oversight in their jurisdiction; the authors accept no responsibility for such use.
