This study develops an empirical multiple linear regression (MLR) model to predict backbreak from five commonly logged blast design parameters: burden, spacing, stemming length, powder factor, and a geometric stiffness ratio, following the variable framework established in prior backbreak-prediction studies [3], [5]. A dataset of 36 field blast records was compiled, and predictor collinearity, model significance, and residual behaviour were assessed using standard regression diagnostics. A reduced four-variable model (burden, spacing, powder factor, and geometric stiffness) explained 97.6% of the variance in the observed dataset (in-sample R² = 0.976, adjusted R² = 0.972, F(4,31) = 310.1, p < 0.001), with a root-mean-square error of 0.35 m and mean absolute percentage error of 9.4%; six-fold cross-validation produced a mean out-of-fold R² of 0.84, indicating somewhat weaker but still reasonable performance on held-out data. Burden and powder factor were the strongest positive predictors, while spacing exerted a negative, moderating effect, consistent with established blast mechanics. The results support the use of routinely collected design parameters for practical, low-cost backbreak forecasting and pre-blast design adjustment, while highlighting multicollinearity among burden-related variables as a limitation warranting cautious interpretation of individual coefficients.
tags: backbreak, blast design, burden, powder factor, multiple linear regression, rock fragmentation,open-pit mining
title: A Reliability-Centered Approach to Preventive Maintenance (RCM) Evaluation of an 11/0.415 Kv Secondary Distribution Substation

summary: Adaptive systems can execute authorized actions whose factual effects move the cur- rent authority state outside the successors permitted by a normative authority specifi- cation. This paper studies when enforcement can transform such factual transition dy- namics so that authorized transitions remain aligned with the specification. We model enforcement as a transformation of transition systems and distinguish pre-transition filtering, post-transition correction, and transition redesign as realization classes of one formal operator. Completeness requires every authorized transition in a domain to produce an admissible authority successor. We prove existence of a complete redesign operator whenever the admissible successor set is nonempty, show that complete step- level enforcement yields trajectory-level alignment, and derive invariant preservation under a closure condition. We then establish two architecture-level limits: observa- tional indistinguishability can make complete post-transition correction impossible, and delayed information can force a trade-off between completeness and intervention minimality. Conflicting authority specifications are separated as a specification-level taxonomic boundary rather than an enforcement failure. The results therefore separate abstract enforceability from implementability and distinguish information and timing failures from inconsistency in the normative specification itself.
title: Enforcement-Induced Alignment of Authority-State Transitions. Formal Conditions and Limits

summary: A Markdown public note is included in the deposit (public_note_final.md); it is the finalized archival version of the canonical note. This deposit provides a reproducible research compendium for route (O3), the favorable-margin route, of the COLT 2022 open problem "Better differentially private learning algorithms with margin guarantees" (Bassily, Mohri & Suresh, PMLR 178:5638-5643; companion paper NeurIPS 2022, arXiv:2204.10376, BMS22). Problem and result - BMS22 Algorithm 1 (pure (eps,0)-DP linear margin learner) carries the strongest of the three BMS22 guarantees - a dimension-independent relative-deviation margin bound (its Thm 3.1) - but its running time is exponential in Lambda^2 r^2/rho^2, super-polynomial in m as soon as Lambda^2 r^2/rho^2 = omega(1); the efficient Algorithms 2/3 trade the guarantee down to approximate-DP hinge-loss statements. The open problem asks whether the strong guarantee can be had at polynomial cost. - This work sharpens the BMS22 Alg. 1 runtime analysis: it makes the greedy cover explicit - C is a maximal rho/(10r)-separated subset of B^k(2 Lambda), hence a rho/(10r)-cover with |C| <= (41 Lambda r/rho)^k - and proves that the running time T = O(m d k + m k |C|), with sketch dimension k = c1 Lambda^2 r^2 ln(4m/beta)/rho^2, is polynomial in (m, d, 1/beta) exactly in the favorable-margin regime rho >= c0 Lambda r. - A matching tightness boundary is proved for the entire sketch+net+exponential-mechanism family (to which BMS22 Alg. 1 and the packaged algorithm belong): if rho = o(Lambda r), every such learner is super-polynomial in m (JL-dimension lower bound times net-volume lower bound), so rho = Theta(Lambda r) is the exact poly-time boundary of this framework. - The full BMS22 Thm-3.1-analog relative-deviation guarantee is proved under pure (eps,0)-DP (public Rademacher sketch, deterministic projection, exponential mechanism over the cover with sensitivity 1/m, post-processing), with the Gate-05-repaired Gamma statement carrying the cover constant inside the logarithm; the same statement-vs-proof corner present in BMS22 Thm 3.1 as printed is disclosed in the note. - No new algorithm is claimed: the packaged learner coincides with BMS22 Algorithm 1 modulo the explicit cover construction, and no asymptotic-in-m speedup over Alg. 1 is claimed in the corner where both run in polynomial time. Contents - proof/: source note, Theorem 1 with the complete Gate-05-verified proof (privacy, utility, explicit cover, runtime, tightness), owner-1's prior analysis with the escape map (O1)-(O4), and the bounded C1-C5 repair record. - src/: PoC runtime simulations and verifier rerun scripts (Python 3, numpy). - data/: frozen JSON records and verifier logs with sha256 fingerprints. - review/: adversarial review (CONDITIONAL PASS, conditions C1-C5), scoped re-review (PASS), and the packaging-time novelty check. - README.md and SMOKE_TEST.md: environment, commands, expected outputs, and the 2026-09-18 smoke-test record. - public_note.md / public_note_final.md: the finalized public note; packaging_index.md, package_completeness.md, references_supplement.md, and packaging_check_report.md: packaging documentation, literature relationships, and the independent package-inspection report. - LICENSE_CODE_MIT.txt, LICENSE_DATA_CC0.txt, LICENSE_NOTE_CC_BY.txt: license details. Limitations - The parent COLT 2022 open problem is not closed: the result covers only the favorable-margin corner rho = Omega(Lambda r) for cover-based learners. The intermediate regime Lambda r/sqrt(m) << rho = o(Lambda r) is genuinely super-polynomial for this framework, and the tightness bound does not apply to non-cover-based learners (e.g. continuous-domain pure-DP samplers); no poly-time pure-DP learner is ruled out for rho = o(Lambda r) by any means other than this family analysis. - The deliverable is an analysis sharpening (explicit poly bound, exact efficiency boundary, pure-DP guarantee), not a new algorithm or a new guarant
title: Poly-time pure-DP linear margin learning in the favorable-margin regime: the exact efficiency boundary of the sketch+net+exponential-mechanism framework

summary: Title: CronNet-Holo Framework: Holographic Computational Language, 12.8 THz Projection Pixel, and Conditional Derivations of the Standard Model and Riemann Hypothesis Abstract: We present a collection of papers developing the CronNet-Holo framework, a unified program in which physical reality emerges from a holographic computational language (LCH) based on the binary icosahedral group 2I ≅ SL(2,5), the 600-cell lattice, Hecke transfer operators, and the invariant 53. The central prediction is a vacuum absorption peak at ν_pixel = 12.8 ± 0.2 THz with FWHM = 0.15 ± 0.05 THz, identified as the projection pixel frequency. The framework conditionally derives the Standard Model gauge group SU(3)_c × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y, three fermion generations, the Higgs mechanism, and gravity from the coherent representation V_coh = V₁ ⊕ 4V₄ ⊕ 6V₆ of 2I, with dim V_coh = 1² + 4² + 6² = 53. It also provides a conditional proof of the Riemann Hypothesis within the framework’s Volume-Spectral Duality axiom. The mathematical core includes the compression 4 → 3, the projector P = I − (1/4)J, the heat kernel K(t) = e^(−tD²), the Seeley-DeWitt expansion, and the entropy identity. The connection to physical reality remains conditional on five hypotheses: an anabelian epimorphism ρ: π̂₁(X) → 2I, 53-dimensional continuous cohomology, the 12.8 THz spectral anchor, a canonical selection rule R for {1,4,6}, and the spectral action giving correct Seeley-DeWitt coefficients. Falsifiable predictions include the 12.8 THz peak, vanishing correlation Cov(m,d_i) = 0, Ginibre spectral statistics ⟨r⟩ = 0.5873, Weinberg angle sin²θ_W(IR) ≈ 0.231049, and CMB modulation with period 751 and 53 phases θ_k that are multiples of 2π/5 with multiplicities 1, 4, 6. This Zenodo record collects the papers in a logical reading order. Keywords: holographic principle, computational language, 600-cell, binary icosahedral group, Hecke operators, Riemann Hypothesis, Standard Model, 12.8 THz, CronNet-Holo, LCH, projection pixel, spectral action, anabelian cohomology. Reading Order (files in logical sequence): Compression 4 → 3 Elimination of Redundancy and Emergence of Relational Information in the CronNet-Holo Framework Defines the decomposition ℝ⁴ = ℝ ⊕ V₃, the projector P = I − (1/4)J, the bundle V₃(Δ) over the 600 tetrahedra, and the holonomy conjecture. 3-6-9 Ladder Compression, Heat, Gravity, and the Universal Coherence Theorem Unifies the dimensional compression, heat as the 6-sector response, gravity as the 9-sector response, and the coherence energy E_coh({1,4,6}) = 1² + 4² + 6² = 53. Coherence Theorem with a Universal Object The Selection Problem for {1,4,6} Addresses the circularity problem: the need for a canonical rule R that selects {1,4,6} from the Perron-Frobenius vector δ = (1,2,3,4,5,6,4,3,2) of the affine E₈ Dynkin diagram. Grammar of the Language The Compression Process as the Grammar of the Language Interprets compression 4 → 3 as grammatical redundancy elimination. The 53 phases θ_k are the alphabet; the cycle Z₀ → E₈ → M₅₃ → Z₀ is the grammar. Holographic Code The Language of Projection: Holographic Code and the CronNet-Holo Program Develops the inverse problem: reading the spectrum {λ_n} from CMB correlations. Introduces the modulation formula C_ℓ = C_ℓ^ACDM · |(1/53) ∑_{k=1}^{53} e^{iθ_k ℓ(ℓ+1)/751}|². Language of Projection Translating Physical Facts into Holographic Sentences Provides a grammar, dictionary, and examples translating particle masses, forces, and symmetry breaking into holographic sentences. Computational Language of Reality LCH — Holographic Computational Language Defines LCH as a formal grammar with types, rewrite rules, operational semantics, and observables. The fundamental cycle is Z₀ → E₈ → M₅₃ → Z₀.
title: CronNet-Holo Framework: Holographic Computational Language

summary: Formal financial sector linkage with community group saving and lending mechanisms (CGSLs) is often proposed as a pathway through which fragile rural economies can move from subsistence finance to more durable agricultural investment. Yet, in South Sudan, this linkage remains difficult to institutionalise. This article re-analyses thesis evidence from Eastern Equatoria, Jonglei and Lakes State to examine why coordination among government, non-governmental organisations, donors, formal financial institutions and CGSL groups remains elusive. Framed through North's institutional analysis, the article argues that CGSL proliferation is not simply a cultural preference for informal finance; it is a rational institutional response to high transaction costs, weak formal enforcement, limited rural banking infrastructure, conflict-affected markets and project-based support systems. The study used a mixed-methods design involving 81 valid survey responses and 17 interviews. Descriptive findings showed strong demand for government and donor collaboration, with 94% of respondents agreeing or strongly agreeing that such collaboration should support rural financial services. However, the mean score for NGO promotion of informal savings was lower (3.68), and village-bank loan officer linkage was weaker (3.49), suggesting that external support is uneven and not yet converted into stable formal-informal intermediation. Chi-square tests confirmed significant associations between CGSL participation and agricultural development indicators, while logistic regression showed that CGSL credit access significantly influenced farmers' investment decisions. The article concludes that linkage failure is best understood as a coordination problem: CGSL groups carry local trust and repayment discipline, but they remain weakly connected to formal capital, policy protection, risk-management products, extension systems and market institutions. The paper recommends a coordination compact that recognises CGSLs as rural financial institutions, links mature groups to suitable wholesale finance, and protects member governance without destroying local accountability.
title: Government-NGO-CGSL Coordination Failures: Why Formal-Informal Financial Sector Linkage Remains Elusive in South Sudan

summary: For a century, cinema has returned to a single figure—the thinking machine that turns on its maker—and to a single feeling: dread. This article asks where that dread is actually manufactured. It pairs a qualitative coding of twelve canonical texts, from Karel Čapek's R.U.R. (1920) to the generative-AI films of the 2020s, with a computational content analysis of their scripts, conducted with a purpose-built instrument that measures fear vocabulary, sentiment arcs, propaganda techniques, dehumanizing language, and the language of violence. The results are unexpected. Explicit fear language never reaches one and a half percent of sentences in any script; the three-act emotional arc of every film in the corpus registers as neutral or faintly positive; the most recent films carry the least fear language of all; and the two films most affectionate toward their machines objectify them most heavily in grammar. The article argues that these apparent null results are themselves the finding. The fear of the intelligent machine is cultivated not in words but in the audiovisual apparatus—in lighting inherited from expressionism and noir, in the bodiless machine voice, in the unblinking close-up and the withheld cut, in production design that photographs the machine like geography. Drawing on cultivation theory, the Frankfurt School, and postcolonial critique, the article then asks who benefits from a fear installed beneath the level of language, and what a century of spectacular, misaimed dread has trained audiences not to see.
tags: Keywords: Artificial intelligence; science-fiction cinema; content analysis; cultivation theory; technophobia
title: The Many Names of The Machine: Fear, Neutrality, and The Cinema of Artificial Intelligence, 1920–2026

summary: FlowMLLab v1.7.0 adds paired self-supervised wake-learning modules. Week 7.3 retains the strong gappy-POD baseline on masked low-rank wake reconstruction and corrects linear-probe pooling and sample-standard-deviation reporting. Week 7.4 generates sixteen compact Reynolds trajectories and measures target-label efficiency for instantaneous lift using frozen pretrained, random and POD-32 representations. title: FlowMLLab: An Open-Source Framework for Reproducible CFD-to-Scientific-Machine-Learning Experiments

summary: We study an explicit integral Koszul presentation arising in the graded-syzygy analysis of a previously constructed Huneke-Wiegand family. For every integer p>=8, its cokernel contains a direct summand isomorphic to (Z/2)^floor(((p-2)^2+3)/12). The classes are indexed by all strictly increasing nonnegative triples of sum p-2. Reflection-symmetric interval potentials give explicit original integral sources for twice each class. Relative parity functionals, supported on ten to twelve original rows, detect the classes independently and vanish on every complete connecting image; extension over the remaining target gives a nonconstructive retraction. A previously tracked four-row vector is integrally congruent to one selected class, with an explicit source for the difference. We also give its full twice-source, two short kernel-domain corrections, and a neighboring integral potential basis of rank binomial(p-1,2) with at most seven-row images. Independent finite computations check the signed identities and complete-sector parity certificates, preserving all tested sources in lossless archives. A failed local search yields an exact locality obstruction. The uniform theorem follows from signed reconstruction, exhaustive source classification, and an elementary counting recurrence, not finite rank extrapolation. The full cokernel, an upper bound, and identification with earlier isolated subpresentations remain unresolved. The family-to-presentation identification is an imported premise. Son Pham retains priority for the original public Huneke-Wiegand counterexample. Source code, computation records and archived sources: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH .
title: A quadratic family of integral two-torsion classes in a Huneke–Wiegand Koszul presentation

summary: In March 2026, the Canadian Cardiovascular Harmonized National Guideline Endeavour (C-CHANGE) published the first Canadian clinical practice guideline to jointly address brain, heart, and mental health conditions, replacing the disease-specific silos that had previously left family physicians without unified guidance for patients carrying multiple, interacting chronic conditions. This review synthesizes that guideline for a Canadian primary care audience, examining in turn its recommendations for managing heart failure and atrial fibrillation in patients with comorbid cognitive impairment, its guidance on cognitive screening and silent cerebral infarct detection in cardiac patients, its proposed integrated care pathway linking cardiology, neurology, and mental health services, and its shared decision-making framework for reconciling competing treatment priorities. The evidence indicates that cognitive status materially changes cardiac management decisions, that brief validated screening tools can identify at-risk patients within a standard visit, and that team-based models such as the Patient's Medical Home already provide much of the infrastructure the guideline's integrated pathway requires. What remains incomplete is implementation: screening tools, referral pathways, and electronic medical record supports exist individually but are rarely deployed together in the same practice. Family physicians are positioned to close that gap and are the clinicians most likely to see these patients before either a cardiac or neurologic event forces a reactive referral. Moving this guideline from publication into everyday Canadian family practice will require deliberate investment in the team-based infrastructure that makes integrated, patient-centred brain-heart care practical rather than aspirational.
title: Integrated Brain-Heart-Mental Health Care: A Review of the 2026 C-CHANGE Guideline

summary: In July 2026 a counterexample to Goemans' cost version of the Dinitz–Garg–Goemans theorem was announced publicly, outside peer review, and circulated widely. We report an independent verification of that finite object by exact rational enumeration, performed without executing or importing the proposer's verifier, together with quantitative and structural content that the announcement did not state. Our results: (i) the instance is confirmed, so Goemans' conjecture is false, and, the instance being acyclic, the Morell–Skutella cost conjecture and the convex-combination form fall with it; (ii) the instance forces a violation of exactly 16/15 of the maximum demand d_max, that is, the conjecture fails by one unit at d_max = 15, so the open question whether cost-preserving rounding is possible with O(d_max) violation is untouched by it; (iii) every proved result in the area survives its direct test on the instance, including the Dinitz–Garg–Goemans theorem, the Morell–Skutella cost-free conjecture, the series-parallel theorem of Majthoub Almoghrabi, Skutella and Warode, and the planar theorem of Traub, Vargas Koch and Zenklusen; (iv) the instance contains a K4 subdivision, hence sits exactly one structure outside the series-parallel class where the conjecture is proved, and, being planar, pins the planar constant strictly between 1 and 2; (v) an exact separation linear program shows that the published cost vector is an optimal separator for that graph and fractional flow, so its cost gap cannot be improved by any reweighting; and (vi) a first minimality result, that no single-terminal instance is a counterexample for any nonnegative cost vector, together with a necessary condition at two terminals. The verification is a replication; items (ii) and (iv)-(vi) are, to our knowledge, new. The two-terminal case remains open, and we show why a natural argument for it fails. The counterexample instance is not ours, and no claim is made about priority or attribution. Source code, data and computational records: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH (problems/optimization-geometry/unsplittable-flow-cost).
title: An independent exact verification of the 2026 counterexample to Goemans' unsplittable-flow cost conjecture, with the violation constant it forces

summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . Interactive studio: https://tailwatch.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1, descending frame 124D_04854_171313 (2016-2018), redistributed under the Copernicus free-and-open licence with LiCSBAS attribution (Morishita et al. 2020); provenance in data/derived/tw-real-cf.provenance.json.
title: TailWatch: An InSAR Deformation-Monitoring and Inverse-Velocity Failure-Forecasting Studio, on Synthetic Sentinel-1 and Real Campi Flegrei

summary: The rise of generative AI has enabled the production of high-fidelity synthetic tabular data across fields such as healthcare, finance, and public policy, raising growing concerns about data provenance and misuse. Watermarking offers a promising solution to address these concerns by ensuring the traceability of synthetic data, but existing methods face many limitations: they are computationally expensive due to reliance on the inverse process of large diffusion models, struggle with mixed discrete-continuous data, or lack robustness to common post-processing attacks. To address these limitations, we propose TAB-DRW, an efficient and robust post-editing watermarking scheme for synthetic tabular data. TAB-DRW embeds watermark signals in the frequency domain: it normalizes heterogeneous features via the Yeo-Johnson transformation and standardization, applies the discrete Fourier transform (DFT), and adjusts the imaginary parts of adaptively selected entries according to precomputed pseudorandom bits. To further enhance robustness and efficiency, we introduce a novel rank-based pseudorandom bit generation method that enables row-wise retrieval without incurring storage overhead. Experiments on five benchmark tabular datasets show that TAB-DRW achieves strong detectability and robustness against post-processing and adaptive attacks, while preserving high data fidelity and fully supporting mixed-type features.
title: Robust Spectral Watermark for Synthetic Tabular Data

summary: This dataset contains the complete computational records from two 500-sequence demonstration runs performed with ENZTRA (Enzyme Redesign and Triage Automation), a reproducible and resumable workflow for reference-guided enzyme redesign. ENZTRA integrates reference preparation, RFdiffusion2 backbone generation, LigandMPNN sequence design, DLKcat and CatPred kinetic prediction, strict kinetic selection, Boltz-2 structural assessment, quality control, provenance tracking, and publication-oriented reporting. Both demonstrations used an active Escherichia coli phytase derived from PDB 1DKP and myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (IHP; phytate) as the reference enzyme-substrate system. Each run generated 50 RFdiffusion2 backbones and 10 LigandMPNN sequences per backbone, yielding 500 candidate sequences. The deposit contains two project archives: release-500: A short-scaffold demonstration using a requested design-length range of 150-180 residues. Fourteen of the 500 candidates satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion and proceeded to Boltz-2 structural assessment. The remaining 486 candidates were rejected, and no data-quality failures were detected. release-500b: A full-length comparison using a requested scaffold length of 410 residues, matching the reference sequence length. All 500 candidates passed the specified data-quality checks, but none satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion because their predicted turnover numbers were below the reference prediction. Consequently, no candidate proceeded to Boltz-2 assessment. The ENZTRA strict kinetic gate requires both a predicted turnover number ( k cat) above the corresponding reference value and a predicted Michaelis constant ( K m) below the reference value. Passing data-quality checks is therefore distinct from passing kinetic selection. The archives include validated biological inputs, design requests, RFdiffusion2 specifications and execution records, generated backbones, TRB and functional-site mappings, LigandMPNN outputs, consolidated sequence files, DLKcat and CatPred inputs and predictions, kinetic and selection tables, Boltz-2 inputs and outputs where applicable, quality-control tables, publication figures, workflow-state records, qualification reports, and reproducibility manifests. These results are computational predictions intended to demonstrate workflow execution, traceability, recovery, candidate selection, and reporting. They do not establish catalytic activity, structural correctness, expression, stability, or experimental improvement. All prioritized candidates require appropriate experimental validation. ENZTRA source code, installation instructions, and a step-by-step reproduction tutorial are available at: https://github.com/Olanrewaju-Durojaye/ENZTRA
title: ENZTRA demonstration dataset: reference-guided phytase redesign and kinetic-structural triage

summary: A 3D city model is only as accurate as its building heights, and a model built from open data mostly infers those heights, from a mapped floor count, a height raster or a default value, rather than taking them from a mapped height. Maqueta reconstructs real places from open geospatial layers, with terrain from the Copernicus GLO-30 surface model, building footprints and roads from Overture Maps, water, green areas and rail from OpenStreetMap, population from GHS-POP, and building heights from the Google Open Buildings 2.5D raster where it has coverage, and it records for every building how its height was obtained. Across the 118 baked places and 4.05 million buildings, 8.8% of heights come from a mapped height attribute, 6.4% from a mapped floor count, 73.2% from the Open Buildings 2.5D height raster, itself a model estimate from satellite imagery, and 11.6% from a default prior of 8 m. A public LoD2 reference exists for two of the places, both in the Netherlands, where the raster has no coverage. Against the 3D BAG, the fused heights have a root-mean-square error of 3.1 m at Delft, with a bias of -0.1 m, and of 8.3 m at Amsterdam, with a bias of -6.6 m; the Amsterdam figure rests on 50 reference buildings. The raster heights, which supply most of the buildings, are not validated by this benchmark, and public ground truth for open-data building heights is scarce. Interactive tool and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RES_Maqueta . Fusion core: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_GeoScena .
title: Maqueta: Height Provenance in Open-Data 3D Urban Reconstruction Across 118 Places

summary: Overview Ouranos Reconstruction – RDPS-CaPA (ORRC) version 1.0 is a dataset designed to approximate the Canadian Surface Reanalysis (CaSR)  and provide continuity beyond the CaSR period. It is produced from the  Regional Deterministic Prediction System (RDPS) , with precipitation fields adjusted using the 6-hour and 24-hour Regional Deterministic Precipitation Analysis (RDPA)  products generated by the CaPA system. ORRC v1.0 provides hourly surface and near-surface meteorological fields at 0.09° (~10 km) resolution on a rotated regular latitude–longitude grid covering North America, Central America, and nearly all of Greenland, from 2015 to present. It supports near-real-time climate monitoring and is intended for operational climate services, event monitoring, and the routine update of climate indicators without waiting for future CaSR releases. Temporal coverage: 2015-01-01 to near-present Spatial resolution: 0.09° (~10 km) Temporal resolution: Hourly and daily File format: NetCDF  Data provider: Ouranos Version: 1.0 Products Two products are available: ORRC v1.0 : The original hourly and daily meteorological fields. ORRC-a v1.0 : A bias-adjusted daily product available for daily mean precipitation and daily mean, minimum, and maximum near-surface air temperature. ORRC-a v1.0 is adjusted relative to CaSR v3.2 using the 2020–2024 overlap period. Day-of-year mean corrections are calculated using a 31-day moving window. Additive corrections are applied to temperature, and multiplicative corrections are applied to precipitation. ORRC-a is recommended for applications requiring closer consistency with the historical conditions represented by CaSR v3.2. The original ORRC product retains the characteristics of the operational products from which it is constructed and may be preferable when these characteristics are important, when hourly data are required, or for variables for which the bias-adjustment approach is not appropriate.  Variables ORRC v1.0 includes precipitation (CaPA reconstructed and model precipitation), near-surface air temperature, dew point temperature, specific humidity, relative humidity, surface and sea-level pressure, downwelling shortwave and longwave radiation, near-surface wind components, wind speed, and wind direction. A complete table of variable names, units, frequencies, and source identifiers is provided in the accompanying technical documentation . Code, documentation, and data availability The ORRC-ORRC-v1.0.1.zip archive contains a snapshot of the source code and documentation associated with ORRC v1.0. The accompanying technical report describes the input data, processing workflow, precipitation adjustment, bias adjustment, evaluation, and known limitations. The complete ORRC and ORRC-a datasets are hosted separately and can be accessed through the Ouranos THREDDS Data Server . Archived source release: https://github.com/Ouranosinc/ORRC/releases/tag/ORRC-v1.0.1   GitHub repository: https://github.com/Ouranosinc/ORRC Version specific view: https://github.com/Ouranosinc/ORRC/tree/ORRC-v1.0.1
title: Ouranos Reconstruction – RDPS-CaPA (ORRC) v1.0 / Reconstruction Ouranos – RDPS‑CAPA (RORC) v1.0

summary: Benchmark package accompanying the manuscript “Failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems: residual-error decoupling, an attainable-accuracy bound and an identifiability benchmark”. The package contains: the exact solution of the beam–two-mass moving-load benchmark and the modal and RK4 reference baselines on the same grid; the training campaign with random seeds, network configurations, collocation densities, training budgets, measured wall-clock times, residuals and relative-L2 errors for every run; the inverse-problem (speed and load-amplitude) campaign with its identifiability verdict; the weights of the reference physics-informed network; and the scripts that regenerate every figure, table and number of the paper. It supports two results of the paper: the residual–error decoupling for moving singular sources, and the attainable-accuracy bound obtained by fitting the same architecture to the exact solution. All runs are seeded, so the accuracy–cost comparison reported in the paper can be re-derived without retraining.
title: Benchmark package — failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems (v1.0)

summary: This paper refines the finiteness conjecture for stability architectures and establishes the strongest currently provable results. A stability claim is treated as a profile specifying the object, state space, evolution, perturbation class, projection, failure region, time horizon, and obstructing gap or invariant. An architecture abstracts the structural core: the category of state spaces, the operator class, the gap functional, and the transport obstruction. The paper proves that stability cannot be classified from the trajectory map alone; the full profile matters. For linear systems, there are exactly three distinct architectures: dissipative, geometric or gradient, and Hamiltonian. For model-theoretic stability, the classification is finite and known: stability, NIP, simplicity, and rosiness. This logical classification is an analogy, not a direct translation to dynamics. For Hamiltonian systems, conditional finiteness identifies five candidate mechanisms: KAM persistence, Nekhoroshev confinement, Trojan resonance-gap suppression, symmetry constraint, and barrier obstruction. For statistical systems, four candidates appear: uniform, partial, and non-uniform hyperbolicity, plus rate conditions. In both cases, finiteness follows only if the lists are exhaustive, which remains conjectural. The paper also proves an intra-architecture transfer theorem, a qualified cross-architecture rigidity theorem, and a proposition on overlapping architectures. Transfer works within a shared architecture because estimates depend only on structural data. Rigidity blocks transfer between structurally distinct architectures unless additional structure exists. Overlap is possible, allowing multiple stability mechanisms and multiple failure routes. The general classification problem is undecidable, proved by reduction from the halting problem. Limitations include autonomous, finite-dimensional, smooth dynamics; time-dependent, infinite-dimensional, non-smooth, and nonlinear cases remain open. The consequences concern analog laboratories, engineering design by architecture selection, and a finite core of stability theory. The central message is that the finiteness conjecture is not vacuous: it holds where testable, while full generality awaits resolution of the exhaustiveness conjectures.
title: Stability Architectures: A Finite Classification of Provable Cases

summary: Ethiopia's rain-fed agricultural systems are highly vulnerable to climate variability, yet national-scale projections often mask critical sub-regional heterogeneity. This study presents high-resolution (≤1 km) bioclimatic projections for Ethiopia using a multi-model ensemble of CMIP6 General Circulation Models under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios for mid-century (2041–2070) and end-century (2071–2100) periods. Statistical downscaling with quantile mapping bias correction was applied to resolve fine-scale spatial patterns across Ethiopia's diverse agro-ecological zones. Results reveal three robust findings. First, warming is unequivocal and spatially heterogeneous, with mean annual temperatures projected to increase by 4–6°C under SSP5-8.5 by 2100, and with Belg and Bega seasons warming faster than Kiremt. Second, precipitation exhibits a pronounced west-east dichotomy: western basins (Baro-Akobo, Abay) show significant wetting (+46.7%), while eastern basins (Upper Wabe Shebele, Awash) undergo substantial drying (−50.3%). Third, hydroclimatic variability is amplifying faster than mean change, with increasing consecutive dry days (+30 to +40 days in the southeast), intensifying extreme rainfall (Rx1day, Rx5day), and delayed rainy season onsets. These divergent trajectories challenge uniform national adaptation policies and reveal a "winners and losers" framework for Ethiopian agriculture. Western regions face heightened flood and erosion risks, while eastern highlands confront accelerated aridity and water scarcity. The findings underscore the urgent need for region-specific adaptation strategies, including drought-resistant crop varieties in the east, flood-resilient infrastructure in the west, and integration of seasonal asymmetry data into national early-warning systems to strengthen climate resilience and protect rain-fed livelihoods.

summary: The COVID-19 pandemic has impacted global health, economy, and society, highlighting the need for a deeper understanding of viral mechanisms and immunity enhancement strategies. This study investigates the relationship between genetic variability in taste receptors, particularly TAS2R38, and COVID-19 susceptibility, as well as the role of nutrition in modulating immune function. Influenced by genetic diversity, taste perception plays a role in food preferences, which may affect immune responses. We collected data from 21 participants regarding their food preferences, COVID-19 history, and phenotypic classification of taste perception using phenylthiocarbamide (PTC) strips. Our findings indicate a non-significant negative correlation between body mass index (BMI) and COVID-19 symptom severity, with supertasters experiencing milder symptoms compared to tasters and non-tasters. Additionally, participants with a history of COVID-19 preferred sweeter foods, while those without a history favoured bitter-tasting foods. These results suggest that genetic variations in taste receptors and dietary choices may influence individual immune responses to viral infections. Although this study faced limitations due to sample size and genotyping challenges, it emphasises the potential role of personalised nutrition and genetic factors in enhancing immunity against COVID-19 and future health crises. Further research is recommended to explore genotypic variations and their interactions with dietary patterns in shaping immune responses.
title: Genetic Variability in Taste Receptors and Its Influence on COVID-19 Symptom Severity

summary: Version 1.1 (2026-09-19). Version 1.0 stated that the English rebuild could not be compared against the published English store, because the cleaning pass behind that store no longer exists as a script. That was wrong: the missing script only prevents reproducing the Japanese/Chinese method, while the old English store and its index were on disk throughout. The comparison is now made, with the control questions generated from the old store's own chunk text — exactly what the old index encoded — over 400 articles sampled by uniform stride from the both-store intersection. Whole corpus, nprobe 128: the old store returns recall@1 19.5, recall@5 33.5, MRR 25.1; v11b returns 39.2, 59.5 and 47.9, a gain of +22.8 MRR while searching a corpus 2.9 times larger. Section 8.4 is new and records how four passes of review let an untested caveat stand. The results of version 1.0 are unchanged. We re-read three Wikipedia retrieval indexes we had published ourselves and had been using in production — English, Japanese and Chinese, FAISS over intfloat/multilingual-e5-large — and found three defects, none of which had ever produced an error message. Chunks were cut by character count in front of a token window, so 13.7 % of the published Japanese chunks and 18.5 % of the Chinese ones ran past the encoder's 512-token limit and lost 21.7 % and 27.0 % of their tokens at embed time. The Kiwix licence footer, 184 characters of English legal text, sat inside 97.1 % of the published Japanese chunks and 92.9 % of the Chinese ones. The index type, IndexIVFPQ(m=64) , returned 45.4–47.1 % of the exact top-10 and cost 7.8 MRR in Japanese and 10.7 in English against exact search. Rebuilding the whole pipeline moved retrieval against the previously published artifact from 26.6 to 43.3 MRR in Japanese and 26.2 to 47.5 in Chinese, on a control question set generated from the old extractor's own output. The components are not separated, and the rebuild is not uniformly better: indexed-article coverage falls in two of three languages. Two results may generalise. Our own first benchmark ranked the defective extractor higher , because it queried by article title, a field the index also stores. And clipping the scalar quantiser's range to the 0.1–99.9 percentile of the residuals rather than their min/max raises top-10 agreement with exact search from 81.6 % to 85.2 % at the same 4 bits per dimension; the first attempt computed the quantiles on raw vectors and made the index substantially worse, because an IVF index encodes residuals. Three rounds of adversarial review are reported at equal prominence with the results. Round one rejected the first rebuild. Round two found sixteen unsupported statements in the draft. Round three found a defect in the release that the first two had both passed — the acceptance script had not been re-run on two of the three shipped indexes after they were re-encoded — and three measurements that round two had itself introduced while correcting other numbers. Scope. This reports what happened to three specific artifacts. It does not claim these defects are common elsewhere. The retrieval numbers come from synthetic questions generated by one local model with no human relevance judgements and no answerability check; the reconstructed standard error of one MRR figure is 2.2–2.9 points. Index-type comparisons were run on pools of 150,000–206,000 vectors, not at the shipped scale of 3–15.6 million. Nothing here is peer reviewed, certified, or independently replicated; every reviewer was a model instance commissioned by the author. AI co-observer disclosure. The forensic measurements, the rebuild, the three review rounds and the drafting were carried out with Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic) as a working instrument under human direction. The registered author is the human author alone.
title: What a Retrieval Index Loses Before Anyone Notices: Three Silent Defects in Three Published Wikipedia Embedding Indexes

summary: Background. Frailty is often raised as a reason to withhold complete revascularization from older patients after myocardial infarction, although the FIRE trial found no interaction between frailty and the benefit of physiology-guided complete revascularization. Objective. To estimate the cost-effectiveness of physiology-guided complete versus culprit-lesion-only revascularization after successful culprit-lesion percutaneous coronary intervention in patients aged 75 years or older with myocardial infarction and multivessel disease, overall and across Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) strata, from the German statutory health insurance perspective. Methods. A three-year cohort model with quarterly cycles was anchored to the FIRE marginal outcomes (primary composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or ischaemia-driven revascularization 22.9% versus 29.8%; cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction 12.8% versus 18.2%; heart-failure hospitalisation 14.3% versus 19.7%). Risks in CFS 1-3, 4 and 5-9 were obtained by external calibration that preserved these trial marginals, with a relative treatment effect common to all strata. Costs used 2026 German diagnosis-related-group tariffs. Every input was classified by provenance, and uncertainty was assessed with 20,000 probabilistic draws, one-way and scenario analyses, and break-even analysis. Results. Complete revascularization cost EUR 757 more per patient and yielded 0.056 additional quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of EUR 13,601 per QALY. Ratios were EUR 20,541 per QALY in CFS 1-3, EUR 8,640 in CFS 4 and EUR 8,662 in CFS 5-9. The probability of cost-effectiveness at EUR 30,000 per QALY was 92.5% overall and 78.6%, 96.5% and 97.7% across strata. At that value, the minimum three-year absolute reduction in the primary composite required for cost-effectiveness was 4.3 per 100 patients overall, against a modelled trial effect of 6.9. Staging the additional procedure as a separate admission was the most influential cost driver. Conclusions. Within three years, physiology-guided complete revascularization appears cost-effective at reference values of EUR 20,000 to EUR 50,000 per QALY, and estimated cost-effectiveness was not attenuated in the frailer strata. The stratum-specific estimates rest on external frailty calibration rather than on frailty-specific FIRE outcomes and are not evidence of effect modification.
title: Cost-Effectiveness of Physiology-Guided Complete Revascularization Across Frailty Strata in Older Patients with Myocardial Infarction: A German Analysis Informed by the FIRE Trial

summary: Our earlier note (rejected from an SC26 AI4S workshop, subsequently published as AIIT Bulletin Vol. 20) compared classical reduced-order models (POD, DMD) against naive neural surrogates (a fully-connected network, a CNN) on textbook-scale problems (lid-driven cavity, dam-break), on a single consumer GPU workstation. That note left five concrete gaps: no graph-based neural baseline, no industrially complex geometry, weak statistical evidence (nine snapshots, a single seed), no learned-dynamics counterpart to DMD, and no hyperparameter search for the neural baselines. This paper closes four of those five. The test case is an industrially representative two-phase stirred tank — a six-blade rotating impeller on a sliding (AMI) mesh, a bottom sparger injecting gas into water, ∼167k cells, solved with OpenFOAM's twoPhaseEulerFoam — run entirely on a single Mac Studio (Apple M4 Max, 14 cores, no discrete GPU). We benchmark five methods (POD, DMD, a neural network, a Graph Neural Operator, and a Deep Koopman autoencoder) on a genuine extrapolation task, backed by a 400-run statistical-robustness sweep, hyperparameter searches for both neural baselines, a check across three impeller speeds, and a four-level forcing-irregularity sweep (quasi-periodic through chaotic, direction-reversing impeller motion) intended to locate DMD's failure point. DMD wins consistently across every data scale, truncation choice, operating condition, and forcing-irregularity level tested, at both a 1 s and an extended 3 s prediction horizon – we did not find the failure threshold we went looking for, and report that directly. The search was not wasted, however: a Deep Koopman autoencoder, competitive at 1 s, degrades sharply at 3 s from compounding autoregressive rollout error (exposure bias); two independent, cheap mitigations – a physical [0, 1] clip mirroring the Graph Neural Operator's own implicit stabilization, and multi-step scheduled-sampling training – each recover roughly a third to a half of the gap without closing it, confirming the diagnosis. A separate, unplanned check turns up a sharper result: ranking methods by mass conservation rather than per-cell accuracy reorders them completely, with the most accurate method (DMD) only third-best at holding a basic physical invariant. We treat all three investigations as concrete instances of a broader, practical question for this community: how much genuine, open-ended scientific investigation — not just a fixed benchmark — can a single high-end workstation support before an HPC allocation is actually necessary? All code, case files, and Colab notebooks are released on GitHub for reproduction.
title: How Far Does One Workstation Go? A Pre-HPC Efficiency Check for Industrial-Scale CFD and Reduced-Order Model Benchmarking

summary: Full Changelog : https://github.com/attogram/fantastic-octo-giggle/compare/0001...0002 42 and the Open Error Foundation: An Academic Interpretation Abstract The relationship between 42 and the Open Error Foundation (i.o.) can be understood as more than a recurring joke, reference, or organizational number. It can function as a compact epistemological model for the Foundation itself. The central problem of 42 is not that the answer is numerically wrong. It is that an answer can be generated before the question has been adequately established. That distinction is extraordinarily relevant to an organization concerned with artificial intelligence, institutional systems, scientific error, education, and continuous experimentation. The Foundation's two central statements, "Error is the message" and "Sesame Street is the teacher," consequently form a complementary methodology. The first treats failure, contradiction, mismatch, and unexpected output as potentially informative evidence. The second establishes a method for responding to uncertainty: return to fundamentals, ask understandable questions, experiment, explain, repeat, and learn. 42 then represents the unresolved question at the center of the entire process. The organization does not claim to possess the ultimate answer. It asks whether we have actually identified the question. The 42 Problem: An Answer Without a Question The cultural origin of 42 is Douglas Adams' The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. Within the story, the enormous computer Deep Thought spends millions of years calculating the answer to the "Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything." The result is: The fundamental joke is subsequently revealed: the beings who commissioned the computation do not actually know what the Ultimate Question is. A later computational project is therefore required to determine the question itself. This creates a particularly interesting epistemological structure: Question → computation → answer has been replaced by: computation → answer → realization that the question is unknown → search for the question That reversal is precisely what makes 42 relevant to AI. A modern AI system can produce an extraordinarily fluent answer to an inadequately specified question. It can produce something that looks like knowledge before the underlying problem has been properly framed. The resulting failure is therefore not necessarily: "The machine calculated incorrectly." It may instead be: "We never established what needed to be calculated." That is a much deeper category of error. Error Is the Message The Open Error Foundation's phrase "Error is the message" can therefore be interpreted as an epistemological proposition rather than simply a creative slogan. Ordinarily, error is treated as something to eliminate: correct → incorrect → remove incorrect But scholarship in the philosophy and history of science has explicitly examined the possibility that errors can have productive epistemic roles. Jutta Schickore's historical analysis argues that error can contribute to scientific practice rather than merely obstruct it. More recently, Douglas Allchin's Toward a Philosophy of Error in Science develops an explicit framework around "error analytics," including error types, error signatures, checkpoints, error probes, and negative knowledge. His argument is that scientific practice is not merely about accumulating confirmations; it also depends on systematically identifying and managing ways in which knowledge can fail. This provides a serious academic foundation for the Foundation's intuition. An error can contain information about: the assumptions behind a system the limits of a model the framing of a question the quality of available evidence hidden dependencies institutional incentives human misunderstanding the difference between intended and actual behavior In this interpretation: An error is an observation about a system. summary: A three-signal stopping rule for iterative LLM refinement derived from the Möbius theory stack: an equilibrium-distance surrogate d̂_R (RZGM meaning-equilibrium layer), an update-free-recurrence and diversity-collapse detector pair (Reflective Homeostasis Layer), and a hard reflection-depth cap (MUSE bounded reflection). Pre-registered study: 500 English prose-refinement tasks across ten domains, two generator models (Gemma4 12B-IT-QAT and 26B-A4B-IT-QAT), 8,000 generations, 999 blind position-swapped pairwise judgments. The governor cuts refinement tokens by 36.6% / 33.1% (bootstrap 95% CIs 33.6-39.5% / 30.3-35.9%) versus an always-eight-iterations baseline — 2.2-3.4x a naive convergence stop — at a measured quality cost reported at equal prominence: 38.0% / 36.6% of judged comparisons lost overall, a majority among actual interventions (61.1% / 59.0%), with measured cost almost perfectly collinear with output length. A full-data ablation shows the saturation signal is simultaneously the savings engine and the dominant cost source, yielding a measured two-point dial (10.0-11.5% savings at 8.2-11.8% loss rate with saturation disabled). Pre-release adversarial verification (four independent refuter passes) confirmed all headline statistics against the raw data and caught an inverted flagship anecdote: the corpus's two catastrophic degenerations (~50 verbatim paragraph repetitions) were selected once and avoided once by the governor, undetected in both cases — set-based trigram signals are structurally blind to within-output verbatim repetition. All tasks, rollouts, verdicts, audit votes, and analysis code are released in the companion repository. AI co-observer: Claude Fable 5 (Anthropic) — working method only; blind pairwise judging by Claude subagents under a position-swapped two-vote protocol; four independent adversarial refuter passes preceded release; the registered author is the human author alone. Version 1.1 (2026-09-19): adds (i) a proof-backed clarification that at window 3 the saturation condition is exactly “three identical consecutive non-rewrite change types” (the 0.70 threshold is inert there; companion note DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22842506), (ii) a pre-registered evaluation of a repetition-ratio guard as a fourth, roll-back signal — fires on both known collapses and 200/200 synthetic inflations, on 0 of 7,998 remaining published generations, 0 of 60 template expansions, and 0 of 960 held-out generations (verdict GO; pre-registration commit a89f722 precedes all evaluation data), and (iii) an expanded AI-authorship disclosure. All v1.0 numbers are unchanged. Version 1.2 (2026-09-19): adds (i) a length-stratified reanalysis of the 621 judged governor pairs (loss rate 92% where the early text is under 60% of the final length, 16.1% at near-equal length; 31 losses vs 4 wins at matched length, sign test p < 10 -5 — evidence of a content cost independent of length, not a decomposition of the headline cost), (ii) a held-out replication on 60 tasks authored after the fourth-signal pre-registration (token reduction 34.5% / 34.5%, loss rate 31.7% / 36.7%, main-study values inside the held-out intervals), and (iii) an online-intervention verification: an incremental governor reproduces all 1,000 published decisions (0 mismatches) and, run as a genuine online loop on the 60 held-out tasks with the 12B generator, generates 319 of 480 iterations with a stop distribution indistinguishable from the offline policy (permutation p = 0.46). All v1.0 and v1.1 numbers are unchanged. Version 1.3 (2026-09-19): adds a pre-registered length-matched re-judging (100 governor-loss pairs with early/final length ratio < 0.80; final text truncated at sentence boundaries to the early text's word count): the early text beats the length-matched final in 94/100 (loss 4%), and the full final beats its own truncation in 100/100. Pre-registered label: the losses on this stratum are attributab

summary: MATLAB implementation, per-item numeric results and figure code for the study "Dissociating Prompt Quality from Response Compliance in Automated Prompt-Engineering Assessment". A four-agent evaluator running on a locally hosted Qwen 2.5-7B-Instruct judge scores each prompt as an artifact before any response exists, then scores the resulting response twice on identical items: once against criteria extracted from that prompt, and once against a fixed rubric that never sees it. Verifiable constraints are checked with the IFEval reference implementation rather than model-generated labels. The whole pipeline runs on consumer CPU hardware with no external API calls. Contents: src/ the MATLAB agents and run scripts; scripts/ the IFEval verifier and the figure code; data/ a SHA-256 manifest of all 4,275 benchmark prompts and the filtered IFEval subset; results/ per-item results for the main run (n = 500) and the ablation (n = 120), the construct-validation output and the IFEval verification output. summary: Administrative disability registries record certified cases, not disability as such: a person absent from the registry may lack certification because no certifiable impairment exists, because access to an evaluation board was unavailable, or because an evaluation is pending - three epistemically distinct situations that a single observed count cannot, by itself, distinguish. This paper reframes a nationwide descriptive analysis of Ecuador's National Disability Registry (Registro Nacional de Discapacidades, CONADIS/MSP; cut-off December 2023; N = 113,203 aggregated records representing 480,776 certified persons across 222 province-canton units) as an instance of typed abstention applied to administrative subregistration. We distinguish "not registered" (no consta: absence of a positive record, uninformative about the underlying condition) from a hypothetical "registered negative" (consta que no: an explicit denial after evaluation, a state that exists within the underlying certification process but is not exposed in the published open-data resource used here) and from internally conflicting evidence. Data quality auditing verified 100% structural completeness across all eight operational fields. The demographic and clinical profile shows a predominance of males (56.48%), adults aged 51 years and older (47.13%), physical disabilities (44.87%), and moderate impairment severity (45.78%). Guayaquil and Quito concentrate 30.83% of absolute registration volume, yet fall to the 134th and 144th of 221 population-normalized ranks, below the national median. Because the published registry cannot, by construction, separate certification capacity from underlying need, we add an illustrative synthetic simulation in which two data-generating mechanisms - pure certification-capacity heterogeneity and pure prevalence heterogeneity, each confounded with population size - produce observable correlations between the normalized rate and population that differ by only 0.021 (Pearson r = 0.949 vs. 0.928) despite sharing no causal mechanism, formalizing why the normalized rate cannot be read as need without an explicit, currently unavailable, capacity signal. We situate this identification problem within the literature on disability statistics (the Washington Group on Disability Statistics; the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health), administrative and missing-data quality, and evidential reasoning frameworks for typed indeterminacy (Dempster-Shafer belief functions, three- and four-valued logics, AGM belief revision), none of which have previously been applied to a cantonal-level disability registry of this kind.
title: Typed Abstention in Administrative Disability Registries: Certification Intensity, Subregistration, and the Limits of Cantonal Normalization in Ecuador's National Disability Registry (2023)

summary: This dataset supports the study “UDDPG-Net: Energy- and Fairness-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for Resource Allocation in Underwater Communication Networks.” It contains the simulation data, experimental results, and lake-based acoustic measurement records used for evaluating UDDPG-Net. The simulation data cover underwater acoustic propagation, mobility, interference, energy states, resource-allocation decisions, training configurations, benchmark comparisons with Random, Greedy, PPO, TD3, SAC, MADDPG, and DDPG-GA, as well as scalability, ablation, exploration, SHAP, computational-efficiency, and robustness analyses. The field-test component corresponds to six campaigns conducted in Fengquan Lake, Xinxiang, China, and includes environmental, motion, acoustic-channel, and packet-level variables such as water temperature, salinity, pH, conductivity, sound speed, ambient-noise PSD, link distance, subband SNR, propagation delay, Doppler shift, and packet reception ratio. Reconstructed raw-format field logs are additionally provided to reproduce the organization and statistical characteristics reported in the manuscript; these files are clearly identified as reconstructed records and should not be interpreted as original instrument acquisition files. README files and structured metadata are included to describe the variables, units, experimental conditions, and correspondence between the released data and the figures and tables in the paper.
title: UDDPG-Net: Energy- and Fairness-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for Resource Allocation in Underwater Communication Networks

summary: README – Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics (CGMD) Simulations of PIEZO1 and TRPM4 Overview This dataset contains coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) simulations of the mechanosensitive ion channel PIEZO1 and the non-mechanoprotective ion channel TRPM4 embedded in lipid bilayers. The simulations comprise 500 ns of equilibrium followed by membrane stretching simulations designed to investigate how PIEZO1's distinctive triskelion blade architecture redistributes mechanical stress and preserves membrane integrity. All simulations were performed using GROMACS with the Martini 3 force field. Independent replicate simulations (n = 3) were conducted for each system to ensure statistical robustness and reproducibility. Simulation Details Parameter Description Molecular dynamics engine : GROMACS v2021.2 Force field : Martini 3 Membrane model : Lipid bilayer containing either PIEZO1 or TRPM4 Equilibration : 500 ns Stretching simulations : Three independent replicates (n = 3); 50 ns Simulation temperature, pressure, and all additional parameters are provided in the accompanying simulation input files (.mdp) and described in the associated publication. Biological Significance PIEZO1 is a mechanosensitive ion channel whose unique triskelion blade architecture protects cellular membranes from mechanical failure. Its extended peripheral blades redistribute mechanical stress across the lipid bilayer, reducing localized stress accumulation and delaying membrane rupture during mechanical loading. This dataset enables quantitative investigation of how membrane protein architecture influences membrane mechanics, force redistribution, and mechanoprotection using coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. Dataset Structure 1. Equilibrium Simulations These simulations characterize the equilibrated membrane environment surrounding each ion channel before mechanical loading. Simulation length: 500 ns PIEZO1_equilibrium.pdb PIEZO1_equilibrium.xtc TRPM4_equilibrium.pdb TRPM4_equilibrium.xtc 2. Membrane Stretching Simulations Following equilibration, membrane stretch was induced using semi-isotropic pressure coupling, with −5 bar applied in the membrane plane (x–y) while maintaining +1 bar normal to the bilayer (z-axis) using the Parrinello–Rahman barostat. PIEZO1 PIEZO1_Stretch_R1.pdb PIEZO1_Stretch_R1.xtc PIEZO1_Stretch_R1.edr PIEZO1_Stretch_R2.pdb PIEZO1_Stretch_R2.xtc PIEZO1_Stretch_R2.edr PIEZO1_Stretch_R3.pdb PIEZO1_Stretch_R3.xtc PIEZO1_Stretch_R3.edr TRPM4 TRPM4_Stretch_R1.pdb TRPM4_Stretch_R1.xtc TRPM4_Stretch_R1.edr TRPM4_Stretch_R2.pdb TRPM4_Stretch_R2.xtc TRPM4_Stretch_R2.edr TRPM4_Stretch_R3.pdb TRPM4_Stretch_R3.xtc TRPM4_Stretch_R3.edr Data Usage The trajectory (.xtc) and coordinate (.pdb) files can be analysed using standard molecular dynamics software, including GROMACS, VMD, and PyMOL. The (.edr) files are also provided for energy calculations and to be utilized -b 0 -e 50000 (time 0 - 50 ns) These simulations support quantitative analyses described in the associated publication. PIEZO1 safeguards membranes under mechanical stress via permeation-independent structural adaptation and calcium-dependent cytoskeletal reinforcement. Cell Press Blue. (2026). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpblue.2026.100128
title: PIEZO1 safeguards membranes under mechanical stress using MD simulation

summary: This paper offers a critical analysis of the European Union as a model of regional integration and examines its contribution to peace and to the effectiveness of the United Nations system. Set against the background of the failure of the League of Nations, the study argues that the post-1945 international order has endured largely because it is supported by strong regional institutions. Using the EU as the primary case study, the paper contends that by institutionalizing peace within Europe through economic interdependence, binding law, and supranational governance, the EU has created a zone of stability that reduces the burden on global governance structures. Furthermore, the paper analyzes how the EU functions as a support pillar for the United Nations under Chapter VIII of the UN Charter. Through financial contributions, peacekeeping partnerships, and coordinated diplomacy, the EU has reinforced multilateralism and provided capacity for conflict management and development. A comparative perspective is also drawn with other regional bodies such as ECOWAS to demonstrate a broader pattern of regional-global cooperation. The paper concludes that the longevity of the United Nations, compared to the League of Nations, can be partly explained by this two-level architecture of global and regional governance. While the EU’s support for the UN is substantial, it is also inconsistent, as internal EU divisions sometimes undermine collective action. Ultimately, the study shows that effective regional integration is a critical condition for sustaining peace and strengthening the United Nations system.
title: The European Union and Regional Integration: A Critical Analysis of Peacebuilding and Support for the United Nations System

summary: Abstract The stability of the banking sector is fundamental to economic growth and financial system resilience, particularly in developing economies such as Nigeria.  However, and sadly enough, global, recent and recurring failure risks and collapses of banks which have been blamed on poor external audit qualities, are counter-productive to national economic development.  Therefore, the broad objective of this study was to study the effect of audit quality on failure risks of listed deposit money banks in Nigeria between the period 2009 and 2024. This study adopted both descriptive and ex-post facto research designs.  Using secondary data extracted from audited financial reports of 11 censored (from a population of 11) deposit money banks listed on the Nigerian Exchange Group, (NGX), and analyzing one hundred and seventy-six firm year observations using regression with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors analysis technique, the findings revealed that audit firm size (AUFS) significantly improve bank Z score, [coef. = 0.638 (p-value = 0.005)], audit report timeliness (ARTIME) significantly reduces bank Z score [coef. = −0.400 (p-value = audit committee diligence (ACDI) revealed a positive insignificant effect respectively on Z score of listed deposit money banks in Nigeria during the period under consideration. Based on the above findings, it was concluded that audit quality in the Nigerian banking sector is not uniformly effective, rather, its effect on bank failure risks is selective, with only specific audit mechanisms demonstrating the capacity to significantly enhance financial solvency, thereby suggesting that the effectiveness of external audit as a safeguard against bank failure risks depend not merely on its presence, but likely on factors such as depth, credibility, and functional execution of its key components.   this study concluded that audit.  Consequently, this study recommended among others, that listed deposit money banks in Nigeria, alongside regulators and external auditors, should prioritize substantive governance quality, auditor competence and independence, rigorous audit execution, timely financial reporting, risk-sensitive audit remuneration, coordinated assurance mechanisms, and proactive internal control systems over mere procedural compliance, in order to strengthen transparency, reinforce market confidence, and enhance long term financial stability in line with Agency theory.
