summary: We present an HTTP threat detection system embedded in a production reverse proxy that achieves sub-500ns per-request inference latency. The system combines a depth-limited CART decision tree with a compact two-layer MLP in an ensemble architecture, where the tree provides fast-path classification and the MLP refines uncertain cases. Model weights are exported as Rust `const` arrays, enabling zero-allocation deployment with no runtime deserialization. We formalize structural safety properties of the ensemble in the Lean~4 theorem prover, establishing a three-tier verification approach covering structural invariants, weight-dependent decision bounds, and floating-point error propagation. In initial small-scale trials on a combined dataset of production logs, CSIC-2010, and CIC-IDS2017-derived features, the ensemble achieves >99% validation accuracy for both scanner and DDoS detection, with tree inference completing in under 2ns and full ensemble inference under 6ns. We discuss limitations of the current training data and outline directions for scaling to larger, human-labeled corpora.
title: Sub-Microsecond HTTP Threat Detection with Decision Tree–MLP Ensembles and Lean 4 Verification

summary: Embarrassingly parallel workloads, such as parameter sweeps, Monte Carlo simulations, and hyperparameter searches, are pervasive in research computing, yet running a single experiment across a mix of laptops, lab servers, cloud virtual machines (VMs), and high-performance computing (HPC) clusters still demands ad hoc Secure Shell (SSH) tunnels, port forwarding, and scheduler-specific scripts. We present DART, a job distributor that turns any such mix of machines into a single shared queue. DART pairs a Dockerized job server with a one-line worker command-line interface (CLI); a hosted Hub automates reverse tunneling, worker authentication, and public endpoint provisioning, so collaborators on any network, including those behind network address translation (NAT) or using a personal laptop, can join an experiment with a single API-key and no firewall changes. This makes DART especially effective for researchers who combine Advanced Cyberinfrastructure Coordination Ecosystem: Services & Support (ACCESS)-provisioned HPC resources [1] with institutional clusters and personal workstations, federating all resources under one queue with no per-site configuration. All communication is encrypted end-to-end, and access is controlled through API-key authentication and a personal identification number (PIN)-protected dashboard. Researchers create experiments, define parameter grids, and monitor jobs entirely from a web dashboard; a work-conserving scheduler dispatches jobs on demand, exploits resource heterogeneity, and automatically re-queues failures. In a real-world deployment of 37,720 jobs across 68 heterogeneous machines spanning an institutional HPC cluster, a national ACCESS resource, and personal computers, the observed run completed in approximately eight days. DART’s dynamic allocation achieved a simulation-derived 35× speedup over static partitioning (≈4 days vs. ≈139 days), reducing a multi-month workload to days.
title: DART: Distributed Assignment of Research Tasks for Heterogeneous Compute Environments

summary: Anticoncentration is a key ingredient in complexity theoretic arguments for quantum advantage from Gaussian boson sampling. Here we prove polynomial small ball anticoncentration for complex Gaussian transpose Gram hafnians and complex symmetric Gaussian hafnians. For a k × 2n matrix X with independent standard complex Gaussian entries, we establish polynomial small ball anticoncentration for haf(XᵀX) under k ≥ 4n and n²/k = O(log n). For hafnians of 2n × 2n complex symmetric Gaussian matrices, polynomial small ball anticoncentration holds for every n ≥ 1. In both ensembles, any prescribed inverse polynomial failure probability can be achieved with an inverse polynomial small ball radius, uniformly over all centers. These results go beyond moment based anticoncentration by controlling the probability of small hafnian amplitudes. The proof combines Fourier compression with conditional Wishart geometry to handle dependent hafnian cofactors. Files: main.pdf contains the main article (14 pages); supplement.pdf contains the supplementary proofs and additional results (33 pages). Related Lean verification sources: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22554594 and https://github.com/HongruZhao/ComplexGramHafnians.
title: Local Anticoncentration for Gaussian Boson Sampling via Conditional Wishart Geometry

summary: This dataset contains analysis-ready spatial data on informal urban conditions, heat and flood exposure, slum population, and malaria burden across sub-Saharan Africa.   The deposit includes a processed subnational dataset with 4,320 administrative units, a 44-feature country/region boundary layer, annual HI406 and WBGT30 heat-exposure rasters for 2011–2020, a slum-population raster, a complete data dictionary, descriptive statistics, raster metadata, provenance documentation, rights guidance, and integrity checksums.   The vector data are provided as ESRI Shapefiles and the gridded data as GeoTIFF files. All spatial datasets use WGS 84 (EPSG:4326). The raster grids contain 1,141 columns by 1,235 rows at approximately 0.060362 degrees per cell.   The malaria indicators are population-weighted estimates mapped from source administrative-unit means onto the common slum-population grid. The original upstream flood and malaria source layers are not redistributed in this record. Users should consult the included README, data dictionary, provenance documentation, sources and limitations, and data-use notes before reuse.   This record contains data and data documentation only. Code, notebooks, manuscripts, figures, and supplementary documents are maintained separately in the project repository: https://github.com/JinRuii/informal-urban-climate-malaria-ssa
title: Analysis-ready spatial data on informal urban conditions, climate exposure and malaria burden across sub-Saharan Africa

summary: Self-contained synthetic seismic–gravity inversion models, Python operators, seeds, archived and profile-initialized fits, regional controls, posterior samples, figures and validation records for the manuscript by Emilson P. Leite and Maiara M. Gonçalves. Version 0.11 adds a four-start calibration on 96 paired noise comparisons, an audit of unchanged displayed seismic median errors, exact n=32 coverage intervals, and empirical bias–variance accounting of the existing regional controls. The four-start shortcut did not reproduce the profile solutions; the manuscript retains 32 profile-initialized noise pairs for each free-geometry configuration. Fixed-geometry ensembles retain 256 realizations. Wide local intervals under a free trend coexist with systematic target-property errors directed towards the prior. No new posterior chains were generated in this revision. Field observations and third-party BP-model data are not required.
title: When gravity adds useful information to interpretation-conditioned post-stack seismic inversion: reproducibility archive

summary: Code and data to reproduce all analyses and the figure in O'Dea et al. (2026) "Failure of a tropical upwelling rapidly collapsed Panama's anchoveta fishery and its exports". Includes Python scripts for the reef-logger upwelling indices, the bay-wide composite index, the observer set records, the anchoveta length and weight series, the unified 1956 to 2025 landings series, and the main figure together with every statistic reported in the paper. Data include weekly sonde casts from the three deep central stations of the Bay of Panama, continuous reef temperature loggers from the Gulf of Panama running since 1995, the Copernicus Marine Service biogeochemical reanalysis of net primary production (1994 to 2026), anchoveta and thread herring landings spliced from the digitised national stock assessment (1956 to 2014) and the ARAP landings register (2015 to 2025, 332,610 records across 206 taxa), 3,077 onboard observer purse-seine set records (2017 to 2025), 645 dockside proximate assays of landed anchoveta (2016 to 2025), and fish oil and fishmeal export tabulations from INEC customs statistics (1997 to 2025). The archive is self-contained and rebuilds the figure and all reported statistics from the raw sources whenever the derived and figures directories are deleted. Instructions for use, including execution order, software dependencies, directory structure, the provenance of every source and the known caveats, are in README.md. Data are released under CC BY 4.0 and code under the MIT Licence.
title: Code and data for: Failure of a tropical upwelling rapidly collapsed Panama's anchoveta fishery and its exports

summary: Abstract Distributed version control preserves source states, ancestry, branching, merging, and collaboration with extraordinary success. It does not ordinarily require engineering intent, failed approaches, claim scope, verification evidence, residual disagreement, or continuation state to exist as typed repository objects. Those records instead tend to be distributed across commit prose, review systems, issue trackers, CI logs, artifact stores, chat, and human memory. This disclosure explores a broader version-control model for software developed by humans and agents without claiming that content addressing, provenance, attestations, change-oriented versioning, or agent memory are new in isolation. Gemel models an evidence-bearing change : a content-addressed relation from an exact input state to an exact output state, linked to intent, operations, producer provenance, claims, evidence, residuals, verification scope, and causal context. Trajectories preserve completed, rejected, interrupted, superseded, and inconclusive work. Claims remain declarations rather than stored truth; support and readiness are derived conservatively from evidence, residuals, freshness, supersession, and policy. Context manifests and checkpoints provide bounded continuation surfaces without requiring private reasoning transcripts. The inspected Rust reference implementation defines deterministic canonical encoding, BLAKE3-256 identities, immutable objects, mutable refs, rebuildable indexes, 24 object families, Git-carried exchange, deterministic Git projection, semantic indexing, native and hosted synchronization, agent queries, policy checks, and an FRF court runner. For this paper, the supplied source archive was independently built in a clean temporary directory and cargo test --all-targets completed 236 tests with zero failures. This result is implementation-specific conformance evidence. It is not evidence that Gemel improves developer productivity, agent reliability, or industrial outcomes. Gemel composes with the Forensic Residual Framework (FRF) as an evidence plane and with FRF-Fuzz as a discovery plane. The paper situates that composition against Git facilities, patch algebra, provenance models, software-supply-chain attestations, reproducible builds, software archives, event sourcing, rationale capture, and agent memory. It discloses alternative embodiments and defines falsifiable evaluations for handoff quality, repeated-error reduction, evidence freshness, reconciliation, interoperability, context cost, storage overhead, and longitudinal fuzzing. Its principal claim is architectural: software history can be represented as an engineering graph in which source state, intent, evidence, residual uncertainty, negative knowledge, and continuation state possess explicit identity and scope. Whether that representation earns its operational cost remains an empirical question. Keywords distributed version control; Git; agentic software development; evidence engineering; provenance; content addressing; Merkle DAG; software agents; developmental trajectories; negative knowledge; residual primacy; FRF; FRF-Fuzz; reproducibility; software archaeology; semantic lineage; source provenance; event sourcing.

summary: Reproducibility release 1.1.0 for Ocean Engineering manuscript OE-D-25-10458. This package supports a controlled Rotterdam-Yokohama comparison of the Suez, Cape and Northern Sea Route corridors using three predefined strategic waypoint philosophies per corridor. The archive contains the Python routing and analysis code, all nine waypoint definitions, frozen maritime-network geometries and scenario/leg distances, dual-coastline quality-assurance and local-repair reports, 0.05/0.025-degree convergence outputs, sourced OpenStreetMap Suez Canal geometry and provenance, downstream time/fuel/CO2 analyses, exponent and vessel-reference sensitivities, and the frozen manuscript sources and figures. The routing method uses searoute 1.4.3, WGS84 distance recomputation and no great-circle fallback. The reproduction command stages the archived routes, regenerates downstream tables and copies the included figure assets. A full routing rerun additionally requires the externally distributed Natural Earth 10 m v5.1.1 and GSHHG 2.3.7 full L1 coastline datasets. Tests and release checks are documented in the archive. The comparison is strategic and does not predict realised voyages or commercial viability.
title: Effects of Route Representation on Distance and Downstream Voyage Implications in Europe–Asia Trade: A Comparison of the Suez, Cape, and Northern Sea Route Corridors

summary: Description : Classeur canonique source-par-source (66 feuilles) sous-tendant l'article "Data-Audited Elastic, Hardness, and Heterostructure-Compatibility Assessment of MAX Phases and MXenes". Contient : l'audit élastique et de dureté des 44 phases MAX canoniques et 11 MXenes ; l'audit de provenance des paramètres de maille ; la matrice de compatibilité dataset-pair des hétérostructures MAX/MAX (461 combinaisons admissibles) ; le screening de durcissement par contraste élastique validé contre des superréseaux expérimentaux (Fiantok et al. 2023) ; les propriétés d'interface (module biaxial, énergie de cohérence) ; la contrainte thermique de désaccord ; et la synthèse applicative orientée revêtements de protection. Chaque feuille documente sa source primaire (DOI), son statut de preuve (EXPERIMENTAL/DFT/UNKNOWN explicite), et une feuille de validation trace les vérifications de non-régression appliquées à chaque étape. Tableaux supplémentaires S1 (tenseur élastique et modules dérivés des 44 phases MAX canoniques), S2 (constantes élastiques 2D et E2D dérivé de 11 systèmes MXene), S3 (valeurs de dureté expérimentales avec charge, méthode, état d'échantillon et niveau de preuve). Format soumission-prêt correspondant aux tableaux cités dans le manuscrit.

summary: Supporting material for the manuscript "Subacute oral glyphosate impairs testicular function in male mice (Mus musculus): a threshold-anchored dose-response study of steroidogenesis, sperm quality, redox balance and spermatogenic histopathology" (Elbeeh, Filfilan, Filfilan and Filfilan), submitted to Drug and Chemical Toxicology (Taylor & Francis). Forty adult male Swiss albino (ICR) mice, 8-10 weeks old and 22.1-25.5 g at allocation, received vehicle (distilled water) or technical-grade glyphosate at 10, 50 or 100 mg/kg/day by oral gavage for 28 days, n = 10 per group. The dose range brackets the regulatory no-observed-adverse-effect level of approximately 50 mg/kg/day. Endpoints measured in the same 40 animals: body and testis weight; serum testosterone, LH and FSH; epididymal sperm concentration, progressive motility, viability and morphology; testicular malondialdehyde, reduced glutathione, superoxide dismutase and catalase; and testis histopathology stained with haematoxylin-eosin and with periodic acid-Schiff, assessed by the Johnsen tubular-maturation score and by measurement of seminiferous tubule diameter, germinal epithelial height and graded lesion severity. Sections were digitised on a Philips UltraFast Scanner at the x20 level (0.5 micrometres per pixel) and reviewed in the Philips PathologySuite viewer; morphometry was performed in ImageJ v1.54 with semi-automated annotation in QuPath v0.4.3 on fields exported at the native scan resolution. Contents: S1, the manufacturer's Certificate of Analysis for the test article (Sigma-Aldrich 337757, lot MKCZ1523, purity at least 96 per cent, CAS 1071-83-6); S2, analytical kits, instruments, assay conditions and intra- and inter-assay coefficients of variation; S3, the analysis and figure-plotting code; S4, the complete per-animal dataset underlying every figure and table; S5, the benchmark-dose model set with BMD and BMDL10 values; and Supplementary Figure S6 with its caption, showing the histomorphometry and graded lesion scores of Table 4 with individual animal values overlaid. README.md gives the full manifest. Every value reported in the manuscript can be recomputed from S4 using the code in S3. Statistics: continuous endpoints were compared by Welch's ANOVA with the Games-Howell post-hoc test; ordinal lesion grades by the Kruskal-Wallis test with Holm-adjusted Dunn's post-hoc test; monotonic trend by the Jonckheere-Terpstra test; and the endpoint family was controlled at a false-discovery rate of 5 per cent (Benjamini-Hochberg). The Johnsen tubular-maturation score was nominated in advance as the primary endpoint; every other endpoint is secondary. Ethics: all procedures were approved by the Bioethics Committee of Umm Al-Qura University, Makkah, Saudi Arabia (approval no. HAPO-02-K-012-2025-04-2781) and were conducted in accordance with the ARRIVE 2.0 guidelines. These 40 animals also support the cardiotoxicity, neurotoxicity and immunotoxicity arms of the same programme, which are reported separately under the same approval number. Licensed CC BY 4.0.
title: Supplementary data and analysis code for: Subacute oral glyphosate impairs testicular function in male mice (Mus musculus)

summary: Supporting material for the manuscript "Subacute oral glyphosate impairs testicular function in male mice (Mus musculus): a threshold-anchored dose-response study of steroidogenesis, sperm quality, redox balance and spermatogenic histopathology" (Elbeeh, Filfilan, Filfilan and Filfilan), submitted to Drug and Chemical Toxicology (Taylor & Francis). Forty adult male Swiss albino (ICR) mice, 8-10 weeks old and 22.1-25.5 g at allocation, received vehicle (distilled water) or technical-grade glyphosate at 10, 50 or 100 mg/kg/day by oral gavage for 28 days, n = 10 per group. The dose range brackets the regulatory no-observed-adverse-effect level of approximately 50 mg/kg/day. Endpoints measured in the same 40 animals: body and testis weight; serum testosterone, LH and FSH; epididymal sperm concentration, progressive motility, viability and morphology; testicular malondialdehyde, reduced glutathione, superoxide dismutase and catalase; and testis histopathology stained with haematoxylin-eosin and with periodic acid-Schiff, assessed by the Johnsen tubular-maturation score and by measurement of seminiferous tubule diameter, germinal epithelial height and graded lesion severity. Sections were digitised on a Philips UltraFast Scanner at the x20 level (0.5 micrometres per pixel) and reviewed in the Philips PathologySuite viewer; morphometry was performed in ImageJ v1.54 with semi-automated annotation in QuPath v0.4.3 on fields exported at the native scan resolution. Contents: S1, the manufacturer's Certificate of Analysis for the test article (Sigma-Aldrich 337757, lot MKCZ1523, purity at least 96 per cent, CAS 1071-83-6); S2, analytical kits, instruments, assay conditions and intra- and inter-assay coefficients of variation; S3, the analysis and figure-plotting code; S4, the complete per-animal dataset underlying every figure and table; S5, the benchmark-dose model set with BMD and BMDL10 values; and Supplementary Figure S6 with its caption, showing the histomorphometry and graded lesion scores of Table 4 with individual animal values overlaid. README.md gives the full manifest. Every value reported in the manuscript can be recomputed from S4 using the code in S3. Statistics: continuous endpoints were compared by Welch's ANOVA with the Games-Howell post-hoc test; ordinal lesion grades by the Kruskal-Wallis test with Holm-adjusted Dunn's post-hoc test; monotonic trend by the Jonckheere-Terpstra test; and the endpoint family was controlled at a false-discovery rate of 5 per cent (Benjamini-Hochberg). The Johnsen tubular-maturation score was nominated in advance as the primary endpoint; every other endpoint is secondary. Ethics: all procedures were approved by the Bioethics Committee of Umm Al-Qura University, Makkah, Saudi Arabia (approval no. HAPO-02-K-012-2025-04-2781) and were conducted in accordance with the ARRIVE 2.0 guidelines. These 40 animals also support the cardiotoxicity, neurotoxicity and immunotoxicity arms of the same programme, which are reported separately under the same approval number. Licensed CC BY 4.0.

summary: This dataset accompanies the SpiderNet paper on modeling directional cell–cell meta-interactions from spatial omics data. It contains saved analysis results, plotting inputs, interactive visualization data, and benchmark outputs for eight study workflows.  Together with the SpiderNet code repository, these files support reproduction of the documented saved-result figures and exploration of trained results. A manifest provides file checksums and restoration paths. The collection does not include all raw inputs required for retraining every analysis.

summary: Data repository for "Newborn neurons in the adult hippocampus regulate representational drift in area CA3 and memory plasticity." Computational environment: Python 3.6, MATLAB 2022a, Windows 10. Dataset: Representative data from 3 mice (IDs: XS149, XS155, XS156) across 4 time points (newborn neuron ages: 4–7 weeks or 8–9 weeks). Each time point contains 3 sessions: a Context A noCLZ baseline, and two post i.p. clozapine injection sessions (Context A CLZ and Context B CLZ). Raw data (2-photon TIFF images and behavioral data) and processed outputs are organized by session in subfolders. Processing pipeline: Imaging and behavioral data aligned via Behavioral data processing.ipynb Raw TIFFs motion-corrected with Suite2p Motion-corrected data denoised with DeepCAD Denoised data reprocessed with Suite2p for motion correction and ROI extraction; ROIs manually inspected via the Suite2p GUI Spatial information computed and place cells classified via Spatially-tuned place cell detection.py Downstream analyses performed with MATLAB scripts in code/Matlab/
title: Newborn neurons in the adult hippocampus regulate representational drift in area CA3 and memory plasticity

summary: This paper asks a narrow question. Lyapunov stability, geometric stability, and statistical stability are all described as spectral-gap properties. The gaps act on different operators, live on different spaces, and survive different perturbations. The informal habit of treating them as one nested hierarchy is correct for convex wells and hyperbolic sinks. It is not correct as a statement about dynamical systems in general. The paper replaces that habit with a comparison theorem. A stability claim is a profile: an evolution, a perturbation class, a projection, and a failure set. Comparative type can change when the map is held fixed and only the projection changes. Three statistical properties are kept distinct. The first is weak continuity of an invariant measure under perturbation. The second is a spectral gap of a transfer or Fokker–Planck operator on a named function space. The third is differentiability of the measure in the perturbation parameter. These three can hold together. They can also separate. The proved implications are scoped. A positive Hessian implies Lyapunov stability of a mechanical equilibrium and a dissipative Jacobian gap for a gradient flow. A hyperbolic sink gives weak continuity of a Dirac family and does not give mixing on a positive-dimensional density space. Uniform hyperbolicity gives a transfer-operator gap on an anisotropic space and, in the perturbation class of Keller and Liverani, weak continuity of an SRB family. Partial hyperbolicity yields a gap only after restriction to the hyperbolic factor. Nonuniform hyperbolicity with a Young tower yields a slower, tail-controlled rate and is compatible with instability of almost every orbit. A prescribed decay for a piecewise expanding map or a hypocoercive generator need not come from any hyperbolic splitting. Architectural estimates do not transfer between structurally distinct operator classes. In one linear-quadratic noise model the three classical tests return the same number. In a double well they separate. The paper does not claim that statistical mechanisms are finite, and it does not prove that averaging a frequency-gap Hamiltonian system produces a kinetic spectral gap.
title: Which Spectral Gaps Imply Which: Lyapunov, Geometric, and Statistical Criteria

summary: ElectromagneticFields v0.9.0 Diff since v0.8.0 Breaking Changes Everything here that requires a change to calling code, and what to do about it. The sections below give the reasoning; this is the checklist. @code , its seven per-preset variants, code and load_equilibrium are gone. Generated code is no longer injected into a module. Build a field by calling FieldFunctions(equ) , which returns a value: it can be constructed inside a function, stored, and passed to a vector field through a problem's parameters , none of which the old module injection allowed. The ~450 scalar functions are ~41 generics returning tensors, each taking the field first. B¹(t, q) becomes B♯(field, t, q)[1] and dAᵢdxⱼ(t, q) becomes DA♭(field, t, q)[i, j] . The names use the musical isomorphisms — ♭ covariant, ♯ contravariant, ♮ physical, the bare letter the magnitude — and Changed below has the full old-to-new table. Every one of the ~444 old scalar values is an entry of one of the new tensors. The per-field submodules are flattened into the package. Solovev.ITER() is SolovevEquilibriumITER() , ThetaPinch.init() is ThetaPinchEquilibrium() , and so on for every field; Solovev.ITER(xpoint = true) and its siblings are gone in favour of the named X-point constructors. The coordinate helpers X , Y , Z , R , r , θ , ϕ and r² are package-level generics and deliberately not exported — reach them as ElectromagneticFields.R or through coordinates(field) . periodicity is no longer answered or exported by this package. GeometricBase.periodic(equ) gives one Bool per coordinate instead, and a chart with no method for it raises a MethodError when a field is built from it, deliberately. Code that assembled a (xmin, xmax) tuple from rangemin / rangemax behind a single flag must now build it from periodic and the bounds. periodicity = periodic(field) is silently wrong , not an error: a three-element Bool vector destructures to (false, false) . parameters(field) for a Solov'ev equilibrium now includes the coefficient vector c . A₃ reads it, so it travels with the other parameters instead of being frozen into the code. A field rebuilt after clear_field_cache!() is equal to a few ULP, not bit for bit. Compare two builds of one field with a tolerance rather than == . SymEngine is no longer a dependency ; Symbolics, StaticArrays, GeometricBase and ConstructionBase are. The Julia floor stays 1.10. Added Aqua.jl runs as part of the test suite , in test/aqua_tests.jl , which calls Aqua.test_all . This package carried no package-level quality check of any kind before, so all eight — method ambiguities, unbound type parameters, undefined exports, the agreement between Project.toml and test/Project.toml , stale dependencies, [compat] bounds, type piracy and persistent tasks — start from a clean pass rather than from a list of known failures. Two of them cover something this package does structurally. test_piracies covers the eight methods added to GeometricBase's periodic , functions and parameters , each of which dispatches on a type defined here; a new chart family brings a periodic method with it, so the property outlasts any list of the sites. test_undefined_exports covers an export list dominated by the musical-isomorphism accessors, which are defined across src/analytic/ rather than beside the export. The test suite has a test/Project.toml of its own , carrying Aqua, CairoMakie, LinearAlgebra, SafeTestsets, StaticArrays and Test, each with a [compat] bound. The [extras] and [targets] sections of the package's Project.toml are gone with it, together with the CairoMakie bound that belonged to them. Test dependencies that only [extras] declared carried no bounds at all, which is what Aqua.test_deps_compat reports. Changed The symbolic engine is replaced from SymEngine.jl to Symbolics.jl. Dependencies change: SymEngine is removed, Symbolics, StaticArrays, GeometricBase and ConstructionBase are added. Julia floor stays 1.10. GeometricBase is there for the generic names functions ,

summary: This paper refines the finiteness conjecture for stability architectures and establishes the strongest currently provable results. A stability claim is treated as a profile specifying the object, state space, evolution, perturbation class, projection, failure region, time horizon, and obstructing gap or invariant. An architecture abstracts the structural core: the category of state spaces, the operator class, the gap functional, and the transport obstruction. The paper proves that stability cannot be classified from the trajectory map alone; the full profile matters. For linear systems, there are exactly three distinct architectures: dissipative, geometric or gradient, and Hamiltonian. For model-theoretic stability, the classification is finite and known: stability, NIP, simplicity, and rosiness. This logical classification is an analogy, not a direct translation to dynamics. For Hamiltonian systems, conditional finiteness identifies five candidate mechanisms: KAM persistence, Nekhoroshev confinement, Trojan resonance-gap suppression, symmetry constraint, and barrier obstruction. For statistical systems, four candidates appear: uniform, partial, and non-uniform hyperbolicity, plus rate conditions. In both cases, finiteness follows only if the lists are exhaustive, which remains conjectural. The paper also proves an intra-architecture transfer theorem, a qualified cross-architecture rigidity theorem, and a proposition on overlapping architectures. Transfer works within a shared architecture because estimates depend only on structural data. Rigidity blocks transfer between structurally distinct architectures unless additional structure exists. Overlap is possible, allowing multiple stability mechanisms and multiple failure routes. The general classification problem is undecidable, proved by reduction from the halting problem. Limitations include autonomous, finite-dimensional, smooth dynamics; time-dependent, infinite-dimensional, non-smooth, and nonlinear cases remain open. The consequences concern analog laboratories, engineering design by architecture selection, and a finite core of stability theory. The central message is that the finiteness conjecture is not vacuous: it holds where testable, while full generality awaits resolution of the exhaustiveness conjectures.

summary: Abstract Distributed version control preserves source states, ancestry, branching, merging, and collaboration with extraordinary success. It does not ordinarily require engineering intent, failed approaches, claim scope, verification evidence, residual disagreement, or continuation state to exist as typed repository objects. Those records instead tend to be distributed across commit prose, review systems, issue trackers, CI logs, artifact stores, chat, and human memory. This disclosure explores a broader version-control model for software developed by humans and agents without claiming that content addressing, provenance, attestations, change-oriented versioning, or agent memory are new in isolation. Gemel models an evidence-bearing change : a content-addressed relation from an exact input state to an exact output state, linked to intent, operations, producer provenance, claims, evidence, residuals, verification scope, and causal context. Trajectories preserve completed, rejected, interrupted, superseded, and inconclusive work. Claims remain declarations rather than stored truth; support and readiness are derived conservatively from evidence, residuals, freshness, supersession, and policy. Context manifests and checkpoints provide bounded continuation surfaces without requiring private reasoning transcripts. The inspected Rust reference implementation defines deterministic canonical encoding, BLAKE3-256 identities, immutable objects, mutable refs, rebuildable indexes, 24 object families, Git-carried exchange, deterministic Git projection, semantic indexing, native and hosted synchronization, agent queries, policy checks, and an FRF court runner. For this paper, the supplied source archive was independently built in a clean temporary directory and cargo test --all-targets completed 236 tests with zero failures. This result is implementation-specific conformance evidence. It is not evidence that Gemel improves developer productivity, agent reliability, or industrial outcomes. Gemel composes with the Forensic Residual Framework (FRF) as an evidence plane and with FRF-Fuzz as a discovery plane. The paper situates that composition against Git facilities, patch algebra, provenance models, software-supply-chain attestations, reproducible builds, software archives, event sourcing, rationale capture, and agent memory. It discloses alternative embodiments and defines falsifiable evaluations for handoff quality, repeated-error reduction, evidence freshness, reconciliation, interoperability, context cost, storage overhead, and longitudinal fuzzing. Its principal claim is architectural: software history can be represented as an engineering graph in which source state, intent, evidence, residual uncertainty, negative knowledge, and continuation state possess explicit identity and scope. Whether that representation earns its operational cost remains an empirical question. Keywords distributed version control; Git; agentic software development; evidence engineering; provenance; content addressing; Merkle DAG; software agents; developmental trajectories; negative knowledge; residual primacy; FRF; FRF-Fuzz; reproducibility; software archaeology; semantic lineage; source provenance; event sourcing.
title: Gemel: Evidence-Native Version Control for Agentic Software Development - Longitudinal Engineering Memory, Residual-Aware Change Graphs, Git Interchange, and Reproducible Agent Handoffs

summary: This paper asks a narrow question. Lyapunov stability, geometric stability, and statistical stability are all described as spectral-gap properties. The gaps act on different operators, live on different spaces, and survive different perturbations. The informal habit of treating them as one nested hierarchy is correct for convex wells and hyperbolic sinks. It is not correct as a statement about dynamical systems in general. The paper replaces that habit with a comparison theorem. A stability claim is a profile: an evolution, a perturbation class, a projection, and a failure set. Comparative type can change when the map is held fixed and only the projection changes. Three statistical properties are kept distinct. The first is weak continuity of an invariant measure under perturbation. The second is a spectral gap of a transfer or Fokker–Planck operator on a named function space. The third is differentiability of the measure in the perturbation parameter. These three can hold together. They can also separate. The proved implications are scoped. A positive Hessian implies Lyapunov stability of a mechanical equilibrium and a dissipative Jacobian gap for a gradient flow. A hyperbolic sink gives weak continuity of a Dirac family and does not give mixing on a positive-dimensional density space. Uniform hyperbolicity gives a transfer-operator gap on an anisotropic space and, in the perturbation class of Keller and Liverani, weak continuity of an SRB family. Partial hyperbolicity yields a gap only after restriction to the hyperbolic factor. Nonuniform hyperbolicity with a Young tower yields a slower, tail-controlled rate and is compatible with instability of almost every orbit. A prescribed decay for a piecewise expanding map or a hypocoercive generator need not come from any hyperbolic splitting. Architectural estimates do not transfer between structurally distinct operator classes. In one linear-quadratic noise model the three classical tests return the same number. In a double well they separate. The paper does not claim that statistical mechanisms are finite, and it does not prove that averaging a frequency-gap Hamiltonian system produces a kinetic spectral gap.
title: Which Spectral Gaps Imply Which: Lyapunov, Geometric, and Statistical Criteria

summary: ElectromagneticFields v0.9.0 Diff since v0.8.0 Breaking Changes Everything here that requires a change to calling code, and what to do about it. The sections below give the reasoning; this is the checklist. @code , its seven per-preset variants, code and load_equilibrium are gone. Generated code is no longer injected into a module. Build a field by calling FieldFunctions(equ) , which returns a value: it can be constructed inside a function, stored, and passed to a vector field through a problem's parameters , none of which the old module injection allowed. The ~450 scalar functions are ~41 generics returning tensors, each taking the field first. B¹(t, q) becomes B♯(field, t, q)[1] and dAᵢdxⱼ(t, q) becomes DA♭(field, t, q)[i, j] . The names use the musical isomorphisms — ♭ covariant, ♯ contravariant, ♮ physical, the bare letter the magnitude — and Changed below has the full old-to-new table. Every one of the ~444 old scalar values is an entry of one of the new tensors. The per-field submodules are flattened into the package. Solovev.ITER() is SolovevEquilibriumITER() , ThetaPinch.init() is ThetaPinchEquilibrium() , and so on for every field; Solovev.ITER(xpoint = true) and its siblings are gone in favour of the named X-point constructors. The coordinate helpers X , Y , Z , R , r , θ , ϕ and r² are package-level generics and deliberately not exported — reach them as ElectromagneticFields.R or through coordinates(field) . periodicity is no longer answered or exported by this package. GeometricBase.periodic(equ) gives one Bool per coordinate instead, and a chart with no method for it raises a MethodError when a field is built from it, deliberately. Code that assembled a (xmin, xmax) tuple from rangemin / rangemax behind a single flag must now build it from periodic and the bounds. periodicity = periodic(field) is silently wrong , not an error: a three-element Bool vector destructures to (false, false) . parameters(field) for a Solov'ev equilibrium now includes the coefficient vector c . A₃ reads it, so it travels with the other parameters instead of being frozen into the code. A field rebuilt after clear_field_cache!() is equal to a few ULP, not bit for bit. Compare two builds of one field with a tolerance rather than == . SymEngine is no longer a dependency ; Symbolics, StaticArrays, GeometricBase and ConstructionBase are. The Julia floor stays 1.10. Added Aqua.jl runs as part of the test suite , in test/aqua_tests.jl , which calls Aqua.test_all . This package carried no package-level quality check of any kind before, so all eight — method ambiguities, unbound type parameters, undefined exports, the agreement between Project.toml and test/Project.toml , stale dependencies, [compat] bounds, type piracy and persistent tasks — start from a clean pass rather than from a list of known failures. Two of them cover something this package does structurally. test_piracies covers the eight methods added to GeometricBase's periodic , functions and parameters , each of which dispatches on a type defined here; a new chart family brings a periodic method with it, so the property outlasts any list of the sites. test_undefined_exports covers an export list dominated by the musical-isomorphism accessors, which are defined across src/analytic/ rather than beside the export. The test suite has a test/Project.toml of its own , carrying Aqua, CairoMakie, LinearAlgebra, SafeTestsets, StaticArrays and Test, each with a [compat] bound. The [extras] and [targets] sections of the package's Project.toml are gone with it, together with the CairoMakie bound that belonged to them. Test dependencies that only [extras] declared carried no bounds at all, which is what Aqua.test_deps_compat reports. Changed The symbolic engine is replaced from SymEngine.jl to Symbolics.jl. Dependencies change: SymEngine is removed, Symbolics, StaticArrays, GeometricBase and ConstructionBase are added. Julia floor stays 1.10. GeometricBase is there for the generic names functions ,

summary: This paper refines the finiteness conjecture for stability architectures and establishes the strongest currently provable results. A stability claim is treated as a profile specifying the object, state space, evolution, perturbation class, projection, failure region, time horizon, and obstructing gap or invariant. An architecture abstracts the structural core: the category of state spaces, the operator class, the gap functional, and the transport obstruction. The paper proves that stability cannot be classified from the trajectory map alone; the full profile matters. For linear systems, there are exactly three distinct architectures: dissipative, geometric or gradient, and Hamiltonian. For model-theoretic stability, the classification is finite and known: stability, NIP, simplicity, and rosiness. This logical classification is an analogy, not a direct translation to dynamics. For Hamiltonian systems, conditional finiteness identifies five candidate mechanisms: KAM persistence, Nekhoroshev confinement, Trojan resonance-gap suppression, symmetry constraint, and barrier obstruction. For statistical systems, four candidates appear: uniform, partial, and non-uniform hyperbolicity, plus rate conditions. In both cases, finiteness follows only if the lists are exhaustive, which remains conjectural. The paper also proves an intra-architecture transfer theorem, a qualified cross-architecture rigidity theorem, and a proposition on overlapping architectures. Transfer works within a shared architecture because estimates depend only on structural data. Rigidity blocks transfer between structurally distinct architectures unless additional structure exists. Overlap is possible, allowing multiple stability mechanisms and multiple failure routes. The general classification problem is undecidable, proved by reduction from the halting problem. Limitations include autonomous, finite-dimensional, smooth dynamics; time-dependent, infinite-dimensional, non-smooth, and nonlinear cases remain open. The consequences concern analog laboratories, engineering design by architecture selection, and a finite core of stability theory. The central message is that the finiteness conjecture is not vacuous: it holds where testable, while full generality awaits resolution of the exhaustiveness conjectures.
title: Stability Architectures: A Finite Classification of Provable Cases

summary: This repository contains the code and data accompanying the article “A Physics-Informed B-Spline Reconstruction of Flow Data,” published in Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering (CMAME). The package includes numerical inputs, model coefficients, and analysis and plotting scripts for the one-dimensional convection–diffusion, two-dimensional Burgers, and lid-driven-cavity examples presented in the paper. For the lid-driven-cavity case, the flow data are included, but the Firedrake solver, its computational environment, and the scripts used to generate these data are not provided. This archive preserves the version associated with the published article. The code will continue to be maintained and updated in the PI-BSR GitHub repository .
title: A Physics-Informed B-Spline Reconstruction of Flow Data: Reproducibility Package

summary: This work presents reusable mathematical bridges extracted from the Chronos formal-verification programme and related Lean developments in constrained dynamics, quantum mechanics, gravity, operator theory, partial differential equations, and Yang–Mills theory.   The purpose of the work is to make formally developed mathematical structures available for reuse beyond the physical problems in which they were originally constructed.   The paper develops four primary reusable connections.   First, it presents an internal-time framework for constrained Hamiltonian systems. When a candidate clock has a nonvanishing rate along a constrained trajectory, the system can be reparameterized with respect to that clock, producing relational evolution. This connects directly with the existing Chronos frozen-to-flow and Wheeler–DeWitt formalization.   Second, it develops a quantum–classical shared-time bridge based on expectation-value evolution. For suitable Hamiltonians, including the constant-force system already treated in the formal programme, quantum expectation values obey exact classical equations of motion.   Third, it extracts a reusable operator-theoretic chain connecting coercive lower bounds to positive spectral bounds, invertibility, and quantitative inverse or resolvent control. Together with cutoff and graph-core machinery developed during the Yang–Mills formalization, this provides reusable infrastructure for unbounded operators in quantum mechanics and partial differential equations.   Fourth, it presents the general inverse-distance field structure underlying the existing Chronos gravity formalization. A radial inverse-distance potential produces an inverse-square gradient, satisfies the three-dimensional vacuum Laplace equation away from the source, and has radius-independent spherical flux. The same mathematical structure can therefore be instantiated in Newtonian gravity, electrostatics, Green-function theory, and other potential problems.   The central goal is compositional reuse. Rather than treating each formal proof as an isolated endpoint, the work identifies intermediate machine-checkable theorem structures that can serve as starting points for additional formal developments.   Immediate applications include relational clock models, Wheeler–DeWitt and constrained systems, Ehrenfest and semiclassical quantum dynamics, electrostatic inverse-square fields, Schrödinger operators, spectral-gap arguments, elliptic PDEs, gauge systems, and other operator-theoretic problems.   This paper accompanies the broader Chronos formal-verification programme and is intended as an openly reusable mathematical and formal-physics resource.
title: Reusable Formal Bridges from Chronos Verification: Internal Time, Quantum–Classical Dynamics, Operator Control, and Inverse-Distance Fields

summary: Resumen La diversidad de formas utilizadas para registrar los campos de autor y afiliación constituye uno de los principales problemas que afectan la normalización de los datos bibliográficos y, en consecuencia, el tiempo de procesamiento, la fiabilidad de los indicadores métricos y la delimitación del corpus utilizado en los análisis bibliométricos. En este contexto, el presente trabajo tiene como objetivo proponer los requerimientos necesarios para mejorar los procesos de normalización de datos en software destinado al análisis métrico de información científica. Para ello, se realizó un diagnóstico de los principales métodos y técnicas empleados internacionalmente para la normalización y desambiguación de datos bibliográficos. Como resultado, se establecen los requerimientos para el desarrollo de una aplicación automatizada de preprocesamiento de datos orientada a estudios métricos. La propuesta contempla la estructura de la base de datos, las tareas y etapas del procesamiento, así como los algoritmos que deberán integrarse en la aplicación. En particular, se plantea la combinación de diferentes algoritmos para abordar la desambiguación de los campos de autor y afiliación institucional. La propuesta busca contribuir al desarrollo de herramientas más eficientes y confiables para el preprocesamiento de datos en estudios bibliométricos. Palabras clave: normalización de datos; desambiguación de autores; normalización de afiliaciones; procesamiento de datos; bibliometría; minería de datos; análisis bibliométrico; preprocesamiento de datos. Abstract The diversity of formats used to record author and affiliation fields represents one of the main challenges affecting the normalization of bibliographic data and, consequently, processing time, the reliability of metric indicators, and the delimitation of the corpus used in bibliometric analyses. In this context, this study aims to propose the requirements needed to improve data normalization processes in software designed for the metric analysis of scientific information. To this end, a diagnosis was conducted of the main methods and techniques used internationally for the normalization and disambiguation of bibliographic data. As a main result, the study establishes the requirements for the development of an automated data preprocessing application for metric studies. The proposal specifies the database structure, processing tasks and stages, as well as the algorithms to be integrated into the application. In particular, it proposes combining different algorithms to address the disambiguation of author and institutional affiliation fields. The proposed approach aims to contribute to the development of more efficient and reliable tools for data preprocessing in bibliometric studies. Keywords: data normalization; author disambiguation; affiliation normalization; data processing; bibliometrics; data mining; bibliometric analysis; data preprocessing.

summary: Read the 74-page Split-Zero paper . Complete LaTeX, cumulative sources, citations and checks ; results and exact proof locators ; matching GitHub source edition . The Split-Zero programme represents finite zero-divisor classes of the completed Riemann zeta function by polynomials in an arithmetic theta-source Hilbert space. The metric on the observation kernel is obtained by minimizing over all original polynomial representatives. This edition calculates how that metric changes with polynomial degree. It gives every Christoffel–Darboux covariance entry, including reflected-node collisions and divided derivatives; retains the full correction after coefficient compression; and expresses the four-cutoff determinant ratio as a product of exact degree-step factors. The paired quartet relation proves a strict finite kernel contraction. Its magnitude at the unresolved large-degree kq scale is not evaluated, and no RH conclusion is claimed. Programme citations in the paper are clickable links to actual public proof sources, with exact locations where available. The same source links are included in the three complete cumulative LaTeX successors. The source archive includes a machine-readable link registry and restores two previously unpublished cited proofs. Older cumulative citations still needing an exact source match remain explicitly identified in that registry; no guessed destination is presented as verified. Classical sources retain their human authorship: Gernot Akemann and Graziano Vernizzi, Characteristic Polynomials of Complex Random Matrix Models , Nuclear Physics B 660 (2003), 532–556 ; the named authors of the NIST DLMF orthogonal-polynomial chapter ; and Jack Sherman and Winifred J. Morrison, Adjustment of an Inverse Matrix Corresponding to a Change in One Element of a Given Matrix (1950) . The last citation is historical and bibliographically checked; the rank-one calculation used here is proved directly. Earlier programme proofs remain separately credited. The reader contains ten complete proof bodies. The new CD and degree-step checkers pass 779 exact finite checks in each of ordinary and optimized Python, with 13 intended failure controls in each mode. These checks do not sample the actual period matrix or establish a large-degree asymptotic. The three large cumulative LaTeX manuscripts have not been freshly compiled in this edition. The 98 earlier standalone papers and archives remain. To respect Zenodo's 100-file limit, the preceding result index is retained byte-for-byte as predecessor062/RESULT_INDEX.json in the new source ZIP. Its original separate download also remains in the preceding immutable edition. Existing authorship, rights notices and access conditions are preserved. This successor does not claim that unfinished parallel-task work has been incorporated.
title: Split-Zero cohomology: exact degree changes in the arithmetic kernel metric

summary: This paper proposes a speculative Holographic–Multiway Theory (HMT) connecting the holographic principle, multiverse/quantum branching concepts, and Wolfram Physics. summary: In a recent publication, we derived a general relativity (RG) gauge-invariant solution modelling a granular universe composed of spherical bodies with a radial Gaussian density profile. In this framework, a cosmological constant Λ emerges natively from the gravitational self-energy of these discrete nodes. Energy conservation dictates a uniform compactness ratio M\/σ^2 across all bodies, a relation closely met by the elliptical galaxies as shown in the GAMA survey. This setup yields: Λ≈1/( 12 π^3 ) (κ a c^2   M/σ^2    )^2which, using the compactness measured in the GAMA survey, evaluates to Λ≈ 0.9×10^(-52)   m^(-2) , a value close to modern observations. The model predicts the R ∝ (1+z)^(-1.5) size scaling confirmed by the 3D-HST+CANDELS survey and, unlike standard ΛCDM theory, the model preserves total energy conservation. Before gas clouds collapsing around z≈3 the universe was mostly homogeneous resulting in this model to Λ≈0. During the Lyman-α forest epoch an intense gas clouds collapsing into stars and black holes occurred. We extended our RG model to purely radial collapsing nodes which gave Λ≈(κ a^3)/(4π^3 ) M/R^2   (d^2 R)/(dt^2 )<0. This backreaction force of the gas cloud collapse reached a peak around z ≈2 , and later declined around z≈1.5 when massive galaxies ran out of cold gas or experienced quenching shutting down their star formation. At this epoch, the galaxies began their assembling into their modern structures, raising the cosmological constant to its current baseline value. Integrating this dynamical Λ(z), while targeting the current Hubble parameter of H_0=73 km/s/Mpc , yields a perfect validation against the Planck cosmic microwave background angular scale θ^*=0.010410 rad and the latest DESI BAO data.   Notably, the model predicts a structure clustering amplitude of S_8≈0.81 in line with the BOSS/DESI Deep Scale Galaxy Clustering data survey. The proposed model successfully bypasses the need for an unexplained, speculative dark energy burst.
title: Addressing the Hubble tension with a dynamical Λ(z) induced by galactic gravitational self-energy and by backreaction force from gas cloud collapse

summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of tasks, motivating two important aspects of deployment: inference efficiency and output provenance, which can be tackled by speculative sampling and watermarking, respectively. However, recent works have shown that combining these two goals is highly nontrivial and can be potentially impossible. In this work, we develop a novel multi-draft speculative sampling algorithm based on Poisson processes that improves the frontier of this fundamental trade-off. The proposed algorithm has strong sampling efficiency on its own and, more interestingly, is naturally watermarkable: we can embed an unbiased watermark without degrading speculative acceptance. Moreover, our algorithm is based on an exact list-coupling-without-communication scheme, which yields a drafter invariance property that benefits both sampling and watermarking. It is the first multi-draft, drafter-invariant speculative sampling scheme that maintains both watermark strength and sampling efficiency, and we experimentally verify its strong performance in both aspects.
title: Watermarkable Multi-Draft Speculative Sampling via Poisson Processes

summary: Traditional unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) methods are designed to flag or localise deviations from a normative distribution, ignoring the underlying generative mechanisms of the anomalies. Yet the nature of an anomaly is often as important as its presence. We reformulate UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem, in which the objective is to infer the most probable corruption responsible for each observation. Our framework yields a probabilistic anomaly score as the energy of the inferred corruption parameters, and serves as a principled recipe for developing new UAD algorithms. We derive several existing methods as instances of the general framework, each corresponding to the same energy score under different modelling choices. Experimentally, we study the framework's components in a controlled setting, and improve object-class AUROC on the MVTec AD dataset by 2.3% by adapting the underlying corruption model. Finally, we validate the framework on a brain MRI benchmark, achieving strong detection performance while producing estimates of pathology intensity, bias, and geometry. Code is available at https://github.com/jgmyles/inverse-uad.

The continuation of this program—including the spectral equivalence conjecture of   with the zeros of , the complete theory of the spectral ratio, and the extensions to function composition and analytic continuation beyond   remains as the author's later work. summary: This article develops a practical, theoretical, methodological, and legal framework for the attribution and attributive analysis of artworks in museum collections. It preserves the core professional focus of museum attribution while reorganizing it into an IMRAD research structure and strengthening the relationship between connoisseurship, provenance research, technical examination, digital humanities, and museum documentation. The study is intended primarily for new and practicing research staff in museum art departments. Classical approaches associated with Giovanni Morelli, Heinrich Wölfflin, and Erwin Panofsky are considered alongside infrared and ultraviolet imaging, radiography, microscopy, spectroscopy, X-ray fluorescence, digital image analysis, and carefully bounded applications of artificial intelligence. Particular attention is given to provenance, evidentiary hierarchy, legal due diligence, and the scientific passport of a museum object. The legal context is discussed with reference to the Law of the Republic of Uzbekistan “On Museums,” the ICOM Code of Ethics for Museums, and the UNESCO 1970 Convention. As a principal result, a five-stage integrated attribution protocol is proposed: preliminary documentation and provenance screening; visual-stylistic and iconographic analysis; technical and material examination; digital/computational assistance; and collegial synthesis with formal documentation. An illustrative training case based on a Fergana Valley painting is used to demonstrate how a museum researcher should distinguish hypotheses from verified evidence.

summary: Code and frozen experimental data accompanying the accepted JCDL 2026 paper A Provenance-First Discovery Layer for Research Gaps, Limitations, and Future Directions in ETDs . The system proposes research-gap, limitation, and future-direction passages from electronic theses and dissertations, aligns retained passages to source text and physical PDF pages, and keeps proposed type and synopsis separately reviewable. Version 1.0.0 includes the implementation, prompts, schemas, evaluation tools, and 31,486 frozen data files: compiled source text and corpus metadata, study splits, model outputs, reference construction, passage audits, the 600-record human-review ledger, training traces, and expected results. The code archive and checksum-pinned data archive support CPU reproduction of the reported statistics, including the original 20,000-resample whole-ETD bootstrap intervals. Fresh model training, inference, and external audits are separate operations; source PDFs and model weights are not included. The GitHub repository provides installation instructions, result lineage, validation receipts, and documented reproduction limits: provenance-first-etd-discovery . summary: Clustering high-dimensional data is a fundamental task in unsupervised machine learning with applications to a variety of domains. In the centralized data scenario, this task is commonly solved using deep clustering methods that utilize deep neural network architectures to learn clustering-friendly latent space representations. In Federated Learning, where data is distributed between clients and is private, deep clustering methods are less explored. In particular, recently introduced federated deep clustering methods, despite showing very promising performance, still fall short in reliably providing good performance if data across clients are non-identically-independently distributed. In this work, we introduce a generalization of Deep Clustering Networks to the federated scenario, named FedDCN, that simultaneously optimizes a reconstruction loss and a clustering loss. To ensure robustness and latent space alignment in non-identically-independently distributed data scenarios, FedDCN generates synthetic data augmentations, and its learning objective includes a geometric regularization for latent space alignment. Through experimental evaluation, the effectiveness of the approach under IID and non-IID assumptions is demonstrated, and future research directions are identified.
title: Federated Deep Clustering Networks for High-Dimensional and Heterogeneous Data

In Federated Learning, where data is distributed between clients and is private, deep clustering methods are less explored. In particular, recently introduced federated deep clustering methods, despite showing very promising performance, still fall short in reliably providing good performance if data across clients are non-identically-independently distributed. In this work, we introduce a generalization of Deep Clustering Networks to the federated scenario, named FedDCN, that simultaneously optimizes a reconstruction loss and a clustering loss. To ensure robustness and latent space alignment in non-identically-independently distributed data scenarios, FedDCN generates synthetic data augmentations, and its learning objective includes a geometric regularization for latent space alignment. Through experimental evaluation, the effectiveness of the approach under IID and non-IID assumptions is demonstrated, and future research directions are identified.

summary: Recent advances in diffusion models have enabled high-performance, instance-adaptive compressed sensing through posterior sampling, without task-specific policy training. Existing methods select sensing probes by maximizing total posterior signal variance and are therefore primarily reconstruction-driven. We introduce a classification-driven extension motivated by the closed-form posterior covariance of a class-conditional Gaussian mixture model, which decomposes into within-class and between-class uncertainty. Using calibrated soft classifier outputs, we estimate these uncertainty terms from diffusion posterior samples and propose a classification-oriented criterion for selecting the dominant sensing direction in the unmeasured subspace. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 compare the resulting classification accuracy, measurement cost, and reconstruction quality with those of reconstruction-oriented counterparts. The results identify regimes in which semantic posterior uncertainty yields a more favorable classification--measurement trade-off and quantify the associated reconstruction cost.
title: Classification-oriented adaptive sensing via posterior sampling

summary: Increasing demand for high-performance optical devices drives the search for improved fabrication and design paradigms. While photonic circuits have traditionally used structures with two discrete 'binary' height levels, grayscale 'wavy' interfaces, or optical Fourier surfaces, have recently become possible. They provide precise control over the Fourier components that govern the optical response. This capability raises the question: When does a wavy device improve performance and why? Here, we show that wavy integrated processors exhibit superior accuracy and efficiency to binary analogs. Inverse-designed wavy interferometers have the design freedom to minimize outscattering to free space and backreflections. They reach a five-fold lower transmission error than binary counterparts and enable bandwidths up to 300 nm. We formalize these findings for other distinct integrated devices, such as photonic crystals, nanocavities, and beam emitters. A Fourier-optics analysis identifies a trade-off: wavy profiles manipulate light more accurately, whereas binary profiles excel in interaction strength. As such, tailored wavy profiles emit high-quality beams. However, binary profiles remain preferable in photonic crystals and nanocavities, where maximal index contrast is required and binarization-induced higher harmonics are benign. Thus, for quantum information, optical computing, and sensing, optical Fourier surfaces offer a route to miniaturized integrated circuits with improved performance.
title: When Integrated Photonics Should Be Wavy

summary: The collinear-antiferromagnetic spin-fluctuation paradigm has long guided unconventional superconductivity research, yet fails to reconcile the noncollinear spin phenomena observed across cuprates, iron-based superconductors, and nickelates. Using extensive first-principles calculations and unbiased large-scale DMRG simulations, we show that Dzyaloshinski-Moriya interaction (DMI)-arising from local inversion-symmetry breaking-is a common ingredient across these families. This DMI unifies hallmark observations in parent compounds-incommensurate orders, spin-wave gaps, and noncollinear textures. Under hole doping, strong DMI drives spin vortices to merge with pi-shifted hole stripes, forming hybrid vortex-hole stripe phases. These phases stabilize charge order while supporting, not suppressing, superconductivity. By contrast, under electron doping, these vortices pin holes and suppress long-range superconductivity. Our results establish DMI as a unifying link between noncollinear magnetism and superconductivity, identifying hole-strip-vortex coupling as a microscopic pairing engine. Given that DMI is common across major superconductor families, these findings challenge the prevailing pairing mechanism and offer an experimentally testable roadmap for materials optimization.
title: Universal Dzyaloshinski-Moriya interaction dictates pairing in unconventional superconductor families

summary: Discovering the structure and kinetics of chemical reaction networks (CRNs) from time-series concentration data is a fundamental challenge in chemical kinetics, with existing approaches relying on prior mechanistic assumptions or suffering from high computational cost and noise sensitivity. In this work, we present integral chemical reaction neural networks (iCRNNs), a framework that combines the interpretable, physics-constrained, architecture of chemical reaction neural networks (CRNNs) with an integral collocation formulation of the governing dynamics. Rather than solving ODEs forward in time at each training step, we approximate the integral of the learned rate functions directly using numerical quadrature. This yields an entirely algebraic forward pass consisting only of matrix operations, eliminating the repeated adaptive ODE solves of standard CRNN and producing smoother, more predictable training. We provide a recovery error analysis characterising the structural sources of ill-conditioning (conservation laws, reaction reversibility, and shared reactant sets) that limit network identifiability. On two benchmark CRNs, iCRNN trains in roughly half the wall-clock time of the baseline CRNN method on a four-species mechanism and between three and four times faster on a five-species mechanism, while completing every training run reliably and attaining comparable or lower loss.
title: Integral chemical reaction neural networks

summary: Privacy leakage in LLM agents is commonly evaluated within individual components such as memory, retrieval, or tool-use pipelines, which makes it difficult to distinguish internal exposure from information that an external observer can actually recover. We present CIPL (Channel Inversion for Privacy Leakage), a channel-aware evaluation framework for black-box privacy leakage in LLM agents. CIPL represents a target through sensitive source, selection, assembly, execution, observation, and extraction stages and evaluates the transition from selected sensitive units to attacker-recoverable output under a shared protocol. Experiments across memory-based, retrieval-mediated, and tool-mediated targets, together with a BrowserUse live-agent case study, show that storage labels alone do not determine recoverability. Memory targets form a near-saturated reference case, retrieval-mediated leakage is frequently partial, and tool-mediated and live-agent leakage varies strongly with observation surface, prompt-to-channel alignment, retrieval depth, and provider behavior. A stratified semantic audit further identifies attacker-useful disclosures that canonical exact matching misses. CIPL therefore provides a common framework for comparing how internal sensitive dependence is realized as externally recoverable leakage across heterogeneous agent pipelines.

summary: We investigate Floquet--spin-orbit compensation in the three-band $α$-$T_3$ system, which interpolates between graphene at $α=0$ and the dice lattice at $α=1$. By tuning the interplay between an off-resonant circularly polarized optical field and intrinsic spin--orbit coupling, we identify three distinct pairwise band-degeneracy conditions in the quasienergy spectrum: (i) valley--spin degeneracy, (ii) spin--band degeneracy, and (iii) flat--dispersive band degeneracy. The flat band is not an artifact of a two-band reduction but rather an exact property of the continuum Hamiltonian at this compensation point, where the complete three-band Hamiltonian supports a momentum-independent dark state. A winding-two low-energy Hamiltonian and a finite-momentum Berry-curvature maximum, whose radius scales as the square root of the detuning, emerge from detuning this contact. We further show that the intrinsic transverse thermoelectric response encodes these spectrum patterns. The flat- and quadratic-band degeneracy can be predicted for $0<α<1/2$ because the two response scales linked to the linear contacts have a monotonic ratio independent of the common spin--orbit energy scale. This allows an inverse determination of $α$ and of the common spectral scale. The analytical results are confirmed by full three-band Kubo calculations, which also define the regime in which this inverse characterization is still observable. These results connect an experimentally accessible, Berry-curvature-sensitive thermoelectric response to tunable Floquet--spin--orbit band geometry.

summary: We study Bousfield--Kan completions through the interaction of free simplicial resolutions, their filtration spectral sequences, and a noncommutative arithmetic square. For every free discrete simplicial group of finite type, we express its integral pronilpotent completion as the homotopy pullback of its rational prounipotent completion and the product of its pro-$p$ completions over an explicit adelic simplicial group. The adelic entry is formed by taking restricted products at finite nilpotent stages and then their inverse limit; no nilpotency assumption on the original group of components is required. Finite subpresentations of contractible presentations provide an explicit application of this construction. Independence of the specified relators makes the positive-degree terms of the rational and mod-$p$ filtration spectral sequences vanish, with convergence verified on the quotient towers. Continuous comparison of free simplicial resolutions then realizes, in characteristic zero, the equivalence with a constant free prounipotent group by morphisms and homotopies in that category. For the corresponding presentation complex $K$ we obtain $R_\infty K\simeq K(F_R(Z),1)$ for $R=\mathbb Q,\mathbb F_p,\mathbb Z$, where $Z$ indexes a complementary basis and $F_R(Z)$ denotes, respectively, the rational points of a free prounipotent group, a free pro-$p$ group, or a free pronilpotent group. Compatible contractions at the nilpotent stages identify all four entries of the arithmetic square in this case.

summary: Ransomware increasingly fragments its file operations across temporary and intermediate files, scattering the semantic context that links individual I/O events to an overarching encryption campaign. This fragmentation defeats existing detectors that reason over isolated file streams -- whether pattern-based methods that match rigid event sequences or learning-based methods that require accumulating statistical evidence across many files. We present DEFEAT, a framework that reconstructs this fragmented, scattered context by grouping causally related file events into File Event Gadgets (FEGs), semantically coherent units that capture the full intent behind sequences of file operations spanning multiple dynamically created files. Unlike provenance graphs (system-wide causal graphs that record relationships among all OS entities, such as processes, files, sockets, and registry keys, across the entire system), FEGs are scoped to the file-operation context of a single user asset, enabling lightweight, targeted analysis without whole-system instrumentation. Each FEG is modelled as an attributed control flow graph (ACFG) and embedded via a graph neural network for unsupervised clustering, enabling analysts to label entire behavioural clusters rather than individual samples, reducing annotation effort by 94%. summary: Solver, driver scripts and every numerical output of a study of the efficiency and the retrieved-mode noise of a Lambda-type atomic quantum memory. The model is the one-dimensional Maxwell-Bloch system of a three-level ensemble with the anti-Stokes four-wave-mixing channel, integrated in JAX/Diffrax so that the derivative of an observable with respect to the control field comes from a reverse pass through the propagation. The noise observable is one row of the Bogoliubov kernel projected on the retrieved temporal mode, obtained without assembling the kernel. The outputs cover: the efficiency-noise front traced over a 32-knot control at two signal detunings; the largest singular value of the storage-retrieval map along that front and its dependence on the four-wave-mixing coupling; the spin-wave growth of the resonant anti-Stokes configuration over 2.5 decades of optical depth and a factor 15 in control amplitude; the efficiency, noise photon number and collinear phase mismatch of a cesium configuration taken from published experimental parameters; the derivative of each front point with respect to the optical depth, the spin decoherence, the phase mismatch and the four-wave-mixing coupling, each from one reverse pass; three optimizers compared at one evaluation budget and at three control dimensions, with the cost of a gradient measured against the cost of an objective on the same working point; the number of temporal modes the storage map resolves, on a ladder in the basis size at two spatial grids; the Doppler-averaged absorption of a warm vapour in closed form; three velocity quadratures measured against that closed form and against its derivative, which is the average the field's source carries; the integrator step a velocity-resolved solve needs, which is not the step the front was traced at; the landed controls of the second detuning read again under a 300 K Maxwellian, at one velocity class and at thirty; the Bogoliubov identity projected on the retrieved mode, evaluated at every front point; the noise the detector gate collects over every temporal mode, by stochastic trace estimation, and the effective mode count it gives against the retrieved-mode count; the same trace against the gate's own length; a manifest of every landed run with its detuning, step specification, bound and outcome; the reproducibility of the front, measured as the disagreement between two runs of one control that reach the same efficiency, and what that reproducibility does to a slope read off the front; and the front re-traced at a constant integrator step over both searches, with the local logarithmic slope read on it at three efficiencies fixed before the set was read.  Every output file is plain text carrying its own configuration in a header and a machine-readable RESULT line; DEPOSIT.md maps the directories and names the script that produces each. The archive is a git archive of one commit, so the tree is exactly what that revision held.

summary: A characteristic corrugated surface morphology of Nb films on Cu is identified, with mesoscopic features comparable to the London penetration depth and coherence length, and its impact on superconducting radio frequency cavity performance metrics is examined. Magnetic field enhancement factors and superheating field suppression factors are calculated within the London model for a representative corrugated geometry. These results demonstrate that roughness trends derived from buffered chemical polished and electropolished Nb cavities do not capture the impact of nanoscale surface morphology on SRF Nb thin film performance, as even surfaces that possess low average roughness can contain geometric features that generate substantial local field enhancement and significantly suppress the Bean Livingston barrier. The influence of surface roughness on impurity diffusion is also investigated, which highlights the roles of increased surface area and local geometric confinement in modifying near surface impurity distributions. Tracking the effect of impurity diffusion on the evolution of magnetic field enhancement, we show that geometrically confined impurity distributions can mitigate nanoscale magnetic field enhancement substantially.
title: Failure of Conventional Roughness Metrics in Assessing Field-Limiting Mesoscopic Topography in SRF Nb Films on Cu
