summary: Long-term memory is essential for large language model (LLM) agents to maintain consistency and personalization over extended interactions. Existing memory systems typically rely on fixed granularities or static schemas, but these designs struggle when heterogeneous information, such as preferences, events, constraints, and temporal updates, is embedded in a single mixed representation. The resulting semantic interference makes top-K retrieval sensitive to noise and often leaves relevant evidence poorly ranked. We present AutoViewMem, a data-driven framework that organizes long-term conversational memory into self-configuring, low-overlap semantic views before indexing. AutoViewMem discovers candidate views from interaction traces, selects a compact complementary view set, and uses these views to guide write-time structured extraction of provenance-grounded memories. This representation-first design moves semantic disentanglement from retrieval time to write time, allowing standard top-K similarity search to retrieve focused evidence without explicit routing or iterative retrieval. We further apply offline consolidation to improve memory compactness and consistency. Experiments on the LoCoMo and PersonaMem benchmarks, under both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B backbones, show that AutoViewMem improves long-horizon question answering and personalization over strong memory baselines while preserving a simple inference pipeline.

summary: The hotspots of powerful radio galaxies are the sites of high-energy particle acceleration, but radio observations give us limited information on the electron energy distributions that they generate, which affects our overall understanding of their physics and energetics. Optical synchrotron counterparts to radio galaxy hotspots, which probe high electron energies, have been known for many years, but have only been studied in a small number of objects selected as being very bright in the radio. By combining Low-Frequency Array (LOFAR) observations with the Euclid Q1 data release in the Euclid Deep Field North, we identify 77 powerful radio galaxies with hotspots and show that a small but significant fraction of them, 7--15\%, may have detected infrared and optical counterparts to their hotspots. The hotspot spectral energy distributions in our clearest cases are consistent with particle acceleration up to (but not beyond) 1\,TeV in energy on the assumption of field strengths close to equipartition, whereas non-detected hotspots either do not reach such high electron energies or would have to have very different electron energy spectra or significantly sub-equipartition magnetic field strengths. Two new candidate optical hotspots are clearly detected matching high-resolution LOFAR data; one is remarkable as both the highest-redshift optical hotspot known to date ($z \approx 1.6$) and also the first optical detection of the hotspot of the inner lobe of a restarting source. We discuss approaches to performing a large-scale study of hotspots with the full wide-area Euclid surveys, particularly when combined with the international baselines of LOFAR, enabling for the first time a statistical analysis of high-energy particle acceleration in hotspots.

summary: Many machine learning systems try to explain complex data - like images or financial time series - in terms of hidden, independent factors that generated them. Recovering the true underlying factors, rather than some scrambled version of them, is the central challenge of nonlinear Independent Component Analysis (nICA). We prove identifiability (exact recovery) up to trivial ambiguities for real analytic generating functions when source probability density functions have a finite number of discontinuities in the first derivative. The Laplace distribution is the most prominent example satisfying this assumption. Our proof relies on the contrast between kinks in the source distribution and the smoothness of real analytic functions. Real analytic functions comprise a broad class of generating mechanisms, and can be approximated with Normalizing Flows or Variational Autoencoders with standard activation functions (e.g., tanh, softplus, GELU), so our result applies with minimal changes to existing training pipelines. We perform experiments on real and synthetic data with both Normalizing Flows and Variational Auto-Encoders demonstrating their identifiability properties. In experiments on CelebA data we recover several interpretable latent factors controlling unique attributes across the dataset.
title: Kinks vs. Smoothness: Identifiability of Real Analytic nICA for Laplace-like Sources

summary: Brane tilings are bipartite graphs on a 2-torus that encode the Lagrangians of 4d N=1 supersymmetric gauge theories arising on D3-branes probing toric Calabi-Yau 3-folds. Among these bipartite graphs, only those that satisfy geometric consistency conditions correspond to well-behaved quantum field theories. We train a convolutional neural network (CNN) to distinguish geometrically consistent from inconsistent brane tilings directly from their Kasteleyn matrices. We study a family of 4d N=1 theories obtained by adding diagonal edges to the hexagonal faces of the brane tiling for the abelian orbifold C^3/Z_3 x Z_3, and find that the CNN identifies geometric inconsistency with high accuracy. For inconsistent brane tilings that can be rendered consistent by Higgsing a single bifundamental chiral field, we show that gradient-based saliency analysis can be used to localize the responsible chiral fields with accuracy well above a matched random baseline. These results demonstrate that explainable AI (XAI) can be used to identify local defects responsible for inconsistencies in supersymmetric gauge theories.
title: Diagnosing Inconsistencies in 4d N=1 Gauge Theories with Explainable AI

summary: Professional graphic design is a long-horizon agentic task in which structured, editable artifacts emerge from many interdependent actions, yet outcomes admit no reliable programmatic oracle. We introduce a continual adaptation framework in which a frozen frontier model operates professional design software through more than 230 tools, while an external procedural memory of natural-language skills accumulates and refines reusable design procedures from experience. The memory widens by acquiring procedures for recurring uncovered subtasks and deepens by revising existing procedures against their own successful and failed executions, while a matched replay gate admits only changes that repair failures without regressing observed successes. Five rounds over 1,406 real user briefs and 1,869 automatically graded trajectories, with no weight updates and no human labels, grow the bank from 76 documentation-derived skills to 139 and raise GenEval2 execution success on Claude-Sonnet-4 from 72.7% to 99.3% (+11.99 points in generation quality), with 61.8% and 67.6% win rates against the no-skill agent across four specialized design benchmarks on Claude-Sonnet-4 and Claude-Opus-4.6. We further show the two mechanisms are effective in combination: on 200 held-out briefs from user-traffic benchmark, widening or deepening alone reaches a 49.4% / 48.6% win rate over the no-skill agent, while their combination reaches 58.5% (p = 0.025). Procedural memory offers a practical route to continual adaptation of agents under noisy, unverifiable feedback.
title: Designer-RSI: Evolving Procedural Memory from User Traffic for Agentic Graphic Design

summary: A desirable property of a world model is the ability to learn continually across tasks, adapting to new environments without forgetting what the agent has already learnt. In particular, the ability to retain and reuse knowledge obtained from prior experiences underpins an agent's ability to efficiently adapt to novel environments, as the dynamics of the physical world can often be described in recurring mechanisms. However, the world model's measure of adaptation entangles two abilities: the speed and capacity to learn unseen tasks, and the reuse of knowledge already acquired, since incoming tasks carry novel content alongside what recurs. In order to isolate knowledge reuse from prior experiences, we propose a compositional continual learning benchmark for world models in robot manipulation. Specifically, we design each task curriculum with compositional tasks that combine aspects of the tasks seen in the sequence. We further factorise this composition along the axes of action and perception to better understand how different input modalities bottleneck knowledge reuse. We evaluate state-of-the-art world models under canonical continual learning methods, alongside a modular world model whose dynamics backbone contains explicitly reusable components. Results show that modularity balances reuse against forgetting better than conventional methods, but none solve the problem fully, leaving clear room for continual world models built to reuse without forgetting. More details are available on our project website: https://object814.github.io/Compositional-Continual-Learning/.
title: Benchmarking World Models for Continual Learning on Compositional Tasks

summary: Counterfactual simulation with a clinical world model means fixing a patient's history, changing the treatment, and reading off the predicted response. Doing so requires deciding what counts as one intervention. In clinical settings, interventions are documented as bundles: a co-occurrence audit of 945,707 patient-hours from MIMIC-IV shows groups of components, such as every parameter of a dialysis circuit, that never appear apart, so an edit that changes one component on its own describes an hour that never occurs in the data. We hypothesize that the granularity at which an intervention is edited changes how a world model responds, and test this with Clin-JEPA, a latent world model of patient trajectories conditioned on hourly treatment text. At 1,019 documented onsets of invasive ventilation, we keep the patient's history and other treatments fixed and compare editing one ventilator setting with editing the complete configuration recorded for a real patient with the most similar recent trajectory. The complete bundle moves the predicted next state further than any single setting, consistently across all five settings, and the difference remains after accounting for how much each edit changes the model's input. Intervention granularity therefore materially affects the response of a clinical world model: single-component edits may understate treatment sensitivity, and bundle-aware editing may offer a better-supported basis for counterfactual treatment simulation.
title: Intervention Granularity Matters: Coherent Treatment Bundles in Counterfactual Simulation with Clinical World Models

summary: This record provides supporting experimental data, source code, selected trained model weights, and reproducibility documentation for the manuscript “RART: A Resource-Aware Recursive Transformer for Stochastic Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling” by Cem Savas Aydin. The study evaluates RART on stochastic resource-constrained project scheduling problems using instances from the Project Scheduling Problem Library (PSPLIB). The primary comparison involves 101 J60 projects, three training seeds per method, and 1,000 common duration scenarios per project. Seven J30 projects provide secondary comparisons. The comparator is an independently trained Wheatley-based graph neural network policy. The uploaded files comprise: ESM_1.pdf: Supplementary methodological documentation, including model features, random streams, evaluation procedures, statistical reconstruction, and provenance. ESM_2.zip: Archived source code, six selected inference checkpoints, project definitions and splits, training records, scenario-level scheduling outcomes, and scripts for reconstructing the reported statistics and figures. Recorded outcomes include mean makespan, upper-tail makespan measured by CVaR90, results before and after schedule repair, and computation times. The README.md file within ESM_2.zip provides instructions for reconstructing the statistical results from the saved simulation outputs without retraining the models.
title: Supporting Data and Code for RART: A Resource-Aware Recursive Transformer for Stochastic Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling

summary: PLANETS SSbD Training on EcoTrace Tool for Digital Product Passports This data entry contains training materials for the EcoTrace Tool and its employment for DPP. It includes: (1) video clip on the intro, bbackground, aiming of DPP in PLANETS, data model of EcoTrace, its connection to SSbD methodology, first testing feedback. (2) a slide set on the topics covered in the video clip, (3) a txt-version as Readme file for the summary of the EcoTrace trraining session. in short: Major take-aways DPP is intended to be a key mechanism for operationalising and communicating SSbD information across product value chains. FAIR data principles are fundamental to DPP implementation , particularly interoperability, machine readability, metadata, identifiers, provenance and controlled accessibility. PLANETS aims to connect the SSbD assessment workflow with DPP data , including information generated across the different assessment tiers and dimensions. EchoTrace is being developed as a flexible, sector-agnostic DPP management tool , allowing customised data models, product types, field groups and user permissions. Different stakeholders require different levels of access ; confidentiality and controlled access are therefore central considerations rather than all DPP information being universally public. Blockchain and Hyperledger Fabric are being explored to support traceability and data integrity , with transactions governed through authorised operations and smart contracts. The practical exercises identified usability and implementation issues , particularly around field groups, permissions, product status, data integrity and how different stakeholders contribute to the same product passport. Industry willingness to provide information is a significant consideration , especially where data involve intellectual property, confidentiality or commercially sensitive information. Future development will focus on standardisation, semantic/metadata dictionaries, blockchain integration and potential EU registry integration. The successful implementation of DPPs will depend not only on technology but also on governance, data granularity, confidentiality, interoperability and stakeholder trust.

summary: Code reproducing the numerical experiments of the manuscript "Reconstruction method based on Fourier series for attenuated photoacoustic tomography in a circular geometry" by S. Moon, J. Oh, and G. Park. The manuscript reconstructs the initial pressure in two-dimensional photoacoustic tomography with frequency-dependent attenuation, on a circular measurement geometry. A Green function representation and Graf's addition theorem reduce the inverse problem to a family of one-dimensional radial integral equations for the angular Fourier coefficients, which are discretized and solved by zero-order Tikhonov regularization with the regularization parameter chosen by the L-curve criterion. This archive contains the Python code and the precomputed results for every figure and table of Section 4, for a thermoviscous attenuation model and a Nachman-Smith-Waag model. See README.md for the requirements and the order in which to run the scripts.

summary: This article develops a formalized methodology for multidimensional assessment of demand–production alignment in the building materials industry. The study specifies the indicators, normalization rules, and aggregation procedure needed to assess quantitative, assortment, spatial-logistics, temporal, and resource-capacity alignment jointly. The methodological design synthesizes established approaches to composite indicators, industrial statistics, forecast evaluation, and missing-data treatment. Five component scores—BQ, BA, BH, BT, and BR—are defined alongside asymmetric normalization of shortages and surpluses, geometric aggregation, a coverage measure (COV), data-quality statuses, and a mandatory constraint triggered by breaches of quality, safety, or environmental requirements. The resulting calculation protocol permits the Integral Matching Index (IMI) to be reported only with its component profile, normalization parameters, uncertainty interval, and data provenance record. A complete industry-level IMI is not calculated because a harmonized panel of orders, inventories, logistics, effective capacity, and resource availability is not currently available. The methodology is intended for subsequent reproducible validation using enterprise data and may be incorporated into sales and operations planning (S&OP) and strategic monitoring. Its practical interpretation focuses on identifying the component that constrains overall alignment rather than merely comparing aggregate scores.

summary: Returning to sport after injury requires more than restoration of physical capacity. Athletes must interpret bodily signals, renegotiate their relationship with sport, and decide whether participation remains both desirable and acceptable. This critical narrative review examines athletic identity, fear of reinjury, and psychological readiness, using anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction as the principal empirical context. Targeted searches of publicly accessible research records, publisher pages, and reference lists identified conceptual, observational, qualitative, measurement, and intervention studies. The synthesis distinguishes evidence about returning to sport from evidence about subsequent injury and treatment effectiveness. Three findings organize the analysis. Athletic identity can remain stable, weaken, or strengthen during rehabilitation; a declining group mean therefore does not describe every athlete. Fear encompasses consequences for everyday life and future participation, and its significance depends on the activity and recovery stage. Psychological readiness is associated with return, but its relationship with subsequent injury differs across samples and assessment times. Recent randomized evidence also cautions against assuming that a plausible psychological intervention will improve return rates. The review develops an interpretive framework in which physical capacity, psychological willingness, and opportunity for supported participation are examined separately and then considered together. Its contribution is a set of testable propositions about confidence calibration, identity flexibility, and decision quality. Psychological care should support informed participation and personally meaningful recovery, while its effects on sustained performance and reinjury require direct evaluation.

summary: Supporting material for the manuscript "Subacute oral glyphosate impairs testicular function in male mice (Mus musculus): a threshold-anchored dose-response study of steroidogenesis, sperm quality, redox balance and spermatogenic histopathology" (Elbeeh, Filfilan, Filfilan and Filfilan), submitted to Drug and Chemical Toxicology (Taylor & Francis). Forty adult male Swiss albino (ICR) mice, 8-10 weeks old and 22.1-25.5 g at allocation, received vehicle (distilled water) or technical-grade glyphosate at 10, 50 or 100 mg/kg/day by oral gavage for 28 days, n = 10 per group. The dose range brackets the regulatory no-observed-adverse-effect level of approximately 50 mg/kg/day. Endpoints measured in the same 40 animals: body and testis weight; serum testosterone, LH and FSH; epididymal sperm concentration, progressive motility, viability and morphology; testicular malondialdehyde, reduced glutathione, superoxide dismutase and catalase; and testis histopathology stained with haematoxylin-eosin and with periodic acid-Schiff, assessed by the Johnsen tubular-maturation score and by measurement of seminiferous tubule diameter, germinal epithelial height and graded lesion severity. Sections were digitised on a Philips UltraFast Scanner at the x20 level (0.5 micrometres per pixel) and reviewed in the Philips PathologySuite viewer; morphometry was performed in ImageJ v1.54 with semi-automated annotation in QuPath v0.4.3 on fields exported at the native scan resolution. Contents: S1, the manufacturer's Certificate of Analysis for the test article (Sigma-Aldrich 337757, lot MKCZ1523, purity at least 96 per cent, CAS 1071-83-6); S2, analytical kits, instruments, assay conditions and intra- and inter-assay coefficients of variation; S3, the analysis and figure-plotting code; S4, the complete per-animal dataset underlying every figure and table; S5, the benchmark-dose model set with BMD and BMDL10 values; Supplementary Figure S6 with its caption, showing the histomorphometry and graded lesion scores of Table 4 with individual animal values overlaid; S7, the completed ARRIVE 2.0 checklist; S8, the full statistical record for all 30 endpoints (Shapiro-Wilk and Levene checks, the test applied, post-hoc comparisons, effect sizes, Benjamini-Hochberg q values, Jonckheere-Terpstra trend statistics, dose-response correlations and benchmark-dose fits) together with the group mean, SEM and n behind every plotted point; and S9, the unmodified field exported from the whole-slide image behind each panel of Figures 4 and 5, both plates before the arrows were drawn, a manifest of exactly what was done to each image, and checksums. README.md gives the full manifest. Every value reported in the manuscript can be recomputed from S4 using the code in S3. Statistics: continuous endpoints were compared by Welch's ANOVA with the Games-Howell post-hoc test; ordinal lesion grades by the Kruskal-Wallis test with Holm-adjusted Dunn's post-hoc test; monotonic trend by the Jonckheere-Terpstra test; and the endpoint family was controlled at a false-discovery rate of 5 per cent (Benjamini-Hochberg). The Johnsen tubular-maturation score was nominated in advance as the primary endpoint; every other endpoint is secondary. Ethics: all procedures were approved by the Bioethics Committee of Umm Al-Qura University, Makkah, Saudi Arabia (approval no. HAPO-02-K-012-2025-04-2781) and were conducted in accordance with the ARRIVE 2.0 guidelines. These 40 animals also support the cardiotoxicity, neurotoxicity and immunotoxicity arms of the same programme, which are reported separately under the same approval number. Licensed CC BY 4.0. Version 2.0.0 adds S8 and S9, replaces S3 with a copy that also carries requirements.txt, a README and the benchmark-dose output table, and replaces the Supplementary Figure S6 image with a copy from which a non-standard private PNG chunk, added in transit and carrying no image information, has been removed. No reported value changed between versions 1.
title: Supplementary data and analysis code for: Subacute oral glyphosate impairs testicular function in male mice (Mus musculus)

summary: This paper proposes a persistent epistemic architecture for AI systems in which durable cognitive state is explicit and independent of any particular language model. The persistent substrate maintains inspectable, scoped beliefs with provenance, distinguishes individual sources and accumulates domain-sensitive trust, retains unresolved questions across interactions, and supports offline consolidation that detects contradictions and generates hypotheses. Its contents participate directly in subsequent learning and action rather than serving only as retrieved memory. A dependency-free prototype instantiates this core, with language models at both linguistic interfaces, to illustrate the cycle by which attributed testimony becomes revisable belief. The central claim is that continual learning requires explicit epistemic structure: a representation of what the system believes, why it believes it, whom it learned it from, and what remains unresolved, if its evolving epistemic state is to remain inspectable and correctable. This becomes increasingly consequential as AI systems contribute to their own development, because increasing capability does not necessarily entail a corresponding improvement in epistemic reliability. Persistent epistemic state provides a substrate on which correction and calibration can accumulate over time while remaining externally auditable. Preprint submitted to arXiv in September 2026. Source code and demonstrator: https://github.com/protopopescu/chloe and  https://lftm.gla.ac.uk/chloe/
title: CHLOE: A Persistent Epistemic Architecture for Inspectable AI

summary: Reproducibility software for confidence-aware, risk-calibrated, multiobjective tuning of an edge-executable battery-supported microgrid energy-management system under finite simulation budgets and distribution shift. The archived software release is tied to a closed confirmatory evidence chain with frozen validation, internal-test, ablation, sensitivity, and external-OOD provenance roots.
title: Confidence-Aware Robust Edge EMS: Reproducibility Software for Risk-Calibrated Multiobjective Tuning

summary: This software package contains the code used for the simulation, analysis, and reproducibility of a study on closed-loop digital-twin validation of federated learning updates for methane control in underground mining. The package includes the plant–twin simulator, federated-learning routines, calibration scripts, intervention-budget analyses, attack calibration and backdoor diagnostics, candidate-update generation and scoring, the fresh-seed confirmatory analysis, twin-mismatch sensitivity experiments, exploratory Krum-based comparisons, FLTrust-style diagnostics, serious-harm analyses, and read-only manuscript audits. The evaluation separates the simulated plant used for operational outcome assessment from the imperfect digital twin used for candidate scoring. The repository also documents the distinction between direct plant evaluation and curve-interpolated budget matching used in different experimental stages. Raw methane measurements are not redistributed in this archive. The study uses the public dataset “Methane” by Sikora and Wróbel, available from Mendeley Data, Version 1, DOI: 10.17632/yd7vw4c5mk.1. Instructions for obtaining and preparing the data are provided in DATA.md. The archive includes reproducibility documentation, script-to-manuscript mapping, provenance notes, execution order, software requirements, and SHA-256 checksums. Historical scripts are retained where necessary to document the progression from early exploratory analyses to the final frozen analysis.
title: SFDT-DTVRA: Reproducibility Code for Closed-Loop Digital-Twin Validation of Federated

summary: This report reconstructs the publication history of The Watermark, the student literary and arts journal of the University of Massachusetts Boston. It was published from 1993 through 2022 under that title. This report draws on physical copies, digital archival holdings from ScholarWorks and personally held hard copies, as well as firsthand research, it examines the journal's institutional and material history. It also documents changes in production and distribution, as well as gaps in the surviving digital record. The report concludes with a reconstructed record of known volumes and is periodized.
title: The Watermark (1993–2022): A Publication History and Reconstruction

summary: Science communication poster and educational resource developed for the 2026 European Researchers’ Night–Nit de la Investigació at the University of Alicante as supporting material for a hands-on activity devoted to coin production. For this activity, an enlarged minting system based on the dies of a silver Carthaginian shekel has been reproduced by means of 3D printing. Participants can directly experience how hammered coinage works by placing a modelling-clay flan between a fixed lower die and a movable upper die, and observing how pressure impresses the obverse and reverse types onto its surface. The poster provides the historical and technological context for this activity through an overview of the evolution of coin production and means of payment, from manual hammered coinage to the mechanisation of coin manufacture and contemporary digital payment systems. It presents in a synthetic way some of the main technological developments, including hammered coinage, mechanised roller minting, the screw press, banknote production and security features, and the progressive dematerialisation of payment methods. Developed within the framework of the PArchTE ( Predictive Archaeology and Transition Economies ) and SEDES (PID2023-152305NB-I00) projects. The activity forms part of “UA Divulga VI. Annual Plan of the UCC+i of the University of Alicante (2025–2026)” (FCT-24-20347), funded by the Spanish Foundation for Science and Technology (FECYT). Activity developed by the University Institute for Research in Archaeology and Historical Heritage (INAPH), University of Alicante.
title: Arqueología de la producción monetal

summary: Preconditioned Total Field Inversion: a single-step method that inverts the total field directly to susceptibility over the whole field-of-view, jointly performing background-field removal and dipole inversion. Uses a preconditioner (χ = P·y, larger outside the brain) so the large out-of-brain background susceptibility is well-conditioned, with MEDI-style L1 morphology regularization. QSM-CI reconstruction method tfi-qsmrs . Browse and run it at https://qsmxt.github.io/QSM-CI/submission.html?method=tfi-qsmrs .
title: QSM-CI method: TFI (QSM.rs) (v4)

summary: Combined multi-echo B0 field mapping by ROMEO (via the QSMxT/QSM.rs engine, `qsmxt fieldmap romeo`) — MCPC-3D-S phase-offset removal, template/temporal multi-echo unwrapping, and a magnitude/TE-weighted B0 estimate. Alternative to Laplacian field mapping. QSM-CI reconstruction method romeo-qsmrs . Browse and run it at https://qsmxt.github.io/QSM-CI/submission.html?method=romeo-qsmrs .
title: QSM-CI method: ROMEO (QSM.rs) (v9)

summary: QSMART: vessel-aware two-stage reconstruction. Consumes the total field and produces susceptibility, doing its own spatially-dependent background field removal and vasculature-aware regularization (Frangi vessel detection + SDF). QSM-CI reconstruction method qsmart-qsmrs . Browse and run it at https://qsmxt.github.io/QSM-CI/submission.html?method=qsmart-qsmrs .
title: QSM-CI method: QSMART (QSM.rs) (v9)

summary: QSMART — the authors' ORIGINAL MATLAB toolbox (v1.0), run as the full pipeline: Laplacian phase unwrapping, magnitude-weighted echo fitting (with its native R_0 reliability mask), Frangi-filter vasculature masking (with N4 bias correction), two-stage spatially-dependent filtering (SDF) background removal, two-stage STI-Suite QSM_iLSQR inversion, and dipole-model offset adjustment. Compiled from MATLAB and run on the license-free MATLAB Runtime (+ ANTs N4 in the image). QSM-CI reconstruction method qsmart-matlab . Browse and run it at https://qsmxt.github.io/QSM-CI/submission.html?method=qsmart-matlab .
title: QSM-CI method: QSMART (MATLAB) (v2)

summary: This record contains replication materials for “AI-intensive scientific collaboration exposes unequal coverage in name-based bibliometrics” by Anirban Adhikary and Sourav Bikash Borah. The archive contains the public analysis code, environment specifications, documentation, public-safe aggregate materials, frozen reference outputs, figure sources, and verification tools associated with the study. The public archive reproduces and verifies results within the documented derived-input boundary. It does not redistribute the approximately 770 GB OpenAlex source snapshot. Certain author-level derived inputs, including identifier-bearing bibliometric, name, affiliation, and network records, are excluded from public release because their combination creates a material reidentification risk. Full controlled reproduction requiring these inputs is available subject to an approved research purpose, identity verification, appropriate data-use conditions, and applicable third-party restrictions. The archive documents the analytical workflow, software environment, input contracts, cryptographic hashes, output lineage, and the distinction between public verification and controlled-input execution. The reported analyses are associational.
title: Replication package for "AI-intensive scientific collaboration exposes unequal coverage in name-based bibliometrics"

summary: Multi-agent active inference gives a natural account of belief sharing: agents hold local posteriors over a shared latent state, communicate those beliefs, and pool them into a colony-level consensus. The same mechanism is fragile when a member is miscalibrated, corrupted, or strategically wrong. Because the standard pool multiplies the reports together, a single confident-but-wrong broadcast that puts near-zero mass on the true state can pull the whole consensus off it, outweighing many honest members. The colony therefore needs a way to preserve the useful structure of belief sharing while limiting the influence of contaminated beliefs. This paper presents Active Fedference, a discrete-categorical framework that connects robust federated generalized variational inference with active inference belief sharing. The main bridge is structural: standard belief sharing appears as the non-robust corner of a broader generalized-Bayes family, while robust losses, conservative server fusion, and explicit aggregation diagnostics describe how the system moves away from that corner under declared contamination mechanisms. The result is not a replacement for belief sharing, but a containment result: ordinary belief sharing is recovered when robustness is turned off. Bounded-loss theory applies on the client axis, while the variational-server axis supplies an objective-backed redescending weight update. Following the manuscript's authoritative three-axis guarantee map, the paper keeps source-conditional client updates, a recovery-only heuristic server rule, and an objective-backed variational server rule as separate claim owners, with no robustness guarantee transferred between them. The study suite then exercises the framework as an end-to-end research system: recovery checks anchor the standard-Bayes limit, belief-sharing studies verify the communication baseline, contamination experiments test robust consensus, and extension studies probe moving agents, hierarchical latent structure, sensitivity to acuity and colony size, parameter recovery, and single-host socket-backed federation traces. All reported quantities are generated from deterministic analysis artifacts and injected into the manuscript by token, so the paper, figures, release package, and validation reports remain tied to the same execution record. The open-source repository is ActiveInferenceInstitute/Active_Fedference. This final-release manuscript uses assigned version DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22149133; the bound deposited PDF and repository release are controlled by separate publication gates.
title: Robust Belief Sharing in Federated Active Inference: A Recovery-Tested Generalized-Variational Framework for Categorical Contamination-Aware Consensus

The same mechanism is fragile when a member is miscalibrated, corrupted, or strategically wrong. Because the standard pool multiplies the reports together, a single confident-but-wrong broadcast that puts near-zero mass on the true state can pull the whole consensus off it, outweighing many honest members. The colony therefore needs a way to preserve the useful structure of belief sharing while limiting the influence of contaminated beliefs. This paper presents Active Fedference, a discrete-categorical framework that connects robust federated generalized variational inference with active inference belief sharing. The main bridge is structural: standard belief sharing appears as the non-robust corner of a broader generalized-Bayes family, while robust losses, conservative server fusion, and explicit aggregation diagnostics describe how the system moves away from that corner under declared contamination mechanisms. The result is not a replacement for belief sharing, but a containment result: ordinary belief sharing is recovered when robustness is turned off. Bounded-loss theory applies on the client axis, while the variational-server axis supplies an objective-backed redescending weight update. Following the manuscript's authoritative three-axis guarantee map, the paper keeps source-conditional client updates, a recovery-only heuristic server rule, and an objective-backed variational server rule as separate claim owners, with no robustness guarantee transferred between them. The study suite then exercises the framework as an end-to-end research system: recovery checks anchor the standard-Bayes limit, belief-sharing studies verify the communication baseline, contamination experiments test robust consensus, and extension studies probe moving agents, hierarchical latent structure, sensitivity to acuity and colony size, parameter recovery, and single-host socket-backed federation traces. All reported quantities are generated from deterministic analysis artifacts and injected into the manuscript by token, so the paper, figures, release package, and validation reports remain tied to the same execution record. The open-source repository is ActiveInferenceInstitute/Active_Fedference. This final-release manuscript uses assigned version DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22149133; the bound deposited PDF and repository release are controlled by separate publication gates.
title: Robust Belief Sharing in Federated Active Inference: A Recovery-Tested Generalized-Variational Framework for Categorical Contamination-Aware Consensus

summary: Recent agentic campaigns show that coordinated AI systems can compress reconnaissance, exploitation, and credential harvesting into machine-tempo operations. This paper asks a narrow question: whether increasing the number of untrusted attack sources changes the authorization outcome of an inline control that mediates every protected path and permits only explicit device-to-device relations. Under stated assumptions of complete mediation, fixed and correct policy, uncompromised trust anchors, no alternate path, and sufficient enforcement capacity, it does not. Additional untrusted source identities create additional denied first-contact events, not a permitted relation. This is a conditional property of the authorization rule, not a claim that throughput, alert volume, or availability are independent of swarm size. A four-run laboratory test of an AutoGen agent using GPT-4o provides a mechanism demonstration: the agent created four fresh network identities, and each was denied at its first observed unauthorized probe. The test does not establish a population rate or current-frontier performance. A closed-form illustration shows why reconnaissance opportunity grows with total probe volume when no relation enforcement exists, while the authorization outcome remains denial under the stated assumptions. Residual risks include fingerprinting, compromise of a trusted endpoint, policy error, incomplete path coverage, implementation bypass, and resource exhaustion. Detection remains necessary for evidence and follow-on response; the narrower claim is that alert-only detection should not be the primary containment mechanism for a machine-tempo campaign.
title: The AI Agent Swarm Meets First Contact: Conditions Under Which Preventive Relation Enforcement Is Scale-Invariant

summary: Abstract Distributed version control preserves source states, ancestry, branching, merging, and collaboration with extraordinary success. It does not ordinarily require engineering intent, failed approaches, claim scope, verification evidence, residual disagreement, or continuation state to exist as typed repository objects. Those records instead tend to be distributed across commit prose, review systems, issue trackers, CI logs, artifact stores, chat, and human memory. This disclosure explores a broader version-control model for software developed by humans and agents without claiming that content addressing, provenance, attestations, change-oriented versioning, or agent memory are new in isolation. Gemel models an evidence-bearing change : a content-addressed relation from an exact input state to an exact output state, linked to intent, operations, producer provenance, claims, evidence, residuals, verification scope, and causal context. Trajectories preserve completed, rejected, interrupted, superseded, and inconclusive work. Claims remain declarations rather than stored truth; support and readiness are derived conservatively from evidence, residuals, freshness, supersession, and policy. Context manifests and checkpoints provide bounded continuation surfaces without requiring private reasoning transcripts. The inspected Rust reference implementation defines deterministic canonical encoding, BLAKE3-256 identities, immutable objects, mutable refs, rebuildable indexes, 24 object families, Git-carried exchange, deterministic Git projection, semantic indexing, native and hosted synchronization, agent queries, policy checks, and an FRF court runner. For this paper, the supplied source archive was independently built in a clean temporary directory and cargo test --all-targets completed 236 tests with zero failures. This result is implementation-specific conformance evidence. It is not evidence that Gemel improves developer productivity, agent reliability, or industrial outcomes. Gemel composes with the Forensic Residual Framework (FRF) as an evidence plane and with FRF-Fuzz as a discovery plane. The paper situates that composition against Git facilities, patch algebra, provenance models, software-supply-chain attestations, reproducible builds, software archives, event sourcing, rationale capture, and agent memory. It discloses alternative embodiments and defines falsifiable evaluations for handoff quality, repeated-error reduction, evidence freshness, reconciliation, interoperability, context cost, storage overhead, and longitudinal fuzzing. Its principal claim is architectural: software history can be represented as an engineering graph in which source state, intent, evidence, residual uncertainty, negative knowledge, and continuation state possess explicit identity and scope. Whether that representation earns its operational cost remains an empirical question. Keywords distributed version control; Git; agentic software development; evidence engineering; provenance; content addressing; Merkle DAG; software agents; developmental trajectories; negative knowledge; residual primacy; FRF; FRF-Fuzz; reproducibility; software archaeology; semantic lineage; source provenance; event sourcing.
title: Gemel: Evidence-Native Version Control for Agentic Software Development - Longitudinal Engineering Memory, Residual-Aware Change Graphs, Git Interchange, and Reproducible Agent Handoffs

summary: Reproducibility release 1.1.0 for Ocean Engineering manuscript OE-D-25-10458. This package supports a controlled Rotterdam-Yokohama comparison of the Suez, Cape and Northern Sea Route corridors using three predefined strategic waypoint philosophies per corridor. The archive contains the Python routing and analysis code, all nine waypoint definitions, frozen maritime-network geometries and scenario/leg distances, dual-coastline quality-assurance and local-repair reports, 0.05/0.025-degree convergence outputs, sourced OpenStreetMap Suez Canal geometry and provenance, downstream time/fuel/CO2 analyses, exponent and vessel-reference sensitivities, and the frozen manuscript sources and figures. The routing method uses searoute 1.4.3, WGS84 distance recomputation and no great-circle fallback. The reproduction command stages the archived routes, regenerates downstream tables and copies the included figure assets. A full routing rerun additionally requires the externally distributed Natural Earth 10 m v5.1.1 and GSHHG 2.3.7 full L1 coastline datasets. Tests and release checks are documented in the archive. The comparison is strategic and does not predict realised voyages or commercial viability.
title: Effects of Route Representation on Distance and Downstream Voyage Implications in Europe–Asia Trade: A Comparison of the Suez, Cape, and Northern Sea Route Corridors

summary: Description : Classeur canonique source-par-source (66 feuilles) sous-tendant l'article "Data-Audited Elastic, Hardness, and Heterostructure-Compatibility Assessment of MAX Phases and MXenes". Contient : l'audit élastique et de dureté des 44 phases MAX canoniques et 11 MXenes ; l'audit de provenance des paramètres de maille ; la matrice de compatibilité dataset-pair des hétérostructures MAX/MAX (461 combinaisons admissibles) ; le screening de durcissement par contraste élastique validé contre des superréseaux expérimentaux (Fiantok et al. 2023) ; les propriétés d'interface (module biaxial, énergie de cohérence) ; la contrainte thermique de désaccord ; et la synthèse applicative orientée revêtements de protection. Chaque feuille documente sa source primaire (DOI), son statut de preuve (EXPERIMENTAL/DFT/UNKNOWN explicite), et une feuille de validation trace les vérifications de non-régression appliquées à chaque étape. Tableaux supplémentaires S1 (tenseur élastique et modules dérivés des 44 phases MAX canoniques), S2 (constantes élastiques 2D et E2D dérivé de 11 systèmes MXene), S3 (valeurs de dureté expérimentales avec charge, méthode, état d'échantillon et niveau de preuve). Format soumission-prêt correspondant aux tableaux cités dans le manuscrit.

title: MAX Phase and MXene Multisource Elastic, Hardness, and Heterostructure-Interface Database, Supplementary Tables S1–S3: Canonical Elastic, MXene, and Hardness Datasets for MAX Phases

summary: Supporting material for the manuscript "Subacute oral glyphosate impairs testicular function in male mice (Mus musculus): a threshold-anchored dose-response study of steroidogenesis, sperm quality, redox balance and spermatogenic histopathology" (Elbeeh, Filfilan, Filfilan and Filfilan), submitted to Drug and Chemical Toxicology (Taylor & Francis). Forty adult male Swiss albino (ICR) mice, 8-10 weeks old and 22.1-25.5 g at allocation, received vehicle (distilled water) or technical-grade glyphosate at 10, 50 or 100 mg/kg/day by oral gavage for 28 days, n = 10 per group. The dose range brackets the regulatory no-observed-adverse-effect level of approximately 50 mg/kg/day. Endpoints measured in the same 40 animals: body and testis weight; serum testosterone, LH and FSH; epididymal sperm concentration, progressive motility, viability and morphology; testicular malondialdehyde, reduced glutathione, superoxide dismutase and catalase; and testis histopathology stained with haematoxylin-eosin and with periodic acid-Schiff, assessed by the Johnsen tubular-maturation score and by measurement of seminiferous tubule diameter, germinal epithelial height and graded lesion severity. Sections were digitised on a Philips UltraFast Scanner at the x20 level (0.5 micrometres per pixel) and reviewed in the Philips PathologySuite viewer; morphometry was performed in ImageJ v1.54 with semi-automated annotation in QuPath v0.4.3 on fields exported at the native scan resolution. Contents: S1, the manufacturer's Certificate of Analysis for the test article (Sigma-Aldrich 337757, lot MKCZ1523, purity at least 96 per cent, CAS 1071-83-6); S2, analytical kits, instruments, assay conditions and intra- and inter-assay coefficients of variation; S3, the analysis and figure-plotting code; S4, the complete per-animal dataset underlying every figure and table; S5, the benchmark-dose model set with BMD and BMDL10 values; and Supplementary Figure S6 with its caption, showing the histomorphometry and graded lesion scores of Table 4 with individual animal values overlaid. README.md gives the full manifest. Every value reported in the manuscript can be recomputed from S4 using the code in S3. Statistics: continuous endpoints were compared by Welch's ANOVA with the Games-Howell post-hoc test; ordinal lesion grades by the Kruskal-Wallis test with Holm-adjusted Dunn's post-hoc test; monotonic trend by the Jonckheere-Terpstra test; and the endpoint family was controlled at a false-discovery rate of 5 per cent (Benjamini-Hochberg). The Johnsen tubular-maturation score was nominated in advance as the primary endpoint; every other endpoint is secondary. Ethics: all procedures were approved by the Bioethics Committee of Umm Al-Qura University, Makkah, Saudi Arabia (approval no. HAPO-02-K-012-2025-04-2781) and were conducted in accordance with the ARRIVE 2.0 guidelines. These 40 animals also support the cardiotoxicity, neurotoxicity and immunotoxicity arms of the same programme, which are reported separately under the same approval number. Licensed CC BY 4.0.
title: Supplementary data and analysis code for: Subacute oral glyphosate impairs testicular function in male mice (Mus musculus)

summary: This dataset accompanies the SpiderNet paper on modeling directional cell–cell meta-interactions from spatial omics data. It contains saved analysis results, plotting inputs, interactive visualization data, and benchmark outputs for eight study workflows.  Together with the SpiderNet code repository, these files support reproduction of the documented saved-result figures and exploration of trained results. A manifest provides file checksums and restoration paths. The collection does not include all raw inputs required for retraining every analysis.
title: SpiderNet: A meta-interaction basis for cell-cell communication in tissues

summary: Data repository for "Newborn neurons in the adult hippocampus regulate representational drift in area CA3 and memory plasticity." Computational environment: Python 3.6, MATLAB 2022a, Windows 10. Dataset: Representative data from 3 mice (IDs: XS149, XS155, XS156) across 4 time points (newborn neuron ages: 4–7 weeks or 8–9 weeks). Each time point contains 3 sessions: a Context A noCLZ baseline, and two post i.p. clozapine injection sessions (Context A CLZ and Context B CLZ). Raw data (2-photon TIFF images and behavioral data) and processed outputs are organized by session in subfolders. Processing pipeline: Imaging and behavioral data aligned via Behavioral data processing.ipynb Raw TIFFs motion-corrected with Suite2p Motion-corrected data denoised with DeepCAD Denoised data reprocessed with Suite2p for motion correction and ROI extraction; ROIs manually inspected via the Suite2p GUI Spatial information computed and place cells classified via Spatially-tuned place cell detection.py Downstream analyses performed with MATLAB scripts in code/Matlab/
title: Newborn neurons in the adult hippocampus regulate representational drift in area CA3 and memory plasticity

summary: This paper asks a narrow question. Lyapunov stability, geometric stability, and statistical stability are all described as spectral-gap properties. The gaps act on different operators, live on different spaces, and survive different perturbations. The informal habit of treating them as one nested hierarchy is correct for convex wells and hyperbolic sinks. It is not correct as a statement about dynamical systems in general. The paper replaces that habit with a comparison theorem. A stability claim is a profile: an evolution, a perturbation class, a projection, and a failure set. Comparative type can change when the map is held fixed and only the projection changes. Three statistical properties are kept distinct. The first is weak continuity of an invariant measure under perturbation. The second is a spectral gap of a transfer or Fokker–Planck operator on a named function space. The third is differentiability of the measure in the perturbation parameter. These three can hold together. They can also separate. The proved implications are scoped. A positive Hessian implies Lyapunov stability of a mechanical equilibrium and a dissipative Jacobian gap for a gradient flow. A hyperbolic sink gives weak continuity of a Dirac family and does not give mixing on a positive-dimensional density space. Uniform hyperbolicity gives a transfer-operator gap on an anisotropic space and, in the perturbation class of Keller and Liverani, weak continuity of an SRB family. Partial hyperbolicity yields a gap only after restriction to the hyperbolic factor. Nonuniform hyperbolicity with a Young tower yields a slower, tail-controlled rate and is compatible with instability of almost every orbit. A prescribed decay for a piecewise expanding map or a hypocoercive generator need not come from any hyperbolic splitting. Architectural estimates do not transfer between structurally distinct operator classes. In one linear-quadratic noise model the three classical tests return the same number. In a double well they separate. The paper does not claim that statistical mechanisms are finite, and it does not prove that averaging a frequency-gap Hamiltonian system produces a kinetic spectral gap.
title: Which Spectral Gaps Imply Which: Lyapunov, Geometric, and Statistical Criteria

summary: This repository contains the code and data accompanying the article “A Physics-Informed B-Spline Reconstruction of Flow Data,” published in Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering (CMAME). The package includes numerical inputs, model coefficients, and analysis and plotting scripts for the one-dimensional convection–diffusion, two-dimensional Burgers, and lid-driven-cavity examples presented in the paper. For the lid-driven-cavity case, the flow data are included, but the Firedrake solver, its computational environment, and the scripts used to generate these data are not provided. This archive preserves the version associated with the published article. The code will continue to be maintained and updated in the PI-BSR GitHub repository .
title: A Physics-Informed B-Spline Reconstruction of Flow Data: Reproducibility Package

summary: This work presents reusable mathematical bridges extracted from the Chronos formal-verification programme and related Lean developments in constrained dynamics, quantum mechanics, gravity, operator theory, partial differential equations, and Yang–Mills theory.   The purpose of the work is to make formally developed mathematical structures available for reuse beyond the physical problems in which they were originally constructed.   The paper develops four primary reusable connections.   First, it presents an internal-time framework for constrained Hamiltonian systems. When a candidate clock has a nonvanishing rate along a constrained trajectory, the system can be reparameterized with respect to that clock, producing relational evolution. This connects directly with the existing Chronos frozen-to-flow and Wheeler–DeWitt formalization.   Second, it develops a quantum–classical shared-time bridge based on expectation-value evolution. For suitable Hamiltonians, including the constant-force system already treated in the formal programme, quantum expectation values obey exact classical equations of motion.   Third, it extracts a reusable operator-theoretic chain connecting coercive lower bounds to positive spectral bounds, invertibility, and quantitative inverse or resolvent control. Together with cutoff and graph-core machinery developed during the Yang–Mills formalization, this provides reusable infrastructure for unbounded operators in quantum mechanics and partial differential equations.   Fourth, it presents the general inverse-distance field structure underlying the existing Chronos gravity formalization. A radial inverse-distance potential produces an inverse-square gradient, satisfies the three-dimensional vacuum Laplace equation away from the source, and has radius-independent spherical flux. The same mathematical structure can therefore be instantiated in Newtonian gravity, electrostatics, Green-function theory, and other potential problems.   The central goal is compositional reuse. Rather than treating each formal proof as an isolated endpoint, the work identifies intermediate machine-checkable theorem structures that can serve as starting points for additional formal developments.   Immediate applications include relational clock models, Wheeler–DeWitt and constrained systems, Ehrenfest and semiclassical quantum dynamics, electrostatic inverse-square fields, Schrödinger operators, spectral-gap arguments, elliptic PDEs, gauge systems, and other operator-theoretic problems.   This paper accompanies the broader Chronos formal-verification programme and is intended as an openly reusable mathematical and formal-physics resource.
title: Reusable Formal Bridges from Chronos Verification: Internal Time, Quantum–Classical Dynamics, Operator Control, and Inverse-Distance Fields

summary: Read the 74-page Split-Zero paper . Complete LaTeX, cumulative sources, citations and checks ; results and exact proof locators ; matching GitHub source edition . The Split-Zero programme represents finite zero-divisor classes of the completed Riemann zeta function by polynomials in an arithmetic theta-source Hilbert space. The metric on the observation kernel is obtained by minimizing over all original polynomial representatives. This edition calculates how that metric changes with polynomial degree. It gives every Christoffel–Darboux covariance entry, including reflected-node collisions and divided derivatives; retains the full correction after coefficient compression; and expresses the four-cutoff determinant ratio as a product of exact degree-step factors. The paired quartet relation proves a strict finite kernel contraction. Its magnitude at the unresolved large-degree kq scale is not evaluated, and no RH conclusion is claimed. Programme citations in the paper are clickable links to actual public proof sources, with exact locations where available. The same source links are included in the three complete cumulative LaTeX successors. The source archive includes a machine-readable link registry and restores two previously unpublished cited proofs. Older cumulative citations still needing an exact source match remain explicitly identified in that registry; no guessed destination is presented as verified. Classical sources retain their human authorship: Gernot Akemann and Graziano Vernizzi, Characteristic Polynomials of Complex Random Matrix Models , Nuclear Physics B 660 (2003), 532–556 ; the named authors of the NIST DLMF orthogonal-polynomial chapter ; and Jack Sherman and Winifred J. Morrison, Adjustment of an Inverse Matrix Corresponding to a Change in One Element of a Given Matrix (1950) . The last citation is historical and bibliographically checked; the rank-one calculation used here is proved directly. Earlier programme proofs remain separately credited. The reader contains ten complete proof bodies. The new CD and degree-step checkers pass 779 exact finite checks in each of ordinary and optimized Python, with 13 intended failure controls in each mode. These checks do not sample the actual period matrix or establish a large-degree asymptotic. The three large cumulative LaTeX manuscripts have not been freshly compiled in this edition. The 98 earlier standalone papers and archives remain. To respect Zenodo's 100-file limit, the preceding result index is retained byte-for-byte as predecessor062/RESULT_INDEX.json in the new source ZIP. Its original separate download also remains in the preceding immutable edition. Existing authorship, rights notices and access conditions are preserved. This successor does not claim that unfinished parallel-task work has been incorporated.
title: Split-Zero cohomology: exact degree changes in the arithmetic kernel metric

summary: This paper proposes a speculative Holographic–Multiway Theory (HMT) connecting the holographic principle, multiverse/quantum branching concepts, and Wolfram Physics. It develops a computational framework in which hypergraph rewriting, multiway evolution, causal structure, branchial graphs, and lower-dimensional information encoding can be used to investigate whether holographic behavior and multiverse-like branching are mathematically compatible. The paper then proposes a Wolfram Physics research program for testing these ideas computationally, followed by an experimental framework for investigating selected hypotheses associated with the Gateway Process. Proposed technologies include Wolfram computational models, artificial neural systems, EEG/fMRI, neurofeedback, noninvasive neuromodulation, and blinded information-retrieval experiments. The work is presented as a research proposal rather than an established theory, with emphasis on falsifiability, quantitative testing, independent replication, and separating demonstrated physics from speculative extensions concerning consciousness, temporal information retrieval, and afterlife-related hypotheses.
title: Toward a Holographic–Multiway Theory of the Multiverse: A Wolfram Physics Framework for Testing Holography, Quantum Branching, and the Gateway Hypothesis

summary: In a recent publication, we derived a general relativity (RG) gauge-invariant solution modelling a granular universe composed of spherical bodies with a radial Gaussian density profile. In this framework, a cosmological constant Λ emerges natively from the gravitational self-energy of these discrete nodes. Energy conservation dictates a uniform compactness ratio M\/σ^2 across all bodies, a relation closely met by the elliptical galaxies as shown in the GAMA survey. This setup yields: Λ≈1/( 12 π^3 ) (κ a c^2   M/σ^2    )^2which, using the compactness measured in the GAMA survey, evaluates to Λ≈ 0.9×10^(-52)   m^(-2) , a value close to modern observations. The model predicts the R ∝ (1+z)^(-1.5) size scaling confirmed by the 3D-HST+CANDELS survey and, unlike standard ΛCDM theory, the model preserves total energy conservation. Before gas clouds collapsing around z≈3 the universe was mostly homogeneous resulting in this model to Λ≈0. During the Lyman-α forest epoch an intense gas clouds collapsing into stars and black holes occurred. We extended our RG model to purely radial collapsing nodes which gave Λ≈(κ a^3)/(4π^3 ) M/R^2   (d^2 R)/(dt^2 )<0. This backreaction force of the gas cloud collapse reached a peak around z ≈2 , and later declined around z≈1.5 when massive galaxies ran out of cold gas or experienced quenching shutting down their star formation. At this epoch, the galaxies began their assembling into their modern structures, raising the cosmological constant to its current baseline value. Integrating this dynamical Λ(z), while targeting the current Hubble parameter of H_0=73 km/s/Mpc , yields a perfect validation against the Planck cosmic microwave background angular scale θ^*=0.010410 rad and the latest DESI BAO data.   Notably, the model predicts a structure clustering amplitude of S_8≈0.81 in line with the BOSS/DESI Deep Scale Galaxy Clustering data survey. The proposed model successfully bypasses the need for an unexplained, speculative dark energy burst.
title: Addressing the Hubble tension with a dynamical Λ(z) induced by galactic gravitational self-energy and by backreaction force from gas cloud collapse

summary: Traditional unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) methods are designed to flag or localise deviations from a normative distribution, ignoring the underlying generative mechanisms of the anomalies. Yet the nature of an anomaly is often as important as its presence. We reformulate UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem, in which the objective is to infer the most probable corruption responsible for each observation. Our framework yields a probabilistic anomaly score as the energy of the inferred corruption parameters, and serves as a principled recipe for developing new UAD algorithms. We derive several existing methods as instances of the general framework, each corresponding to the same energy score under different modelling choices. Experimentally, we study the framework's components in a controlled setting, and improve object-class AUROC on the MVTec AD dataset by 2.3% by adapting the underlying corruption model. Finally, we validate the framework on a brain MRI benchmark, achieving strong detection performance while producing estimates of pathology intensity, bias, and geometry. Code is available at https://github.com/jgmyles/inverse-uad.
title: A Principled Approach to Unsupervised Anomaly Detection

summary: Split-Zero cohomology and the zeta-function research programme is a cumulative collection of mathematical papers, complete LaTeX proofs, formalization sources, calculations and literature-based research notes. Its central question is how the zeros of the Riemann zeta function can be studied through explicitly constructed arithmetic cohomology, spectral actions and quantitative metric estimates. The collection also retains the related heat-flow, arithmetic-trace, fluid, complexity and thermal-geometry investigations from which parts of this programme developed. Project and reading guide · Research contents · Machine-readable workbench index . Papers remain separate readable PDFs; the source archives supply the corresponding editable mathematics and supporting materials. What the collection contains Split-Zero coefficients, geometry and cohomology. The construction retains a ring's internal zero and a separate symbol for absence, so a zero element in a specified support fibre is not confused with an absent fibre. The papers construct coefficient maps, quotients, homology, finite spectral jets and their relation to the infinite theta quotient. Deligne's Weil II provides a motivating source for the cohomology–duality–weight-control programme; its finite-field theorem is not asserted to apply automatically to the Riemann zeta function. Read the cohomology and weight-control paper and the foundational objects and maps . Arithmetic theta sources and analytic control. The central analytic complex is [V → B], with theta map Θ and quotient B/ΘV. Scaling acts by D = −x∂x; the Mellin-side arithmetic function is 2ξ(s), where ξ is the completed Riemann zeta function. The papers carry finite zero packets, including multiplicities, through the original source maps and least-norm quotient metrics. They develop source recovery, residue and period maps, tensor and exterior constructions, Mellin and Gamma estimates, orthogonal-polynomial kernels, Hankel–Toda determinant identities, boundary terms, and growing-degree volume and covariance calculations. The cumulative Split-Zero reader , its proof companion , and the separate kernel, conductor and source-transport papers retain the complete arguments. Conductor geometry and spectral observation. Further papers calculate the original relation and conductor maps, kernels, quotient volumes, real-period resonances, inverse spectra and finite observation bounds. The native spectral paper , real-period paper , resonance-direction paper and inverse-power observation paper have distinct, explicit scopes. Geometric examples are not represented as identified arithmetic zeta-zero packets. Formalization and reproducible calculation. The Lean sources and formalization notes cover specified algebraic, quotient and homological interfaces. Source packages retain exact finite checkers, numerical or interval calculations where supplied, figures, manifests and verification records. A Lean check of an interface, a finite algebra test and an analytic proof are documented as different forms of evidence; none silently certifies the others. The wider zeta literature and connected investigations. The separate zeta reader , fluid/Navier–Stokes reader , de Bruijn–Newman heat-flow reader , Connes/arithmetic-trace reader , geometric-complexity reader and vacuum and thermal-geometry reader preserve the earlier research routes and their stated limitations. Related Unified Flow calculations concern specified black-hole, thermal, spectral-zeta and geometric-flow probes. The CUE research map connects existing random-unitary-matrix, Mellin and finite-phase-space work. An analogy or proposed connection is not presented as an established implication between major conjectures. How to read and assess the work This is an ongoing research programme, not a claimed proof or disproof of RH or the other major conjectures discussed in the connected notes. The remaining arithmetic estimates and identifications are stated in the individual paper
title: Split-Zero cohomology and the zeta-function research programme

summary: Clustering high-dimensional data is a fundamental task in unsupervised machine learning with applications to a variety of domains. In the centralized data scenario, this task is commonly solved using deep clustering methods that utilize deep neural network architectures to learn clustering-friendly latent space representations. In Federated Learning, where data is distributed between clients and is private, deep clustering methods are less explored. In particular, recently introduced federated deep clustering methods, despite showing very promising performance, still fall short in reliably providing good performance if data across clients are non-identically-independently distributed. In this work, we introduce a generalization of Deep Clustering Networks to the federated scenario, named FedDCN, that simultaneously optimizes a reconstruction loss and a clustering loss. To ensure robustness and latent space alignment in non-identically-independently distributed data scenarios, FedDCN generates synthetic data augmentations, and its learning objective includes a geometric regularization for latent space alignment. Through experimental evaluation, the effectiveness of the approach under IID and non-IID assumptions is demonstrated, and future research directions are identified.
title: Federated Deep Clustering Networks for High-Dimensional and Heterogeneous Data

summary: Recent advances in diffusion models have enabled high-performance, instance-adaptive compressed sensing through posterior sampling, without task-specific policy training. Existing methods select sensing probes by maximizing total posterior signal variance and are therefore primarily reconstruction-driven. We introduce a classification-driven extension motivated by the closed-form posterior covariance of a class-conditional Gaussian mixture model, which decomposes into within-class and between-class uncertainty. Using calibrated soft classifier outputs, we estimate these uncertainty terms from diffusion posterior samples and propose a classification-oriented criterion for selecting the dominant sensing direction in the unmeasured subspace. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 compare the resulting classification accuracy, measurement cost, and reconstruction quality with those of reconstruction-oriented counterparts. The results identify regimes in which semantic posterior uncertainty yields a more favorable classification--measurement trade-off and quantify the associated reconstruction cost.
title: Classification-oriented adaptive sensing via posterior sampling

summary: Increasing demand for high-performance optical devices drives the search for improved fabrication and design paradigms. While photonic circuits have traditionally used structures with two discrete 'binary' height levels, grayscale 'wavy' interfaces, or optical Fourier surfaces, have recently become possible. They provide precise control over the Fourier components that govern the optical response. This capability raises the question: When does a wavy device improve performance and why? Here, we show that wavy integrated processors exhibit superior accuracy and efficiency to binary analogs. Inverse-designed wavy interferometers have the design freedom to minimize outscattering to free space and backreflections. They reach a five-fold lower transmission error than binary counterparts and enable bandwidths up to 300 nm. We formalize these findings for other distinct integrated devices, such as photonic crystals, nanocavities, and beam emitters. A Fourier-optics analysis identifies a trade-off: wavy profiles manipulate light more accurately, whereas binary profiles excel in interaction strength. As such, tailored wavy profiles emit high-quality beams. However, binary profiles remain preferable in photonic crystals and nanocavities, where maximal index contrast is required and binarization-induced higher harmonics are benign. Thus, for quantum information, optical computing, and sensing, optical Fourier surfaces offer a route to miniaturized integrated circuits with improved performance.
title: When Integrated Photonics Should Be Wavy

summary: The collinear-antiferromagnetic spin-fluctuation paradigm has long guided unconventional superconductivity research, yet fails to reconcile the noncollinear spin phenomena observed across cuprates, iron-based superconductors, and nickelates. Using extensive first-principles calculations and unbiased large-scale DMRG simulations, we show that Dzyaloshinski-Moriya interaction (DMI)-arising from local inversion-symmetry breaking-is a common ingredient across these families. This DMI unifies hallmark observations in parent compounds-incommensurate orders, spin-wave gaps, and noncollinear textures. Under hole doping, strong DMI drives spin vortices to merge with pi-shifted hole stripes, forming hybrid vortex-hole stripe phases. These phases stabilize charge order while supporting, not suppressing, superconductivity. By contrast, under electron doping, these vortices pin holes and suppress long-range superconductivity. Our results establish DMI as a unifying link between noncollinear magnetism and superconductivity, identifying hole-strip-vortex coupling as a microscopic pairing engine. Given that DMI is common across major superconductor families, these findings challenge the prevailing pairing mechanism and offer an experimentally testable roadmap for materials optimization.
title: Universal Dzyaloshinski-Moriya interaction dictates pairing in unconventional superconductor families

summary: Discovering the structure and kinetics of chemical reaction networks (CRNs) from time-series concentration data is a fundamental challenge in chemical kinetics, with existing approaches relying on prior mechanistic assumptions or suffering from high computational cost and noise sensitivity. In this work, we present integral chemical reaction neural networks (iCRNNs), a framework that combines the interpretable, physics-constrained, architecture of chemical reaction neural networks (CRNNs) with an integral collocation formulation of the governing dynamics. Rather than solving ODEs forward in time at each training step, we approximate the integral of the learned rate functions directly using numerical quadrature. This yields an entirely algebraic forward pass consisting only of matrix operations, eliminating the repeated adaptive ODE solves of standard CRNN and producing smoother, more predictable training. We provide a recovery error analysis characterising the structural sources of ill-conditioning (conservation laws, reaction reversibility, and shared reactant sets) that limit network identifiability. On two benchmark CRNs, iCRNN trains in roughly half the wall-clock time of the baseline CRNN method on a four-species mechanism and between three and four times faster on a five-species mechanism, while completing every training run reliably and attaining comparable or lower loss.
title: Integral chemical reaction neural networks
