summary: Invasive plant species pose a significant threat to global biodiversity, particularly within protected areas. This study investigated the diversity, community structure and distribution of invasive plants in Margalla Hills National Park (MHNP), Pakistan, combining a systematic quadrat-based field survey with soil physicochemical analysis and a GIS/remote-sensing framework. Surveys were conducted along 300 m transects, with separate quadrats for trees (10 × 10 m), shrubs (5 × 5 m) and herbs (1 × 1 m). The survey yielded 26 growth-form records representing 24 taxonomically distinct invasive species. Ricinus communis and Annona squamosa were each recorded as both a tree and a shrub. Overall records comprised 12 tree, 8 shrub and 6 herb growth forms. Because quadrat areas differed among growth forms, density was standardized to individuals m⁻² for cross-form comparison, on which basis herbs were by far the densest (5.19 m⁻²), followed by shrubs (0.77 m⁻²) and trees (0.14 m⁻²). Within growth forms, Sophora japonica led the trees (26.54 individuals quadrat⁻¹), Tecoma stans the shrubs (20.90) and Silybum marianum the herbs (5.58). Herbs also recorded the highest mean cover (24.99 ± 6.61%). Across the park, Broussonetia papyrifera, Parthenium hysterophorus and Lantana camara were the most frequently recorded dominants. The invasive assemblage was most species-rich and diverse in the tree layer (Shannon–Wiener H ≈ 2.52) and least diverse in the herb layer (≈ 1.98), reflecting the broad suite of woody invaders established in the park and the sustained pressure this places on native woody communities. Soils were neutral to slightly acidic (pH 6.63–7.22) with low electrical conductivity (0.81 dS m⁻¹) and very low organic matter (0.13 ± 0.01%), conditions associated with hardy, disturbance-adapted invaders. These findings confirm active invasion across all growth forms and provide a spatially explicit baseline for targeted management and long-term monitoring of this protected Himalayan ecosystem.
title: Community structure, edaphic drivers and ecological impacts of invasive plant species in Margalla Hills National Park, Pakistan
An Interpretable Synthetic Benchmark for Machine Learning in Low-Strain Pile Integrity Testing

summary: Hashing Is Not Retrieval is a prospectively frozen three-arm evaluation of context accumulation in small-model multi-agent code cartography. It compares three ways for an orchestrator to hand work to a worker: 1. FULL HISTORY — retransmit prior worker outputs. 2. OPAQUE REF — replace the previous output with an unretrievable SHA-256 digest. 3. RETRIEVED — resolve the digest through a tenant-scoped content-addressed store and inject the recovered bytes. All arms receive identical source-derived evidence. The apparatus measures the exact message content sent to workers and records token counts, model and provider identifiers, generation IDs, usage, cost, retries, and retrieval proofs. A five-task gate preceded a fixed 50-task controlled benchmark, followed by a separate state-required evaluation across 24 deterministic fixtures and a five-scale Medusa case study. Key result: in the controlled benchmark, RETRIEVED reduced paired peak context by 38.3% relative to FULL HISTORY. The state-required follow-up shows that opaque references fail when state must be recovered, while verified retrieval preserves substantially more structural information. This is bounded-context evidence for automatic orchestrator-resolved state passing inside a specific two-worker code-cartography harness — not a universal claim about autonomous memory, long-context capability, or reasoning quality. The release includes the corrected author-identified preprint, executable apparatus, frozen results, task fixtures, telemetry, and verification instructions. Version 1.0.2 supplies the curated, verifier-passing reproducibility archive. It supersedes the uncurated archive from version 1.0.1 and includes the exact pinned apparatus, state-required fixtures, frozen results, and archive verifier. Submission status: This preprint was submitted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Long Context Foundation Models (LCFM). LCFM is a non-archival workshop; this Zenodo record is a public preprint and does not indicate acceptance or publication. Workshop information: https://longcontextfm.github.io/ Research website: https://abdulmoizahmed.com/research Concept DOI (all versions): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22844754 License: CC BY 4.0.
title: Hashing Is Not Retrieval: A Three-Arm Study of Context Accumulation in Small-Model Code Cartography

summary: Code, result tables, and figures for a two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) study in which instruments for coronary artery disease (CAD) were filtered by colocalization (coloc.abf, PPH4 ≥ 0.8) with brain cell-type-specific cis-eQTLs from single-nucleus transcriptomics of human cortex (Bryois et al., Nature Genetics 2022). Of 274 CAD lead loci, 32 colocalized with brain-cell eQTLs, yielding 32 cell-annotated instruments (excitatory neurons 12, pericytes 7 after palindrome exclusion, oligodendrocytes 5, astrocytes 3, microglia 2, inhibitory neurons 1, OPC 1) explaining 3.4–5.6% of CAD liability on the liability scale. Random-effects inverse-variance weighted estimates (with weighted median, MR-Egger, leave-one-out, Cochran's Q and I², MR-PRESSO-analog global permutation, outlier correction, and MR-Steiger sensitivity analyses) are provided for ischemic stroke (OR 1.335, 95% CI 1.189–1.498, p = 1.0e-6), any stroke (OR 1.309, p = 8.5e-7), Alzheimer's disease (proxy-inclusive, and a clinically diagnosed replication arm), and major depression (null negative control). Cell-type-stratified analyses attribute the stroke effect to neuronal and neurovascular-unit (pericyte) expression programs. Contents: full analysis pipeline (R 4.6 / Python 3.13), all derived result tables (instruments, colocalization posteriors, harmonized exposure–outcome pairs, primary and stratified MR, leave-one-out, Steiger), publication figures (SVG/PDF vector plus ≥300 dpi PNG), the manuscript (v1.7), supplementary tables S1–S8, and the completed STROBE-MR checklist. Raw GWAS summary statistics are not redistributed; all sources are public (GWAS Catalog accessions GCST90132315, GCST006908, GCST006906, GCST90027158, GCST007511, GCST005839; eQTL record 10.5281/zenodo.7276971) and every number needed to reproduce the tables and figures is included.
title: Cell-type-stratified Mendelian randomization implicates neuronal and neurovascular expression programs in the causal effect of coronary artery disease on stroke: analysis code, result tables, and figures

summary: Within the Complementarity-First and Reciprocal Internal Complementarity research program, we study the linear perturbations of the smooth massive magnetic core constructed in the companion paper. The host is a supplied flat-space SU(2) Yang–Mills theory with one adjoint scalar, unit magnetic degree, and equal scalar and vector masses. The action and physical scales are not derived from reciprocity. Starting from the full Cartesian second variation and linear Gauss constraint, we organize the physical angular sectors without excluding translations, boundary phase, or neutral radiation. A positive whole-half-line comparison gives a 4/25 lower bound in the two-profile magnetic radial sector. The separate spherical electric-flux operator has a positive but unquantified gap after charge and boundary data are separated. Explicit first-nonradial matrices, a compact-annulus Schur reduction, symbolic-angular-momentum higher matrices, and rational core certificates give all-angular nonnegativity conditional on the stated background and sufficient certificate predicates. The framed kernel consists of three translations and one phase tangent. In a covariant derivative-and-mass completion, a compact-remainder argument gives coercivity modulo this collective space with an unquantified positive constant. The kinetic wave operator nevertheless has essential spectrum [0,∞): exactly Gauss-dressed photon packets retain the zero threshold. An exact translation–photon overlap constructs fields orthogonal to the full kernel in L2 whose energy tends to zero while their local core tends to a nonzero translation. Thus energy-space or local-moment projection, not ordinary L2 orthogonality, is required for the stated coercivity. The result is a conditional linear sign, kernel, and norm-control theorem, not nonlinear orbital stability, decay, a numerical mode spectrum, or a monopole population prediction.
tags: Complementarity-First; Reciprocal Internal Complementarity; magnetic monopole; Yang–Mills– Higgs Hessian; coercivity; collective modes; photon continuum; computer-assisted proof; Lean.
title: All-Angular Positivity and Threshold-Compatible Coercivity

summary: Topic models, in particular Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), have been adapted to hyperspectral imagery (HSI) as a route to interpretable spectral mixtures: each spectral unit (canonically a pixel) becomes a document of quantised band-frequency tokens and the inferred topic-word distributions act as non-negative basis spectra. Yet the dominant evaluation criterion remains downstream classification accuracy, an accuracy-only view that is silent on whether the basis is reproducible, band-robust, calibrated, or actually outperforms standard linear baselines. We propose and instantiate a twelve-axis evaluation framework for LDA-style topic models on HSI that quantifies, on the same set of benchmarks: (F-1) classification macro-F1 compared across five method families (paired differences and a hierarchical Bayesian model), (F-2) topic-word coherence (c_v, c_NPMI, U-Mass), (F-3) seed stability for both LDA and two neural variants (ProdLDA, ETM), (F-4) capacity sensitivity across K in {4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16}, (F-5) band-mask robustness, (F-6) cross-method clustering agreement (LDA vs Felzenszwalb, SLIC, patches, pixels), (F-7) topic-label coupling via P(L | t) entropy and KL, (F-8) per-topic Hungarian-aligned identity tracking, (F-9) HIDSAG cross-preprocessing stability, (F-10) cross-scene topic transfer, (F-11) rate-distortion of the topic representation, and (F-12) external alignment of the topics with a spectral library and a method-rank cross-comparison. We apply the framework to six standard HSI benchmarks (Indian Pines, Salinas, Salinas-A, Pavia University, Kennedy Space Center, Botswana) and five subsets of the HIDSAG mineralogical database (GEOMET, MINERAL1, MINERAL2, GEOCHEM, PORPHYRY). The framework yields three findings that the accuracy-only view does not surface. First, on the labelled scenes the topic-routed soft classifier, which routes the raw spectrum to per-topic logistic experts, matches the raw-spectrum logistic baseline in macro-F1 (0.915 against 0.910, a paired difference of 0.005), while a logistic regression on the topic proportions theta alone trails the baseline by 0.325: the topics add an interpretable routing to the raw spectrum but do not replace it. Second, on Salinas-A under the SWIR-only band mask the paired ARI between canonical and masked dominant-topic maps reaches 0.766, while on Kennedy Space Center under every mask, and on Botswana under the SWIR mask, the same paired ARI collapses to approximately 0.01, separating scenes on which an interpretability claim is band-robust from scenes on which it is not. Third, the theta-only deficit holds on HIDSAG: over its nineteen mineralogical targets the topic-logistic classifier trails raw-logistic by 0.268 macro-F1 (lower on 18 of 19 targets), contrary to the prima-facie expectation that mineralogical mixtures favour topic decomposition over the raw spectrum. We release 3895 deterministic derived artefacts (449 MB), the builder source, the FastAPI backend, the React frontend, and a 109-endpoint test harness as a public, MIT-licensed reproducibility package. Code and derived artefacts: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_LDA_HSI . Interactive web application: https://lda-hsi.fasl-work.com . Manuscript sources: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_LDA_HSI_Paper . Funding: The Advanced Mining Technology Center (AMTC) Basal project (ANID/PIA Project AFB220002) and ANID FONDECYT Postdoctorado 3220094.
title: Beyond Accuracy: A Multi-Axis Evaluation Framework for Interpretable Topic Models on Hyperspectral Imagery

summary: The COVID-19 pandemic altered human mobility and natural-resource management, potentially affecting wildlife in rural landscapes where conservation and livestock production coexist. This work evaluated temporal variation in mammal detections in the Bienes Comunales Santa Cruz Nuevo Wildlife Management Unit, Puebla, Mexico, using camera-trap data from two pre-pandemic surveys (2018 and 2019) and a post-restriction survey (2022). Sampling comprised 39 station-years and 3,193.31 effective camera-days. The work compared encounter rates, station-level occurrence, and observed and estimated species richness among years, and also examined associations between wild mammals, domestic animals, human activity, altitude, and vegetation attributes. Species richness varied substantially among years: 14 species were recorded in 2018, nine in 2019, and 11 in 2022. Chao2 estimates and station-based rarefaction supported this interannual variability rather than a consistent directional change. Gray fox ( Urocyon cinereoargenteus ) detections declined significantly during the post-restriction survey relative to the pre-pandemic baseline (rate ratio = 0.280, 95% CI = 0.129–0.604, FDR-adjusted q = 0.025). Other species showed uncertain or non-estimable temporal effects because of sparse detections or complete zeros. Raccoon detections were negatively associated with altitude, whereas gray fox and coyote detections were associated with livestock occurrence. These findings demonstrate species-specific temporal responses and emphasize that nondetection or nonsignificant results do not necessarily indicate ecological stability. Although the observed changes coincided with the COVID-19 period, they cannot be attributed exclusively to pandemic restrictions because the year also represented climatic, ecological, and management variation.
title: Fauna–Vegetation correlations and relative abundance in a fragmented landscape of Southwest Mexico: Pre- and Post-COVID-19 analysis

summary: MATLAB implementation, per-item numeric results and figure code for the study "Dissociating Prompt Quality from Response Compliance in Automated Prompt-Engineering Assessment". A four-agent evaluator running on a locally hosted Qwen 2.5-7B-Instruct judge scores each prompt as an artifact before any response exists, then scores the resulting response twice on identical items: once against criteria extracted from that prompt, and once against a fixed rubric that never sees it. Verifiable constraints are checked with the IFEval reference implementation rather than model-generated labels. The whole pipeline runs on consumer CPU hardware with no external API calls. Contents: src/ the MATLAB agents and run scripts; scripts/ the IFEval verifier and the figure code; data/ a SHA-256 manifest of all 4,275 benchmark prompts and the filtered IFEval subset; results/ per-item results for the main run (n = 500) and the ablation (n = 120), the construct-validation output and the IFEval verification output. title: Dissociating Prompt Quality from Response Compliance in Automated Prompt-Engineering Assessment: evaluator, results and figure code

summary: Extended reasoning can increase response time and computational cost without improving an answer. Models may revisit unproductive steps or build further reasoning on an earlier mistake. This study evaluates whether Jev, a probabilistic decision maker, can provide an inexpensive error signal to help decide when additional reasoning is needed. We compare Jev with GPT-5.6 Luna on generated ordering and logic-grid puzzles and on the official released ZebraLogic test set. The generated questions are four-choice items with one correct answer among four. The official test set is used open-ended: Luna produces the full grid, Jev checks it without the solution key, and Luna may revise once when Jev does not judge the answer consistent. On the generated multiple-choice problems, Jev is 5 to 60 percentage points more accurate than Luna with reasoning disabled, at lower measured API cost, and every observed top-choice disagreement identifies a Luna error. On a stratified sample of 200 official ZebraLogic puzzles, exact-grid accuracy rises from 41.0% with reasoning disabled to 90.5% with high-effort reasoning. A revision pass adds two points in both settings, but a revision-only control shows the gain comes from the extra attempt, not from Jev's information: on the answers Jev flags, a plain second look is at least as accurate as the Jev-informed revision (16 versus 13 correct without reasoning, and 70 versus 70 at high effort). Jev detects 93% of the weak reasoner's errors with 92% precision, but only 10% of its high-effort flags identify errors. These results motivate using Jev or similar decision models in a model harness: software that controls when to continue, reconsider, retrieve evidence, or allocate more reasoning. An early check could help avoid spending further computation on a mistaken line of reasoning. The experiments measure checking of final answers, however, and do not measure reductions in hallucination or repetitive reasoning inside a harness. On the official benchmark, extra reasoning accounts for most of the accuracy, and the checker's information does not improve on a second attempt. Larger studies with balanced answer positions, selective triggers, and step-level feedback are needed to test whether checking improves accuracy or reduces total cost.
title: Evaluating Jev for Cost-Effective Candidate Verification: An Exploratory Study

summary: This dataset provides a curated and reproducible compilation of data used to analyze long-term trends in external-cause mortality in Ecuador from 1990 through 2024. The primary data sources are official mortality statistics and population estimates and projections published by Ecuador’s National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censos, INEC). The dataset includes annual mortality counts and population-based indicators for major external-cause categories, including land transport injuries, other transport accidents and accidental injuries, suicide, homicide, events of undetermined intent, and other external causes. Where available, the data are organized by calendar year, sex, age or age group, geographic unit, ICD classification, and cause of death. Population denominators, crude mortality rates, confidence intervals, absolute and relative changes, mortality composition measures, sex-specific rate ratios, and variables used in the statistical analyses are documented separately from the original source data. The repository also contains information used to support the reproducibility of the associated scientific study, including analytical datasets, variable definitions, ICD harmonization information, population denominators, model-related variables, sensitivity-analysis data, quality-control documentation, data provenance, and records of differences identified between historical editions of INEC statistical tables. Hospital discharge datasets reviewed during data curation are documented at the variable and source level. Individual-level hospital discharge microdata are not included in the public dissemination package when their inclusion could create unnecessary privacy or re-identification risks. Original source information is kept distinct from derived variables and researcher-calculated indicators to preserve full provenance and auditability. The package follows FAIR data principles and includes machine-readable CSV files together with the original curated Excel database, a data dictionary, methodology documentation, provenance and transformation records, quality-control information, ethics and privacy considerations, citation metadata, licensing information, and version history. No missing values were imputed solely for publication, and no undocumented assumptions were used to generate unavailable data. Values for recent years should be interpreted according to the provisional or revised status indicated by the original INEC sources. This dataset is intended to support reproducibility, secondary epidemiological analyses, public health surveillance, methodological review, and research on injuries, violence, suicide, homicide, road traffic mortality, and other external causes of death in Ecuador.
title: Ecuador External-Cause Mortality, Population Denominators, and Reproducibility Dataset, 1990–2024

summary: We are pleased to announce the release of ASPECT 3.1.0. ASPECT is the Advanced Solver for Planetary Evolution, Convection, and Tectonics. It uses modern numerical methods such as adaptive mesh refinement, multigrid solvers, and a modular software design to provide a fast, flexible, and extensible mantle convection solver. ASPECT is available from                    https://aspect.geodynamics.org/ and the release is available from         https://geodynamics.org/resources/aspect and         https://github.com/geodynamics/aspect/releases/tag/v3.1.0 Among others this release includes the following significant changes: - Support for modeling surface deformation has been significantly   extended. Fastscape erodibility can now vary in space and time according to   climate and sea level data, checkpointing functionality has been improved,   tangential boundary velocities along deformed boundaries are more accurate,   and support for initially deformed boundaries has been improved. Preliminary   coupling to the landscape evolution library Landlab is available as well.   (Liang Xue, Derek Neuharth, Michael Pons, Daniel Douglas, Zhibin Lei, Anne    Glerum, Ninghui Tian, Bob Myhill, Rene Gassmoeller, Timo Heister, Wolfgang    Bangerth) - Modeling crystal-preferred orientation and anisotropic viscosity has been   significantly improved. summary: This technical note investigates whether operator-relative noncentrality can predict the relative empirical power of complementary localized scan statistics in correlated spectra. The motivating real-data benchmark compares BABAR and BESIII measurements of the e⁺e⁻ → π⁺π⁻ cross section in the ρ-resonance region on a common 5 MeV grid from 0.600 to 0.880 GeV. The real-data comparison remains negative, with no statistically supported localized shape tension identified. The methodological study compares a coherent-yield scan with a covariance-profiled shape scan and defines the frozen coordinate Θ = log(ES/EY), where ES and EY represent maximum local operator-accessible signal strengths. An archival confirmatory replication used 50,000 null calibration draws per covariance environment, 15,000 independent null-validation draws per environment, 1,440 signal/covariance conditions, and 576,000 injected pseudoexperiments. Θ predicted which scan had greater empirical power with pooled AUC 0.9820 and mean leave-one-covariance-environment-out AUC 0.9740; its correlation with the empirical power difference was 0.9185. Independent Type-I error estimates ranged from 0.0466 to 0.0540. The results support operator-relative noncentrality as a useful empirical coordinate for complementary globally calibrated scans within the tested benchmark. The underlying ingredients, including Gaussian noncentrality, covariance-weighted subspace detection, quadratic scanning, and Monte Carlo calibration, are established; the contribution is a reproducible computational synthesis and controlled characterization rather than a claim of a new general statistical law
title: Operator-Relative Noncentrality in Localized Correlated-Spectrum Scans: A BABAR–BESIII Benchmark

summary: xinvert v0.3.0 Complete CUDA GPU back-end, a rename pass on the module and public API, and a thread-safe progress reporter. This release also folds in everything that had accumulated since v0.2.0 — v0.2.1 and v0.2.2 were developed but never published, so 0.3.0 is the next version on PyPI after 0.2.0. (Earlier gaps exist in this project too: 0.1.4–0.1.6 were tagged but never released.) Highlights GPU back-end for every equation type architect='gpu' now works for all seven solvers, not just the standard 2-D Poisson case: | equation type | CPU kernel | GPU kernel | | --- | --- | --- | | standard 1D | invert_standard_1D | invert_standard_1D_gpu | | standard 2D | invert_standard_2D | invert_standard_2D_gpu | | standard 2D full (flux form) | invert_standard_2D_full | invert_standard_2D_full_gpu | | standard 3D | invert_standard_3D | invert_standard_3D_gpu | | general 2D | invert_general_2D | invert_general_2D_gpu | | general 3D | invert_general_3D | invert_general_3D_gpu | | general 2D biharmonic | invert_general_bih_2D | invert_general_bih_2D_gpu | Red-Black SOR kernels with a shared loop skeleton ( _run_sor_2d_loop , _run_sor_3d_loop ), adaptive convergence-check intervals, and an optional per-call thread-block shape via iParams['gpu_block2d'] . GPU solves are bounded to one at a time ( gpus._GPU_MAX_CONCURRENT ) so dask can pipeline disk I/O against them, and CUDA context creation is done on the main thread. Measured on an RTX 3090: single timestep, 300 x 720: 17.3x (1.73 s GPU vs 29.99 s on one core) 12 timesteps, 300 x 720: ~1.6x over 12-core dask CPU (21.3 s vs 33.3 s) — at this size the solve is launch-bound, not execution-bound large grids, fixed 1000 iterations: up to 17.1x See the benchmark docs for the full sweep and the launch-overhead analysis. Module rename: numbas.py → cpus.py The CPU kernel module is now named for what it contains. xarray 's dask backend remains the multi-core path. API renames (breaking) Four public names lose a _test suffix that misdescribed them as test-only — they implement real discretizations used by shipped applications: | old | new | | --- | --- | | invert_standard_2D_test | invert_standard_2D_full | | inv_standard2D_test | inv_standard2D_full | | invert_GillMatsuno_test | invert_GillMatsunoFlux | | invert_Stommel_test | invert_StommelFlux | Users calling the old names must update; there are no aliases. The private __coeffs_*_test helpers became __coeffs_*Flux . Thread-safe live progress output printInfo output from dask worker threads and distributed clusters no longer interleaves. Each message is emitted as a single atomic write with the right parent header, so Jupyter and worker logs stay readable. Tests Seven CPU/GPU consistency suites ( tests/test_Gpu*.py plus tests/test_CpuGpuConsistency.py , ~1700 lines) asserting the analytic solution where one exists and CPU/GPU agreement otherwise; GPU cases skip cleanly when no CUDA device is present. Benchmark suite under tests/ , with machine-readable results in tests/results/*.json and figure regeneration via tests/plot_benchmarks.py . CI matrix: Python 3.9 – 3.12, 38 passed, 37 skipped . Housekeeping .gitattributes line-ending policy plus a one-off renormalization — the repository had a CRLF/LF mix that inflated diffs by thousands of lines. deriv() with the central scheme no longer converts numpy-backed input to dask; the rechunk is applied only to genuinely chunked data. Documentation: GPU status table, benchmark page and the parallel-inversions notebook brought in line with the implementation. Upgrade notes Breaking: the four API renames above. CUDA support is optional — import xinvert still works on machines without a GPU, and architect='cpu' remains the default. If you pin gpu_block2d , the default is still (16, 16) . Full diff: https://github.com/miniufo/xinvert/compare/v0.2.0...v0.3.0

summary: Reproducibility package for the manuscript "Distinct conformational and interaction signatures of the FGFR1 V561M and N546K resistance-associated mutations: a multi-replicate molecular dynamics study" . This package contains everything needed to regenerate every table, figure and reported number in the manuscript from the analysis outputs, except the raw trajectories. Systems and sampling: three FGFR1 kinase domain systems (wild type, V561M, N546K) in complex with erdafitinib, three independent 500 -ns replicates each , analysed over the 200 -500 ns plateau. Nominal sampling 4.5 us; realised aggregate production sampling 4.491 us. All three systems share a 9.28387 nm cubic SPC water box with 0.15 M NaCl (total atoms 78 , 608 / 78 , 609 / 78 , 624 ). Contents: - scripts/ - 14 analysis and plotting scripts (Python 3.10 ) covering every main and supplementary figure panel - tables/ - 38 per-replicate and summary result tables (CSV) - matrices/ - 24 DCCM matrices, common-subspace PCA projections and RMSD series (NumPy .npy) - mdp/ - GROMACS run-control files (minimisation, ions, NVT, NPT, production) plus the fully expanded grompp parameter file - tpr/ - the nine production run inputs (complete, with all parameters baked in ) - topology/ - GROMACS topology files ( system and protein topologies, posre.itp, ligand parameters, index files ) - README.md - directory layout, frame-selection rules, uncertainty conventions, table/figure provenance, and full run parameters Software: GROMACS 2024.6 (production) and 2024.3 (analysis), gmx_MMPBSA 1.6 .5 , MDTraj 1.10 .3 , Python 3.10 (NumPy 2.2 .6 , SciPy 1.15 .2 , Matplotlib). summary: This work studies whether internal rotation changes the longevity of source-free localized excitations in the reduced Enchan local time-rate field. The frozen scalar dynamics are S_tt = div[mu(D) grad S] - S with D = |grad S| and mu(D) = 1/(1 + D^(3/2)); no continuing external torque, centrifugal force, primitive matter source, or added rotational potential is used during the reported evolutions. Stage A supplies the non-rotating source-free baseline. Stage B1 initializes rotating phase-space states at omega = 4, 8, and 12 and evolves the extended runs to dimensionless time t = 100. Over 80 <= t <= 100, the mean localized-energy fractions are approximately 0.002207 for the non-rotating baseline and 0.006006, 0.149470, and 0.368846 for omega = 4, 8, and 12. The result is a graded rotation-associated longevity hierarchy: weak rotation gives little practical rescue, intermediate rotation substantially extends localization, and the strongest tested branch remains transient-localized through t = 100. Matched-energy near-zero-J_z controls provide a separate causality check and show that net canonical angular momentum alone is not a monotonic explanation of every late-time difference. Stage B2 separately tests spontaneous self-spin from exactly zero initial total angular momentum and finds no validated convergent counter-rotating branch in the tested scalar-only initial-data families. The ordered scan supports a physical formation picture in which a localized grain can move from weak rotational asymmetry through progressive spin-up into a strong-rotation long-lived branch. Time, space, and omega are dimensionless reduced-branch quantities; t = 100 is not assigned an SI duration in this work. The deposit contains the Version 1.0 manuscript PDF, a reproducibility ZIP with the publication source, code, selected archived numerical outputs, README, LICENSE, and SHA-256 integrity manifest. The final main.pdf is the default preview. License: Enchan Research & Verification License v1.0. Copyright (c) 2026 Mitsuhiro Kobayashi.
title: Can Rotation Make Spacetime Grains Last? Internal Angular Momentum and Longevity of Source-Free Enchan Grains

summary: Industry 4.0 transforms manufacturing through cyber-physical systems, the Industrial Internet of Things, digital twins, and data-driven intelligence, yet the volume of latency-sensitive data these technologies generate strains conventional cloud-only computing. Edge and fog computing have emerged as the central enabling paradigm, distributing computation across a device–fog–cloud continuum. This paper surveys the enabling technologies of Industry 4.0 with an emphasis on edge–cloud computing and formulates the resulting computation-offloading problem as a constrained, load-dependent optimization model that jointly minimizes task latency and device energy under deadline and capacity constraints. A genetic algorithm and a particle swarm optimizer are developed and benchmarked against five baseline strategies on synthetic industrial workloads. Across one hundred tasks averaged over ten instances, the genetic algorithm reduced the weighted objective by 34.1 percent relative to a greedy heuristic and by 82.6 percent relative to cloud-only execution, while lowering deadline violations to 1.6 percent. The latency–energy trade-off, convergence, and scalability are analyzed, and managerial implications for industrial deployment are discussed.
title: Energy- and Latency-Aware Computation Offloading in Edge–Fog–Cloud Architectures for Industry 4.0

On held-out benchmark poems the label is recoverable from the words xiangsi (相思) and xiangyi (相忆); in a source-audited corpus of 52,253 Tang poems, xiangsi is followed as a formula with a history, from pre-Tang song to Tang poems of farewell and exchange, across 116 poets, and into fifteen close readings. summary: Abstract The stability of the banking sector is fundamental to economic growth and financial system resilience, particularly in developing economies such as Nigeria.  However, and sadly enough, global, recent and recurring failure risks and collapses of banks which have been blamed on poor external audit qualities, are counter-productive to national economic development.  Therefore, the broad objective of this study was to study the effect of audit quality on failure risks of listed deposit money banks in Nigeria between the period 2009 and 2024. This study adopted both descriptive and ex-post facto research designs.  Using secondary data extracted from audited financial reports of 11 censored (from a population of 11) deposit money banks listed on the Nigerian Exchange Group, (NGX), and analyzing one hundred and seventy-six firm year observations using regression with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors analysis technique, the findings revealed that audit firm size (AUFS) significantly improve bank Z score, [coef. = 0.638 (p-value = 0.005)], audit report timeliness (ARTIME) significantly reduces bank Z score [coef. = −0.400 (p-value = audit committee diligence (ACDI) revealed a positive insignificant effect respectively on Z score of listed deposit money banks in Nigeria during the period under consideration. Based on the above findings, it was concluded that audit quality in the Nigerian banking sector is not uniformly effective, rather, its effect on bank failure risks is selective, with only specific audit mechanisms demonstrating the capacity to significantly enhance financial solvency, thereby suggesting that the effectiveness of external audit as a safeguard against bank failure risks depend not merely on its presence, but likely on factors such as depth, credibility, and functional execution of its key components.   this study concluded that audit.  Consequently, this study recommended among others, that listed deposit money banks in Nigeria, alongside regulators and external auditors, should prioritize substantive governance quality, auditor competence and independence, rigorous audit execution, timely financial reporting, risk-sensitive audit remuneration, coordinated assurance mechanisms, and proactive internal control systems over mere procedural compliance, in order to strengthen transparency, reinforce market confidence, and enhance long term financial stability in line with Agency theory. Keywords: Audit Quality, Failure Risks of Listed Deposit Money Banks, Bank Z-Score, Agency Theory.

summary: Concern about low-information-content publications—least publishable units, salami-sliced outputs, redundant papers, benchmark increments, and false-positive findings dressed as discoveries—is distributed unevenly across the sciences. Some fields appear to convert procedural effort into publishable "findings" almost at will, whereas others force nearly every contribution into the slow form of a convergence result or an error audit. Existing accounts attribute the disparity to incentives, statistical flexibility, or disciplinary culture, but incentives are universal while the output pattern is not, and flexibility alone cannot explain fields whose verdicts are stringent and objective yet are gamed at industrial scale. This paper develops a structural account centered on two features of a research program: the closure of its decision space by formal and empirical constraints, and the gameability of the verdicts that adjudicate its claims. Stringency, fidelity to the epistemic target, and resistance to rehearsal are distinct properties of a verdict; a benchmark can be maximally stringent and objective while remaining trivially gameable. Because the underlying dimensions are ordinal and non-compensatory, susceptibility to low-information publication cannot be expressed as a scalar ratio and is better represented as a typology. Four regimes are distinguished: convergent programs with dual closure and ungameable verdicts; formally bounded programs with thin empirical closure; programs governed by stringent but gameable verdicts; and open-latitude programs with weak closure and subjective adjudication. Each regime channels publication pressure into a different production line—flexibility monetization, verdict gaming, or fragmentation and repackaging—and each requires interventions matched to its production line rather than a generic reform package. The model explains why string theory and fixed-benchmark machine learning, often misread by single-axis accounts, exhibit such different pathologies, and it predicts which reforms will work, fail, or backfire in each regime.
title: The Structural Determinants of Low-Information Publication in Science: A Constraint–Verdict Typology

summary: Embarrassingly parallel workloads, such as parameter sweeps, Monte Carlo simulations, and hyperparameter searches, are pervasive in research computing, yet running a single experiment across a mix of laptops, lab servers, cloud virtual machines (VMs), and high-performance computing (HPC) clusters still demands ad hoc Secure Shell (SSH) tunnels, port forwarding, and scheduler-specific scripts. We present DART, a job distributor that turns any such mix of machines into a single shared queue. DART pairs a Dockerized job server with a one-line worker command-line interface (CLI); a hosted Hub automates reverse tunneling, worker authentication, and public endpoint provisioning, so collaborators on any network, including those behind network address translation (NAT) or using a personal laptop, can join an experiment with a single API-key and no firewall changes. This makes DART especially effective for researchers who combine Advanced Cyberinfrastructure Coordination Ecosystem: Services & Support (ACCESS)-provisioned HPC resources [1] with institutional clusters and personal workstations, federating all resources under one queue with no per-site configuration. All communication is encrypted end-to-end, and access is controlled through API-key authentication and a personal identification number (PIN)-protected dashboard. Researchers create experiments, define parameter grids, and monitor jobs entirely from a web dashboard; a work-conserving scheduler dispatches jobs on demand, exploits resource heterogeneity, and automatically re-queues failures. In a real-world deployment of 37,720 jobs across 68 heterogeneous machines spanning an institutional HPC cluster, a national ACCESS resource, and personal computers, the observed run completed in approximately eight days. DART’s dynamic allocation achieved a simulation-derived 35× speedup over static partitioning (≈4 days vs. ≈139 days), reducing a multi-month workload to days.
title: DART: Distributed Assignment of Research Tasks for Heterogeneous Compute Environments

summary: Anticoncentration is a key ingredient in complexity theoretic arguments for quantum advantage from Gaussian boson sampling. Here we prove polynomial small ball anticoncentration for complex Gaussian transpose Gram hafnians and complex symmetric Gaussian hafnians. For a k × 2n matrix X with independent standard complex Gaussian entries, we establish polynomial small ball anticoncentration for haf(XᵀX) under k ≥ 4n and n²/k = O(log n). For hafnians of 2n × 2n complex symmetric Gaussian matrices, polynomial small ball anticoncentration holds for every n ≥ 1. In both ensembles, any prescribed inverse polynomial failure probability can be achieved with an inverse polynomial small ball radius, uniformly over all centers. These results go beyond moment based anticoncentration by controlling the probability of small hafnian amplitudes. The proof combines Fourier compression with conditional Wishart geometry to handle dependent hafnian cofactors. Files: main.pdf contains the main article (14 pages); supplement.pdf contains the supplementary proofs and additional results (33 pages). Related Lean verification sources: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22554594 and https://github.com/HongruZhao/ComplexGramHafnians.
title: Local Anticoncentration for Gaussian Boson Sampling via Conditional Wishart Geometry

summary: Research and educational instrument. Not for clinical use, for the care of any patient, or to determine or influence any drug dose. A simulation-calibrated informatics pipeline that fits a single-compartment exponential approximation to published population pharmacokinetic models of unfractionated heparin during cardiopulmonary bypass, and renders the result as an institution-specific decay nomogram. This is the supporting code and archived analysis for manuscript JCVA-D-26-01511. Published models of heparin disposition are biexponential and require a computer to evaluate. The pipeline asks how well a single decay constant k — calibrated to an institution's own dosing, weight and bypass-time distributions — can approximate a chosen reference model, and quantifies where it fails. The answer differs sharply by model: at the reversal timepoint the approximation holds to 0.38% mean absolute error for Lanoiselée and 0.44% for Jia, but to 10.3% for Delavenne, rising to 72% after repeated supplemental boluses. Contents. Five reference-model implementations with their published parameters and provenance; seeded cohort sampling and calibration; agreement statistics; nomogram geometry and rendering; a Streamlit dashboard; an automated test suite; and a frozen analysis run comprising 20 result tables, the main-text and supplementary figures, a run manifest and a manuscript-ready summary. A sixth model (PRODOSE-2) is implemented and tested but withheld from the active pipeline pending validation and peer review. Reproduction. Every reported number regenerates from one seeded command: pip install -r requirements-frozen.txt python run_analysis.py --seed 20260912 --outdir /tmp/check python check_frozen.py /tmp/check All randomness comes from explicitly seeded generators, each analysis stage drawing from its own independent stream. Re-running reproduces every archived result to within floating-point rounding on any machine, and byte-for-byte on the machine the archive was built on. The manifest records the seed, the commit, the package versions and every analysis decision. Continuous integration runs the suite on two Python versions, each test file again in isolation, and the reproduction check on every push. Verification, and its limits. Automated checks confirm that each closed-form solution actually solves its own differential equations and satisfies the identities they imply, and six landmark values from a published simulation are reproduced to within 3%. No participant-level data from any source study is held, so no model is re-fitted and no prediction is compared with an observation. What is demonstrated is faithful implementation of the published models — not that the published models are correct. No external or predictive validation is claimed. Scope. The pipeline represents the pharmacokinetic central-compartment amount only. It does not model the pharmacodynamic layer — anti-factor Xa activity or activated clotting time — nor peripheral-compartment heparin, antithrombin, protamine pharmacology or heparin rebound. Converting a residual amount into a protamine dose requires an institutional ratio that this software does not supply. Intended purpose. This software is a research and educational instrument whose purpose is to demonstrate and teach an informatics method under simulated conditions. Within that intended purpose it is not a medical device. Nothing here has been cleared, approved or evaluated by any regulatory authority; outputs have not been validated against measured anti-factor Xa activity, activated clotting time or clinical reversal in patients, and no clinical benefit has been demonstrated. Anyone using it outside the intended purpose does so on their own responsibility and may bring the tool within medical-device oversight in their jurisdiction; the authors accept no responsibility for such use. Version 2.0.0 changes every statistic reported by 1.x and corrects two errors in previou
title: Heparin decay nomogram pipeline

summary: Within the Complementarity-First and Reciprocal Internal Complementarity research program, we study regular perturbations of a supplied smooth massive degree-one SU(2) Yang–Mills–Higgs monopole with equal scalar and vector masses. A neutral transverse readout satisfies an exact nonlinear equation whose source is a divergence of an L2 tensor plus an L6/5 remainder. An additional affine infrared class is preserved on compact regular intervals and transported to admitted framed gauge and collective charts. Ordinary kinetic collective subtraction need not preserve its homogeneous negative norm; a compensating sum retains the relevant cancellation. Pure spatial transport is skew, while complete coordinate corrections admit an endpoint Duhamel identity. These statements concern finite-time admissibility, not uniform all-time localization. Assuming the companion’s nonnegative physical Hessian, complete framed kernel, local-moment coercivity and explicit threshold-packet estimates, a Gauss projection of a compact weighted translation yields a sharper test in the same monopole background. Its affine tail label differs from its actual initial local center rate, and its collective-orthogonal velocity lies outside the domain of the physical Hessian’s inverse square root. Its global linearized local-moment connection residual is unbounded in kinetic L2 while remaining bounded in the energy norm. We obtain an exponentially weighted time-average lower bound, not a universal pointwise growth law. Fixed-time differentiability excludes a time-uniform linear-scale nonlinear strong-residual estimate on this class, but does not establish nonlinear Lyapunov instability. The actual spectral inverse-square-root domain is necessary and sufficient for bounded unforced linear radiative position. We identify the nonlinear physical source that would need stronger control. The example proves that affine admissibility does not imply spectral admissibility; it does not classify their full inclusion relation or prove all-time nonlinear spectral propagation.
tags: Complementarity-First; Reciprocal Internal Complementarity; magnetic monopole; infrared control; affine tail class; spectral inverse domain; collective modulation; threshold wave; Lean.
title: Affine and Spectral Infrared Control of Monopole Perturbations

summary: This record contains the experimental reproducibility package accompanying the study “Model for Improving the Quality of Uncertain Clustering.” The package provides the complete Jupyter notebook, generated figures, run-level results, aggregated summaries, parameter-sensitivity analyses, bootstrap-stability estimates, drift-response measurements, and paired statistical comparisons. The experimental evaluation compares Fuzzy C-Means (FCM), Possibilistic C-Means (PCM), Possibilistic Fuzzy C-Means (PFCM), and entropy-regularized FCM across five datasets: Iris, Wine, Breast Cancer Wisconsin, Digits represented by four unsupervised principal components, and an imbalanced overlapping synthetic dataset. summary: Abstract Modern enterprise AI systems increasingly operate across multiple authorized data sources, memories, applications, and tools. This creates a security problem that is not adequately described as conventional data theft. An AI workload may be individually authorized to read support records, engineering information, source-control activity, supplier data, budgets, hiring information, and calendars. No individual source may contain a sensitive strategic conclusion. However, the AI system may combine those independently authorized fragments and reconstruct a new high-value object: an unreleased product direction, likely launch window, supplier dependency, market strategy, organizational weakness, or other forward-looking enterprise knowledge. The security boundary therefore changes. The relevant questions are no longer only: Who may read data A? or: Who may read data B? They also become: Who may establish the relationship A-to-B? Who may retain or disclose the resulting inference? Who may cause an external action because of that reconstructed meaning? This paper describes a threat model in which the AI assistant becomes a computational graph across previously separate enterprise systems. The resulting risk may exist even when each underlying retrieval complies with its ordinary source-level permissions. The sensitive object is not necessarily a stolen database record; it may be a new semantic object created through authorized association. The architecture therefore separates two security transitions: Authorized Data | v Authorized Reconstruction | v Computed Meaning | v Authorized Effectuation | v External Consequence The first transition concerns association authority : permission to read independently authorized fragments does not automatically imply permission to join those fragments into a new semantic relationship. The second concerns execution-time finality : permission to compute, generate, or prepare an output does not automatically imply permission for that output to become externally consequential. The proposed architectural model therefore introduces controls around independently governed relationship mapping, session-bound reconstruction, minimum-necessary temporary views, provenance-aware release, and a mandatory effectuation boundary. Candidate outputs or actions remain non-effective until the consequence-controlling component verifies the applicable authority, provenance, destination, policy state, disclosure conditions, and other protected execution state immediately before release or effectuation. In compact form: Access != Association Association != Authority to Disclose Computation != Authority to Cause Consequence The execution-time consequence boundary may be implemented through existing mechanisms such as policy-enforcement points, reference monitors, authorization servers, secure execution environments, transaction coordinators, capability systems, protected dispatchers, database commit controls, network command gates, or equivalent mechanisms. The important property is functional rather than terminological: A computed result or proposed action remains non-effective until the component with mandatory control over the actual consequence verifies that the exact pending effect is permitted under current protected authority and state. This architecture is intended to complement conventional identity, access control, encryption, zero-trust, data-loss prevention, confidential-computing, logging, and authorization systems rather than replace them. Those mechanisms continue to protect identities, stores, channels, and individual permissions. The additional problem addressed here is governance of the relationship created between authorized fragments and governance of the transition from computed meaning to actual consequence . The paper presents this as a forward-looking threat model rather than an allegation concerning any specific enterprise or AI product. The objective is to identify an architectural risk
title: Enterprise AI as a Reconstruction Layer: Governing Derived Knowledge and Execution-Time Consequences

summary: This paper proposes a persistent epistemic architecture for AI systems in which durable cognitive state is explicit and independent of any particular language model. The persistent substrate maintains inspectable, scoped beliefs with provenance, distinguishes individual sources and accumulates domain-sensitive trust, retains unresolved questions across interactions, and supports offline consolidation that detects contradictions and generates hypotheses. Its contents participate directly in subsequent learning and action rather than serving only as retrieved memory. A dependency-free prototype instantiates this core, with language models at both linguistic interfaces, to illustrate the cycle by which attributed testimony becomes revisable belief. The central claim is that continual learning requires explicit epistemic structure: a representation of what the system believes, why it believes it, whom it learned it from, and what remains unresolved, if its evolving epistemic state is to remain inspectable and correctable. This becomes increasingly consequential as AI systems contribute to their own development, because increasing capability does not necessarily entail a corresponding improvement in epistemic reliability. Persistent epistemic state provides a substrate on which correction and calibration can accumulate over time while remaining externally auditable. Preprint submitted to arXiv in September 2026. Source code and demonstrator: https://github.com/protopopescu/chloe and  https://lftm.gla.ac.uk/chloe/
title: CHLOE: A Persistent Epistemic Architecture for Inspectable AI

summary: Multi-agent active inference gives a natural account of belief sharing: agents hold local posteriors over a shared latent state, communicate those beliefs, and pool them into a colony-level consensus. The same mechanism is fragile when a member is miscalibrated, corrupted, or strategically wrong. Because the standard pool multiplies the reports together, a single confident-but-wrong broadcast that puts near-zero mass on the true state can pull the whole consensus off it, outweighing many honest members. The colony therefore needs a way to preserve the useful structure of belief sharing while limiting the influence of contaminated beliefs. This paper presents Active Fedference, a discrete-categorical framework that connects robust federated generalized variational inference with active inference belief sharing. The main bridge is structural: standard belief sharing appears as the non-robust corner of a broader generalized-Bayes family, while robust losses, conservative server fusion, and explicit aggregation diagnostics describe how the system moves away from that corner under declared contamination mechanisms. The result is not a replacement for belief sharing, but a containment result: ordinary belief sharing is recovered when robustness is turned off. Bounded-loss theory applies on the client axis, while the variational-server axis supplies an objective-backed redescending weight update. Following the manuscript's authoritative three-axis guarantee map, the paper keeps source-conditional client updates, a recovery-only heuristic server rule, and an objective-backed variational server rule as separate claim owners, with no robustness guarantee transferred between them. The study suite then exercises the framework as an end-to-end research system: recovery checks anchor the standard-Bayes limit, belief-sharing studies verify the communication baseline, contamination experiments test robust consensus, and extension studies probe moving agents, hierarchical latent structure, sensitivity to acuity and colony size, parameter recovery, and single-host socket-backed federation traces. All reported quantities are generated from deterministic analysis artifacts and injected into the manuscript by token, so the paper, figures, release package, and validation reports remain tied to the same execution record. The open-source repository is ActiveInferenceInstitute/Active_Fedference. This final-release manuscript uses assigned version DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22149133; the bound deposited PDF and repository release are controlled by separate publication gates.
title: Robust Belief Sharing in Federated Active Inference: A Recovery-Tested Generalized-Variational Framework for Categorical Contamination-Aware Consensus

summary: Recent agentic campaigns show that coordinated AI systems can compress reconnaissance, exploitation, and credential harvesting into machine-tempo operations. This paper asks a narrow question: whether increasing the number of untrusted attack sources changes the authorization outcome of an inline control that mediates every protected path and permits only explicit device-to-device relations. Under stated assumptions of complete mediation, fixed and correct policy, uncompromised trust anchors, no alternate path, and sufficient enforcement capacity, it does not. Additional untrusted source identities create additional denied first-contact events, not a permitted relation. This is a conditional property of the authorization rule, not a claim that throughput, alert volume, or availability are independent of swarm size. A four-run laboratory test of an AutoGen agent using GPT-4o provides a mechanism demonstration: the agent created four fresh network identities, and each was denied at its first observed unauthorized probe. The test does not establish a population rate or current-frontier performance. A closed-form illustration shows why reconnaissance opportunity grows with total probe volume when no relation enforcement exists, while the authorization outcome remains denial under the stated assumptions. Residual risks include fingerprinting, compromise of a trusted endpoint, policy error, incomplete path coverage, implementation bypass, and resource exhaustion. Detection remains necessary for evidence and follow-on response; the narrower claim is that alert-only detection should not be the primary containment mechanism for a machine-tempo campaign.
title: The AI Agent Swarm Meets First Contact: Conditions Under Which Preventive Relation Enforcement Is Scale-Invariant

summary: Abstract Distributed version control preserves source states, ancestry, branching, merging, and collaboration with extraordinary success. It does not ordinarily require engineering intent, failed approaches, claim scope, verification evidence, residual disagreement, or continuation state to exist as typed repository objects. Those records instead tend to be distributed across commit prose, review systems, issue trackers, CI logs, artifact stores, chat, and human memory. This disclosure explores a broader version-control model for software developed by humans and agents without claiming that content addressing, provenance, attestations, change-oriented versioning, or agent memory are new in isolation. Gemel models an evidence-bearing change : a content-addressed relation from an exact input state to an exact output state, linked to intent, operations, producer provenance, claims, evidence, residuals, verification scope, and causal context. Trajectories preserve completed, rejected, interrupted, superseded, and inconclusive work. Claims remain declarations rather than stored truth; support and readiness are derived conservatively from evidence, residuals, freshness, supersession, and policy. Context manifests and checkpoints provide bounded continuation surfaces without requiring private reasoning transcripts. The inspected Rust reference implementation defines deterministic canonical encoding, BLAKE3-256 identities, immutable objects, mutable refs, rebuildable indexes, 24 object families, Git-carried exchange, deterministic Git projection, semantic indexing, native and hosted synchronization, agent queries, policy checks, and an FRF court runner. For this paper, the supplied source archive was independently built in a clean temporary directory and cargo test --all-targets completed 236 tests with zero failures. This result is implementation-specific conformance evidence. It is not evidence that Gemel improves developer productivity, agent reliability, or industrial outcomes. Gemel composes with the Forensic Residual Framework (FRF) as an evidence plane and with FRF-Fuzz as a discovery plane. The paper situates that composition against Git facilities, patch algebra, provenance models, software-supply-chain attestations, reproducible builds, software archives, event sourcing, rationale capture, and agent memory. It discloses alternative embodiments and defines falsifiable evaluations for handoff quality, repeated-error reduction, evidence freshness, reconciliation, interoperability, context cost, storage overhead, and longitudinal fuzzing. Its principal claim is architectural: software history can be represented as an engineering graph in which source state, intent, evidence, residual uncertainty, negative knowledge, and continuation state possess explicit identity and scope. Whether that representation earns its operational cost remains an empirical question. Keywords distributed version control; Git; agentic software development; evidence engineering; provenance; content addressing; Merkle DAG; software agents; developmental trajectories; negative knowledge; residual primacy; FRF; FRF-Fuzz; reproducibility; software archaeology; semantic lineage; source provenance; event sourcing.
title: Gemel: Evidence-Native Version Control for Agentic Software Development - Longitudinal Engineering Memory, Residual-Aware Change Graphs, Git Interchange, and Reproducible Agent Handoffs

summary: Supporting material for the manuscript "Subacute oral glyphosate impairs testicular function in male mice (Mus musculus): a threshold-anchored dose-response study of steroidogenesis, sperm quality, redox balance and spermatogenic histopathology" (Elbeeh, Filfilan, Filfilan and Filfilan), submitted to Drug and Chemical Toxicology (Taylor & Francis). Forty adult male Swiss albino (ICR) mice, 8-10 weeks old and 22.1-25.5 g at allocation, received vehicle (distilled water) or technical-grade glyphosate at 10, 50 or 100 mg/kg/day by oral gavage for 28 days, n = 10 per group. The dose range brackets the regulatory no-observed-adverse-effect level of approximately 50 mg/kg/day. Endpoints measured in the same 40 animals: body and testis weight; serum testosterone, LH and FSH; epididymal sperm concentration, progressive motility, viability and morphology; testicular malondialdehyde, reduced glutathione, superoxide dismutase and catalase; and testis histopathology stained with haematoxylin-eosin and with periodic acid-Schiff, assessed by the Johnsen tubular-maturation score and by measurement of seminiferous tubule diameter, germinal epithelial height and graded lesion severity. Sections were digitised on a Philips UltraFast Scanner at the x20 level (0.5 micrometres per pixel) and reviewed in the Philips PathologySuite viewer; morphometry was performed in ImageJ v1.54 with semi-automated annotation in QuPath v0.4.3 on fields exported at the native scan resolution. Contents: S1, the manufacturer's Certificate of Analysis for the test article (Sigma-Aldrich 337757, lot MKCZ1523, purity at least 96 per cent, CAS 1071-83-6); S2, analytical kits, instruments, assay conditions and intra- and inter-assay coefficients of variation; S3, the analysis and figure-plotting code; S4, the complete per-animal dataset underlying every figure and table; S5, the benchmark-dose model set with BMD and BMDL10 values; and Supplementary Figure S6 with its caption, showing the histomorphometry and graded lesion scores of Table 4 with individual animal values overlaid. README.md gives the full manifest. Every value reported in the manuscript can be recomputed from S4 using the code in S3. Statistics: continuous endpoints were compared by Welch's ANOVA with the Games-Howell post-hoc test; ordinal lesion grades by the Kruskal-Wallis test with Holm-adjusted Dunn's post-hoc test; monotonic trend by the Jonckheere-Terpstra test; and the endpoint family was controlled at a false-discovery rate of 5 per cent (Benjamini-Hochberg). The Johnsen tubular-maturation score was nominated in advance as the primary endpoint; every other endpoint is secondary. Ethics: all procedures were approved by the Bioethics Committee of Umm Al-Qura University, Makkah, Saudi Arabia (approval no. HAPO-02-K-012-2025-04-2781) and were conducted in accordance with the ARRIVE 2.0 guidelines. These 40 animals also support the cardiotoxicity, neurotoxicity and immunotoxicity arms of the same programme, which are reported separately under the same approval number. Licensed CC BY 4.0.

summary: This paper asks a narrow question. Lyapunov stability, geometric stability, and statistical stability are all described as spectral-gap properties. The gaps act on different operators, live on different spaces, and survive different perturbations. The informal habit of treating them as one nested hierarchy is correct for convex wells and hyperbolic sinks. It is not correct as a statement about dynamical systems in general. The paper replaces that habit with a comparison theorem. A stability claim is a profile: an evolution, a perturbation class, a projection, and a failure set. Comparative type can change when the map is held fixed and only the projection changes. Three statistical properties are kept distinct. The first is weak continuity of an invariant measure under perturbation. The second is a spectral gap of a transfer or Fokker–Planck operator on a named function space. The third is differentiability of the measure in the perturbation parameter. These three can hold together. They can also separate. The proved implications are scoped. A positive Hessian implies Lyapunov stability of a mechanical equilibrium and a dissipative Jacobian gap for a gradient flow. A hyperbolic sink gives weak continuity of a Dirac family and does not give mixing on a positive-dimensional density space. Uniform hyperbolicity gives a transfer-operator gap on an anisotropic space and, in the perturbation class of Keller and Liverani, weak continuity of an SRB family. Partial hyperbolicity yields a gap only after restriction to the hyperbolic factor. Nonuniform hyperbolicity with a Young tower yields a slower, tail-controlled rate and is compatible with instability of almost every orbit. A prescribed decay for a piecewise expanding map or a hypocoercive generator need not come from any hyperbolic splitting. Architectural estimates do not transfer between structurally distinct operator classes. In one linear-quadratic noise model the three classical tests return the same number. In a double well they separate. The paper does not claim that statistical mechanisms are finite, and it does not prove that averaging a frequency-gap Hamiltonian system produces a kinetic spectral gap.
title: Which Spectral Gaps Imply Which: Lyapunov, Geometric, and Statistical Criteria

summary: This work presents reusable mathematical bridges extracted from the Chronos formal-verification programme and related Lean developments in constrained dynamics, quantum mechanics, gravity, operator theory, partial differential equations, and Yang–Mills theory.   The purpose of the work is to make formally developed mathematical structures available for reuse beyond the physical problems in which they were originally constructed.   The paper develops four primary reusable connections.   First, it presents an internal-time framework for constrained Hamiltonian systems. When a candidate clock has a nonvanishing rate along a constrained trajectory, the system can be reparameterized with respect to that clock, producing relational evolution. This connects directly with the existing Chronos frozen-to-flow and Wheeler–DeWitt formalization.   Second, it develops a quantum–classical shared-time bridge based on expectation-value evolution. For suitable Hamiltonians, including the constant-force system already treated in the formal programme, quantum expectation values obey exact classical equations of motion.   Third, it extracts a reusable operator-theoretic chain connecting coercive lower bounds to positive spectral bounds, invertibility, and quantitative inverse or resolvent control. Together with cutoff and graph-core machinery developed during the Yang–Mills formalization, this provides reusable infrastructure for unbounded operators in quantum mechanics and partial differential equations.   Fourth, it presents the general inverse-distance field structure underlying the existing Chronos gravity formalization. A radial inverse-distance potential produces an inverse-square gradient, satisfies the three-dimensional vacuum Laplace equation away from the source, and has radius-independent spherical flux. The same mathematical structure can therefore be instantiated in Newtonian gravity, electrostatics, Green-function theory, and other potential problems.   The central goal is compositional reuse. Rather than treating each formal proof as an isolated endpoint, the work identifies intermediate machine-checkable theorem structures that can serve as starting points for additional formal developments.   Immediate applications include relational clock models, Wheeler–DeWitt and constrained systems, Ehrenfest and semiclassical quantum dynamics, electrostatic inverse-square fields, Schrödinger operators, spectral-gap arguments, elliptic PDEs, gauge systems, and other operator-theoretic problems.   This paper accompanies the broader Chronos formal-verification programme and is intended as an openly reusable mathematical and formal-physics resource.
title: Reusable Formal Bridges from Chronos Verification: Internal Time, Quantum–Classical Dynamics, Operator Control, and Inverse-Distance Fields

summary: Read the 74-page Split-Zero paper . Complete LaTeX, cumulative sources, citations and checks ; results and exact proof locators ; matching GitHub source edition . The Split-Zero programme represents finite zero-divisor classes of the completed Riemann zeta function by polynomials in an arithmetic theta-source Hilbert space. The metric on the observation kernel is obtained by minimizing over all original polynomial representatives. This edition calculates how that metric changes with polynomial degree. It gives every Christoffel–Darboux covariance entry, including reflected-node collisions and divided derivatives; retains the full correction after coefficient compression; and expresses the four-cutoff determinant ratio as a product of exact degree-step factors. The paired quartet relation proves a strict finite kernel contraction. Its magnitude at the unresolved large-degree kq scale is not evaluated, and no RH conclusion is claimed. Programme citations in the paper are clickable links to actual public proof sources, with exact locations where available. The same source links are included in the three complete cumulative LaTeX successors. The source archive includes a machine-readable link registry and restores two previously unpublished cited proofs. Older cumulative citations still needing an exact source match remain explicitly identified in that registry; no guessed destination is presented as verified. Classical sources retain their human authorship: Gernot Akemann and Graziano Vernizzi, Characteristic Polynomials of Complex Random Matrix Models , Nuclear Physics B 660 (2003), 532–556 ; the named authors of the NIST DLMF orthogonal-polynomial chapter ; and Jack Sherman and Winifred J. Morrison, Adjustment of an Inverse Matrix Corresponding to a Change in One Element of a Given Matrix (1950) . The last citation is historical and bibliographically checked; the rank-one calculation used here is proved directly. Earlier programme proofs remain separately credited. The reader contains ten complete proof bodies. The new CD and degree-step checkers pass 779 exact finite checks in each of ordinary and optimized Python, with 13 intended failure controls in each mode. These checks do not sample the actual period matrix or establish a large-degree asymptotic. The three large cumulative LaTeX manuscripts have not been freshly compiled in this edition. The 98 earlier standalone papers and archives remain. To respect Zenodo's 100-file limit, the preceding result index is retained byte-for-byte as predecessor062/RESULT_INDEX.json in the new source ZIP. Its original separate download also remains in the preceding immutable edition. Existing authorship, rights notices and access conditions are preserved. This successor does not claim that unfinished parallel-task work has been incorporated.
title: Split-Zero cohomology: exact degree changes in the arithmetic kernel metric

summary: This paper proposes a speculative Holographic–Multiway Theory (HMT) connecting the holographic principle, multiverse/quantum branching concepts, and Wolfram Physics. It develops a computational framework in which hypergraph rewriting, multiway evolution, causal structure, branchial graphs, and lower-dimensional information encoding can be used to investigate whether holographic behavior and multiverse-like branching are mathematically compatible. The paper then proposes a Wolfram Physics research program for testing these ideas computationally, followed by an experimental framework for investigating selected hypotheses associated with the Gateway Process. Proposed technologies include Wolfram computational models, artificial neural systems, EEG/fMRI, neurofeedback, noninvasive neuromodulation, and blinded information-retrieval experiments. The work is presented as a research proposal rather than an established theory, with emphasis on falsifiability, quantitative testing, independent replication, and separating demonstrated physics from speculative extensions concerning consciousness, temporal information retrieval, and afterlife-related hypotheses.
title: Toward a Holographic–Multiway Theory of the Multiverse: A Wolfram Physics Framework for Testing Holography, Quantum Branching, and the Gateway Hypothesis

summary: In a recent publication, we derived a general relativity (RG) gauge-invariant solution modelling a granular universe composed of spherical bodies with a radial Gaussian density profile. In this framework, a cosmological constant Λ emerges natively from the gravitational self-energy of these discrete nodes. Energy conservation dictates a uniform compactness ratio M\/σ^2 across all bodies, a relation closely met by the elliptical galaxies as shown in the GAMA survey. This setup yields: Λ≈1/( 12 π^3 ) (κ a c^2   M/σ^2    )^2which, using the compactness measured in the GAMA survey, evaluates to Λ≈ 0.9×10^(-52)   m^(-2) , a value close to modern observations. The model predicts the R ∝ (1+z)^(-1.5) size scaling confirmed by the 3D-HST+CANDELS survey and, unlike standard ΛCDM theory, the model preserves total energy conservation. Before gas clouds collapsing around z≈3 the universe was mostly homogeneous resulting in this model to Λ≈0. During the Lyman-α forest epoch an intense gas clouds collapsing into stars and black holes occurred. We extended our RG model to purely radial collapsing nodes which gave Λ≈(κ a^3)/(4π^3 ) M/R^2   (d^2 R)/(dt^2 )<0. This backreaction force of the gas cloud collapse reached a peak around z ≈2 , and later declined around z≈1.5 when massive galaxies ran out of cold gas or experienced quenching shutting down their star formation. At this epoch, the galaxies began their assembling into their modern structures, raising the cosmological constant to its current baseline value. Integrating this dynamical Λ(z), while targeting the current Hubble parameter of H_0=73 km/s/Mpc , yields a perfect validation against the Planck cosmic microwave background angular scale θ^*=0.010410 rad and the latest DESI BAO data.   Notably, the model predicts a structure clustering amplitude of S_8≈0.81 in line with the BOSS/DESI Deep Scale Galaxy Clustering data survey. The proposed model successfully bypasses the need for an unexplained, speculative dark energy burst.
title: Addressing the Hubble tension with a dynamical Λ(z) induced by galactic gravitational self-energy and by backreaction force from gas cloud collapse

summary: Traditional unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) methods are designed to flag or localise deviations from a normative distribution, ignoring the underlying generative mechanisms of the anomalies. Yet the nature of an anomaly is often as important as its presence. We reformulate UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem, in which the objective is to infer the most probable corruption responsible for each observation. Our framework yields a probabilistic anomaly score as the energy of the inferred corruption parameters, and serves as a principled recipe for developing new UAD algorithms. We derive several existing methods as instances of the general framework, each corresponding to the same energy score under different modelling choices. Experimentally, we study the framework's components in a controlled setting, and improve object-class AUROC on the MVTec AD dataset by 2.3% by adapting the underlying corruption model. Finally, we validate the framework on a brain MRI benchmark, achieving strong detection performance while producing estimates of pathology intensity, bias, and geometry. Code is available at https://github.com/jgmyles/inverse-uad.
title: A Principled Approach to Unsupervised Anomaly Detection

summary: Split-Zero cohomology and the zeta-function research programme is a cumulative collection of mathematical papers, complete LaTeX proofs, formalization sources, calculations and literature-based research notes. Its central question is how the zeros of the Riemann zeta function can be studied through explicitly constructed arithmetic cohomology, spectral actions and quantitative metric estimates. The collection also retains the related heat-flow, arithmetic-trace, fluid, complexity and thermal-geometry investigations from which parts of this programme developed. Project and reading guide · Research contents · Machine-readable workbench index . Papers remain separate readable PDFs; the source archives supply the corresponding editable mathematics and supporting materials. What the collection contains Split-Zero coefficients, geometry and cohomology. The construction retains a ring's internal zero and a separate symbol for absence, so a zero element in a specified support fibre is not confused with an absent fibre. The papers construct coefficient maps, quotients, homology, finite spectral jets and their relation to the infinite theta quotient. Deligne's Weil II provides a motivating source for the cohomology–duality–weight-control programme; its finite-field theorem is not asserted to apply automatically to the Riemann zeta function. Read the cohomology and weight-control paper and the foundational objects and maps . Arithmetic theta sources and analytic control. The central analytic complex is [V → B], with theta map Θ and quotient B/ΘV. Scaling acts by D = −x∂x; the Mellin-side arithmetic function is 2ξ(s), where ξ is the completed Riemann zeta function. The papers carry finite zero packets, including multiplicities, through the original source maps and least-norm quotient metrics.
